title: Adaptive Workflow Intelligence: A Cognitive Architecture for Context-Driven Enterprise Automation
comment: 12 pages, simulation-based evaluation of adaptive workflow agents
summary: Enterprise systems increasingly rely on automated workflows, yet many AI-driven solutions remain brittle under non-stationary conditions, evolving policies, and delayed operational feedback. While reinforcement learning and large language model (LLM) agents offer partial adaptability, they do not by themselves provide persistent reflection mechanisms or straightforward integration with policy-constrained enterprise operations. This paper introduces Adaptive Workflow Intelligence (AWI), a cognitive architecture for context-driven enterprise agents organized around a four-layer Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection (PCAR) loop. AWI treats reflection as a mechanism for continuous policy refinement and combines hybrid reasoning with reflective memory and feedback-driven adaptation to support decision making under environmental drift and operational constraints. We evaluate AWI in a simulated enterprise decision workflow characterized by delayed outcomes and a controlled regime shift. In a drift-and-delay stress test, guardrail-constrained adaptive approaches recover more rapidly than static automation while maintaining policy compliance. Within this setting, AWI's reflective components modestly reduce behavioral oscillation and feedback variance, illustrating the stability-agility trade-off introduced by reflective policy adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Adaptive Workflow Intelligence (AWI), a four-layer Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection (PCAR) cognitive architecture for enterprise agents that uses reflection for continuous policy refinement. Evaluated in a simulated workflow with delayed outcomes and a regime shift, guardrail-constrained adaptive approaches recover faster than static automation, while AWI's reflective components modestly reduce behavioral oscillation and feedback variance.
AI.motivation: Enterprise systems rely on automated workflows, but many AI-driven solutions are brittle under non-stationary conditions, evolving policies, and delayed operational feedback. Reinforcement learning and LLM agents provide only partial adaptability: they lack persistent reflection mechanisms and straightforward integration with policy-constrained enterprise operations.
AI.method: AWI is a cognitive architecture for context-driven enterprise agents organized around a four-layer Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection (PCAR) loop. It treats reflection as a mechanism for continuous policy refinement and combines hybrid reasoning with reflective memory and feedback-driven adaptation to support decision making under environmental drift and operational constraints. It is evaluated in a simulated enterprise decision workflow with delayed outcomes and a controlled regime shift, using a drift-and-delay stress test.
AI.result: In the drift-and-delay stress test, guardrail-constrained adaptive approaches recover more rapidly than static automation while maintaining policy compliance. Within this setting, AWI's reflective components modestly reduce behavioral oscillation and feedback variance, illustrating the stability-agility trade-off introduced by reflective policy adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Reflective policy adaptation via the PCAR loop supports faster recovery under drift and delay while preserving policy compliance, but its gains are modest and come with a stability-agility trade-off, evidenced by reduced oscillation and feedback variance.

title: Accelerating Floating-Point Satisfiability Solving via Gradient Normalization
summary:
Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers are foundational to software verification, program analysis, and compiler testing, particularly over the theory of Quantifier-Free Floating-Point (QF_FP). While recent optimization-based SMT solvers have successfully applied gradient descent to continuous relaxations of logical formulas, they are fundamentally bottlenecked by gradient domination, a phenomenon where a small subset of difficult clauses hijacks the optimization trajectory, preventing the solver from satisfying the broader formula and trapping it in local minima.
  To overcome this, we present GradSAT, a novel framework that bridges optimization-based SMT solving with Multi-Task Learning (MTL). GradSAT reformulates the constraint satisfaction process by treating each SMT clause as an independent MTL task. By applying dynamic gradient normalization (GradNorm), GradSAT actively balances the gradient magnitudes across all clauses at runtime, systematically penalizing dominant gradients and accelerating lagging clauses to ensure uniform convergence. GradSAT implements this through a highly optimized, two-stage hybrid pipeline. First, a GPU-accelerated PyTorch backend leveraging symbolic compilation and operator fusion navigates the continuous relaxation to a high-quality basin. Second, the candidate assignment is handed off to a bit-precise local search engine to rapidly resolve the exact, rigorous assignment. By stabilizing the continuous search dynamics, GradSAT mitigates the brittleness of prior gradient-based solvers and provides a robust, highly parallelizable architecture for complex constraint solving.

AI.tldr: GradSAT bridges optimization-based SMT solving with Multi-Task Learning by treating each clause as an independent task and applying dynamic gradient normalization to balance gradients, combined with a two-stage GPU plus bit-precise local search pipeline.
AI.motivation: Optimization-based SMT solvers over QF_FP suffer from gradient domination, where a small subset of difficult clauses hijacks the optimization trajectory, causing local minima and preventing satisfaction of the broader formula.
AI.method: Reformulates constraint satisfaction as Multi-Task Learning, treating each SMT clause as an independent task. Uses dynamic gradient normalization (GradNorm) to balance gradient magnitudes at runtime, penalizing dominant gradients and accelerating lagging clauses. Implements a two-stage hybrid pipeline: a GPU-accelerated PyTorch backend with symbolic compilation and operator fusion to navigate the continuous relaxation to a high-quality basin, followed by a bit-precise local search engine to resolve the exact rigorous assignment.
AI.result: Stabilizes continuous search dynamics, mitigates the brittleness of prior gradient-based solvers, and provides a robust, highly parallelizable architecture for complex constraint solving.
AI.conclusion: GradSAT offers a novel MTL-based framework addressing gradient domination in optimization-based SMT solving, delivering a robust and parallelizable architectural solution for complex constraint satisfaction.

title: Route-Verify-Vote: Procedure-Conditioned Self-Consistency for Mixed-Domain Reasoning
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, and 8 tables. Accepted for oral presentation at CCL26-Eval
summary:
Compositional generalization remains challenging when language models must combine familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The Scenario-Based Commonsense Reasoning Evaluation (SCoRE) 2026 tests this ability on three mixed domains absent from training and requires models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question.
  We introduce Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that uses language models without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning procedure that guides the model in representing and applying the relevant constraints. Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints. Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with a small vote-count margin between the two most frequent sets. Samples for each question follow the same domain-specific procedure.
  On the official test set, voting over 16 sampled answer sets per question achieves an exact-set accuracy of 74.6%. Adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%, and combining models on selected domain routes raises accuracy to 79.4%. The final system ranked second among participating systems. These results support domain-specific reasoning procedures and answer-set disagreement as useful tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain reasoning.

AI.tldr: RVV is a training-free, procedure-conditioned self-consistency framework that routes each question to a domain-specific reasoning procedure, verifies options against extracted constraints, and votes over complete answer sets with adaptive sample allocation, reaching 79.4% exact-set accuracy and second place on the SCoRE 2026 benchmark.
AI.motivation: Language models struggle with compositional generalization when familiar reasoning operations must be combined in unfamiliar ways. SCoRE 2026 specifically tests this on three mixed domains unseen during training and requires identifying the full set of correct options per question, making standard single-answer prompting insufficient.
AI.method: Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a procedure-conditioned self-consistency framework operating without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning procedure that guides the model in representing and applying relevant constraints. Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints. Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with a narrow vote-count margin between the two most frequent sets. All samples for a question follow the same domain-specific procedure.
AI.result: On the official test set, voting over 16 sampled answer sets per question achieves 74.6% exact-set accuracy; adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%; combining models on selected domain routes reaches 79.4%. The system ranked second among participating systems.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific reasoning procedures and answer-set disagreement are effective tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain reasoning, enabling strong compositional generalization without parameter updates.

title: An Empirical Study of Agent Skills' Downstream Utility
summary: Agent Skills package procedural guidance and resources for reuse, but a relevant Skill does not necessarily improve task performance. Existing studies characterize Skill content and evaluate downstream performance, yet provide limited explanations of how utility depends on content, execution configuration, and multi-Skill organization. We conduct an empirical study on 87 SkillsBench tasks, defining downstream utility as the pass-rate difference from No-Skill on the same tasks under the same model--harness configuration. We compare the same Skills across nine configurations, then examine alternative published Skills and organizations of fixed Skill sets under three selected configurations. We retrieve marketplace candidates from a curated corpus of 37,596 Skills. LLM-assisted analysis of content, execution traces, and final artifacts, followed by author review, relates provided support to actual use and task outcomes. The same Skills help some configurations and hurt others on 36.78\% of tasks, with trajectories showing that recommended procedures can become an execution burden. Relevance rankings overlook more useful candidates. Within the evaluated candidate sets, reranking by support for required operations raises first-choice pass rates by 4.35--5.80 percentage points across the three configurations. We derive 17 authoring practices linking executable procedures to recovery, preservation of task requirements, and checks on final artifacts. Stage Plan and Dependency DAG outperform use order alone, with DAG's additional benefits concentrated in tasks supplied with five or six Skills. These findings guide developers to assess usable operation support, allow procedure adaptation while preserving task requirements, and make artifact dependencies explicit when organizing Skills.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of 87 SkillsBench tasks shows a relevant Skill's utility depends on content, execution configuration, and multi-Skill organization: the same Skills help some configurations and hurt others on 36.78% of tasks, and reranking candidates by support for required operations raises first-choice pass rates by 4.35-5.80 pp.
AI.motivation: Agent Skills package procedural guidance and resources for reuse, but a relevant Skill does not necessarily improve task performance. Prior work characterizes Skill content and evaluates downstream performance but offers limited explanation of how utility depends on content, execution configuration, and multi-Skill organization.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical study on 87 SkillsBench tasks, defining downstream utility as the pass-rate difference from No-Skill under the same model-harness configuration. They compare identical Skills across nine configurations, then examine alternative published Skills and organizations of fixed Skill sets under three selected configurations. Marketplace candidates are retrieved from a curated corpus of 37,596 Skills. LLM-assisted analysis of content, execution traces, and final artifacts, followed by author review, links provided support to actual use and outcomes.
AI.result: The same Skills help some configurations and hurt others on 36.78% of tasks; trajectories show recommended procedures can become an execution burden. Relevance rankings overlook more useful candidates. Within the evaluated candidate sets, reranking by support for required operations raises first-choice pass rates by 4.35-5.80 percentage points across the three configurations. Seventeen authoring practices are derived linking executable procedures to recovery, preservation of task requirements, and artifact checks. Stage Plan and Dependency DAG outperform use order alone, with DAG's additional benefits concentrated in tasks supplied with five or six Skills.
AI.conclusion: Skill utility is configuration- and organization-dependent rather than intrinsic to relevance. Findings guide developers to assess usable operation support, allow procedure adaptation while preserving task requirements, and make artifact dependencies explicit when organizing Skills.

title: A Review Of Robotic World Models For Dynamic Environments Based On Factor And Scene Graphs
summary: Models based on graphs have emerged in robotics as a powerful foundation for internal world representations, where factor and scene graphs are among the most prominent model types found in the related literature and in successful robotic solutions. Initially, many of these models were assuming static environments as a simplification. Herein, factor graphs mainly provide uncertainty-aware geometric estimations while scene graphs enable a structured semantic abstraction. However, real-world robotic environments are often dynamic, posing severe challenges for purely static world representations. Therefore, this review presents a comprehensive view on how dynamic aspects of real-world environments can be addressed in such graph-based world models. We organize our assessments around three main aspects: (I) suitable representations, (II) pipelines to construct and update the representations, and (III) their exploitation for downstream tasks. We review approaches that are either based on factor or scene graphs, but put special emphasis on novel approaches that combine both types to form hybrid models. We mainly analyze how different types of dynamics can be modeled herein, and categorize common architectural patterns. Finally, emerging trends and open challenges are identified, including uncertainty propagation from learned perception through the representation layers, the observability of dynamic-entity motion and scale under minimal sensing, scalable lifelong maintenance, and the lack of datasets and evaluation protocols that ground world-model quality in downstream task performance under dynamics.

AI.tldr: A review of graph-based world models (factor graphs, scene graphs, and hybrids) in robotics, organized by representations, construction/update pipelines, and downstream exploitation, focused on how dynamic real-world environments are handled, with emerging trends and open challenges identified.
AI.motivation: Graph-based models—factor graphs and scene graphs—have become powerful foundations for internal world representations in robotics, but early work largely assumed static environments. Real-world robotic environments are often dynamic, so purely static representations are inadequate and pose severe challenges. There is a need for a comprehensive view of how dynamic aspects can be addressed in graph-based world models.
AI.method: A review organized around three aspects: (I) suitable representations, (II) pipelines to construct and update these representations, and (III) their exploitation for downstream tasks. It covers approaches based on either factor graphs or scene graphs, with special emphasis on hybrid models that combine both. The review analyzes how different types of dynamics can be modeled and categorizes common architectural patterns.
AI.result: The review classifies common architectural patterns for handling dynamics in graph-based world models, spanning factor-graph-centric, scene-graph-centric, and hybrid designs, and identifies where each is suited. It also surfaces emerging trends and open challenges.
AI.conclusion: Key open challenges include uncertainty propagation from learned perception through representation layers, the observability of dynamic-entity motion and scale under minimal sensing, scalable lifelong maintenance, and the lack of datasets and evaluation protocols that ground world-model quality in downstream task performance under dynamics.

title: How Could AI Eliminate Humanity? A Failure-Mode Analysis of Civilizational Risk
summary: This article develops a failure-mode framework for analyzing how advanced artificial intelligence could contribute to human extinction, irreversible civilizational collapse, or permanent human disempowerment. The central thesis is that catastrophic AI risk does not require consciousness, hostility, or an explicit intention to harm humanity. Instead, risk may arise through several distinct but interacting pathways, including autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, and competitive deployment. The severity of these pathways depends on factors such as capability, autonomy, external access, persistence, institutional safeguards, and the preservation of recovery capacity. The analysis is deliberately non-operational: it identifies causal conditions, empirically tractable intermediate quantities, and defensive research questions rather than procedures for causing harm.

AI.tldr: Proposes a failure-mode framework for catastrophic AI risk based on causal pathways, not consciousness or malice.
AI.motivation: Concern that advanced AI could cause extinction, irreversible collapse, or permanent disempowerment, and that such risk is often mischaracterized as requiring hostile intent.
AI.method: Conceptual, non-operational failure-mode analysis identifying interacting pathways—autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, competitive deployment—and severity factors including capability, autonomy, access, persistence, safeguards, and recovery capacity.
AI.result: A structured taxonomy of causal conditions and measurable intermediate quantities, plus defensive research questions rather than harm-enabling procedures.
AI.conclusion: Catastrophic AI risk can be analyzed without assuming consciousness or hostility, enabling tractable defensive research.

title: SAFE: Unified Slip and Fracture Detection with Low-Cost Acoustic Sensing in Robotic Grasping
summary: Manipulating fragile objects remains challenging as robots must understand the state of what they grasp, such as slip or fracture, to respond appropriately, especially when material properties are unknown. In this paper, we present SAFE: a low-cost, general-purpose sensing approach that detects both slip and fracture in real time using two passive polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) acoustic sensors and motor proprioception, without relying on vision or prior material knowledge. The sensors are mounted on a compliant Fin Ray gripper, and a unified HistGradientBoosting classifier reports the state (normal, slip, or fracture) from a 79-dimensional feature vector. Under leave-one-grasp-out cross-validation, SAFE achieves an Alert-F1 of 0.884 with near-zero slip-fracture confusion, and ablations confirm that acoustic sensing is indispensable. An adaptive grasp controller built on this detection layer runs at 104 Hz on a Jetson Orin Nano, achieving 91.3% success across 46 closed-loop robot trials spanning diverse object categories, while each fixed-force strategy drops to 0% on object conditions that mismatch its preset. It further reaches 82.4% success on novel objects unseen during training, demonstrating robust, failure-aware grasp control without object-specific calibration.

AI.tldr: SAFE is a low-cost sensing approach using two passive PVDF acoustic sensors plus motor proprioception to detect slip and fracture in real time, enabling failure-aware grasping of fragile objects without vision or prior material knowledge.
AI.motivation: Robots manipulating fragile objects must recognize grasp states such as slip or fracture to respond appropriately, yet this is difficult when material properties are unknown. Existing approaches typically depend on vision or prior material knowledge, which limits generality.
AI.method: Two passive polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) acoustic sensors are mounted on a compliant Fin Ray gripper, combined with motor proprioception and no vision. A unified HistGradientBoosting classifier predicts the state (normal, slip, or fracture) from a 79-dimensional feature vector. An adaptive grasp controller is built on this detection layer, running at 104 Hz on a Jetson Orin Nano.
AI.result: Under leave-one-grasp-out cross-validation, SAFE achieves an Alert-F1 of 0.884 with near-zero slip-fracture confusion; ablations confirm acoustic sensing is indispensable. The closed-loop controller reaches 91.3% success across 46 robot trials on diverse object categories, versus 0% for fixed-force strategies on mismatched object conditions, and 82.4% success on novel unseen objects.
AI.conclusion: SAFE demonstrates robust, failure-aware grasp control without object-specific calibration, using only low-cost acoustic sensing and proprioception, and generalizes to novel objects.

title: Humanize: Judgement Engineering for Agentic Coding
summary:
Agentic coding makes code generation cheap, but reliable completion remains difficult: the agent that writes the code is a weak judge of whether it is done.
  We present Humanize, a multi-agent orchestration workflow for agentic coding built around judgement engineering: explicit, mechanically enforced decisions at the boundaries between planning, implementation, review, and learning. A human approves a plan contract, a builder agent implements it in rounds, and a reviewer agent from another vendor decides completion; deterministic hooks, not a model, route work between these roles and enforce 72 mechanical gates. Viewed as a Markov chain over repository states, alternating builder and reviewer samples jointly from two models, so a defect survives only if both miss it. We study Humanize through its deployment, 118 public postmortems of real loops, and its applications. Over 68 versions in 108 days, it gathered 1,468 GitHub stars.
  Applications include a 567-file gem5 build-system migration under upstream review; Kernel Design Agents, which extend the loop with a kernel knowledge base and profiling feedback and placed in the top three of all three Full-Agent tracks of the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer contest; and, through Humanize Olympiad Agents (HOA), full scores in IOI 2026, IMO 2026, IPhO 2026, and IBO 2024, 418.5/437 in IChO 2026 (gold-medal). Humanize also achieves 672/672 on PutnamBench and ranks first (251/303) on Lean-Eval's leaderboard even competiting with professional mathematicians. The postmortems show that independent review catches unsupported builder claims, but stopping remains a key weakness. In reports that separate rounds by phase, two thirds of rounds occurred after implementation was accepted. This evidence is observational, not a controlled comparison of workflows.

AI.tldr: Humanize is a multi-agent orchestration workflow for agentic coding that applies "judgement engineering"—mechanically enforced decision boundaries between planning, implementation, review, and learning. Using a human-approved plan contract, a builder agent, and a cross-vendor reviewer agent connected by deterministic hooks and 72 mechanical gates, it achieves strong benchmark results (including top scores on IOI/IMO/IPhO/IBO/IChO-style tasks, 672/672 on PutnamBench) while revealing that stopping, not reviewing, remains the key weakness.
AI.motivation: Agentic coding makes code generation cheap, but reliable completion is hard because the agent that writes code is a weak judge of whether the task is truly done. The paper aims to address this "who judges completion" problem by separating generation from completion judgement.
AI.method: Humanize is a multi-agent orchestration workflow built on judgement engineering: explicit, mechanically enforced decisions at boundaries between planning, implementation, review, and learning. A human approves a plan contract; a builder agent implements in rounds; a reviewer agent from another vendor decides completion. Deterministic hooks—not a model—route work and enforce 72 mechanical gates. The design is analyzed as a Markov chain over repository states where alternating builder/reviewer samples from two models, so a defect survives only if both miss it.
AI.result: The system is studied via deployment, 118 public postmortems of real loops, and applications. Over 68 versions in 108 days it gained 1,468 GitHub stars. Applications include a 567-file gem5 build-system migration under upstream review; Kernel Design Agents (with a kernel knowledge base and profiling feedback) placing top-three in all three Full-Agent tracks of MLSys 2026 FlashInfer contest; Humanize Olympiad Agents (HOA) achieving full scores in IOI 2026, IMO 2026, IPhO 2026, and IBO 2024, and 418.5/437 (gold) in IChO 2026; 672/672 on PutnamBench; and first place (251/303) on Lean-Eval despite competition from professional mathematicians.
AI.conclusion: Postmortems show independent review effectively catches unsupported builder claims, but stopping is a key weakness: in phase-separated reports, two-thirds of rounds occurred after implementation was accepted. The evidence is observational rather than a controlled comparison of workflows.

title: Context-Aware Adaptive Pesticide Spraying for Agricultural Robots under Changing Weather and Terrain Using Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted for publication in Computers and Electronics in Agriculture
summary: Precision pesticide spraying is essential for optimizing application efficiency and ensuring uniform chemical distribution. Spraying performance is influenced by multiple factors, including environmental conditions such as temperature and wind speed, pesticide type, and the robot's capability to accurately perceive crops and target spray locations. Existing approaches predominantly emphasize crop detection and rely on predefined spraying parameters, whereas human operators dynamically adjust their spraying strategies by considering environmental conditions, region-specific crop characteristics, and the type of pesticide being applied. In this study, we propose a context-aware adaptive spraying framework based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs), which enables robots to leverage spatial reasoning and integrate information from multiple sources, including crop type, pesticide type, and weather data, to make adaptive and optimized spraying decisions. Subsequently, a trajectory-tracking controller based on Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is employed to ensure precise navigation and accurate spraying at crop locations. The comparative results demonstrate that the proposed method improves accuracy by at least 30% in detecting crop rows. In addition, the experimental evaluations conducted in two environments further demonstrate the robot's ability to flexibly adjust spraying volume and travel speed, while reducing pesticide drift.

AI.tldr: A context-aware adaptive spraying framework using Vision-Language Models enables robots to fuse crop type, pesticide type, and weather data for optimized spraying decisions, paired with an MPPI-based trajectory-tracking controller for precise navigation and spraying.
AI.motivation: Precision pesticide spraying is essential for application efficiency and uniform chemical distribution, but performance depends on many factors: environmental conditions (temperature, wind speed), pesticide type, and the robot's ability to perceive crops and target spray locations. Existing approaches emphasize crop detection and rely on predefined spraying parameters, unlike human operators who dynamically adapt strategies based on environmental conditions, region-specific crop characteristics, and pesticide type.
AI.method: The authors propose a context-aware adaptive spraying framework based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs), enabling robots to leverage spatial reasoning and integrate multi-source information (crop type, pesticide type, weather data) to make adaptive, optimized spraying decisions. A trajectory-tracking controller based on Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is then employed to ensure precise navigation and accurate spraying at crop locations.
AI.result: Comparative results show the proposed method improves crop-row detection accuracy by at least 30%. Experimental evaluations in two environments further demonstrate the robot's ability to flexibly adjust spraying volume and travel speed while reducing pesticide drift.
AI.conclusion: The VLM-based context-aware framework, combined with MPPI trajectory tracking, enables adaptive, context-sensitive spraying that outperforms predefined-parameter approaches, improving detection accuracy and reducing pesticide drift across two test environments.

title: Sequential Probabilistic Uncertainty Estimation for Parallel Multi-Agent Reasoning Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have attracted growing attention for improving reasoning through interaction among multiple agents. In this work, we focus on parallel multi-agent reasoning systems, where several agents solve the same problem over multiple rounds and aggregate their outputs into a final answer. Despite their strong reasoning performance, uncertainty estimation for such systems remains underexplored: the reliability of a MAS depends not only on individual generations, but also on how agents interact and evolve across rounds. We propose SAUCE (Sequential Agent Uncertainty through Consensus Evolution), a lightweight, training-free uncertainty estimator that formulates MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief. SAUCE aggregates round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals through a filtering-style update. Across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two MAS protocols, SAUCE improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over a broad set of uncertainty estimation baselines, including standard log-likelihood-based methods and MAS-specific estimators.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAUCE, a lightweight, training-free uncertainty estimator for parallel LLM-based multi-agent systems that treats MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty estimation for parallel multi-agent reasoning systems is underexplored, yet reliability depends not only on individual agent generations but also on how agents interact and evolve across rounds.
AI.method: SAUCE (Sequential Agent Uncertainty through Consensus Evolution) formulates MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief, aggregating round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals via a filtering-style update. It is lightweight and training-free.
AI.result: Across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two MAS protocols, SAUCE improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over a broad set of baselines, including standard log-likelihood-based methods and MAS-specific estimators.
AI.conclusion: SAUCE offers an effective, training-free approach for estimating uncertainty in parallel LLM-based multi-agent systems, outperforming existing baselines across diverse settings.

title: Taming an End-to-End Autonomous Driving Policy for Urban Navigation of Quadruped Robots
comment: Accepted to IROS 2026 Workshop on AI Meets Autonomy
summary: We present Go2-DrivoR, a goal-conditioned adaptation of the end-to-end autonomous driving trajectory planning framework DrivoR for urban navigation with quadrupedal robots. By conditioning trajectory generation on a local-frame subgoal through a goal token and adapting the vehicle-centric scoring formulation, the method extends DrivoR to short-horizon goal-conditioned local planning without redesigning its core decoders. Specifically, we redefine drivable-area compliance for sidewalk-oriented navigation and reformulate the original ego progress term as goal-conditioned ego progress. Trained exclusively on TartanGround simulation data, Go2-DrivoR improves waypoint-conditioned planning performance on unseen simulation environments and transfers zero-shot to open-loop real-world trajectory prediction.

AI.tldr: Go2-DrivoR adapts the end-to-end driving planner DrivoR for quadrupedal robot urban navigation by adding goal-conditioning via a goal token, redefining drivable-area compliance for sidewalks, and replacing ego progress with goal-conditioned progress.
AI.motivation: DrivoR targets vehicle-centric autonomous driving and lacks goal-conditioning needed for goal-directed local planning on legged robots in urban environments.
AI.method: Condition trajectory generation on a local-frame subgoal via a goal token; adapt the vehicle-centric scoring formulation; redefine drivable-area compliance for sidewalk-oriented navigation; reformulate ego progress as goal-conditioned ego progress. Core decoders are left unchanged.
AI.result: Trained only on TartanGround simulation data, Go2-DrivoR improves waypoint-conditioned planning on unseen simulated environments and transfers zero-shot to open-loop real-world trajectory prediction.
AI.conclusion: Goal-conditioning can be retrofitted onto an existing vehicle-centric planner with minimal modifications, yielding improved generalization and sim-to-real transfer for quadrupedal urban navigation.

title: Agent Plasticity: Measuring Self-Improvement Through Experience
summary: AI agents increasingly operate in environments where they can diagnose failures and improve through experience, yet existing evaluations largely measure what an agent can do at a fixed point in time rather than how effectively it learns. Evaluating self-improvement requires answering three questions: does future performance improve and generalize beyond the interactions that enabled learning; how efficiently are new capabilities acquired; and where does the self-improvement process break down? To answer these questions, we study self-improvement in a controlled setting where agents amortize past experience into reusable artifacts that are inherited by future instances. At each checkpoint, we measure performance on training and held-out environment interactions while accounting for learning cost. We introduce agent plasticity, the efficiency with which an agent converts experience into gains in future held-out performance. Across multiple environments, frontier models exhibit sharply different improvement trajectories despite comparable opportunities to learn. Some achieve substantial and persistent gains, while others remain near or below their initial performance, and gains within the training regime often transfer only partially to out-of-distribution conditions. Endpoint capability and acquisition efficiency also diverge: the agent that ultimately performs best need not be the one that improves most efficiently. Tracing failures through the improvement loop further reveals different candidate bottlenecks. Agents with low plasticity often fail to reuse relevant artifacts, whereas more plastic agents may still fail despite reusing relevant artifacts, pointing to limitations in artifact quality, generalization, or application. Evaluating self-improving agents requires measuring not only what they can do, but how effectively they become better through experience.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that evaluating self-improving AI agents requires measuring learning dynamics—improvement, generalization, and efficiency—not just endpoint capability. It introduces "agent plasticity," the efficiency of converting experience into held-out gains, and finds frontier models differ sharply in improvement trajectories, transfer, and bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations measure what an agent can do at a fixed point rather than how effectively it learns, which is inadequate as AI agents increasingly diagnose failures and improve through experience. A framework is needed to assess whether future performance improves and generalizes, how efficiently capabilities are acquired, and where the self-improvement loop breaks down.
AI.method: A controlled setting is used in which agents amortize past experience into reusable artifacts inherited by future instances. At each checkpoint, performance is measured on training and held-out environment interactions while accounting for learning cost. The authors define agent plasticity as the efficiency with which an agent converts experience into gains in future held-out performance, and trace failures through the improvement loop.
AI.result: Across multiple environments, frontier models show sharply different improvement trajectories despite comparable learning opportunities. Some achieve substantial, persistent gains while others remain near or below initial performance; within-training-regime gains transfer only partially out-of-distribution. Endpoint capability and acquisition efficiency diverge—the best-performing agent is not necessarily the most efficient improver. Low-plasticity agents often fail to reuse relevant artifacts, whereas more plastic agents may fail despite reusing them, indicating limitations in artifact quality, generalization, or application.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating self-improving agents must measure not only what they can do but how effectively they become better through experience. The plasticity framework exposes distinct bottlenecks, showing that endpoint capability, improvement magnitude, and acquisition efficiency are separable dimensions requiring separate measurement.

title: Autonomous Droplet Navigation via Model-Based Reinforcement Learning: Zero-Shot Transfer and Emergent Dynamics
comment: Accepted for presentation at the Robotics & Automation in Self-Driving Laboratories 2026 Workshop, IROS 2026. https://sites.tufts.edu/selfdrivinglabs-iros2026/
summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are transforming chemical and materials discovery through closed-loop automation, yet automated infrastructure for physical manipulation of soft, deformable matter remains beyond current robotic platforms. A critical instance is autonomous droplet transport on an open surface, where contact-angle hysteresis, capillary pinning, and surface heterogeneity produce partially observable dynamics that pose significant challenges for classical model-based controllers. We introduce the first robotic platform for closed-loop autonomous liquid droplet navigation on an open, unconfined surface using model-based reinforcement learning. A two-axis tilting board coated with a thin silicone oil film drives the droplet, while an overhead camera provides real-time feedback. A learned policy was trained on just 50 to 150 physical episodes depending on geometric complexity, without simulation or analytical models. Beyond performance alone, the platform demonstrates three capabilities of interest to the SDL community: it robustly transfers zero-shot to unseen geometries; it autonomously discovers an oscillatory depinning strategy to free the droplet when it sticks; and it completes its full training pipeline in under 90 minutes. These results extend reinforcement-learning manipulation from rigid microrobots to deformable soft-matter systems for next-generation SDLs.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first robotic platform for closed-loop autonomous droplet navigation on an open, unconfined surface using model-based reinforcement learning, achieving zero-shot transfer, autonomous depinning discovery, and sub-90-minute training.
AI.motivation: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are transforming chemical and materials discovery through closed-loop automation, but automated infrastructure for physical manipulation of soft, deformable matter remains beyond current robotic platforms. A critical instance is autonomous droplet transport on an open surface, where contact-angle hysteresis, capillary pinning, and surface heterogeneity produce partially observable dynamics that pose significant challenges for classical model-based controllers.
AI.method: The authors introduce a robotic platform for closed-loop autonomous liquid droplet navigation on an open, unconfined surface using model-based reinforcement learning. A two-axis tilting board coated with a thin silicone oil film drives the droplet, while an overhead camera provides real-time feedback. A learned policy was trained on just 50 to 150 physical episodes depending on geometric complexity, without simulation or analytical models.
AI.result: The platform demonstrates three capabilities: it robustly transfers zero-shot to unseen geometries; it autonomously discovers an oscillatory depinning strategy to free the droplet when it sticks; and it completes its full training pipeline in under 90 minutes.
AI.conclusion: These results extend reinforcement-learning manipulation from rigid microrobots to deformable soft-matter systems for next-generation self-driving laboratories.

title: AdaGuard: Enhancing Safety and Policy Compliance with Reasoning-Enabled LLM-As-A-Judge Guardrails
summary: Enterprise generative AI applications require robust safety mechanisms that can accommodate diverse risk postures, evolving policies, and varying latency constraints. Current guardrail solutions often suffer from rigidity, relying on fixed policy sets and offering limited transparency or reasoning flexibility. We present Adaguard, an adaptive LLM-as-a-Judge framework designed to address these challenges through dynamic policy enforcement and adaptive reasoning-budget allocation. Built using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO), AdaGuard generalizes to user-defined safety and compliance policies at runtime without requiring frequent model updates. A core innovation of our approach is the ability to dynamically infer the complexity of input-policy pairs, allowing the model to switch between high-speed black-box inference and explainable, reasoning-enabled moderation. This flexibility enables developers to balance stringent latency requirements with the need for actionable transparency. This adaptive capability allows AdaGuard to rival other guardrail and frontier models several times its size, while its auto-reasoning mode recovers the accuracy of always-on reasoning at a fraction of the latency

AI.tldr: Adaguard is an adaptive LLM-as-a-Judge guardrail framework that dynamically applies user-defined safety and compliance policies at runtime and allocates reasoning budget based on inferred input-policy complexity, matching larger guardrail and frontier models while reducing latency.
AI.motivation: Enterprise generative AI applications need safety mechanisms that handle diverse risk postures, evolving policies, and varying latency constraints. Existing guardrail solutions are rigid: they rely on fixed policy sets and provide limited transparency or reasoning flexibility, forcing a poor trade-off between speed and explainability.
AI.method: AdaGuard is an adaptive LLM-as-a-Judge framework built with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning via GRPO. It generalizes to user-defined safety and compliance policies specified at runtime, avoiding frequent model updates. Its key innovation is dynamically inferring the complexity of input-policy pairs, allowing the model to switch between high-speed black-box inference and explainable, reasoning-enabled moderation (an auto-reasoning mode).
AI.result: AdaGuard rivals other guardrail and frontier models several times its size. Its auto-reasoning mode recovers the accuracy of always-on reasoning at a fraction of the latency, enabling developers to balance stringent latency requirements with actionable transparency.
AI.conclusion: AdaGuard demonstrates that adaptive policy enforcement and complexity-aware reasoning-budget allocation can deliver flexible, transparent, and efficient safety moderation for enterprise generative AI, achieving strong accuracy with substantially lower latency than always-on reasoning approaches.

title: CIRRA: Dual-Level Continual Instruction Reconciliation with Ongoing Execution for Embodied Robot Agents in Interactive Household Tasks
summary: Household robots must accommodate new user instructions while executing ongoing tasks. Existing agents often regenerate or extensively revise the remaining task sequence, introducing plan ambiguity, logical inconsistency, and redundant execution. We formulate continual instruction reconciliation and propose CIRRA (Continual Instruction Reconciliation for Robot Agents), a dual-level framework combining LLM-based semantic reasoning with rule-constrained structural integration. CIRRA first grounds incoming instructions to unique executable skills and resolves underspecified actions and execution locations. It then preserves the ongoing subtask sequence as an execution backbone and generates integration candidates by inserting incoming subtasks into location-matched segments. The semantic reasoner evaluates only modified segments to identify dependencies and conflicts and select the most logically coherent local integration. This structure-preserving process maintains alignment with ongoing execution, mitigates ambiguity and inconsistency, and reuses shared subtasks to reduce redundant execution. We also introduce CHIRP (Continual Household Instruction Reconciliation and Planning), a text-based benchmark of 120 episodes across eight household environments and six categories of everyday activities. On CHIRP, CIRRA achieves 74.2% decision agreement, exceeding the strongest replanning baseline by 30 percentage points; every correct fusion decision yields a correctly placed, conflict-free schedule. On a Unitree G1 humanoid, CIRRA interrupts ongoing skills at the correct moment in every trial and significantly outperforms all baselines on every metric.

AI.tldr: CIRRA is a dual-level LLM-plus-rule framework for integrating new instructions into ongoing household robot task plans while preserving the existing execution backbone, avoiding the ambiguity, inconsistency, and redundancy of full replanning; it also introduces the CHIRP benchmark and demonstrates strong results in simulation and on a Unitree G1 humanoid.
AI.motivation: Household robots must accommodate new user instructions while executing ongoing tasks, but existing agents often regenerate or heavily revise the remaining task sequence, causing plan ambiguity, logical inconsistency, and redundant execution.
AI.method: The paper formulates continual instruction reconciliation and proposes CIRRA, a dual-level framework combining LLM-based semantic reasoning with rule-constrained structural integration. CIRRA grounds incoming instructions to unique executable skills, resolves underspecified actions and execution locations, preserves the ongoing subtask sequence as an execution backbone, generates integration candidates by inserting incoming subtasks into location-matched segments, and uses a semantic reasoner to evaluate only modified segments for dependencies and conflicts, selecting the most logically coherent local integration.
AI.result: The paper introduces CHIRP, a text-based benchmark of 120 episodes across eight household environments and six categories of everyday activities. On CHIRP, CIRRA achieves 74.2% decision agreement, exceeding the strongest replanning baseline by 30 percentage points, with every correct fusion decision yielding a correctly placed, conflict-free schedule. On a Unitree G1 humanoid, CIRRA interrupts ongoing skills at the correct moment in every trial and significantly outperforms all baselines on every metric.
AI.conclusion: The structure-preserving reconciliation approach maintains alignment with ongoing execution, mitigates ambiguity and inconsistency, and reuses shared subtasks to reduce redundant execution, proving effective in both benchmark and real-robot settings.

title: Can AI Agents Make Open-Ended Scientific Discovery? Evidence from Station
summary: Recent AI systems have made rapid progress in scientific discovery when given well-defined metrics, but whether they can autonomously undertake open-ended scientific discovery remains unclear. We investigate AI's ability to tackle open-ended tasks in Station, an open-world environment in which multiple agents simulate a scientific ecosystem. To tackle challenges specific to open-ended tasks, we propose augmenting Station with two mechanisms: a Supervisor mechanism and periodic Meta Reflection, which encourage persistent exploration even when intermediate metrics are lacking. We construct open-ended tasks from three recent oral papers presented at ICLR. We give agents the main research question studied in each paper while withholding the paper's results and disabling web access. We then measure how many of the original findings-partitioned into individual criteria-agents rediscover. We find that Station rediscovers 62.7% of the criteria on average, compared with 15.4% for Codex Multiagent-v2 and 14.4-20.6% for AI Scientist-v2. Ablation and behavioral analyses indicate that adding the two mechanisms together improves research coverage and continuity. We further evaluate Station on two open-ended tasks without oracle papers and find that some of the discoveries made by the agents closely match discoveries reported by researchers after the knowledge cutoff date. Together, these results indicate that a suitable environment can enable agents to autonomously make meaningful progress in open-ended scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether AI agents can autonomously perform open-ended scientific discovery. It introduces Station, a multi-agent open-world environment augmented with a Supervisor mechanism and periodic Meta Reflection, and shows agents rediscover 62.7% of findings from three ICLR oral papers, far outperforming Codex Multiagent-v2 and AI Scientist-v2.
AI.motivation: Prior AI systems excel at scientific discovery only when given well-defined metrics. Whether AI can autonomously undertake open-ended scientific discovery, where intermediate metrics are absent and progress is hard to measure, remains unclear. The authors aim to test and enable such autonomous open-ended discovery.
AI.method: The authors build Station, an open-world environment where multiple agents simulate a scientific ecosystem. They augment it with a Supervisor mechanism and periodic Meta Reflection to encourage persistent exploration despite lacking intermediate metrics. Open-ended tasks are constructed from three recent ICLR oral papers: agents receive each paper's main research question while the paper's results are withheld and web access is disabled. Findings are partitioned into individual criteria to measure rediscovery. Ablation and behavioral analyses isolate the contribution of the two mechanisms. Station is also evaluated on two open-ended tasks without oracle papers.
AI.result: Station rediscovers 62.7% of criteria on average, versus 15.4% for Codex Multiagent-v2 and 14.4-20.6% for AI Scientist-v2. Ablations show that combining the two mechanisms improves research coverage and continuity. On two open-ended tasks without oracle papers, some agent discoveries closely match findings reported by researchers after the knowledge cutoff date.
AI.conclusion: A suitable environment can enable agents to autonomously make meaningful progress in open-ended scientific discovery, suggesting environment design with mechanisms like Supervisor and Meta Reflection is key to overcoming the lack of well-defined metrics.

title: Trajectory Planning without Trajectory Data: A Manifold-Guided Approach
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code can be found in https://github.com/SilongYong/Ariadne/
summary: A common way for trajectory planning is to leverage generative models trained on large collections of expert trajectories. At inference time, the model generates executable trajectories by conditioning on task goal constraints. However, trajectory-based methods rely on costly supervision, scale poorly with sequence length, and often generalize poorly to unseen constraints such as novel start-goal pairs. We propose an alternative to learn the underlying state-space manifold and use the geometry of the manifold for trajectory planning. This approach requires only state observations and enables generalization to unseen constraints by con- structing trajectories on the learned manifold of the state space. Experiments on Maze2D and robotic motion-planning benchmarks show that Ariadne constructs feasible paths from state-only supervision and generalizes to unseen start-goal combinations. On high-dimensional dual-arm planning, it remains competitive with trajectory-supervised and classical planners, while requiring no trajectory data for training.

AI.tldr: Ariadne learns a state-space manifold from state-only observations and plans trajectories using the manifold's geometry, avoiding costly trajectory supervision and generalizing to unseen start-goal pairs.
AI.motivation: Trajectory planning typically relies on generative models trained on large expert trajectory datasets. These trajectory-based methods suffer from expensive supervision, poor scaling with sequence length, and weak generalization to unseen constraints such as novel start-goal pairs.
AI.method: Instead of learning from trajectories, the paper learns the underlying state-space manifold and exploits its geometry for planning. The method requires only state observations and constructs trajectories directly on the learned manifold, enabling generalization to unseen constraints.
AI.result: On Maze2D and robotic motion-planning benchmarks, Ariadne constructs feasible paths from state-only supervision and generalizes to unseen start-goal combinations. On high-dimensional dual-arm planning, it remains competitive with trajectory-supervised and classical planners, despite requiring no trajectory data for training.
AI.conclusion: Learning the geometry of the state-space manifold offers an effective alternative to trajectory-supervised planning, achieving competitive performance with weaker supervision and better generalization.

title: Humanity's Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models
summary: Humans perceive far more in a scene than what is explicitly depicted: a single glance captures past causes and future trajectories; a quick peek determines if a vehicle can fit between two parked cars; a few seconds of video reveals who holds authority in a room; and a fleeting clip highlights subtle abstract patterns like unwritten rules or hidden labels. This capacity reflects a form of humanity's sixth sense: an intuitive reasoning mechanism that recovers implicit information beyond raw sensory perception. Crucially, this rapid, zero-shot visual intuition underpins everyday navigation and social interaction, making it a vital capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) deployed alongside people. Existing visual benchmarks, however, target either deliberate expert-level analysis in academic and mathematical domains or low-level perception, leaving the intuitive reasoning that people perform largely untested. To bridge this gap, we introduce Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning. HSS spans diverse image and video inputs, organizes items under a structured taxonomy, and pairs each with human-written prompts probing the implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structure that people infer at a glance. Frontier MLLMs fall short of human performance: participants reach 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, reaches only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. Despite excelling in many complex tasks that require advanced perception and knowledge, current models still struggle significantly on these visual tasks that are intuitive for humans. We further explore agentic setup that apply dynamic visual manipulation to HSS, which narrows but does not close the gap. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and directs attention to a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has so far left behind.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Humanity's Sixth Sense (HSS), a benchmark for intuitive visual reasoning that tests MLLMs on implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract information inferred at a glance from images and videos. Humans reach 93.1% accuracy while the best model scores only 53.6%, revealing a major capability gap.
AI.motivation: Humans rapidly and zero-shot recover implicit information beyond raw sensory perception (past causes, future trajectories, social hierarchy, unwritten rules), a "sixth sense" vital for navigation and social interaction. This capability is critical for MLLMs deployed alongside people, yet existing visual benchmarks target either deliberate expert-level analysis in academic/mathematical domains or low-level perception, leaving everyday intuitive reasoning largely untested.
AI.method: The authors build HSS, a benchmark spanning diverse image and video inputs, organized under a structured taxonomy. Each item is paired with human-written prompts that probe the implicit temporal, spatial, social, and abstract structure people infer at a glance. They additionally explore an agentic setup applying dynamic visual manipulation to HSS.
AI.result: Frontier MLLMs fall short of human performance: human participants reach 93.1% accuracy, while the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, reaches only 53.6% even at maximum reasoning effort. The agentic setup narrows but does not close the gap.
AI.conclusion: Despite excelling at many complex tasks requiring advanced perception and knowledge, current models still struggle significantly on visual tasks that are intuitive for humans. HSS establishes intuitive visual reasoning as a measurable axis and directs attention to a capability that scaling on current benchmarks has so far left behind.

title: From Wearable Interfaces to Dexterous Policies: Contact Shifts and Tactile Representations
summary: Unlike conventional teleoperation, wearable interfaces allow operators to collect dexterous demonstrations through their own hand motions while directly interacting with task objects. This direct interaction reduces dependence on the target robot during collection, but it also makes the collection hardware part of the physical process that generates each demonstration. Interface geometry can influence both how a task is performed and what tactile observations are recorded for learning. We study two versions of a DexUMI-family exoskeleton that share the same robot command definition, mapping procedure, and tactile module type but differ in hand-side geometry. The revised interface reduces reported physical demand, improves selected device ratings, enables tactile access in a precision grasp that is mechanically blocked by the baseline, and produces task-dependent changes in recorded contact. Lid twisting primarily exhibits a change in contact location, whereas egg carton opening primarily exhibits a change in contact occurrence. We then train matched policies using either a binary aggregate input or a spatial-plus-force input. On lid twisting and egg carton opening, policies trained on revised-interface demonstrations achieve higher success than those trained on baseline demonstrations, with a significant pooled interface effect. Across these and two additional tasks, USB insertion and soldering tool pick and place, the spatial-plus-force input likewise outperforms binary aggregation. These results show that wearable collection hardware is part of the data-generation process for robot learning. Such interfaces should therefore be evaluated not only through operator experience, but also through the tactile interactions they make recordable and the policy performance their demonstrations support.

AI.tldr: Wearable exoskeleton interface geometry is shown to be part of the data-generation process for robot learning: a revised geometry improves operator experience, enables tactile sensing in a precision grasp, changes recorded contact in a task-dependent way, and yields higher policy success than the baseline.
AI.motivation: Wearable interfaces let operators collect dexterous demonstrations via their own hand motions while directly touching task objects, reducing reliance on the target robot. However, this direct interaction makes the collection hardware part of the physical process generating each demonstration, so interface geometry can shape both task execution and the tactile observations available for learning. The authors argue such hardware should be evaluated not only by operator experience but also by the tactile data it makes recordable and the policy performance it supports.
AI.method: Two versions of a DexUMI-family exoskeleton sharing the same robot command definition, mapping procedure, and tactile module type but differing in hand-side geometry are compared. The revised interface is assessed on reported physical demand, device ratings, tactile accessibility in a precision grasp, and recorded contact during lid twisting and egg carton opening. Matched policies are then trained with either a binary aggregate tactile input or a spatial-plus-force input, and evaluated on lid twisting, egg carton opening, USB insertion, and soldering tool pick and place.
AI.result: The revised interface reduces reported physical demand, improves selected device ratings, enables tactile access in a precision grasp that is mechanically blocked by the baseline, and produces task-dependent changes in recorded contact: lid twisting mainly shows a change in contact location, while egg carton opening mainly shows a change in contact occurrence. Policies trained on revised-interface demonstrations achieve higher success than those on baseline demonstrations for lid twisting and egg carton opening, with a significant pooled interface effect. Across all four tasks, the spatial-plus-force input outperforms binary aggregation.
AI.conclusion: Wearable collection hardware is a constitutive part of the data-generation process in robot learning. Interface design should therefore be evaluated along two axes: operator experience and the tactile interactions it renders recordable, together with the downstream policy performance of the resulting demonstrations.

title: Socio-Foundation: A Model for Generalizable Individual Behavior Simulation via Hierarchical Capability Distillation
summary: Simulating individual behavior requires large language models (LLMs) to preserve persona traits while adapting to dynamic social contexts. However, general-purpose LLMs often flatten distinct personas, while task-specific tuning suffers from fragmentation and generalization. To overcome these challenges, we organize individual simulation into the \textbf{FONTS Taxonomy}, comprising five complementary capability dimensions: \emph{persona fidelity} (\textbf{F}), \emph{outcome realization} (\textbf{O}), \emph{behavioral naturalness} (\textbf{N}), \emph{trajectory coherence} (\textbf{T}), and \emph{social grounding} (\textbf{S}). Grounded in this taxonomy, we curate a standardized training corpus library of approximately 10 million instances across 14 representative datasets and present \textbf{Socio-Foundation}. Socio-Foundation decouples specialization from integration via a three-stage pipeline: learning task experts via DAPO, consolidating them into capability experts via off-policy distillation, and unifying them via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). We also establish \textbf{IndiEval}, consolidating 29 metrics across the FONTS dimensions. Experiments show that Socio-Foundation outperforms its \textit{Qwen3-8B} base by 11.0 points and approaches frontier models such as \textit{GLM-5.2}, with ablations and out-of-distribution evaluations further demonstrating the effectiveness and generalization of our model.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FONTS, a taxonomy for individual behavior simulation with LLMs, and builds Socio-Foundation, a three-stage training pipeline with a 10M-instance corpus and IndiEval benchmark, surpassing its Qwen3-8B base by 11.0 points.
AI.motivation: Simulating individual behavior requires LLMs to preserve persona traits while adapting to dynamic social contexts. General-purpose LLMs tend to flatten distinct personas, while task-specific tuning causes fragmentation and poor generalization.
AI.method: The authors define the FONTS Taxonomy with five dimensions: persona fidelity, outcome realization, behavioral naturalness, trajectory coherence, and social grounding. Based on it, they curate a ~10M-instance standardized corpus over 14 datasets and build Socio-Foundation via a three-stage pipeline: DAPO-based task experts, off-policy distillation into capability experts, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) for unification. They also introduce IndiEval with 29 metrics.
AI.result: Socio-Foundation outperforms its Qwen3-8B base by 11.0 points and approaches frontier models such as GLM-5.2. Ablations and out-of-distribution evaluations confirm effectiveness and generalization.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling specialization from integration through the FONTS-grounded three-stage pipeline yields a unified, generalizable LLM for individual behavior simulation, validated by strong benchmark gains.

title: Toward Evidence-Driven Human-Agent-Robot Teaming for Earth-Independent Anomaly Triage
comment: Accepted to the Space Robotics Workshop at 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
summary: Deep-space crews cannot rely on real-time ground support for urgent off-nominal events. Initial alerts may underdetermine cause, while discriminating evidence may reside in crew observations or at locations that are unsafe, costly, or unavailable for crew inspection. We present an evidence-driven architecture for human-agent-robot teaming in Earth-independent anomaly triage. Agentic AI is treated as a stateful coordinator over bounded, inspectable services rather than as a fully autonomous vehicle controller. A triage state manager maintains hypotheses, evidence provenance, uncertainty, operational context, and tool status; a crew-facing embodied agent elicits observations and explains assessment changes; and a mobile robot acquires targeted, localized evidence. Typed interfaces separate dialogue and orchestration from monitoring, robot command, context retrieval, and safety-critical control. Two scenarios illustrate the architecture: a crewed deep-space mission based on an actual ISS ammonia false alarm, where suspected contamination restricts crew access, and a power-interface anomaly at a crewed lunar base, where robotic inspection distinguishes a local connector fault from other causes ambiguous in remote telemetry. Our main contribution is an authority-bounded closed evidence-loop architecture, exercised in a hardware-in-the-loop integration prototype using Reachy Mini and an Innate MARS mobile robot.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an authority-bounded, evidence-driven architecture for human-agent-robot teaming that supports Earth-independent anomaly triage on deep-space missions, where crews cannot rely on real-time ground support.
AI.motivation: Deep-space crews cannot depend on real-time ground support during urgent off-nominal events. Initial alerts often underdetermine the cause, and discriminating evidence may lie in crew observations or in locations that are unsafe, costly, or inaccessible for crew inspection. This creates a need for autonomous, Earth-independent anomaly triage.
AI.method: The authors design an evidence-driven human-agent-robot teaming architecture in which agentic AI acts as a stateful coordinator over bounded, inspectable services rather than a fully autonomous vehicle controller. A triage state manager tracks hypotheses, evidence provenance, uncertainty, operational context, and tool status. A crew-facing embodied agent elicits observations and explains assessment changes, while a mobile robot acquires targeted, localized evidence. Typed interfaces separate dialogue and orchestration from monitoring, robot command, context retrieval, and safety-critical control.
AI.result: The architecture is illustrated through two scenarios: a crewed deep-space mission based on an actual ISS ammonia false alarm, where suspected contamination restricts crew access, and a power-interface anomaly at a crewed lunar base, where robotic inspection distinguishes a local connector fault from causes that remain ambiguous in remote telemetry. The approach is exercised in a hardware-in-the-loop integration prototype using Reachy Mini and an Innate MARS mobile robot.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is an authority-bounded closed evidence-loop architecture for Earth-independent anomaly triage, validated in a hardware-in-the-loop integration prototype. This establishes a design for coordinating human, agent, and robotic roles under bounded authority during deep-space off-nominal events.

title: Verify Less, Evolve More: Training Idea-Level Critics for Verification-Efficient ML Evolving Agents
summary: As large language models become more powerful, self-evolving agents are able to tackle challenging tasks including AI for machine learning (AI4ML). In AI4ML, while empirical verification is available, it often requires computationally costly model training and evaluation, limiting the speed and scale of agent evolution. Yet verification efficiency remains under-explored, and frontier models provide only limited gains when used directly as idea selectors. We address this gap with specialized idea-level critic models that predict whether a proposed ML modification will improve upon the current solution, allowing agents to screen ideas and concentrate verification resources on the most promising candidates. We train the critic models through supervised fine-tuning on high-quality critiques synthesized by Gemini-3.1-Pro, followed by GRPO to further improve their predictive accuracy. Empirically, our critic models outperform Gemini-3.1-Pro in static idea evaluation, and these gains extend to agent inference, continual learning, and policy training. During inference-time evolution, they improve final solution quality under the same verification budget by selecting more promising ideas, with further gains from continual learning. During policy training, they serve as learned reward models, reserving empirical verification for uncertain cases and enabling substantially more policy updates with the same verification resources. Together, these results show that idea-level critic models help ML agents discover better solutions and learn stronger proposal policies under limited verification budgets.

AI.tldr: Specialized idea-level critic models, trained via SFT on synthesized critiques and GRPO, predict whether a proposed ML modification improves the current solution, enabling self-evolving ML agents to screen ideas and allocate costly verification more efficiently, outperforming Gemini-3.1-Pro and improving inference, continual learning, and policy training under fixed verification budgets.
AI.motivation: In AI4ML, self-evolving agents can propose and verify ML modifications, but verification requires computationally costly training and evaluation, bottlenecking evolution speed and scale. Verification efficiency is under-explored, and frontier models used directly as idea selectors yield only limited gains—motivating dedicated idea-level critics.
AI.method: Train specialized idea-level critic models that predict whether a proposed ML modification improves the current solution. Training uses supervised fine-tuning on high-quality critiques synthesized by Gemini-3.1-Pro, followed by GRPO to improve predictive accuracy. The critics screen ideas so agents spend verification on the most promising candidates.
AI.result: Critics outperform Gemini-3.1-Pro in static idea evaluation, with gains transferring to agent inference, continual learning, and policy training. At inference time they improve final solution quality under the same verification budget; continual learning adds further gains. As learned reward models in policy training, they reserve empirical verification for uncertain cases, enabling more policy updates with equal verification resources.
AI.conclusion: Idea-level critic models let ML agents find better solutions and learn stronger proposal policies under limited verification budgets, establishing verification-efficient critiquing as a key mechanism for self-evolving AI4ML agents.

title: HULK: Learning Whole-Body Forceful Loco-Manipulation for Humanoids
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation 2027
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation of large, heavy objects demands forceful interaction across the entire body. However, such payloads shift a humanoid's center of mass and impose sustained loads across the upper body, challenging balance and command tracking. We present HULK, a whole-body control framework for forceful loco-manipulation. Using model predictive control (MPC) to guide reinforcement learning with predictions of the loaded dynamics, we train two teachers: one tracks arm motions under wrist forces, and the other locomotes while holding large objects against the body. A capture-point control barrier function augments the wrist-force teacher during training to improve balance under load. We distill both teachers into a single policy. Evaluation spans simulation and the Unitree G1. In simulation, the teacher with the barrier function achieves the lowest forward and lateral velocity tracking errors at 10 kg per arm among evaluated controllers and reduces aggregate divergent component of motion (DCM) excursion magnitude by 35.7% relative to MPC-guided reinforcement learning alone. Our wrist-force teacher withstands torso push disturbances of up to 130 N.

AI.tldr: HULK is a whole-body MPC-guided RL framework that distills two teachers (wrist-force arm tracking and object-holding locomotion) into one humanoid policy, improving balance and velocity tracking under heavy payloads.
AI.motivation: Humanoid loco-manipulation of large, heavy objects requires forceful whole-body interaction, but such payloads shift the center of mass and impose sustained upper-body loads, challenging balance and command tracking.
AI.method: Model predictive control guides reinforcement learning with predictions of loaded dynamics. Two teachers are trained: one tracks arm motions under wrist forces, the other locomotes while holding large objects against the body. A capture-point control barrier function augments the wrist-force teacher during training to improve balance under load. Both teachers are distilled into a single policy.
AI.result: Evaluation spans simulation and the Unitree G1. In simulation, the teacher with the barrier function achieves the lowest forward and lateral velocity tracking errors at 10 kg per arm among evaluated controllers, and reduces aggregate divergent component of motion (DCM) excursion magnitude by 35.7% relative to MPC-guided RL alone. The wrist-force teacher withstands torso push disturbances up to 130 N.
AI.conclusion: HULK demonstrates that MPC-guided RL with a capture-point control barrier function enables forceful humanoid loco-manipulation, improving balance and command tracking under heavy payloads and external disturbances.

title: How Fragile Is On-Device Language Model Safety? Localizing Safety-Critical Parameters for Sparse Fault Analysis
summary: As small language models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained and on-device platforms, including as components of agentic systems, the integrity of locally stored model parameters becomes an important safety concern. We investigate whether safety-sensitive behavior in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat is concentrated within a sparse subset of parameters, creating a reduced fault surface for targeted analysis. We study two complementary localization methods: low-rank safety-associated subspace analysis and parameter-level safety--utility importance filtering. Both approaches reveal highly non-uniform safety sensitivity across the network, with the MLP down_proj consistently emerging as a prominent safety-sensitive component and o_proj providing a smaller contribution. Using parameter-level localization, modifying only 0.19% of model weights in down_proj yields 53% Basic ASR and 56% GCG ASR, while tinyBenchmarks accuracy remains at 51.6% compared with a 52.2% unmodified baseline. These results motivate targeted fault analysis and selective integrity protection for language models deployed in resource-constrained, on-device, and agentic settings.

AI.tldr: Safety-relevant behavior in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat is concentrated in a sparse subset of parameters, with down_proj dominating; altering just 0.19% of these weights yields ~53-56% attack success while preserving benchmark accuracy.
AI.motivation: SLMs are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained, on-device, and agentic platforms, making the integrity of locally stored parameters a safety concern. The authors ask whether safety-sensitive behavior is concentrated in a sparse parameter subset, which would create a reduced fault surface for targeted analysis and protection.
AI.method: Two complementary localization methods are used: (1) low-rank safety-associated subspace analysis, and (2) parameter-level safety-utility importance filtering, applied to LLaMA-2-7B-Chat.
AI.result: Both methods show highly non-uniform safety sensitivity. MLP down_proj consistently emerges as the most safety-sensitive component, with o_proj contributing less. Parameter-level localization modifying only 0.19% of down_proj weights achieves 53% Basic ASR and 56% GCG ASR, while tinyBenchmarks accuracy stays at 51.6% versus a 52.2% unmodified baseline.
AI.conclusion: Safety behavior is sparsely localized, motivating targeted fault analysis and selective integrity protection for models deployed in resource-constrained, on-device, and agentic settings.

title: PhysEvo: Astra Can Act, Let It
summary: Astra can act, yet reliable manipulation depends on the system through which it observes and controls the world.
