We introduce PhysEvo, a framework for physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) around a single frozen model. A task agent executes robot tasks; a meta-agent uses the resulting trajectories to diagnose failures, revise tools and skills, and test corrections. The meta-agent can also improve its own diagnostic tools, so retained revisions support both later action and later self-improvement. This process develops joint-level control, evidence-seeking observation, and reusable manipulation skills without model-weight updates or a separately trained action policy. Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, held-out-layout evaluation of retained task-specific deployment versions yields a five-dimension average score of 68.14/100 and 62.00% success, compared with 47.17% for RoboDawn's one-shot Astra agent, the strongest published reference in our comparison. On eight manipulation tasks challenging direct Astra, PhysEvo achieves 55.00% success, compared with 1.25% for the direct-Astra reference. Deploying the simulation-evolved harness on AgileX PiPER and continuing skill revision yields 90.60/100 average score and 84.00% success across 25 trials on five real-world tasks. PhysEvo turns the consequences of action into persistent, testable changes to how a frozen model acts and improves.

AI.tldr: PhysEvo is a physical recursive self-improvement framework that, around a single frozen foundation model, lets a meta-agent diagnose failures from executed trajectories and revise tools/skills (including its own diagnostic tools), yielding persistent, testable improvements to action and self-improvement without weight updates.
AI.motivation: Reliable robot manipulation depends not only on the model's ability to act but on the observation-and-control system through which it acts. The paper targets enabling recursive self-improvement in the physical domain around one frozen model, addressing the gap left by one-shot agents that cannot accumulate improvements.
AI.method: A task agent executes robot tasks; a meta-agent uses resulting trajectories to diagnose failures, revise tools and skills, and test corrections. The meta-agent can also improve its own diagnostic tools so retained revisions serve both later action and later self-improvement. Evolution proceeds without model-weight updates or a separately trained action policy, developing joint-level control, evidence-seeking observation, and reusable manipulation skills.
AI.result: On 42 RoboDojo tasks, held-out-layout evaluation of retained task-specific deployment versions reaches a five-dimension average score of 68.14/100 and 62.00% success, vs. 47.17% for RoboDawn's one-shot Astra agent. On eight manipulation tasks challenging direct Astra, PhysEvo attains 55.00% success vs. 1.25%. Deploying the simulation-evolved harness on AgileX PiPER with continued skill revision yields 90.60/100 average score and 84.00% success over 25 trials on five real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: PhysEvo converts the consequences of action into persistent, testable changes to how a frozen model acts and improves, demonstrating physical recursive self-improvement and effective sim-to-real transfer of the evolved harness.

title: Learning to Report Unsafe Tasks in a Multi-Agent Game
summary: When agents share a reward for completed tasks, reporting unsafe work can reduce the reporter's reward by stopping a task. Audits can make reporting optimal without ensuring that further training teaches a silent team to report. We study this learning problem in a game where any witness can stop a task by reporting. With $k$ witnesses per task sharing a policy and drawing independently, the expected-reward derivative with respect to their shared silence probability counts each task's benefit $k$ times at universal silence. The comparison with universal reporting counts it once. For arbitrary policy groups, we give an audit condition sufficient for exact policy-gradient updates to reach universal reporting and, apart from boundary cases, necessary near universal silence. In a balanced family, the cheapest audits meeting the condition with prescribed positive margins cost exactly $k$ times as much for full sharing as for one policy per role. We train PPO policies on 24 witness graphs from learned silence. Separating co-witnesses reduces unsafe completion by 33.59 percentage points compared with shuffled groups of the same sizes under the same audits (95% graph-bootstrap interval: 21.03-45.13). Only 9 of 48 witness-group runs achieve below 1% unsafe completion while retaining at least 90% legitimate completion. At the same audit budget, a fully shared network meets both thresholds in none of 48 runs with independent action draws and all 48 with a common draw.

AI.tldr: This paper studies when reward-sharing agents can learn to report unsafe work (stopping tasks) rather than stay silent, showing the expected-reward gradient counts a task's benefit k times under universal silence when k co-witnesses share a policy, and derives audit conditions for policy-gradient learning to reach universal reporting.
AI.motivation: When agents share rewards for completed tasks, reporting unsafe work reduces the reporter's reward by stopping the task, creating a misalignment between individual incentives and safe reporting. Audits can make reporting individually optimal but do not guarantee that further training produces a team that actually reports, so the underlying learning dynamics of silence versus reporting need study.
AI.method: The authors model a game where any witness can stop a task by reporting, with k witnesses per task sharing a policy and drawing independently. They analyze the expected-reward derivative with respect to shared silence probability, compare universal silence versus universal reporting, and derive an audit condition sufficient for exact policy-gradient updates to reach universal reporting (and, apart from boundary cases, necessary near universal silence). They quantify audit costs in a balanced family and train PPO policies on 24 witness graphs from learned silence.
AI.result: The expected-reward derivative counts each task's benefit k times at universal silence versus once at universal reporting. In a balanced family, cheapest audits meeting the condition with prescribed positive margins cost exactly k times as much for full sharing as for one policy per role. Training PPO on 24 witness graphs, separating co-witnesses reduces unsafe completion by 33.59 percentage points versus shuffled groups of the same sizes under the same audits (95% graph-bootstrap interval: 21.03-45.13). Only 9 of 48 witness-group runs achieve below 1% unsafe completion while retaining at least 90% legitimate completion. At the same audit budget, a fully shared network meets both thresholds in none of 48 runs with independent action draws and all 48 with a common draw.
AI.conclusion: Shared-policy co-witnesses create a systematic bias toward silence in reward-sharing settings, making universal reporting hard to learn. Separating co-witnesses and appropriate audit design substantially improve safe reporting, and whether a shared network meets safety and legitimacy thresholds hinges critically on correlated (common) versus independent action draws.

title: MimicX: Policy-in-the-Loop Supervision Refinement for Video-Driven Humanoid Motion Tracking
comment: 33 pages, 26 figures, 19 tables, including references and appendices. Project website: https://nebulis-lab.com/MimicX
summary: Human videos provide rich motion targets for humanoid learning, yet visually plausible references can still produce persistent failures under physics-based execution. These failures reveal where training supervision should change. We present MimicX, a policy-in-the-loop framework that uses execution feedback to refine video-driven humanoid motion tracking. Starting from reconstructed and retargeted motion, MimicX localizes difficult transitions and affected body regions, then jointly adapts tracking objectives and the reset curriculum for policy continuation. Repeated rollout verification selects execution-priority improvements subject to tracking guards. Across four core video tasks, MimicX consistently improves tracking accuracy and Robust Execution Horizon relative to the Fixed Reference baseline. Task-averaged results show a 25.7% reduction in body-tracking error and a 255.6% increase in execution horizon. Additional video, motion-reference, and collision-scene studies evaluate the method beyond the core tasks, while MimicX-HLoop accelerates feedback through heterogeneous execution. Overall, MimicX turns policy failure into actionable supervision for deciding what to refine and which refinement to retain.

AI.tldr: MimicX is a policy-in-the-loop framework that refines video-driven humanoid motion tracking using execution feedback, localizing failure transitions and body regions, jointly adapting tracking objectives and the reset curriculum, and selecting improvements via rollout verification.
AI.motivation: Human videos offer rich motion targets for humanoid learning, but visually plausible references can still cause persistent failures under physics-based execution. These failures indicate where training supervision should be changed.
AI.method: Starting from reconstructed and retargeted motion, MimicX localizes difficult transitions and affected body regions, then jointly adapts tracking objectives and the reset curriculum for policy continuation. Repeated rollout verification selects execution-priority improvements subject to tracking guards. MimicX-HLoop accelerates feedback through heterogeneous execution.
AI.result: Across four core video tasks, MimicX consistently improves tracking accuracy and Robust Execution Horizon versus the Fixed Reference baseline, with task-averaged 25.7% reduction in body-tracking error and 255.6% increase in execution horizon. Additional video, motion-reference, and collision-scene studies evaluate the method beyond the core tasks.
AI.conclusion: MimicX turns policy failure into actionable supervision for deciding what to refine and which refinement to retain. It is validated across core tasks and additional studies.

title: Sigma-Hunter: A Domain-Specific Language Model for Threat Hunting and Detection Engineering
summary: Detection engineers must translate threat reports, forensic observations, and hunt hypotheses into precise, testable rules. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) can draft such rules, but often produce invalid YAML, incorrect log sources, unsupported fields, or overly broad detection logic. This paper presents \emph{Sigma-Hunter}, a domain-adapted LLM for analyst-assistive Sigma rule generation and threat hunting. We build an instruction-tuning dataset from 3,635 validated open-source Sigma rules, expanded into 7,663 question-answer and analyst-reasoning examples. Each source rule is assigned to a single train, validation, or test partition before this expansion, so no rule leaks across splits. We fine-tune a 7B Mistral model and a Phi-4 model with LoRA and score held-out rule generations on syntax, approximate field consistency, and a semantic judgment of detection logic, completeness, selectivity, and log-source alignment. Sigma-Hunter-Mistral scores 8.17 overall, against 7.88 for the strongest general-purpose baseline and 4.61 for untuned Mistral. Two findings stand out: domain adaptation enables a compact 7B model to perform competitively with larger general-purpose models on this structured task, and syntactic validity is a weak proxy for semantic rule quality, as several baselines emit well-formed YAML carrying weak detection logic. The adapted models run locally, which suits detection engineering in disconnected environments where analysts cannot reach hosted model services.

AI.tldr: Sigma-Hunter is a domain-adapted 7B LLM that generates Sigma detection rules and threat-hunting logic from natural-language analyst inputs, fine-tuned on 7,663 examples derived from 3,635 validated Sigma rules with leak-free partitioning.
AI.motivation: Detection engineers must convert threat reports, forensic observations, and hunt hypotheses into precise, testable Sigma rules. General-purpose LLMs can draft such rules but frequently produce invalid YAML, wrong log sources, unsupported fields, or overly broad detection logic, making them unreliable for structured detection engineering, especially in disconnected environments without hosted model access.
AI.method: The authors build an instruction-tuning dataset from 3,635 validated open-source Sigma rules, expanded into 7,663 question-answer and analyst-reasoning examples. Each source rule is assigned to a single train/validation/test partition before expansion to prevent leakage across splits. They fine-tune a 7B Mistral model and a Phi-4 model with LoRA, then score held-out rule generations on syntax, approximate field consistency, and a semantic judgment of detection logic, completeness, selectivity, and log-source alignment.
AI.result: Sigma-Hunter-Mistral achieves an overall score of 8.17, compared with 7.88 for the strongest general-purpose baseline and 4.61 for untuned Mistral. Two key findings emerge: domain adaptation lets a compact 7B model perform competitively with larger general-purpose models on this structured task, and syntactic validity is a weak proxy for semantic rule quality, since several baselines emit well-formed YAML carrying weak detection logic.
AI.conclusion: Domain-adapted compact LLMs (Sigma-Hunter) can generate analyst-grade Sigma rules competitively with larger general-purpose models, and syntactic validity alone does not guarantee semantic detection quality. The adapted models run locally, suiting detection engineering in disconnected environments where analysts cannot reach hosted model services.

title: Workhorse: Learning Robust Whole-Body Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from Human Data
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Project page: https://hsb0508.github.io/workhorse/
summary: Humanoid robots still struggle to plan contact-rich whole-body manipulation from egocentric RGB and proprioception. Workhorse learns such manipulation from robot-free human demonstrations. A visual planner predicts five-link targets: the poses of the torso, both wrists, and both feet. A reinforcement-learning whole-body tracker follows them on the robot. Both policies train separately on the same recorded human poses, without retargeting. We augment the training data of each policy to imitate the errors that the other makes at deployment. On a real Unitree G1, Workhorse sorts boxes with its hands and a kick, catches a thrown box, and topples and climbs a suitcase. During box sorting, we show recoveries after a person pushes the robot or takes the box away. In a simulated copy of the demonstration room, the system completes box sorting in 77% of episodes, and in 64% under 40 N.s pushes. With both policies retrained from the same demonstrations, a simulated second humanoid completes box sorting in 83% of episodes without pushes.

AI.tldr: Workhorse learns contact-rich whole-body humanoid manipulation from robot-free human demonstrations using a separate visual planner (predicting torso, wrist, and foot targets) and an RL whole-body tracker, with cross-augmentation to imitate each other's deployment errors, achieving box sorting, catching, and climbing on a real Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots still struggle to plan contact-rich whole-body manipulation from egocentric RGB and proprioception. The paper aims to learn such manipulation from robot-free human demonstrations, avoiding the need for costly robot data or retargeting.
AI.method: A visual planner predicts five-link targets (poses of torso, both wrists, both feet) from egocentric RGB and proprioception. An RL whole-body tracker follows these targets on the robot. Both policies train separately on the same recorded human poses without retargeting. Training data for each policy is augmented to imitate the errors the other makes at deployment.
AI.result: On a real Unitree G1, Workhorse sorts boxes with hands and a kick, catches a thrown box, and topples and climbs a suitcase, with recoveries after pushes or box removal. In simulation, it completes box sorting in 77% of episodes, and 64% under 40 N.s pushes. A second simulated humanoid, with both policies retrained from the same demonstrations, completes box sorting in 83% of episodes without pushes.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates that contact-rich whole-body humanoid manipulation can be learned from robot-free human demonstrations via a decoupled planner-tracker design with cross-policy error augmentation, generalizing across robots and exhibiting recovery behaviors.

title: Whose Memory Is It? Scope-Aware Commit Rules for Long-Term LLM Memory
summary: Persistent memory allows an LLM agent to carry experience across conversations, but it also turns a local reasoning mistake into a durable one. During deliberation, an agent may consider a plan, simulate a tool result, report another speaker's belief, and then reject all of them. If memory retains only the resulting sentences, those once-useful possibilities can later return as facts. The record is neither fabricated nor irrelevant; it has simply been detached from the context in which it was valid. We identify this missing context as \emph{discourse ownership}: the world, branch, or speaker that licenses a proposition. Our first finding is counterintuitive. Language models already carry a causally active signal for ownership, yet conventional memory interfaces discard it when they convert reasoning into records. We introduce CASK (Causally Anchored Scoping Keys), a commit rule that preserves this signal so that shared-world facts enter durable memory while provisional content remains available only within its original scope. Our second finding is that the most obvious way to preserve the signal---storing the discovered internal coordinates---is unreliable because equivalent representations need not keep the same coordinates. CASK instead preserves the stable relations that express ownership. Controlled long-conversation conflicts and tool-agent traces show that this design improves memory admission and prevents provisional content from contaminating later answers while complementing runtime provenance. The resulting commit boundary lets agents explore more possibilities without granting every intermediate sentence authority over future behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "discourse ownership" as the missing context that distinguishes durable facts from provisional reasoning in LLM memory. It shows that language models already carry a causally active ownership signal that conventional memory interfaces discard, and proposes CASK (Causally Anchored Scoping Keys), a commit rule that preserves this signal via stable relations rather than internal coordinates. CASK improves memory admission and prevents provisional content from contaminating later answers.
AI.motivation: Persistent memory lets LLM agents carry experience across conversations but also turns local reasoning mistakes into durable ones. When agents deliberate, they may consider plans, simulate tool results, or report another speaker's belief, then reject them. If memory stores only the resulting sentences, these once-useful possibilities can later resurface as facts—not fabricated or irrelevant, but detached from the context in which they were valid.
AI.method: The authors first identify "discourse ownership"—the world, branch, or speaker that licenses a proposition—as the missing context. They find that language models already carry a causally active ownership signal, but conventional memory interfaces discard it when converting reasoning into records. They propose CASK (Causally Anchored Scoping Keys), a commit rule that preserves this signal so shared-world facts enter durable memory while provisional content remains available only within its original scope. Critically, rather than storing discovered internal coordinates (unreliable, since equivalent representations need not keep the same coordinates), CASK preserves the stable relations that express ownership.
AI.result: Controlled long-conversation conflicts and tool-agent traces show that CASK improves memory admission and prevents provisional content from contaminating later answers, while complementing runtime provenance.
AI.conclusion: The resulting commit boundary lets agents explore more possibilities without granting every intermediate sentence authority over future behavior.

title: FlashNeRD: Performance-First Contact-Rich Neural Robot Dynamics
summary: Compared with analytical physics, learned dynamics models promise robot simulation that is faster, inherently differentiable, and easily adaptable to real data. Neural Robot Dynamics (NeRD) pursues this by keeping collision detection analytical and replacing a simulator's numerical dynamics for the robot with a learned model. Three limitations remain. NeRD offers little speedup over the simulator it learned from, accepts contact only at predefined points, and has no two-way coupling with objects it manipulates. FlashNeRD removes all three with a parallel streaming architecture that makes each prediction faster and more accurate, an encoder that accepts contacts wherever they occur, and two-way coupling with objects simulated by analytical solvers. Experiments across five robots show faster and more accurate dynamics, faster policy learning, and faster inference-time planning. Across three robots, FlashNeRD's dynamics model is up to $55\times$ faster than an optimized NeRD and more accurate over long rollouts. This speedup extends to policy learning, where PPO trains an ANYmal locomotion policy in 34 seconds, $3.8\times$ faster than the analytical simulator and $2.7\times$ faster than an optimized NeRD. With DIAL-MPC, a sampling-based MPC method, the robot climbs all six test platforms where fixed-contact NeRD manages one, at approximately half the analytical simulator's planning time. Cube-reorientation policies trained with FlashNeRD complete within 2% of the simulator-trained policy's target count.

AI.tldr: FlashNeRD is a parallel streaming neural robot dynamics model removing three key limitations of NeRD: slow inference, fixed contact points, and one-way coupling. It achieves up to 55x speedup, higher accuracy, and enables faster policy learning and planning across multiple robots.
AI.motivation: Learned dynamics models can make robot simulation faster, differentiable, and adaptable to real data. NeRD realizes this by keeping collision detection analytical while learning the robot's dynamics, but suffers three limitations: little speedup over the source simulator, contact restricted to predefined points, and no two-way coupling with manipulated objects.
AI.method: FlashNeRD uses a parallel streaming architecture for faster and more accurate per-step prediction, an encoder that accepts contacts wherever they occur (not just predefined points), and two-way coupling with objects simulated by analytical solvers.
AI.result: Across five robots, FlashNeRD yields faster/more accurate dynamics, faster policy learning, and faster planning. On three robots it is up to 55x faster than optimized NeRD with better long-rollout accuracy. PPO trains an ANYmal locomotion policy in 34s (3.8x faster than the analytical simulator, 2.7x faster than optimized NeRD). With DIAL-MPC, the robot climbs all six test platforms versus one for fixed-contact NeRD, at ~half the analytical simulator's planning time. Cube-reorientation policies reach within 2% of the simulator-trained target count.
AI.conclusion: FlashNeRD overcomes NeRD's speed, contact, and coupling limitations, delivering faster and more accurate dynamics that translate into efficient policy learning and planning while matching analytical-simulator quality in downstream tasks.

title: Enabling Dynamic Computation in Looped LMs
summary: Looped LMs are parameter efficient and promise dynamic computation (saving memory and FLOPs on easy tokens). However, state-of-the-art open Looped LMs trained with this dynamic computation capability (Ouro models) do not realize it in practice as each loop iteration (depth) requires its own level of KV-cache, necessitating all loop computations. Moreover, Ouro's early-exit prior is enforced on each token equally, which results in static lower-depth like processing of all tokens regardless of difficulty. In this work, we propose a simple "best-available" KV caching strategy that works out-of-the-box, creating a new frontier in the performance vs depth space. Our approach enables up to 30% reduction in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance, showing the true flexibility of Looped LMs. Furthermore, training looped LMs with awareness about this KV caching strategy improves performance and efficiency. Finally, we apply a small but effective fix to the early-exit prior enforcement objective that makes tokens exit at truly heterogeneous depths based on effort. Our findings are validated on Ouro models as well as smaller looped LMs pre-trained from scratch.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "best-available" KV caching strategy for Looped LMs that enables up to 30% reductions in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance, and improves both training and early-exit heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Looped LMs are parameter efficient and theoretically support dynamic computation, promising memory and FLOP savings on easy tokens. However, state-of-the-art open Looped LMs with dynamic computation (Ouro models) fail to realize this in practice: each loop iteration (depth) requires its own KV-cache level, forcing all loop computations. Additionally, Ouro's early-exit prior is applied equally to every token, producing uniformly lower-depth processing irrespective of token difficulty.
AI.method: The authors propose a simple "best-available" KV caching strategy that works out-of-the-box, opening a new frontier in the performance vs depth trade-off. They further train looped LMs with awareness of this KV caching strategy to boost performance and efficiency, and apply a small but effective fix to the early-exit prior enforcement objective so tokens exit at truly heterogeneous depths based on effort.
AI.result: The approach enables up to 30% reduction in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance. Training with awareness of the KV caching strategy improves both performance and efficiency, and the early-exit prior fix yields genuinely heterogeneous exit depths. Findings are validated on Ouro models as well as smaller looped LMs pre-trained from scratch.
AI.conclusion: The proposed best-available KV caching unlocks the true flexibility of Looped LMs, delivering substantial FLOP and KV memory savings without sacrificing full-depth performance, and combining it with cache-aware training and a corrected early-exit prior further enhances performance, efficiency, and token-adaptive computation.

title: World Models Dream of Success: Diagnosing and Repairing Failure Insensitivity in Robot World Models
summary: Robot world models support policy evaluation, planning, and synthetic data generation, but these applications require predictions that distinguish successful actions from failures. Across four released checkpoints from two architecture families, we observe weak sensitivity to action changes and success-like predictions on verified failures. Although recent work incorporates failures into model training, which data can repair released checkpoints without changing their architecture or training objective still remains underexplored. To this end, we introduce CureWM, which constructs alternative actions from successful demonstrations across a severity grid, verifies their outcomes through execution in simulation or on hardware, and fine-tunes released models on the resulting failures and surviving successes alongside nominal demonstrations. This construction provides controlled action contrasts from shared starting contexts. On 484 held-out LIBERO failure counterfactuals, optimism falls from 80\% after fine-tuning on the official data to 30--43\% across four independently fine-tuned CureWM models (38\% mean). In two separate evaluations on a physical robot arm, failure predictions scored as success-like by a latent-distance diagnostic decrease from 90\% after fine-tuning on successful demonstrations alone to 33\% with CureWM. With failure counts per task, successful replay data, and training budget matched, counterfactual failures yield a success--failure value gap of 0.124, compared with 0.014 for freshly collected on-policy failures. These findings support execution-verified counterfactual replay for post-hoc repair and show why reduced optimism must be evaluated alongside success--failure discrimination. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/CureWM.

AI.tldr: Robot world models are insensitive to action changes and predict success on verified failures; CureWM repairs released checkpoints via execution-verified counterfactual failures, cutting optimism from 80% to 38% mean on LIBERO and improving failure discrimination on hardware.
AI.motivation: Robot world models are used for policy evaluation, planning, and synthetic data generation, all of which require predictions that separate successful actions from failures. However, released checkpoints across two architecture families show weak sensitivity to action changes and optimistic, success-like predictions on verified failures. Prior work adds failures to training, but it is unclear which data can repair already-released checkpoints without altering architecture or training objective.
AI.method: CureWM builds alternative actions from successful demonstrations along a severity grid, verifies their outcomes by execution in simulation or on hardware, and fine-tunes released models on the resulting failures and surviving successes together with nominal demonstrations. This yields controlled action contrasts from shared starting contexts, i.e., execution-verified counterfactual replay, requiring no architecture or objective changes.
AI.result: On 484 held-out LIBERO failure counterfactuals, optimism drops from 80% (official-data fine-tuning) to 30-43% across four independently fine-tuned CureWM models (38% mean). On a physical robot arm, failure predictions rated success-like by a latent-distance diagnostic fall from 90% (successful-demonstration fine-tuning only) to 33% with CureWM. With failure counts per task, successful replay data, and training budget matched, counterfactual failures give a success-failure value gap of 0.124 versus 0.014 for freshly collected on-policy failures.
AI.conclusion: Execution-verified counterfactual replay is effective for post-hoc repair of released robot world models, and reduced optimism must be assessed together with success-failure discrimination rather than optimism alone.

title: PAIR: Bridging Perception and Action in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions. This task requires a transition from representations that describe the scene and instruction to representations that support action generation. Many continuous-action VLAs leave this transition implicit and supervise it mainly through the final action-prediction loss. We introduce PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation between these two spaces. During training, a Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens. A Bridge Module extracts task-relevant features from the current visual-language representations. PAIR aligns these features with the Action Latent Tokens to form Bridge Tokens that preserve task information and capture the structure of expert actions. The Bridge Tokens are then projected into the action-token space and injected into the initial Action Tokens, providing an action-ready starting point for Action Expert refinement. At inference, the autoencoder is removed, and the Bridge Tokens are generated only from the current observation and instruction. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC-D show gains for the evaluated OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter models. On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%. Representation analyses show that Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement. These results support a shared intermediate representation as a useful interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs.

AI.tldr: PAIR is a training framework for continuous-action vision-language-action (VLA) models that learns a shared perception-action representation by aligning visual-language features with action latent tokens, yielding consistent success-rate gains across simulation and real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Continuous-action VLAs must transition from scene/instruction representations to action-generation representations, but this transition is typically left implicit and supervised only by the final action-prediction loss, which provides a weak and indirect learning signal for the intermediate mapping.
AI.method: A Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens. A Bridge Module extracts task-relevant features from current visual-language representations, which are aligned with the Action Latent Tokens to form Bridge Tokens. These Bridge Tokens are projected into action-token space and injected into the initial Action Tokens to seed Action Expert refinement. At inference the autoencoder is removed and Bridge Tokens are generated solely from the current observation and instruction.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN ABC-D, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%.
AI.conclusion: A shared intermediate representation serves as an effective interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs. Representation analyses confirm that Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement.

title: A Unified Kinematic Representation Enables Reusable Biological Joint Moment Estimation
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Objective: Data-driven models that estimate physiological states, particularly biological joint moments, are widely used in exoskeleton control. However, these estimators are often coupled to device-specific sensor configurations, limiting controller transfer and the use of open-source biomechanics datasets. Methods: We proposed joint kinematics as an intermediate representation that decouples hardware-specific sensing from downstream biological joint moment estimation. A joint-moment estimator using joint angles and angular velocities was trained exclusively on open-source biomechanics data and evaluated using kinematics from a hip exoskeleton, knee exoskeleton, and inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor suite during level-ground, ramp-ascent, and ramp-descent walking. Results: The estimator achieved an root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.17 Nm/kg and coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.79 using hip exoskeleton kinematics, 0.19 Nm/kg and 0.62 using knee exoskeleton kinematics, and 0.15 Nm/kg and 0.85 using kinematics derived from IMUs across bilateral hip, knee, and ankle joints. Conclusion: Joint kinematics enabled an estimator trained only on open-source data to operate across distinct wearable platforms. Significance: This framework may reduce target-device data collection and support transferable biological joint moment estimation for exoskeleton control and wearable biomechanics.

AI.tldr: Joint kinematics serve as an intermediate representation to decouple device-specific sensing from biological joint moment estimation, enabling an estimator trained solely on open-source biomechanics data to generalize across hip exoskeleton, knee exoskeleton, and IMU sensor configurations.
AI.motivation: Data-driven joint moment estimators used in exoskeleton control are typically tied to device-specific sensor setups, which restricts controller transferability and prevents reuse of open-source biomechanics datasets.
AI.method: The authors propose joint kinematics as an intermediate representation between hardware sensing and joint moment estimation. A joint-moment estimator taking joint angles and angular velocities as input was trained exclusively on open-source biomechanics data, then evaluated using kinematics sourced from a hip exoskeleton, a knee exoskeleton, and an IMU suite during level-ground, ramp-ascent, and ramp-descent walking.
AI.result: RMSE of 0.17 Nm/kg and R2 of 0.79 with hip exoskeleton kinematics; 0.19 Nm/kg and R2 of 0.62 with knee exoskeleton kinematics; 0.15 Nm/kg and R2 of 0.85 with IMU-derived kinematics across bilateral hip, knee, and ankle joints.
AI.conclusion: Joint kinematics allow an estimator trained only on open-source data to operate across distinct wearable platforms.

title: Not Every Call Needs a Frontier Model: Per-Call-Site Evaluation of Small Language Models in a Deployed Agentic Home-Automation System
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, accepted in NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on SLMs for Agentic Systems, Paris,
summary: An agentic system issues several structurally different kinds of LLM calls. It routes intent, classifies actions, grounds language in a device registry, plans multi-agent pipelines and writes the Python code those pipelines run. The difficulty of these call sites varies by an order of magnitude, yet in practice a single model, chosen for the hardest site, serves all of them. In this work, we evaluate 9 models from 0.8B to a frontier hosted model across the five call sites of a deployed open-source home-automation framework (Wactorz), using its unmodified production prompts and two real Home Assistant installations (280 cases, 2520 scored calls). We find that capability is not ordered the same way at every site, and that larger models are not uniformly better: one 4B model is worse than its 2B sibling at grounded actuation. Paired testing shows the best local model to be statistically indistinguishable from both hosted models at four of five sites. Only code generation separates them, against a small hosted model (p = 0.039) as well as a frontier one (p = 0.002). Aggregate accuracy also hides a safety failure specific to actuation, where small models resolve the accuracy/refusal trade-off in degenerate ways: one model (Gemma4 E2B) actuates on 87.2% of requests for devices the site does not own, while another refuses every request it receives. Routing each site to its best local model reaches 91.8% against 95.4% at no per-call cost. In a live deployment judged by a user, hosting only the two generative sites matches hosting everything (39/43 against 39/43) for 28% of the spend, and the actuation gap the benchmark predicted appears as exactly one case in twenty-six. Benchmark, harness and all records are released at https://github.com/waldiez/slm-callsite-eval.

AI.tldr: Evaluating 9 models (0.8B to frontier) across the five distinct LLM call sites of a deployed home-automation framework, the study shows capability is not uniformly ordered across sites, best local models match hosted models at four of five sites, and per-site routing or hosting only the two generative sites can offer near-parity accuracy at substantially lower cost.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems issue structurally different LLM calls (intent routing, action classification, language grounding, multi-agent planning, code generation) whose difficulty varies by an order of magnitude, yet practitioners typically deploy a single model chosen for the hardest site to serve all sites, potentially wasting compute and money. The paper questions whether this one-model-for-all-sites practice is justified.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 9 models ranging from 0.8B to a frontier hosted model across the five call sites of Wactorz, a deployed open-source home-automation framework, using unmodified production prompts and two real Home Assistant installations, yielding 280 cases and 2520 scored calls. They perform paired statistical testing, analyze aggregate versus per-site accuracy, and examine safety behavior at the actuation site. A live user-judged deployment compares hosting only the two generative sites against hosting all sites.
AI.result: Capability is not ordered identically across sites, and larger models are not uniformly better: a 4B model underperforms its 2B sibling at grounded actuation. The best local model is statistically indistinguishable from both hosted models at four of five sites; only code generation separates them (p = 0.039 vs. a small hosted model, p = 0.002 vs. a frontier one). Aggregate accuracy masks a safety failure at actuation: a small model actuates on 87.2% of requests for devices the site does not own, while another refuses every request. Per-site routing to the best local model reaches 91.8% versus 95.4% for the best single choice at no per-call cost. In live deployment, hosting only the two generative sites matches hosting everything (39/43 vs. 39/43) at 28% of the spend, with the predicted actuation gap appearing as one case in twenty-six.
AI.conclusion: Model selection should be made per call site rather than globally, since capability rankings and scale benefits differ across sites and aggregate metrics can conceal safety failures. Routing each site to its best local model, or hosting only the generative sites in deployment, achieves near-parity performance at markedly lower cost, providing practical guidance for deploying small language models in agentic systems. The benchmark, harness, and all records are released publicly.

title: geodex: A Library for Motion Planning on Riemannian Manifolds
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Code, documentation, and tutorials at https://geodex.readthedocs.io
summary: Planning motions that respect the intrinsic geometry of a robot's configuration space, including its curvature and a configuration-dependent notion of cost, yields shorter, lower-energy, and more natural trajectories than planning under the ambient flat metric. Existing libraries for optimization on manifolds provide rich geometric primitives but do not plan around obstacles. While general-purpose motion planning libraries support many state spaces and custom distance functions, they do not yet treat a configuration-dependent Riemannian metric as the geometry that drives distance, interpolation, and geodesics. We present geodex, an open-source C++20 library with Python bindings. The library exposes the manifold, its Riemannian metric, the retraction, and the sampler as independent, interchangeable components through a single sampling-based motion planning interface. The same planner runs unchanged on canonical spaces $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\mathbb{T}^n$, $\mathbb{S}^n$, matrix Lie groups such as $SO(2)$, $SE(2)$, $SO(3)$, and $SE(3)$, products of these spaces, and articulated-robot configuration spaces, each equipped with a user-defined Riemannian metric. We make geodex publicly available with documentation, tests, and a reproducible benchmark suite.

AI.tldr: geodex is an open-source C++20 library with Python bindings for sampling-based motion planning on Riemannian manifolds, enabling planners to use configuration-dependent metrics, curvature, and geodesics to produce shorter, lower-energy trajectories across canonical spaces, Lie groups, and articulated robots.
AI.motivation: Respecting the intrinsic geometry of a robot's configuration space (curvature and configuration-dependent cost) yields shorter, lower-energy, and more natural trajectories than planning under an ambient flat metric. However, existing manifold-optimization libraries lack obstacle-aware planning, while general-purpose motion planning libraries do not treat a configuration-dependent Riemannian metric as the geometry driving distance, interpolation, and geodesics.
AI.method: The authors present geodex, an open-source C++20 library with Python bindings. It exposes the manifold, its Riemannian metric, the retraction, and the sampler as independent, interchangeable components behind a single sampling-based motion planning interface, with a user-defined Riemannian metric.
AI.result: The same planner runs unchanged on canonical spaces (R^n, T^n, S^n), matrix Lie groups (SO(2), SE(2), SO(3), SE(3)), products of these spaces, and articulated-robot configuration spaces, each equipped with a user-defined Riemannian metric. The library is released with documentation, tests, and a reproducible benchmark suite.
AI.conclusion: geodex fills the gap between manifold-optimization libraries and general-purpose motion planners by offering a unified, geometry-aware sampling-based planning interface, and is made publicly available with documentation, tests, and a reproducible benchmark suite.

title: BEACON-SP: Ontology-Grounded GraphRAG Framework for Clinical Suicide Risk Assessment
summary: We present BEACON-SP, an ontology-grounded Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) framework for clinician-facing decision support in behavioral health settings such as suicide prevention, where effective assessment requires integrating heterogeneous clinical, behavioral, social, and temporal evidence. BEACON-SP combines patient knowledge graphs with ontology-guided retrieval to support multi-hop reasoning across diagnoses, medications, risk and protective factors, life events, and temporal relationships. The framework is enabled by a comprehensive suicide prevention ontology that integrates the Three-Step Theory, the Integrated Motivational-Volitional Model, and the Suicide Social Determinants of Health Ontology into a unified representation of patient risk factors. We construct ontology-grounded patient knowledge graphs and evaluate BEACON-SP for clinician-facing question answering. Compared with a vector-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) baseline on a 1,500-query benchmark spanning 15 clinical categories and 100 patients, BEACON-SP improves completeness, clinical relevance, and evidence grounding under a corrected comparative evaluation protocol, with a small gain on factual accuracy. In paired criterion-level comparisons, GraphRAG is preferred in 76.4% of cases. These results demonstrate the potential of ontology-guided GraphRAG to provide structured, contextualized patient evidence for clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: BEACON-SP is an ontology-grounded GraphRAG framework that combines patient knowledge graphs with ontology-guided retrieval to support clinician-facing decision support in behavioral health, particularly suicide prevention. Evaluated on a 1,500-query benchmark across 15 clinical categories and 100 patients, it outperforms a vector-based RAG baseline in completeness, clinical relevance, and evidence grounding, and is preferred in 76.4% of paired criterion-level comparisons.
AI.motivation: Effective behavioral health assessment, such as in suicide prevention, requires integrating heterogeneous clinical, behavioral, social, and temporal evidence. Standard vector-based RAG may not adequately capture the multi-hop reasoning and structured relationships needed across diagnoses, medications, risk and protective factors, life events, and temporal relationships.
AI.method: BEACON-SP constructs ontology-grounded patient knowledge graphs and performs ontology-guided retrieval for multi-hop reasoning. It is enabled by a comprehensive suicide prevention ontology integrating the Three-Step Theory, the Integrated Motivational-Volitional Model, and the Suicide Social Determinants of Health Ontology into a unified representation of patient risk factors. It is evaluated for clinician-facing question answering against a vector-based RAG baseline.
AI.result: On a 1,500-query benchmark spanning 15 clinical categories and 100 patients, BEACON-SP improves completeness, clinical relevance, and evidence grounding under a corrected comparative evaluation protocol, with a small gain on factual accuracy. In paired criterion-level comparisons, GraphRAG is preferred in 76.4% of cases.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-guided GraphRAG has the potential to provide structured, contextualized patient evidence for clinical decision support in behavioral health settings.

title: Beyond Reconstruction: What Matters in Action Tokenization for Robot Policies?
summary: Autoregressive action-token policies such as vision-language-action models require action tokenizers to translate discrete token sequences into precise control actions in continuous space. Many action tokenizers learn the mapping between tokens and actions via a reconstruction objective. However, as we show through extensive analysis, sufficiently accurate action reconstruction is only one part of what makes a downstream robot policy successful. It is also critical that the policy is able to predict the right tokens for new observations, and that unseen policy token predictions still decode into reasonable actions. These properties are downstream of tokenizer training and are not directly incentivized by a reconstruction objective alone. In this work, we introduce Predictable and Robust Action Tokenization (ProAct), a tokenizer training method that strategically augments reconstruction with the goal of improving downstream predictability and robustness. ProAct is policy-agnostic and uses only action datasets for training. Across the Robomimic, LIBERO, and RoboTwin benchmarks and a diverse set of tokenizer architectures, ProAct improves rollout success by an average of 11.3 percentage points. These improvements also translate to vision-language-action policies and real-world robotic manipulation, yielding average gains of 21.8 and 36.7 percentage points, respectively. These results suggest that effective action tokenization should be designed as a policy interface that balances fidelity, predictability, and robustness, rather than as a reconstruction problem alone.

AI.tldr: ProAct is a policy-agnostic action tokenizer training method that augments reconstruction with objectives promoting downstream predictability and robustness, improving rollout success by 11.3 points on average across benchmarks and larger gains on VLA policies and real robots.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive action-token policies (e.g., VLA models) rely on action tokenizers to map discrete tokens to precise continuous control. Existing tokenizers are trained mainly via reconstruction, but the authors show reconstruction accuracy alone is insufficient: a successful policy also needs to predict the right tokens for new observations and to decode unseen token predictions into reasonable actions—properties not directly incentivized by reconstruction.
AI.method: The authors propose Predictable and Robust Action Tokenization (ProAct), a tokenizer training method that strategically augments the reconstruction objective to explicitly improve downstream predictability and robustness. ProAct is policy-agnostic and is trained using only action datasets.
AI.result: Across Robomimic, LIBERO, and RoboTwin benchmarks and diverse tokenizer architectures, ProAct improves rollout success by an average of 11.3 percentage points. Gains extend to vision-language-action policies (21.8 points) and real-world robotic manipulation (36.7 points).
AI.conclusion: Effective action tokenization should be designed as a policy interface balancing fidelity, predictability, and robustness, rather than as a pure reconstruction problem.

title: Shared-Roadmap Generation and Evaluator for Multi-Agent Path Planning Using Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network
summary: Multi-agent path planning (MAPP) in continuous environments often relies on roadmaps to balance safety and search efficiency. However, traditional roadmap generation methods, such as lattice grids or standard sampling-based approaches, frequently face a trade-off between graph density and the likelihood of finding feasible, high-quality solutions. In this paper, we propose a scalable heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for the automated generation and evaluation of shared multi-agent roadmaps. Our model covers the representation of waypoints, agent locations, and task locations as distinct nodes in a heterogeneous graph, allowing it to reason over global connectivity and inter-agent interactions. By training on occupation density maps aggregated and collected from expert solver trajectories, the GNN learns to identify critical points of interest and prune redundant nodes and edges. This process produces a compact, coordination-aware roadmap that is invariant to task permutations and is reusable for multi-agent pick and delivery tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework can reduce planning effort and can potentially find better solutions, reaching at least 40% reduction in runtime and in graph size for dense roadmaps.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a scalable heterogeneous GNN framework that automatically generates and evaluates shared multi-agent roadmaps, learning from expert solver trajectories to prune redundant nodes/edges and yield compact, coordination-aware roadmaps that cut runtime and graph size by at least 40%.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent path planning (MAPP) in continuous environments relies on roadmaps to balance safety and search efficiency. However, traditional roadmap generation methods (lattice grids, standard sampling-based approaches) face a trade-off between graph density and the likelihood of finding feasible, high-quality solutions.
AI.method: A scalable heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework is proposed for automated generation and evaluation of shared multi-agent roadmaps. Waypoints, agent locations, and task locations are represented as distinct node types in a heterogeneous graph, enabling reasoning over global connectivity and inter-agent interactions. The GNN is trained on occupation density maps aggregated from expert solver trajectories, learning to identify critical points of interest and prune redundant nodes and edges, producing a compact, coordination-aware, task-permutation-invariant roadmap reusable for multi-agent pick-and-delivery tasks.
AI.result: The framework reduces planning effort and can potentially find better solutions, achieving at least 40% reduction in runtime and in graph size for dense roadmaps.
AI.conclusion: The heterogeneous GNN-based approach yields compact, coordination-aware, reusable roadmaps, demonstrating improved efficiency (runtime and graph size reductions of at least 40%) for continuous multi-agent path planning.

title: CAP: Codebook-Aligned Prediction for Tokenized Robot Policies
summary: Action tokenization converts continuous robot actions into discrete symbols that can be modeled autoregressively. However, existing tokenizer-based policies typically ignore the tokenizer's learned latent code structure: after tokenization, the policy treats tokens as unrelated class indices and learns a new classifier from scratch. We show that this discarded structure is valuable. We introduce Codebook-Aligned Prediction (CAP), a method that directly reuses the tokenizer's code vectors as policy class prototypes while leaving the tokenizer and policy backbone otherwise unchanged. Across four quantizer families, three simulation benchmarks, and two real-robot tasks, CAP consistently improves task success over standard token classification heads while holding the tokenizer (and therefore its reconstruction quality) fixed. Our analysis further shows that these gains are not explained by higher token accuracy or changes in the policy head alone. Instead, reusing the tokenizer codebook provides the policy with valuable information about the tokenizer's learned latent structure across tokens, making token prediction errors more benign in action space and improving the representations learned by the policy backbone. These results suggest that action tokenizers learn useful action-aware latent structure beyond discrete targets that should be preserved when training downstream policies.

AI.tldr: CAP reuses the action tokenizer's codebook vectors as policy class prototypes instead of learning a fresh classifier, consistently improving task success across quantizers, benchmarks, and real-robot tasks by preserving the tokenizer's learned latent structure.
AI.motivation: Existing tokenizer-based policies discard the tokenizer's learned latent code structure: after tokenization, tokens are treated as unrelated class indices and the policy learns a new classifier from scratch. The authors argue this discarded structure is valuable and should be preserved.
AI.method: Codebook-Aligned Prediction (CAP): directly reuse the tokenizer's code vectors as the policy's class prototypes (logits computed via alignment with codebook vectors), leaving both the tokenizer and policy backbone otherwise unchanged. Evaluated across four quantizer families, three simulation benchmarks, and two real-robot tasks, holding the tokenizer (and its reconstruction quality) fixed.
AI.result: CAP consistently improves task success over standard token classification heads. Analysis shows gains are not attributable to higher token accuracy or changes in the policy head alone; instead, reusing the codebook supplies information about the tokenizer's learned latent structure across tokens, making token prediction errors more benign in action space and improving the policy backbone's learned representations.
AI.conclusion: Action tokenizers learn useful action-aware latent structure beyond discrete targets; this structure should be preserved when training downstream policies, as CAP demonstrates.

title: When the Governor Becomes the Disturbance: Control-Generated Disturbance and Cost-Aware Backoff in Governed Tool-Using Agents
comment: Includes ancillary experimental data and a Python script for reproducing numerical summaries. Code: https://github.com/CriticalAttentionSystems/CASAgentGovernor
summary: Supervisory governors can interfere with the tool-using agents they regulate. We study this possibility in a controlled file-recovery environment where increases in regulatory intensity trigger experimentally imposed tool failures. A cost-blind governor can turn these failures into persistent blocking that prevents task completion. We compare this governor with a backoff rule that reduces intervention probability using a moving average of known induced events. On a hand-coded stochastic-policy agent, the failure pattern appears under both result replacement and execution of corrupted tool arguments. For the persistent policy, adaptive backoff improves completion relative to a fixed weak governor with approximately matched intervention frequency. A Gemini 2.5 Flash experiment comprising 576 episodes across 6 tasks also shows reduced blocking and improved completion under backoff; among the tested settings, intermediate backoff strength achieves the highest observed aggregate success. These results identify an interaction between intervention cost and persistent action blocking, together with a possible mitigation. The cost mechanisms are imposed and their induced events are directly observable to the backoff rule; applicability beyond this controlled environment remains an empirical question.

AI.tldr: In a controlled file-recovery setting, a cost-blind governor's interventions turn induced tool failures into persistent task blocking; a backoff rule that lowers intervention probability using a moving average of known induced events mitigates this, improving completion on a hand-coded stochastic-policy agent and in a 576-episode Gemini 2.5 Flash experiment, with intermediate backoff strength yielding the best observed aggregate success.
AI.motivation: Supervisory governors that regulate tool-using agents can interfere with the very agents they oversee, but the consequences of such interference—especially when regulatory intensity itself induces tool failures—are not well understood. The paper asks whether a cost-blind governor can convert its own induced failures into persistent blocking of task completion, and whether this can be mitigated.
AI.method: The authors build a controlled file-recovery environment in which increases in regulatory intensity trigger experimentally imposed tool failures. They compare a cost-blind governor against a backoff rule that reduces intervention probability based on a moving average of known induced events. They evaluate on a hand-coded stochastic-policy agent under two failure modes—result replacement and execution of corrupted tool arguments—and run a Gemini 2.5 Flash experiment of 576 episodes across 6 tasks, including a fixed weak governor with approximately matched intervention frequency as a baseline.
AI.result: For the persistent policy, adaptive backoff improves completion relative to the fixed weak governor at approximately matched intervention frequency. In the Gemini 2.5 Flash experiment, backoff reduces blocking and improves completion; among tested settings, intermediate backoff strength achieves the highest observed aggregate success. The failure pattern appears under both result replacement and execution of corrupted tool arguments for the hand-coded agent.
AI.conclusion: The results identify an interaction between intervention cost and persistent action blocking, along with a possible mitigation via adaptive backoff. Because the cost mechanisms are imposed and their induced events are directly observable to the backoff rule, applicability beyond this controlled environment remains an empirical question.

title: Embedded Evaluation of Task Admission Coalescing in Decentralized Multi-Robot Systems
summary: Multi-robot task allocators in dynamic missions commonly admit newly released tasks immediately, potentially invoking allocation for each new arrival. We evaluate task-admission coalescing as a mechanism for controlling allocator processor work while accounting for target-service latency, using CBAA, ACBBA, PI, and HIPC as a representative MRTA suite. The study comprises a 3,000-mission AGX Orin campaign with measured computation delay, 3,000 paired zero-compute missions, and a 96-mission Pololu 3pi+ RP2040 allocator hardware-in-the-loop campaign. Immediate (Eager) admission is compared with thresholds of two, four, and eight tasks and a four-task policy with a 10-s waiting bound across three arrival rates. Across the AGX experiments, coalescing reduces both allocator calls and processor work in 31 of 48 evaluated conditions, although the magnitude of the saving varies by allocator. The principal cost appears under sparse arrivals, where four-task batching increases online-target mean latency by 20.08-23.57 s, predominantly through admission waiting. Bounded admission reduces mean work in ten of twelve allocator-load conditions, including a 19.35% reduction with a 1.40-s mean latency increase for high-arrival HIPC. RP2040 experiments show that this tradeoff can become more favorable as processor constraints tighten. Across four matched medium-arrival HIPC scenarios, Count b=4 reduces mean RP2040 work by 59.85% and service latency by 39.47%, while the corresponding AGX cases increase latency by 27.69%. These results show that the usefulness of task-admission coalescing depends on arrival intensity, allocator-specific behavior, and the relative cost of computation on the execution platform.

AI.tldr: Task-admission coalescing (batching newly released tasks before allocation) is evaluated for multi-robot task allocators (CBAA, ACBBA, PI, HIPC) as a way to control allocator processor work while accounting for target-service latency, across AGX Orin and RP2040 hardware campaigns.
AI.motivation: Dynamic MRTA allocators typically admit newly released tasks immediately, which can trigger an allocation computation for every new arrival. This is wasteful when tasks arrive in bursts or when the allocator's processor is constrained. The paper asks whether coalescing task admissions can reduce allocator calls and processor work without imposing unacceptable latency on target service.
AI.method: Three campaigns: (1) a 3,000-mission AGX Orin campaign with measured computation delay; (2) 3,000 paired zero-compute missions (to isolate admission effects); (3) a 96-mission Pololu 3pi+ RP2040 hardware-in-the-loop campaign. Policies compared: Eager (immediate) admission versus thresholds of 2, 4, and 8 tasks and a 4-task policy with a 10-s waiting bound, across three arrival rates, using CBAA, ACBBA, PI, and HIPC.
AI.result: On AGX, coalescing reduces allocator calls and processor work in 31 of 48 conditions, with magnitude varying by allocator. The main cost appears under sparse arrivals: 4-task batching increases online-target mean latency by 20.08-23.57 s, mostly from admission waiting. Bounded admission reduces mean work in 10 of 12 allocator-load conditions, e.g., a 19.35% work reduction for a 1.40-s latency increase for high-arrival HIPC. On RP2040, the tradeoff can become more favorable: in four matched medium-arrival HIPC scenarios, Count b=4 reduces mean work by 59.85% and service latency by 39.47%, whereas matched AGX cases increase latency by 27.69%.
AI.conclusion: The usefulness of task-admission coalescing is not universal; it depends on arrival intensity, allocator-specific behavior, and the relative cost of computation on the execution platform. Coalescing pays off most where processor constraints are tight (e.g., RP2040), while bounded admission policies help avoid the latency penalty of pure batching under sparse arrivals.

title: From High Recall to High Utility: Dataset-Adaptive Post-Processing of LLM-Generated Customer Intents
summary: Large language models can extract useful signals from heterogeneous enterprise data, but high-recall extraction often produces outputs that are duplicated, uneven in granularity, semantically overlapping, or too numerous for downstream systems and human reviewers to use effectively. We present a dataset-adaptive post-processing architecture developed for Customer Intent Extraction (CIE), where unstructured customer language is transformed into stable, traceable intent units. The approach separates recall-oriented extraction from utility-oriented reduction. Source-specific preprocessing first isolates evidence from multimodal plans, sparse operational records, and structured opportunity data. Candidate intents are then standardized and deduplicated, optionally enriched with metadata for embedding computation, represented in a shared semantic vector space, and grouped using a clustering strategy selected according to the candidate set's characteristics. Cluster-level keywords provide an explainability layer, while singleton reassignment requires agreement between embedding and keyword similarity. Finally, constrained language-model aggregation produces one concise intent per cluster without introducing unsupported concepts, and the resulting unit retains provenance, clustering, embedding, and generation metadata. This treats post-processing not as cosmetic cleanup, but as a semantic reduction layer converting high-recall LLM outputs into reusable enterprise intelligence. We also describe two downstream applications: Machine-Generated Intents, which infer likely objectives for customers lacking direct evidence from peer customers with similar profiles, and intent-guided semantic retrieval and mapping, which uses the stable intent as a query against a downstream decision space, illustrated here by mapping customer intents to business outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a dataset-adaptive post-processing architecture for Customer Intent Extraction that separates high-recall LLM extraction from utility-oriented semantic reduction, producing stable, traceable intent units and enabling downstream applications.
AI.motivation: LLMs can extract useful signals from heterogeneous enterprise data, but high-recall extraction yields duplicated, unevenly granular, semantically overlapping, or overly numerous outputs that downstream systems and human reviewers cannot use effectively.
AI.method: A recall-oriented extraction stage is followed by utility-oriented reduction: source-specific preprocessing isolates evidence from multimodal plans, sparse operational records, and structured opportunity data; candidate intents are standardized, deduplicated, optionally enriched with metadata for embeddings, represented in a shared semantic vector space, and grouped via a clustering strategy selected by candidate-set characteristics. Cluster-level keywords provide explainability, singleton reassignment requires embedding-keyword similarity agreement, and constrained LLM aggregation yields one concise intent per cluster retaining provenance, clustering, embedding, and generation metadata.
AI.result: The architecture converts high-recall LLM outputs into reusable enterprise intelligence rather than cosmetic cleanup, and supports two downstream applications: Machine-Generated Intents, which infer likely objectives for customers lacking direct evidence using similar peer customers, and intent-guided semantic retrieval and mapping, which uses the stable intent as a query against a downstream decision space (e.g., mapping customer intents to business outcomes).
AI.conclusion: Post-processing should be treated as a semantic reduction layer that makes noisy, high-recall LLM extraction usable, stable, and traceable for enterprise intelligence and downstream decision tasks.

title: Belief-Space Planning with Planner-Conditioned Estimator Error under Intermittent Observations
summary: Belief-space planners with separately designed or off-the-shelf estimators may have access to state-relevant information the estimator does not observe. Consequently, even an estimator that minimizes mean-squared error under its own information can have a nonzero error mean when conditioned on planner information. When future corrections are intermittent and stochastic, differences between accepted and rejected error means introduce additional uncertainty terms to correction events that zero-mean assumptions ignore. In this paper, we propose a belief-space planning approach that predicts, propagates, and penalizes planner-conditioned estimator error along evaluated trajectories. A planner-conditioned estimator-error model combines affine error dynamics with a moment recursion that preserves stochastically-induced correction uncertainty. We describe a method by which to predict estimator error dynamics within specified operating regimes and incorporate predicted error moments into a task-weighted quadratic risk objective. We evaluate the approach in simulation for a tilt-rotor VTOL landing on a ship deck using receding-horizon planning. We find that conditioning on planner information reduced error-prediction loss for a command-blind EKF by 13.4% relative to a planner-ignorant model, with strongly regime and horizon-dependent forecasting abilities. In a small set of 16 paired closed-loop trials, the planner lowered the median terminal task gauge from 1.60 to 0.99, and predicted estimator error beyond 2s within a factor of 1.3, versus a 5.7-fold underprediction by covariance-only planning.

AI.tldr: Belief-space planners can access state-relevant information unseen by their estimators, causing planner-conditioned error means that violate zero-mean assumptions. This work predicts, propagates, and penalizes such planner-conditioned estimator error within trajectory optimization via a regime-conditioned affine error model with a moment recursion.
AI.motivation: Separately designed or off-the-shelf estimators may not observe all state-relevant information available to the planner. As a result, an estimator minimizing MSE under its own information can still exhibit nonzero error mean when conditioned on planner information. Under intermittent, stochastic future corrections, differing accepted vs. rejected error means add uncertainty terms to correction events that zero-mean assumptions neglect, degrading closed-loop performance.
AI.method: A belief-space planning approach that predicts, propagates, and penalizes planner-conditioned estimator error along candidate trajectories. A planner-conditioned estimator-error model combines affine error dynamics with a moment recursion preserving stochastically-induced correction uncertainty. Estimator error dynamics are predicted within specified operating regimes, and predicted error moments are incorporated into a task-weighted quadratic risk objective, evaluated via receding-horizon planning.
AI.result: In tilt-rotor VTOL ship-deck landing simulation, conditioning on planner information reduced error-prediction loss for a command-blind EKF by 13.4% versus a planner-ignorant model, with strongly regime- and horizon-dependent forecasting. Across 16 paired closed-loop trials, the planner lowered median terminal task gauge from 1.60 to 0.99 and predicted estimator error beyond 2s within a factor of 1.3, versus 5.7-fold underprediction by covariance-only planning.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling planner-conditioned estimator error yields more accurate error forecasting and improved closed-loop task performance relative to covariance-only or planner-ignorant planning, though benefits are regime- and horizon-dependent.

title: Justice After Identity: Large Language Models and the View from Everywhere
summary: The search for a common view of justice and fairness has challenged human collective activity, as our diverging judgments are unavoidably shaped by the self-interests of social position, personal benefit, cultural inheritance, and historical circumstance. John Rawls famously attempted to overcome this limitation through popularizing a philosophical tradition known by the phrase "the original position" - a thought experiment by which people select principles of justice without knowing the identities or advantages they will possess. Critics, however, have long questioned whether people can meaningfully suspend their social identities and suppress morally relevant forms of lived experience. Artificial intelligence engaged to calculate algorithmic and agentic fairness introduces a novel possibility. LLMs have no singular class, race, gender, nationality, or biography, yet their parameters encode linguistic representations of a vast range of human identities and moral traditions. Perhaps the ethical judgments of LLMs could approximate an integrative original position - a "view from everywhere" generated not by excluding social identities but by computationally incorporating their diversity.It is unlikely that humankind will "hand over the keys" to computational systems by simply delegating complete agentic control of distributive and procedural collective processes. But AI may play a role, perhaps a positive one, interacting with individual and collective human judgment as we often confront increasingly polarized views on what is fair and just. We present data comparing human, base model, and frontier/fine-tuned model judgments about classic moral dilemmas while systematically varying identity relationships and Rawlsian constraints on identity. We conclude by speculating whether, if advanced AI systems provide humans with thoughtful advice, humans would actually be likely to accept it.

AI.tldr: This paper explores whether LLMs can approximate a Rawlsian "original position" for justice judgments, since AI lacks a singular social identity but encodes diverse human perspectives, and presents data comparing human, base, and fine-tuned model judgments on moral dilemmas under varied identity conditions and Rawlsian constraints.
AI.motivation: Human collective judgments about justice and fairness are inevitably biased by self-interest tied to social position, personal benefit, cultural inheritance, and historical circumstance. Rawls's "original position" thought experiment sought to overcome this via identity-blind principle selection, but critics question whether people can genuinely suspend their social identities and suppress morally relevant lived experience. LLMs present a novel possibility: lacking a singular class, race, gender, nationality, or biography, yet encoding linguistic representations of diverse human identities and moral traditions, they might approximate an integrative "view from everywhere" original position.
AI.method: The authors empirically compare human, base model, and frontier/fine-tuned model judgments about classic moral dilemmas, systematically varying identity relationships and Rawlsian constraints on identity.
AI.result: Data are presented on how the three groups (humans, base models, frontier/fine-tuned models) differ in moral dilemma judgments across identity relationship manipulations and Rawlsian identity constraints.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues that full delegation of agentic control over distributive and procedural collective processes to AI is unlikely, but AI may play a positive role interacting with human judgment amid polarization. It speculates whether humans would actually accept thoughtful advice from advanced AI systems on matters of fairness and justice.

title: Fast Planning for Multi-object Multi-target Throwing
comment: Accepted to IROS 2026. 8 pages, 9 figures. Zhengming Zhu and Yang Liu contributed equally. Video Summary: https://liuyangdh.github.io/momt-video
summary: Robot throwing has emerged as a promising technique for improving efficiency in logistics and warehouse automation, by enlarging the workspace and speeding up the process. To significantly increase the throwing system's throughput, we develop strategies for throwing multiple objects in one swipe. Such multi-object multi-target throwing (MOMT) leverages the large degrees of freedom of anthropomorphic hands. The key is to quickly generate fast and feasible throwing motions, which involves a complex trade-off between short trajectory duration and short planning time. We solve this problem in two stages. Offline, we build a model of the feasible set by combining object's inverted flying dynamics and the robot's kinematics and dynamics. Online, we generate feasible throws through fast solution matching and filtering of object's valid detach state and robot's feasible state that can compose sequences of throws in less than 5 ms. We validate the framework on a 7-DoF manipulator equipped with a multi-fingered hand. In simulation, coordinated two-object throwing reduces execution time by up to 46% compared to independent single-object planning, and this improvement is maintained when scaling to three objects. Real-world experiments with two objects confirm a 29% reduction; the remaining gap to the theoretical 50% is attributed to inter-throw transition overhead. When target positions are randomly changed mid-execution, the system re-plans and successfully reaches the new targets within 100 ms latency without stopping the robot.
