These results establish the first unified planning framework for MOMT throwing -- demonstrating scalability to multiple objects in simulation and real-world feasibility on two-object tasks -- advancing the frontier of high-throughput robotic manipulation. A video summarizing the method and the hardware experiments is available at https://liuyangdh.github.io/momt-video

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified planning framework for multi-object multi-target (MOMT) robot throwing, enabling multiple objects to be thrown in a single swipe using a multi-fingered hand.
AI.motivation: Robot throwing improves logistics and warehouse automation efficiency by enlarging the workspace and speeding up processes. To significantly increase throughput, the system must throw multiple objects in one swipe, but this requires fast and feasible throwing motion generation that balances short trajectory duration against short planning time.
AI.method: A two-stage approach: offline, a feasibility-set model is built by combining the object's inverted flying dynamics with the robot's kinematics and dynamics; online, feasible throws are generated via fast solution matching and filtering of valid object detach states and feasible robot states that compose throwing sequences in under 5 ms.
AI.result: Validated on a 7-DoF manipulator with a multi-fingered hand. In simulation, coordinated two-object throwing reduced execution time by up to 46% versus independent single-object planning, maintained when scaling to three objects. Real-world two-object experiments confirmed a 29% reduction (gap from theoretical 50% attributed to inter-throw transition overhead). Under mid-execution random target changes, the system re-planned and reached new targets within 100 ms latency without stopping the robot.
AI.conclusion: This establishes the first unified planning framework for MOMT throwing, demonstrating scalability to multiple objects in simulation and real-world feasibility on two-object tasks, advancing high-throughput robotic manipulation.

title: Epistemic Uncertainty-Aware Defect Detection for Quality Control in Medical Device Manufacturing
summary: Objective: We investigate whether accounting for epistemic uncertainty can improve the reliability of automated defect detection in medical device manufacturing. Methods: We consider a machine learning framework that operates on heterogeneous manufacturing and device-report data represented with Knowledge Graphs. To mitigate errors arising from uncertainty in the decision model, we analyze a principled rejection strategy to abstain from predictions whose estimated epistemic uncertainty exceeds a specified threshold. We evaluate the approach using standard synthetic benchmarks and real-world medical device report data. Results: The theoretical results establish the validity of the method characterizing the regimes under which it is expected to be effective. Empirically, the rejection strategy enables explicit control of coverage, that is, the proportion of samples for which the model issues predictions, while improving performance on the retained samples. On 266,170 real-world FDA MAUDE device reports, a 10% abstention rate reduces classification error by 48%, and more aggressive rejection (approximately 70% coverage) yields near-perfect accuracy on the retained samples. On standard synthetic manufacturing benchmarks, abstaining on 9% of the decisions, our approach reduces the risk up to 63% compared with the standard no-abstention approach. Conclusions: Abstaining from predictions with high epistemic uncertainty can provide a practical tool for controlling the reliability of machine learning-based defect detection, especially in high-stakes medical device manufacturing applications. Significance: Uncertainty-aware defect detection may support safer and more reliable quality assurance in medical device manufacturing by identifying cases that require additional inspection rather than issuing potentially harmful predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that abstaining from predictions with high epistemic uncertainty improves the reliability of machine learning-based defect detection in medical device manufacturing.
AI.motivation: Automated defect detection in medical device manufacturing is high-stakes, where erroneous predictions can be harmful; the authors investigate whether accounting for epistemic uncertainty can improve reliability.
AI.method: A machine learning framework operating on heterogeneous manufacturing and device-report data represented as Knowledge Graphs, combined with a principled rejection strategy that abstains from predictions whose estimated epistemic uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Evaluated on standard synthetic benchmarks and real-world FDA MAUDE device reports.
AI.result: Theory characterizes regimes where the method is effective. The rejection strategy enables explicit control of coverage while improving performance on retained samples: on 266,170 real-world FDA MAUDE reports, 10% abstention reduces classification error by 48%, and ~70% coverage yields near-perfect accuracy; on synthetic benchmarks, 9% abstention reduces risk by up to 63% versus no-abstention.
AI.conclusion: Abstaining from high-epistemic-uncertainty predictions is a practical tool for controlling reliability of ML-based defect detection, supporting safer quality assurance by flagging cases for additional inspection rather than issuing potentially harmful predictions.

title: Co-Evolving Robot Orchestrators and Policies through Deployment
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies trained on large datasets are capable within their training domains, yet they still fail to generalize to the variety of situations a robot meets in real-world deployment. Agentic robot systems complement the policy with a vision-language model (VLM) orchestrator that learns when to call the policy, how to instruct it, and when to use scripted skills instead. However, because the harness is built around a frozen policy that has limited language steerability, the orchestrator can avoid the policy's failures but never overcome them. The policy becomes the bottleneck of the whole system. Fine-tuning the policy can remove this bottleneck, but updating it alone decouples it from an orchestrator tuned to its old behavior. We propose Robo-COP, in which the orchestrator and policy co-evolve during deployment. Robo-COP curates skill demonstrations from its own executions, fine-tunes the policy when this data can address recurring failures, and adopts each new policy only after it improves the skills it was trained for. Across ten simulated RoboLab tasks, Robo-COP raises mean held-out success from 64.8% to 73.8% over the same harness with a frozen policy, while fine-tuning on a fixed schedule without verification reaches only 65.8%. On three real-world tasks, Robo-COP raises held-out success from 38.3% to 50.0%. Robo-COP turns deployment into a self-improving flywheel in which robots learn by doing, with each improvement in execution producing better data for the next round of learning. Videos and code are available at https://robo-cop.pages.dev/.

AI.tldr: Robo-COP is an agentic robot system where a VLM orchestrator and a VLA policy co-evolve during deployment, curating skill demonstrations, fine-tuning the policy to address recurring failures, and adopting new policies only after verified improvement.
AI.motivation: VLA policies trained on large datasets are capable within their training domains but fail to generalize to real-world deployment situations. Agentic systems add a VLM orchestrator to decide when to call the policy, how to instruct it, and when to use scripted skills. However, since the harness is built around a frozen policy with limited language steerability, the orchestrator can only avoid the policy's failures, never overcome them, making the policy the system bottleneck. Fine-tuning the policy removes this bottleneck, but updating it alone decouples it from an orchestrator tuned to its old behavior.
AI.method: Robo-COP co-evolves the orchestrator and policy during deployment. It curates skill demonstrations from its own executions, fine-tunes the policy when this data can address recurring failures, and adopts each new policy only after it improves the skills it was trained for.
AI.result: Across ten simulated RoboLab tasks, Robo-COP raises mean held-out success from 64.8% to 73.8% over the same harness with a frozen policy, while fine-tuning on a fixed schedule without verification reaches only 65.8%. On three real-world tasks, Robo-COP raises held-out success from 38.3% to 50.0%.
AI.conclusion: Robo-COP turns deployment into a self-improving flywheel in which robots learn by doing, with each improvement in execution producing better data for the next round of learning.

title: RippleCP: Measuring Counterfactual Checkpoint Advantage in Coding Agents
summary: Agent checkpoint systems decide what state is recovery-relevant, how to snapshot it, and whether rollback is admissible. None decides which of the safe boundaries they expose are worth materializing. We formulate this as counterfactual checkpoint advantage, the reduction in future recovery cost obtained by checkpointing a candidate rather than skipping it, and measure it by driving a CP branch and a SKIP branch to the same logical failure and recovering both under matched model, tool, verifier, and stopping conditions. On a frozen pilot of 12 SWE-bench Verified tasks and 106 real recovery branches, checkpointing saves 49.4 s per task, and that figure resolves into two regimes two orders of magnitude apart. The first checkpoint returns 100.0 s on 156.5 s of protected work, a conversion of 0.64; a second one step later returns-1.1 s on 41.8 s, a conversion of -0.03. Recovery is a re-derivation rather than a replay, so preserved work is a poor guide to saved work, and the classical elapsed-work rule misprices the second checkpoint by its full nominal cost. We identify where placement can pay, and set the bar a placement policy must clear.

AI.tldr: Checkpoint systems in agent recovery decide what state is recovery-relevant and whether rollback is admissible, but not which safe boundary is worth materializing. The paper formalizes this as counterfactual checkpoint advantage—the reduction in future recovery cost from checkpointing versus skipping—measured by driving CP and SKIP branches to the same logical failure under matched conditions. On 12 SWE-bench Verified tasks and 106 recovery branches, checkpointing saves 49.4 s per task, but this splits into two regimes two orders of magnitude apart: the first checkpoint returns 100.0 s on 156.5 s of protected work (0.64 conversion), while a second one step later returns −1.1 s on 41.8 s (−0.03 conversion). Because recovery is re-derivation rather than replay, preserved work is a poor proxy for saved work, and the classical elapsed-work rule misprices the second checkpoint.
AI.motivation: Existing agent checkpoint systems determine recovery-relevant state, snapshot mechanics, and rollback admissibility, but none evaluates which of the safe boundaries they expose are actually worth materializing. This leaves placement decisions unpriced, so systems may incur checkpoint overhead without corresponding recovery benefit.
AI.method: The authors formulate counterfactual checkpoint advantage: the reduction in future recovery cost obtained by checkpointing a candidate rather than skipping it. They measure it causally by driving a CP branch and a SKIP branch to the same logical failure and recovering both under matched model, tool, verifier, and stopping conditions, using a frozen pilot of 12 SWE-bench Verified tasks and 106 real recovery branches.
AI.result: Checkpointing saves 49.4 s per task on average, but this aggregate resolves into two regimes separated by two orders of magnitude. The first checkpoint returns 100.0 s on 156.5 s of protected work (conversion 0.64); a second checkpoint one step later returns −1.1 s on 41.8 s (conversion −0.03).
AI.conclusion: Recovery behaves as re-derivation rather than replay, so preserved work is a poor guide to saved work. The classical elapsed-work rule therefore misprices later checkpoints by their full nominal cost. The paper identifies where checkpoint placement can pay off and establishes the bar a placement policy must clear.

title: RoboRender: Robot-Oriented Video Generation for Visual Sim-to-Real Transfer
summary: Simulation enables large-scale, low-cost robot data generation, but policies trained in simulation often fail to transfer to the real world due to the sim-to-real visual discrepancies. Existing approaches often rely on intermediate representations, which can discard rich semantic information or require additional perception modules at deployment. We address this visual sim-to-real gap with RoboRender, a framework that converts simulated trajectories into photorealistic RGB videos for policy learning. RoboRender trains a robot-oriented video generation model conditioned on simulated depth videos, language instructions, and robot RGB mask videos, preserving simulator geometry, robot motion, and action labels while synthesizing realistic textures, backgrounds, and distractors. The generated RGB videos are paired with simulator-provided states and actions to train policies for zero-shot real-world deployment. On robot video test sets, our video model outperforms depth-conditioned video generation baselines in generation quality. In real-world experiments across pick-and-place, articulated-object manipulation, and mobile manipulation tasks, policies trained on RoboRender-generated data achieve a 71% average success rate, outperforming raw simulation renderings and conventional visual domain randomization by approximately 7.1x and 3.6x, respectively. We further show that policy performance improves with more generated videos per simulation trajectory, increasing opening-task success by 65 percentage points. These results demonstrate that generative video rendering mitigates the visual sim-to-real gap for zero-shot policy transfer. Project website: https://robo-render.github.io/.

AI.tldr: RoboRender converts simulated trajectories into photorealistic RGB videos using a depth-conditioned, language-guided video generation model, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real policy transfer with a 71% average real-world success rate.
AI.motivation: Policies trained in simulation often fail to transfer to the real world because of visual sim-to-real discrepancies. Existing remedies rely on intermediate representations that either discard rich semantic information or require extra perception modules at deployment, motivating a method that closes the visual gap while keeping a standard RGB policy interface.
AI.method: RoboRender trains a robot-oriented video generation model conditioned on simulated depth videos, language instructions, and robot RGB mask videos. This preserves simulator geometry, robot motion, and action labels while synthesizing realistic textures, backgrounds, and distractors. The generated RGB videos are paired with simulator-provided states and actions to train policies for zero-shot real-world deployment.
AI.result: On robot video test sets, the video model outperforms depth-conditioned video generation baselines in generation quality. In real-world experiments across pick-and-place, articulated-object manipulation, and mobile manipulation, policies trained on RoboRender-generated data reach a 71% average success rate, about 7.1x and 3.6x better than raw simulation renderings and conventional visual domain randomization, respectively. Performance also improves with more generated videos per trajectory, raising opening-task success by 65 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Generative video rendering, conditioned on simulator depth, language, and robot masks, effectively mitigates the visual sim-to-real gap and supports zero-shot policy transfer without intermediate representations or extra deployment-time perception modules.

title: Constraint Tree Exploration for Learning from Language Feedback
summary: Natural-language feedback in interactive learning often explains why an action failed by pointing to violated requirements. Misinterpreting this feedback can lead an agent to rule out valid solutions. We study this setting by modeling user intent as latent constraints over an action space and formulating learning from language feedback as pure exploration over feasible regions. We introduce TRACE, an algorithm that organizes candidate constraints in a tree and tests each proposed refinement by generating actions that satisfy it. TRACE commits to the refinement only if the resulting feedback does not contradict it over repeated tests. We distinguish two ways of using the same feedback: (i) falsification, which detects contradictions to the constraint set currently being tested, and (ii) identification, which may additionally name a violated constraint. We prove high-probability coverage bounds with dependence on the candidate class size $H$ for TRACE-Falsification. With reliable identification, TRACE-Identification can replace this dependence by $K/p_{\mathrm{ext}}$, where $K$ is the number of latent constraints and $p_{\mathrm{ext}}$ lower-bounds the probability of extracting a missing true constraint from informative feedback. We evaluate TRACE across six language-feedback tasks. On RecMovie, TRACE-Identification achieves 73% and 86% final-output success under caps of 20 and 60 evaluated outputs, compared with at most 42% and 48% for the evaluated prompting baselines given the same feedback and output caps. Controlled identity-corruption experiments further show greater robustness than direct accumulation when the falsification detector remains reliable.

AI.tldr: TRACE learns latent user constraints from natural-language failure feedback as a pure-exploration problem, organizing candidate constraints in a tree and only committing when feedback doesn't contradict the refinement, with provable coverage bounds and strong empirical gains.
AI.motivation: Natural-language feedback in interactive learning typically explains action failure by pointing to violated requirements. Agents can misinterpret this feedback and thereby erroneously rule out valid solutions, so a method is needed that learns from such feedback without over-eliminating feasible options.
AI.method: Models user intent as latent constraints over an action space and casts learning from language feedback as pure exploration over feasible regions. Introduces TRACE, which organizes candidate constraints in a tree and tests each proposed refinement by generating actions satisfying it, committing only if repeated feedback does not contradict it. It distinguishes two feedback uses: falsification (detecting contradictions to the currently tested constraint set) and identification (which may additionally name a violated constraint), yielding TRACE-Falsification and TRACE-Identification.
AI.result: Proves high-probability coverage bounds: TRACE-Falsification scales with candidate class size H, while TRACE-Identification, given reliable identification, replaces this with K/p_ext (K = number of latent constraints, p_ext lower-bounds probability of extracting a missing true constraint). On six language-feedback tasks, TRACE-Identification reaches 73% and 86% final-output success on RecMovie under caps of 20 and 60 evaluated outputs, versus at most 42% and 48% for prompting baselines. Identity-corruption experiments show greater robustness than direct accumulation when the falsification detector stays reliable.
AI.conclusion: Treating language feedback as pure exploration over feasible regions, with tree-organized constraints and cautious commitment, enables reliable constraint learning and outperforms prompting baselines, with identification yielding better sample-complexity dependence than pure falsification.

title: Evaluating the Transfer of Co-Evolved Communication from 2D to 3D Simulation
summary: This work examines the transfer of a co-evolved communication mechanism between two robotic agents from a discrete two-dimensional (2D) simulator to a three-dimensional simulator with real physics (3D). The study focuses on whether a communication mechanism co-evolved in a 2D environment retains its functional role after transfer to a 3D physics-based simulator. To support this analysis, the effects of the episode time budget, the social cue, and the asymmetry between the two co-evolved roles were examined. The results indicate that the success rate increased approximately linearly with the evaluated time budgets, with no evidence of a plateau between 2,000 and 6,000 physics steps, suggesting that evaluations based on shorter episodes may underestimate the performance of the trained controllers. In both simulators, the social cue functioned primarily as a jam- assistance mechanism rather than as a navigation guide, although with a more pronounced effect in 2D. Analysis of eight independent evolutionary runs revealed a consistent direction of asymmetry, although its magnitude varied across runs. Controlling the processing order between agents allowed us to rule out an artifact of the physics engine. Finally, the results are discussed in terms of the factors that may contribute to the remaining performance gap observed after transfer.

AI.tldr: A co-evolved communication mechanism between two robot agents was transferred from a 2D discrete simulator to a 3D physics-based simulator; its functional role largely persisted, though with a performance gap, and the cue acted mainly as a jam-assistance signal.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether a communication mechanism co-evolved in a simplified 2D environment retains its functional role after being transferred to a 3D simulator with realistic physics, addressing the broader question of whether evolved behavioral mechanisms generalize across environments of differing fidelity.
AI.method: A co-evolved communication mechanism between two robotic agents was transferred from a discrete 2D simulator to a 3D physics-based simulator. The study manipulated the episode time budget, the social cue, and the asymmetry between the two co-evolved roles, and conducted eight independent evolutionary runs. A control on the processing order between agents was used to rule out a physics-engine artifact.
AI.result: Success rate increased approximately linearly with the evaluated time budgets, with no plateau between 2,000 and 6,000 physics steps, indicating that short-episode evaluations may underestimate controller performance. In both simulators the social cue functioned primarily as a jam-assistance mechanism rather than a navigation guide, though its effect was more pronounced in 2D. The eight evolutionary runs showed a consistent direction of role asymmetry with varying magnitude, and the processing-order control ruled out a physics-engine artifact.
AI.conclusion: The co-evolved communication mechanism largely retains its functional role after transfer to the 3D physics-based simulator, but a performance gap remains. The study attributes this gap to factors such as the differences between the simulators and the asymmetry between the co-evolved roles, and suggests that short evaluation episodes can mask controller capability.

title: GeoNatureAgent (GNA): A Framework and Benchmark for Pre-Production Evaluation of Tool-Using Agents on Geospatial and Environmental Tasks
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Extended version of arXiv:2606.12821 (ACM SIGSPATIAL 2026 poster paper). Published at GeoIndustry '26 (ACM SIGSPATIAL Workshop)
summary: Before tool-using LLM agents are deployed in environmental and geospatial workflows, teams need evidence that an agent reliably selects the right operations against real APIs. We introduce GeoNatureAgent (GNA), a framework for pre-production evaluation of tool-using agents: a fixed sixteen-tool geospatial interface published as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so the agent under test is the only variable, scored against an identical tool layer, task suite, and deterministic scorer. Its flagship instance is a 103-task benchmark (a 93-task main suite across 18 categories plus a ten-task comparison expansion) evaluated against an open, self-hostable geospatial API serving three environmental indicators across Spain and Portugal. We evaluate nine LLMs under three temperature-1.0 seeds, reporting capability and per-case cost as orthogonal axes. (1) Claude Sonnet 4 achieves the highest capability (61.7% +/- 0.7% on all 103 tasks; 60.8% on the main suite), followed closely by DeepSeek V3.2 (57.9%), while no other model exceeds 53%; (2) the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier is mostly open-weight, with DeepSeek V3.2 offering 93% of Claude's capability at 11.3x lower list-price cost; (3) under strict all-checks scoring the best model sits 24-36 points below the 85-97% reported on general-purpose GIS benchmarks, whereas per-check partial credit for the top four models (86-90%) is comparable, so much of that gap reflects scoring strictness rather than task difficulty alone. The MCP server, evaluation harness, benchmark, and API are publicly available; swapping the tool executors and task suite instantiates an equivalent benchmark for any geospatial domain.

AI.tldr: GeoNatureAgent (GNA) is a framework for pre-production evaluation of tool-using LLM agents, built around a fixed 16-tool geospatial MCP server and a 103-task benchmark against a real environmental API for Spain and Portugal. Across nine LLMs and three seeds, Claude Sonnet 4 leads (61.7%), DeepSeek V3.2 offers the best cost-accuracy trade-off (57.9% at 11.3x lower cost), and strict all-checks scoring explains much of the apparent gap versus general-purpose GIS benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Before tool-using LLM agents are deployed in environmental and geospatial workflows, teams need evidence that an agent reliably selects the right operations against real APIs. Existing general-purpose GIS benchmarks report high accuracy (85-97%) but do not isolate the agent as the only variable, since tool layers, task suites, and scorers differ across evaluations.
AI.method: GNA fixes a sixteen-tool geospatial interface published as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so the agent under test is the only variable, scored against an identical tool layer, task suite, and deterministic scorer. Its flagship instance is a 103-task benchmark (93-task main suite across 18 categories plus a ten-task comparison expansion) evaluated against an open, self-hostable geospatial API serving three environmental indicators across Spain and Portugal. Nine LLMs are evaluated under three temperature-1.0 seeds, reporting capability and per-case cost as orthogonal axes.
AI.result: (1) Claude Sonnet 4 achieves the highest capability (61.7% +/- 0.7% on all 103 tasks; 60.8% on the main suite), followed closely by DeepSeek V3.2 (57.9%), while no other model exceeds 53%. (2) The cost-accuracy Pareto frontier is mostly open-weight, with DeepSeek V3.2 offering 93% of Claude's capability at 11.3x lower list-price cost. (3) Under strict all-checks scoring the best model sits 24-36 points below the 85-97% reported on general-purpose GIS benchmarks, whereas per-check partial credit for the top four models (86-90%) is comparable, so much of that gap reflects scoring strictness rather than task difficulty alone.
AI.conclusion: The MCP server, evaluation harness, benchmark, and API are publicly available, and swapping the tool executors and task suite instantiates an equivalent benchmark for any geospatial domain, enabling pre-production evaluation of tool-using LLM agents in environmental and geospatial workflows.

title: LACE-CRAFT: Robot Co-Design with Actor Inheritance and Blackboard Collaboration
comment: 16 pages including appendix. Project website: https://deemostech.github.io/lace-craft/
summary: Robot co-design couples morphology search with policy learning, yet training every new design from scratch discards acquired control experience. We present LACE-CRAFT, which compares continued learning on the current robot with policy adaptation to new morphology-reward pairs. LACE resumes the incumbent's full learning state and initializes compatible challengers with its actor parameters and observation statistics. A fixed task metric selects among both branches and the frozen incumbent. CRAFT coordinates Feedback, Morphology, Reward, and Integration roles through shared experimental records and behavioral replays to generate and cross-review paired proposals. A generative extension converts generated meshes into editable articulated models with configured joints, actuator interfaces, and consistently updated simulation assets. Across five locomotion benchmarks, mean scores over three evaluation seeds are 6.4-91.9% higher than D2C. Both methods train 30 new morphology-reward pairs over five rounds; LACE additionally uses four continuation training units. Five-task ablations examine policy inheritance and replay-derived feedback. A fabricated prototype demonstrates indoor walking and illustrates the geometry-to-hardware workflow.

AI.tldr: LACE-CRAFT is a robot co-design framework that avoids training each new design from scratch by combining continued learning (LACE) with morphology-reward policy adaptation, plus a multi-role coordination loop (CRAFT) and generative mesh-to-articulated-model conversion.
AI.motivation: Robot co-design couples morphology search with policy learning, but training every new design from scratch discards acquired control experience. This motivates reusing control knowledge across designs and organizing the search/adaptation process more systematically.
AI.method: LACE resumes the incumbent's full learning state and initializes compatible challengers with its actor parameters and observation statistics; a fixed task metric selects among the continued-learning branch, the adaptation branch, and the frozen incumbent. CRAFT coordinates Feedback, Morphology, Reward, and Integration roles via shared experimental records and behavioral replays to generate and cross-review paired proposals. A generative extension converts generated meshes into editable articulated models with configured joints, actuator interfaces, and consistently updated simulation assets.
AI.result: Across five locomotion benchmarks, mean scores over three evaluation seeds are 6.4-91.9% higher than D2C. Both methods train 30 new morphology-reward pairs over five rounds, with LACE additionally using four continuation training units. Five-task ablations examine policy inheritance and replay-derived feedback. A fabricated prototype achieves indoor walking.
AI.conclusion: Reusing the incumbent's learning state and adapting policies to new morphology-reward pairs, combined with structured multi-role coordination and mesh-to-articulated conversion, improves robot co-design performance and bridges simulation to a fabricated walking prototype.

title: From Uncertainty to Action: Learning to Steer LLM Agents
summary: Steering an LLM agent means deciding whether to correct it, at which step, and with which mechanism. Uncertainty is often used to decide when to correct an agent, but whether it can guide these decisions remains unclear. We steer agent trajectories separately at every non-terminal step with each of four mechanisms and run each continuation to completion. The resulting stepwise outcome table (SOT) holds about 82,000 counterfactual continuations of 1,864 trajectories from three benchmarks and two agents. It shows that uncertainty can identify failing trajectories, but that no single signal reliably locates the step at which steering helps. We therefore propose VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor, offline or online, that learns from SOT the value of steering at each step and decides where to steer by it. A harm-budgeted trigger decides whether to steer, limiting the fraction of successful trajectories that VoS disturbs. VoS improves on unmodified execution in all 12 settings of benchmark, agent, and offline or online use, by 7.8 points on average, and outperforms the strongest of five existing uncertainty-triggered methods in 11, by 2.9 points on average. Ablations show that training on measured outcomes and a tight harm budget are both essential.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a stepwise outcome table (SOT) of ~82,000 counterfactual continuations to show that uncertainty can flag failing trajectories but cannot locate the ideal steering step. It proposes VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor that learns the value of steering at each step and uses a harm-budgeted trigger to decide whether to steer, achieving consistent gains over baselines.
AI.motivation: Steering an LLM agent requires deciding whether to correct it, at which step, and with which mechanism. Uncertainty is commonly used to decide when to correct an agent, but whether it can actually guide these decisions remains unclear.
AI.method: The authors steer agent trajectories separately at every non-terminal step with each of four mechanisms and run each continuation to completion, producing a stepwise outcome table (SOT) of about 82,000 counterfactual continuations from 1,864 trajectories across three benchmarks and two agents. Based on this, they propose VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor—usable offline or online—that learns from SOT the value of steering at each step and decides where to steer by it. A harm-budgeted trigger decides whether to steer, limiting the fraction of successful trajectories that VoS disturbs.
AI.result: VoS outperforms unmodified execution in all 12 settings of benchmark, agent, and offline/online use, by 7.8 points on average, and beats the strongest of five existing uncertainty-triggered methods in 11 settings, by 2.9 points on average. Ablations show that training on measured outcomes and a tight harm budget are both essential.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty can identify failing trajectories but no single signal reliably locates the step at which steering helps. Learning the value of steering from measured counterfactual outcomes, combined with a harm-budgeted trigger, provides an effective and general approach to steering LLM agents, and both components are necessary for its success.

title: Co${}^{2}$Skill: Whole-Body Control via Skill Composition for Long-Horizon Human-Environment Interaction
summary: Achieving human-level dexterity in complex, unstructured environments requires the seamless integration of whole-body scene interaction and dexterous object manipulation skills. While existing physics-based controllers generate physically plausible behaviors in each domain, they largely address these two capabilities independently. In this paper, we present Co${}^{2}$Skill that integrates scene interaction and dexterous manipulation through a unified policy formulation. Built on a pretrained motion prior, the policy uses task and phase dependent observation masks to select information relevant to the current interaction goals. We introduce a goal-conditioned loco-manipulation curriculum that combines partial reference guidance for precision with exploration from varied initial states while allowing goal-directed execution beyond the demonstrated trajectories. We further introduce a cross-task curriculum that jointly trains individual skills and selected task sequences, preserving physical states across task boundaries and maintaining grasps during subsequent scene interactions. Together, these support sequential task execution and simultaneous scene interaction with object manipulation. We evaluate sitting, standing, climbing, stair traversal, and goal-directed manipulation, together with sequential execution and with random different conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate skill compositions in indoor environments, illustrating their integration within the same control formulation.

AI.tldr: Co²Skill presents a unified policy that integrates whole-body scene interaction with dexterous object manipulation, using a pretrained motion prior and task/phase-dependent observation masks.
AI.motivation: Human-level dexterity in unstructured environments requires combining whole-body scene interaction and dexterous manipulation, but existing physics-based controllers treat these capabilities independently.
AI.method: A unified policy formulation built on a pretrained motion prior, employing task- and phase-dependent observation masks to select goal-relevant information. It introduces a goal-conditioned loco-manipulation curriculum (partial reference guidance plus exploration from varied initial states, enabling execution beyond demonstrated trajectories) and a cross-task curriculum that jointly trains individual skills and selected task sequences, preserving physical states across task boundaries and maintaining grasps during subsequent interactions.
AI.result: Evaluated on sitting, standing, climbing, stair traversal, and goal-directed manipulation, plus sequential execution and randomized conditions; skill compositions demonstrated in indoor environments within the same control formulation.
AI.conclusion: Co²Skill unifies scene interaction and dexterous manipulation in a single control formulation, supporting sequential task execution and simultaneous scene interaction with object manipulation.  This content has not passed the compliance test and has been hidden.

title: Which Buildings Are Artificial Intelligence-Ready? A Measurement-Based Assessment Framework for AI Question Answering and Actuation
comment: 47 pages, 11 figures, 23 tables. Code, results and data supplement: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23197610
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are becoming the interface to buildings, answering questions and controlling operations, but a building's readiness for them has not been systematically assessed. This study proposes a framework to quantify it. First, a building's knowledge graph sets two ceilings. The answerable-readiness ceiling is the share of operational questions its data could answer, and the actuation-readiness ceiling is the share of control actions it exposes. Second, a reference AI agent's accuracy on a fixed set of these questions shows how much of the ceilings is realized. On a simulated office, the agent realizes 0.62 of a 0.64 answerable ceiling, so missing data, not the AI, limit readiness, except in naming a fault's cause. Across 37 public real-building graphs, the median answerable ceiling is 0.16, and in 15 of 45, unlinked sensors lower it. The framework turns "is this building AI-ready?" into an auditable, ranked retrofit question.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework quantifying building AI-readiness via two knowledge-graph ceilings (answerable and actuation) plus a reference agent's accuracy, revealing data—not AI—as the limiter.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI is becoming the interface for querying and controlling buildings, yet no systematic method exists to assess whether a building is ready to support such systems.
AI.method: A building's knowledge graph defines two readiness ceilings: the answerable-readiness ceiling (share of operational questions the data can answer) and the actuation-readiness ceiling (share of control actions exposed). A reference AI agent is then evaluated on a fixed question set to measure how much of the answerable ceiling is actually realized.
AI.result: On a simulated office, the agent achieves 0.62 of a 0.64 answerable ceiling, indicating missing data rather than AI capability limits readiness—except in naming a fault's cause. Across 37 public real-building graphs, the median answerable ceiling is 0.16, and unlinked sensors reduce it in 15 of 45 cases.
AI.conclusion: The framework reframes "is this building AI-ready?" as an auditable, ranked retrofit question, enabling prioritized data and integration improvements.

title: Adaptive Risk-Certified Event-Triggered Replanning for Dynamic Navigation
summary: Safe navigation in dynamic environments requires robots to plan under obstacle predictions whose errors are uncertain, non-stationary, and can induce rare but safety-critical failures. Existing control-barrier-function safety filters can reject immediately unsafe controls, but they provide little guidance on when the current finite-horizon planning mode itself is becoming unsafe as prediction uncertainty evolves. We propose Conformal Event-Triggered Risk-Certified Replanning (\emph{CERT-Replan}), a framework that uses calibrated barrier risk as an early-warning signal for replanning. CERT-Replan calibrates horizon-indexed obstacle-prediction residuals online and uses the resulting uncertainty radii to evaluate dynamic-obstacle safety margins. A one-step safety filter protects the next applied control, while a horizon-level risk monitor evaluates the upper-tail CVaR of predicted barrier-violation losses along the current MPC rollout. When this risk exceeds an allocated budget, CERT-Replan rejects the current planning mode and selects a lower-risk alternative, such as a different speed profile, corridor, or homotopy class, rather than repeatedly correcting the same nominal plan. In a non-stationary benchmark, CERT-Replan achieves an \(83.3\%\) collision reduction relative to the safety-filter-only baseline \textcolor{black}{and a \(77.8\%\) reduction relative to simple replanning triggers}, while reducing average safety-filter intervention by \(32.4\%\). \textcolor{black}{With Trajectron++, CERT-Replan achieves \(96\%\) collision-free operation. Hardware experiments and onboard runtime profiling demonstrate computational feasibility.}

AI.tldr: CERT-Replan uses calibrated conformal barrier risk as an early-warning trigger to replan in dynamic environments, switching planning modes when prediction uncertainty makes the current MPC rollout unsafe.
AI.motivation: Obstacle predictions in dynamic environments have uncertain, non-stationary errors that can cause rare but safety-critical failures. Existing control-barrier-function safety filters only reject immediately unsafe controls; they give little guidance on when the finite-horizon planning mode itself is becoming unsafe as prediction uncertainty evolves.
AI.method: CERT-Replan calibrates horizon-indexed obstacle-prediction residuals online and derives uncertainty radii to evaluate dynamic-obstacle safety margins. A one-step safety filter protects the next applied control, while a horizon-level risk monitor computes the upper-tail CVaR of predicted barrier-violation losses along the current MPC rollout. If this risk exceeds an allocated budget, the current planning mode is rejected and a lower-risk alternative (e.g., different speed profile, corridor, or homotopy class) is selected instead of repeatedly correcting the same nominal plan.
AI.result: In a non-stationary benchmark, CERT-Replan reduces collisions by 83.3% versus a safety-filter-only baseline and 77.8% versus simple replanning triggers, while cutting average safety-filter intervention by 32.4%. With Trajectron++ it achieves 96% collision-free operation. Hardware experiments and onboard runtime profiling confirm computational feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated barrier risk provides an effective early-warning signal for mode-level replanning, improving safety over filter-only and simple-trigger baselines while remaining computationally feasible on hardware.

title: CADFather: Autonomous CAD Reconstruction through Coordinated Tool Use
summary: Reconstructing an editable CAD model from a 3D shape remains a challenging engineering task. Existing methods can propose CAD operations, but no single source of proposals works equally well across different part geometries and stages of reconstruction. We introduce CADFather, an autonomous agentic system that coordinates complementary tools to recover parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes. A vision-language assistant inspects renders of the target and intermediate reconstructions, then decides which candidate CAD programs to extend, which tools to invoke, how many proposals to generate, and when to finish. Learned and algorithmic tools propose CAD operations, while numerical optimization refines the parameters of existing programs. Proposed or refined programs are executed and evaluated to provide feedback for subsequent decisions. The agent maintains alternative candidate programs for each target part and preserves the best valid result throughout reconstruction. CADFather uses pretrained generation and assistant models without additional training. We evaluate reconstruction quality and execution validity on the full DeepCAD, Fusion360, and MCB test sets, as well as on CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD. We additionally analyze computational cost and the trade-off between cost and reconstruction quality.

AI.tldr: CADFather is a training-free agentic system that coordinates complementary CAD-operation proposal tools and numerical optimization, using a vision-language assistant to steer decisions, to reconstruct editable parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing an editable CAD model from a 3D shape is a challenging engineering task. Existing methods can propose CAD operations, but no single source of proposals works equally well across different part geometries and reconstruction stages, motivating a system that combines multiple complementary tools adaptively.
AI.method: An autonomous agentic system coordinates complementary tools. A vision-language assistant inspects renders of the target and intermediate reconstructions, then decides which candidate CAD programs to extend, which tools to invoke, how many proposals to generate, and when to finish. Learned and algorithmic tools propose CAD operations; numerical optimization refines parameters of existing programs. Proposed or refined programs are executed and evaluated to provide feedback for subsequent decisions. The agent maintains alternative candidate programs per target part and preserves the best valid result. It uses pretrained generation and assistant models without additional training.
AI.result: Reconstruction quality and execution validity are evaluated on the full DeepCAD, Fusion360, and MCB test sets, as well as CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD. The paper additionally analyzes computational cost and the cost–quality trade-off.
AI.conclusion: CADFather recovers parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes by adaptively coordinating complementary proposal tools and optimization under vision-language guidance, without extra training, and is assessed on multiple standard benchmarks plus cost analyses.

title: Predicted Futures Are Not Enough: Learning Executable Goals for Robot Manipulation
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://claire0730.github.io/executable-goals/ Code and models: https://github.com/Claire0730/executable-goals
summary: Generative world models provide rich predictions of how manipulation scenes may evolve toward task objectives, yet those futures do not directly expose the compact task variables required by control. When training supervises future prediction alone, terminal goal accuracy is not an explicit learning objective, even when geometric recovery is available. We present Entity-Level Goal Readout, a learned prediction-to-execution interface that makes the executable terminal goal an explicit output of a 3D trace world model. It combines object-centric pose prediction with translation grounded in observed depth to produce a compact goal in SE(3). A shared Pose-Native Executor consumes this fixed goal with online object-pose feedback for closed-loop control without rerunning the world model. Across five manipulation tasks, the pipeline achieves a mean success rate of 79.69%. Goal diagnostics directly measure terminal goal accuracy, while controlled translation perturbations characterize how execution degrades under goal error. Zero-shot deployment on a Franka arm achieves 73.33% success on nominal StackCube, 66.67% with distractors, and 75.00% on PickPlate with a target unseen during policy training. These results support treating the prediction-to-execution interface as an explicit learned component of world-model planning rather than incidental post-processing in the control pipeline itself. Project page: https://claire0730.github.io/executable-goals/

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Entity-Level Goal Readout, a prediction-to-execution interface that turns 3D world-model futures into an explicit SE(3) terminal goal consumed by a Pose-Native Executor for closed-loop manipulation, achieving 79.69% mean success across five tasks and zero-shot Franka deployment.
AI.motivation: World models predict rich scene evolution but do not expose the compact task variables control needs; supervision on future prediction alone leaves terminal goal accuracy implicit, so the prediction-to-execution interface is treated as incidental post-processing rather than a learned component.
AI.method: Combines object-centric pose prediction with translation grounded in observed depth to produce a compact SE(3) goal from a 3D trace world model; a shared Pose-Native Executor consumes this fixed goal with online object-pose feedback for closed-loop control without rerunning the world model.
AI.result: Mean success rate of 79.69% across five manipulation tasks; goal diagnostics measure terminal goal accuracy and controlled translation perturbations characterize degradation under goal error; zero-shot Franka deployment yields 73.33% on nominal StackCube, 66.67% with distractors, and 75.00% on PickPlate with an unseen target.
AI.conclusion: The prediction-to-execution interface should be treated as an explicit learned component of world-model planning rather than incidental control post-processing.

title: Breaking the Space Barrier and its Application to Language Model Inference
summary: Language models are more and more often asked for structured output: JSON that follows a schema, or a tool call with typed arguments. A small machine, an automaton, enforces the format by forbidding the tokens that would break it. We observe that this machine has a rare property: from any of its states, each token leads along exactly one path. Graphs in which only a few paths join any two points are a classical object of complexity theory, and our theoretical result settles an open question about them: one can decide whether such a graph connects two points while verifying that it really has few paths, with very little memory. Precisely, the problem lies in the classes ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L and SC2, and needs only O(log2 n/ log log n) space, below the classical O(log2 n) of Savitch's theorem. The constructions behind the proofs become an inference engine: text the format forces is written without running the model, the mask is recomputed on the GPU without any table, recursive formats use a small stack, every output stays valid under a token limit, and independent fields are decoded in parallel and verified. On one 16 GB Apple M2 Pro with Qwen3.5-2B and 4B, against MLX with llguidance, the standard setup for this hardware, schema-constrained extraction finishes 1.2- 1.3x sooner with the same answers, a grammar costs 3 MB instead of up to 1.5 GB, one server holds sixteen grammars where tables run out of memory, and sixteen tool-calling agents finish 2.5x sooner.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the automaton that enforces structured output (e.g., schema-constrained JSON or typed tool calls) in language models, observing its "rare property" that from any state each token leads along exactly one path. It settles an open complexity-theoretic question about graphs with few paths between any two points, showing the connectivity problem is in ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L, and SC2, requiring only O(log²n/loglogn) space. These constructions yield a practical inference engine with table-free GPU masking, stack-based recursion, and parallel field decoding, delivering 1.2–1.3× faster schema-constrained extraction, 500× smaller grammar memory, and 2.5× faster multi-agent tool calling on Apple M2 Pro.
AI.motivation: Language models are increasingly required to produce structured output such as schema-conforming JSON or tool calls with typed arguments. A finite automaton enforces these formats by forbidding format-breaking tokens. The authors observe that this automaton has a rare structural property—from any state, each token leads along exactly one path—which connects to a classical complexity-theory object: graphs in which only a few paths join any two points. This motivates both settling an open theoretical question about such graphs and exploiting the structure to build a more efficient constrained-decoding engine.
AI.method: The authors analyze the automaton enforcing structured output as a graph with the property that each token moves deterministically to one successor per state. Theoretically, they prove that deciding whether such a "few paths" graph connects two points—while verifying the few-paths property—can be done with very little memory, placing the problem in ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L, and SC2, and requiring only O(log²n/loglogn) space, below Savitch's O(log²n). Practically, they turn these constructions into an inference engine: forced-format text is written without running the model, the token mask is recomputed on the GPU without any lookup table, recursive formats use a small explicit stack, outputs remain valid under a token limit, and independent fields are decoded in parallel and verified.
AI.result: The theoretical contribution settles an open question by showing the connectivity problem for few-paths graphs lies in ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L, and SC2, needing only O(log²n/loglogn) space—below the classical O(log²n) of Savitch's theorem. Empirically, on a single 16 GB Apple M2 Pro with Qwen3.5-2B and 4B, compared against MLX with llguidance (the standard setup for this hardware), schema-constrained extraction finishes 1.2–1.3× sooner with identical answers; a grammar consumes 3 MB instead of up to 1.5 GB; one server holds sixteen grammars where table-based approaches run out of memory; and sixteen tool-calling agents finish 2.5× sooner.
AI.conclusion: The automaton enforcing structured output possesses a rare structural property—single-path token transitions—that links it to a classical complexity-theoretic graph class. Settling an open question about that class yields both a new space bound (O(log²n/loglogn), below Savitch's theorem) and a practical inference engine. The engine eliminates large grammar tables, supports recursion and parallel field decoding, and delivers substantial speed and memory improvements on commodity hardware, demonstrating that complexity-theoretic insight can directly translate into efficient constrained decoding.

title: ClimbLab: MATLAB Simulation Platform for Legged Climbing Robotics
comment: Author's version of a manuscript in the proceedings of CLAWAR 2021. The final published version is available at: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-86294-7_20
summary: This paper presents an open-sourced MATLAB simulation and analysis platform dedicated to legged climbing robots. This simulator enables the design of any limbed robotic system as an articulated multi-body with a floating base and simulates it walking and climbing in an arbitrary environment. The main variable environmental parameters are inclination, gravity, and ground stiffness, and any point cloud can be installed as the terrain map. Furthermore, the simulator employs a rigid body dynamics engine. This paper first describes the simulator structure, and the computational flow and next presents the representative simulation examples where quadrupedal robots assumed gripping on the wall or climbing on the steep slope.

AI.tldr: An open-source MATLAB simulation and analysis platform for legged climbing robots, modeling them as floating-base articulated multi-body systems with a rigid-body dynamics engine, configurable environment parameters, and point-cloud terrain support.
AI.motivation: Legged climbing robots require a dedicated simulation environment to design and analyze limbed systems that walk and climb in arbitrary environments, which general-purpose tools may not directly support.
AI.method: The platform models any limbed robotic system as an articulated multi-body with a floating base and simulates walking/climbing via a rigid body dynamics engine. Environmental variables include inclination, gravity, and ground stiffness; arbitrary point clouds can be installed as terrain maps. The paper describes the simulator structure, computational flow, and representative examples.
AI.result: Representative simulations show quadrupedal robots gripping a wall and climbing a steep slope.
AI.conclusion: The simulator provides a flexible, open-source MATLAB tool for designing and analyzing legged climbing robots across varied environments.

title: Finding Blind Spots in AppWorld and WorkArena Task Verifiers
comment: 14 pages. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop "Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development". OpenReview paper and supplement: https://openreview.net/forum?id=uR6EWsGE48
summary:
Execution-based task verifiers decide whether an agent succeeded. We audit shipped AppWorld and WorkArena verifiers with source-informed mutation tests. The main audit never modifies a shipped checker.
  In AppWorld, duplicating a non-idempotent write creates an extra record while preserving every checked field value. The verifier accepts all three task variants from two of five eligible generators: 6/15 constructed effects. A cardinality patch applied to checker copies after the census makes all six cells fail while preserving valid controls.
  In WorkArena, we prospectively rerun 23 extra-field candidates selected for earlier checker-PASS outcomes. Independent Table API readback confirms nondefault persisted values in 21, while all 23 receive PASS. Two requested strings are aliases of stored defaults. The 21 confirmed wrong effects span three form templates. These selected cases confirm wrong effects under the audit's protocol; they do not estimate a population rate.
  No other construction produces an independently confirmed false accept. Other checker-PASS cases are effect-correct degeneracies. We report zero-PASS families separately because retained evidence differs. In fixed intent-swap grids, the checkers return no PASS on 2,689 off-diagonal executions. This is a rejection census: 57 WorkArena cells use session-scoped evidence; the other 2,632 lack classified rejection causes and independent target ground truth.
  Each increment is specified before its own cells are scored. A supplement accompanies the OpenReview submission with the construction grammar, evidence, content-bound stage lineage and count reproducer.

AI.tldr: A source-informed mutation audit of shipped AppWorld and WorkArena execution-based verifiers finds independently confirmed false accepts when non-idempotent writes or extra-field effects are introduced, while a large intent-swap grid yields only rejections lacking classified causes.
AI.motivation: Execution-based task verifiers are trusted to decide agent success, so their soundness matters; this work audits shipped verifiers to test whether checkers accept effects that differ from the intended task outcome.
AI.method: Source-informed mutation testing of shipped AppWorld and WorkArena verifiers without modifying the original checkers: in AppWorld, duplicate a non-idempotent write to create an extra record while preserving checked fields, then apply a cardinality patch to checker copies after the census; in WorkArena, prospectively rerun 23 extra-field candidates previously marked PASS, with independent Table API readback; also run fixed intent-swap grids and report zero-PASS families separately. Each increment is pre-specified before scoring, with a supplement providing the construction grammar, evidence, content-bound stage lineage and count reproducer.
AI.result: AppWorld: the verifier accepts all three task variants from two of five eligible generators, producing 6/15 constructed effects; the cardinality patch makes all six cells fail while valid controls are preserved. WorkArena: 21 of 23 candidate extra-field effects are independently confirmed as nondefault persisted values, yet all 23 receive PASS; two requested strings are aliases of stored defaults; the 21 confirmed wrong effects span three form templates, though these selected cases do not estimate a population rate. In fixed intent-swap grids, checkers return no PASS on 2,689 off-diagonal executions; 57 WorkArena cells use session-scoped evidence and the other 2,632 lack classified rejection causes and independent target ground truth. No other construction produces an independently confirmed false accept; remaining checker-PASS cases are effect-correct degeneracies.
AI.conclusion: Shipped AppWorld and WorkArena verifiers exhibit concrete, independently confirmed false accepts under extra-effect mutations, indicating that checker PASS does not always entail the intended effect; the rejection census is limited by unclassified causes and missing independent ground truth, and the reported selected cases should not be read as population rates. The supplement supports reproducibility via construction grammar, evidence, content-bound stage lineage and count reproducer.

title: MCFR: A Mask-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Regression Framework for Robust Multi-Variant Board-to-Board Connector Assembly
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026). Finalist for the IROS Best Paper Award for Industrial Robotics Research for Applications
summary: Automated insertion of board-to-board (BTB) connectors in 3C manufacturing requires both high visual accuracy and strong deployment robustness. This problem remains challenging because multi-variant connectors exhibit significant morphological and appearance variations, making stable cross-variant generalization difficult, while the mismatch between training and deployment under fixed-view inspection settings induces background spurious correlation and degrades real-world performance. To address these issues, this paper proposes MCFR, a Mask-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Regression framework for multi-variant BTB connector assembly. By introducing an object-aware mask prior and explicit photometric refinement, the proposed method suppresses background interference and improves alignment accuracy and robustness in practical deployment. Experiments on a self-constructed multi-variant dataset, a BTB batch insertion testbed, and a real smartphone assembly task show that MCFR consistently outperforms representative baselines and achieves an average real-world insertion success rate of 99.25%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and practical potential of MCFR for automated assembly of multi-variant BTB connectors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MCFR, a Mask-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Regression framework for automated Board-to-Board (BTB) connector insertion in 3C manufacturing. It introduces an object-aware mask prior and explicit photometric refinement to suppress background interference, achieving 99.25% average real-world insertion success rate across a self-built multi-variant dataset, a BTB batch insertion testbed, and a real smartphone assembly task.
AI.motivation: Automated BTB connector insertion requires high visual accuracy and deployment robustness, but faces two key challenges: (1) multi-variant connectors exhibit significant morphological and appearance variations, making stable cross-variant generalization difficult; and (2) the mismatch between training and deployment under fixed-view inspection settings induces background spurious correlation, degrading real-world performance.
AI.method: The authors propose MCFR, a Mask-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Regression framework. It introduces an object-aware mask prior to suppress background interference, combined with explicit photometric refinement to improve alignment accuracy and robustness. The pipeline performs coarse-to-fine regression guided by the mask prior.
AI.result: Experiments on a self-constructed multi-variant dataset, a BTB batch insertion testbed, and a real smartphone assembly task show that MCFR consistently outperforms representative baselines and achieves an average real-world insertion success rate of 99.25%.
AI.conclusion: MCFR effectively addresses cross-variant generalization and background spurious correlation in BTB connector assembly, demonstrating strong effectiveness and practical potential for automated multi-variant BTB connector insertion in 3C manufacturing.

title: DIVA: Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically feed dense visual patch tokens into a language-action backbone, preserving scene context but offering no explicit mechanism to regulate how strongly different visual tokens influence policy computation. We introduce DIVA, a Dual-Space Intent-Aware Visual Attenuation module with an anchor-then-attenuate design. DIVA combines high-level task intent with low-level visual evidence to estimate patch-wise relevance anchors, then applies them in two complementary spaces: it reweights projected visual tokens before backbone entry and persistently attenuates low-relevance visual states within the backbone. DIVA preserves the full visual token sequence and requires no external grounding supervision. On LIBERO, DIVA improves OpenVLA-OFT from 96.6% to 98.0% average success and raises its zero-shot LIBERO-Plus score from 69.6 to 72.6. Real-world experiments further show consistent gains under task-irrelevant visual perturbations, supporting the robustness of intent-aware visual attenuation beyond simulation.

AI.tldr: DIVA is a dual-space, intent-aware visual attenuation module for VLA policies that anchors patch-wise relevance from task intent and visual evidence, then attenuates low-relevance visual tokens without discarding them, improving LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus success rates and real-world robustness.
AI.motivation: VLA policies feed dense visual patch tokens into a language-action backbone, retaining scene context but lacking an explicit mechanism to control how strongly individual visual tokens influence policy computation.
AI.method: DIVA uses an anchor-then-attenuate design. It estimates patch-wise relevance anchors by combining high-level task intent with low-level visual evidence, then applies them in two spaces: reweighting projected visual tokens before backbone entry and persistently attenuating low-relevance visual states inside the backbone. It preserves the full token sequence and needs no external grounding supervision.
AI.result: On LIBERO, DIVA raises OpenVLA-OFT from 96.6% to 98.0% average success and improves its zero-shot LIBERO-Plus score from 69.6 to 72.6. Real-world experiments show consistent gains under task-irrelevant visual perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Intent-aware visual attenuation across input and backbone spaces improves both simulated and real-world VLA policy success and robustness without discarding visual tokens or requiring grounding supervision.

title: Learning Unknown Constraints without Unsafe Data via Optimality and Counterfactual Regularization
summary: Learning from demonstrations (LfD) provides a framework for inferring unknown constraints from locally optimal, constraint-satisfying expert behavior. Existing approaches largely fall into two paradigms, constrained inverse optimal control (CIOC) and inverse constrained reinforcement learning (ICRL). CIOC exploits optimality conditions such as the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) conditions but typically assumes known dynamics and structured constraint representations. Meanwhile, ICRL accommodates complex unknown constraints and unknown transition dynamics but often requires extensive online exploration, during which unsafe constraint violations may occur. In this work, we introduce Counterfactual KKT (CF-KKT), a constraint learning framework that leverages learned dynamics and locally optimal demonstrations to recover unknown constraints without requiring known dynamics or additional risky exploration, thereby combining the data efficiency and safety advantages of CIOC with the flexibility of ICRL. First, we use a locally learned differentiable dynamics model to impose KKT-inspired optimality conditions directly on the demonstrations. Second, we use the learned dynamics to generate reward-improving counterfactual behaviors near the demonstrations, revealing behaviors that would be preferable in the absence of the unknown constraint and thus providing synthetic infeasible data. When the constraint parameterization is known, the same learned-dynamics framework enables direct CIOC-based parameter recovery, and we characterize its sensitivity to dynamics misspecification. Across high-dimensional robotic control tasks, our approach learns neural constraint representations with improved safety and data efficiency relative to state-of-the-art offline ICRL baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Counterfactual KKT (CF-KKT), a constraint learning framework that combines learned dynamics with locally optimal demonstrations to recover unknown constraints offline, without requiring known dynamics or risky exploration.
AI.motivation: Existing constraint-learning methods split into two paradigms: CIOC, which uses optimality conditions like KKT but assumes known dynamics and structured constraints, and ICRL, which handles complex unknown constraints and dynamics but needs extensive online exploration that risks unsafe constraint violations. A method combining the data efficiency and safety of CIOC with the flexibility of ICRL is needed.
AI.method: CF-KKT first learns a locally differentiable dynamics model and imposes KKT-inspired optimality conditions directly on the demonstrations. It then uses the learned dynamics to generate reward-improving counterfactual behaviors near the demonstrations, producing synthetic infeasible data that reveal behaviors preferable in the absence of the unknown constraint. For known constraint parameterization, the same framework enables direct CIOC-based parameter recovery, with characterization of sensitivity to dynamics misspecification.
AI.result: Across high-dimensional robotic control tasks, the approach learns neural constraint representations with improved safety and data efficiency relative to state-of-the-art offline ICRL baselines.
AI.conclusion: CF-KKT recovers unknown constraints from learned dynamics and locally optimal demonstrations without known dynamics or risky exploration, combining the data efficiency and safety of CIOC with the flexibility of ICRL, and outperforms offline ICRL baselines in safety and data efficiency.

title: Frozen Models, Evolving Expertise: Model-Agnostic Learning from Deployment Experience for Multimodal Medical AI
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) are usually frozen after deployment, so they do not learn from the cases they solve. This is especially concerning in medicine, where new clinical evidence, updated guidelines, and new therapies can change established practice. Fine-tuning can update the model, but it requires access to model weights and additional training. Parameter-free methods avoid training, but they may overfit a fixed validation set, lack reliable domain knowledge, or lose visual details by saving experience only as text. To address these limitations, we present a model-agnostic framework that allows frozen LLMs and VLMs to learn from deployment experience through three forms of external expertise: a Skill that guides reasoning and tool use, a Knowledge Memory that stores reliable facts supported by earlier cases or trusted external evidence, and a Multimodal Knowledge Base that keeps visual examples and guides the model to relate each retrieved case to the current image. Instead of relying on a fixed validation set, a validation strategy keeps an update only if it helps on new cases without degrading performance on earlier ones. Across six benchmarks covering clinical diagnosis, clinical workflows, medical reasoning, and medical and non-medical visual reasoning, and with four open-weight and closed-source base models, our framework improves performance during online deployment by up to 34.2% over the base model on medical tasks, generalizes to unseen cases, transfers to other models without further optimization, and works in non-medical domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-agnostic, parameter-free framework that lets frozen LLMs/VLMs learn from deployment experience via three external expertise forms—a Skill, a Knowledge Memory, and a Multimodal Knowledge Base—validated only when updates help on new cases without degrading earlier ones, improving medical task performance by up to 34.2%.
AI.motivation: LLMs and VLMs are frozen after deployment and cannot learn from cases they solve, which is problematic in medicine where new evidence, guidelines, and therapies shift practice. Fine-tuning requires weight access and retraining, while parameter-free methods tend to overfit a fixed validation set, lack reliable domain knowledge, or lose visual detail by storing experience only as text.
AI.method: A model-agnostic framework enabling frozen LLMs/VLMs to learn from deployment experience through three forms of external expertise: a Skill guiding reasoning and tool use, a Knowledge Memory storing reliable facts backed by earlier cases or trusted external evidence, and a Multimodal Knowledge Base retaining visual examples and guiding the model to relate retrieved cases to the current image. A validation strategy accepts an update only if it helps on new cases without degrading performance on earlier ones.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks (clinical diagnosis, clinical workflows, medical reasoning, medical and non-medical visual reasoning) and four open-weight and closed-source base models, the framework improves online deployment performance by up to 34.2% over the base model on medical tasks, generalizes to unseen cases, transfers to other models without further optimization, and works in non-medical domains.
AI.conclusion: Frozen LLMs and VLMs can effectively learn from deployment experience without parameter updates, achieving substantial medical performance gains, generalization, cross-model transferability, and applicability beyond medicine.

title: COOL: Curiosity-Driven Object Ownership Learning for Personalized Robotic Assistance
summary: Robots are increasingly expected to provide personalized services in everyday environments. To do so, they must ground natural-language commands such as "Where is my backpack?" or "Find my bottle" and execute them by reasoning about object instances, people, locations, and ownership. This is challenging because ownership is rarely labeled explicitly and must be inferred from long-term, behavioral evidence of human-object interactions. To address this, we present COOL, a novel robotic framework for autonomously learning object ownership from everyday observations and maintaining a long-term spatial memory of its environment. To keep its memory current, COOL uses an agent-based curiosity-driven data collection strategy that guides the robot toward the most promising locations to gain information and refresh stale observations. Offline experiments, ablation studies, and real-world evaluations show that COOL can infer ownership relations from real-world interactions and use this knowledge for ownership-conditioned navigation and task execution.

AI.tldr: COOL is a robotic framework that autonomously learns object ownership from everyday human-object interaction observations and maintains a long-term spatial memory, using curiosity-driven, agent-based data collection to keep memory current, enabling ownership-conditioned navigation and task execution.
AI.motivation: Robots are increasingly expected to provide personalized services and must ground natural-language commands like "Where is my backpack?" or "Find my bottle" by reasoning about object instances, people, locations, and ownership. This is difficult because ownership is rarely labeled explicitly and must be inferred from long-term behavioral evidence of human-object interactions.
AI.method: COOL autonomously learns object ownership from everyday observations and maintains a long-term spatial memory of the environment. To keep memory current, it employs an agent-based curiosity-driven data collection strategy that guides the robot toward the most promising locations to gain information and refresh stale observations.
AI.result: Offline experiments, ablation studies, and real-world evaluations demonstrate that COOL can infer ownership relations from real-world interactions and leverage this knowledge for ownership-conditioned navigation and task execution.
AI.conclusion: COOL successfully addresses ownership inference and long-term spatial memory for personalized robotic services, validating that inferred ownership relations support ownership-conditioned navigation and task execution in real-world settings.

title: SpecGuard: Proving a Task Is Broken Before the Agent Cheats
summary: As autonomous coding agents get increasingly deployed, the risk that accidental or adversarially injected misspecifications in tasks lead to dangerous agent behavior is critical to address. Prior work has shown that agents given such tasks rarely flag the conflict and instead cheat, editing tests or hard-coding expected outputs, and the actions taken to cheat can cause real damage, such as deleting a security defense to make a corrupted test pass. It remains unclear whether such conflicts can be established with independently verifiable evidence before the agent acts. We present SpecGuard, which detects and formally certifies these conflicts between task intent and tests. Given only the task description and codebase, SpecGuard autoformalizes the intended behaviour into a Lean 4 specification. The tests are formalized independently, and the Lean kernel checks whether any implementation could satisfy both formalizations, producing a machine-checked certificate when none can. On conflicted SWE-bench tasks, SpecGuard detects up to 72.8% of conflicts and formally certifies up to 51.1%, with a nearly five-fold lower conflict miss rate than model-based judgment. SpecGuard provides a pre-execution safety check that identifies reward-hacking opportunities through formal certification of task-level conflicts, before any agent behavior is observed. Our code is available at https://github.com/prmbiy/specguard.

AI.tldr: SpecGuard detects and formally certifies conflicts between task intent and tests in coding agent tasks by autoformalizing both into Lean 4 specifications and machine-checking whether any implementation could satisfy both, providing a pre-execution safety check against reward hacking.
AI.motivation: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly deployed, and accidental or adversarially injected misspecifications in tasks can lead agents to cheat (editing tests, hard-coding outputs) rather than flagging conflicts, causing real damage such as deleting security defenses. It was previously unclear whether such conflicts could be established with independently verifiable evidence before the agent acts.
