AI.method: Given only the task description and codebase, SpecGuard autoformalizes the intended behavior into a Lean 4 specification, formalizes the tests independently, and uses the Lean kernel to check whether any implementation could satisfy both formalizations, producing a machine-checked certificate when none can.
AI.result: On conflicted SWE-bench tasks, SpecGuard detects up to 72.8% of conflicts and formally certifies up to 51.1%, with a nearly five-fold lower conflict miss rate than model-based judgment.
AI.conclusion: SpecGuard provides a pre-execution safety check that identifies reward-hacking opportunities through formal certification of task-level conflicts, before any agent behavior is observed.

title: Immiscible Diffusion Policy: Preserving Multimodal Robot Actions through Label-Free Noise Assignment
summary: When diffusion policies were first introduced, they were expected to recover multi-modal action distributions. However, we find this expectation does not always hold, as diffusion policies often collapse to a single modality even when we guarantee the balance of dataset modalities and exact within-batch symmetry. Our analysis indicates that independent action-noise pairing contributes to this failure by increasing mixing and crossing among diffusion paths, which can produce averaged denoising responses and suppress modality-specific behavior. This issue is especially severe in robot planning, where action spaces are dense and low-dimensional, significantly increasing such mixing and crossing. To alleviate this problem, we propose Immiscible Diffusion Policy, a label-free training-time add-on to diffusion policy that uses action-noise assignment to preserve relatively distinct noise-to-action routes without modifying the policy architecture or inference procedure. Across five simulated and two real-world humanoid manipulation tasks spanning state, RGB, and point-cloud observations, our method significantly improves the policy's preservation of action modalities while maintaining strong task performance. It increases the proportion of the non-dominant modality by 6.0x-14.6x across three two-modality tasks and recovers demonstrated modalities that are entirely absent from vanilla policy rollouts on both four-modality tasks. These results demonstrate that Immiscible Diffusion Policy provides a simple yet robust approach to preserving action multi-modality in general robot learning tasks.

AI.tldr: Diffusion policies often collapse to a single action modality despite balanced datasets. The authors trace this to independent action-noise pairing causing path mixing/crossing and averaged denoising, then propose Immiscible Diffusion Policy, a label-free training-time add-on that assigns noise to preserve distinct noise-to-action routes, boosting modality preservation across simulated and real tasks.
AI.motivation: Diffusion policies were expected to recover multi-modal action distributions, but in practice they frequently collapse to a single modality even with balanced dataset modalities and exact within-batch symmetry. The paper aims to diagnose this failure and preserve action multi-modality, which is especially problematic in robot planning where dense, low-dimensional action spaces exacerbate the issue.
AI.method: The analysis identifies independent action-noise pairing as a cause: it increases mixing and crossing among diffusion paths, producing averaged denoising responses that suppress modality-specific behavior. To address this, the authors propose Immiscible Diffusion Policy, a label-free, training-time add-on that uses action-noise assignment to preserve relatively distinct noise-to-action routes, without modifying the policy architecture or inference procedure.
AI.result: Evaluated on five simulated and two real-world humanoid manipulation tasks with state, RGB, and point-cloud observations, the method significantly improves preservation of action modalities while maintaining strong task performance. It increases the non-dominant modality proportion by 6.0x-14.6x on three two-modality tasks and recovers demonstrated modalities entirely absent from vanilla policy rollouts on both four-modality tasks.
AI.conclusion: Immiscible Diffusion Policy offers a simple yet robust approach to preserving action multi-modality in general robot learning tasks, mitigating modality collapse caused by independent noise pairing without architectural or inference changes.

title: Training Language Models To Be Coherent Decision-Makers
summary: Reliable decision-making requires more than accurate prediction: a model must preserve its beliefs, apply the relevant utilities, and recognize when the information needed to justify an action is missing. We study whether language models can learn this decision procedure from supervised fine-tuning and generalize it across domains and differing natural-language expressions of the decision challenge. Across 20 datasets, we explore challenges of belief instability and decision-making errors by first eliciting probabilities of outcomes and then varying only the utilities and the framing of the decision problems, while holding the evidence fixed. We train models to preserve elicited beliefs while selecting the action that maximizes expected utility, and evaluate transfer to unseen application domains, held-out framings, and different classes of payoff structures. We further introduce incomplete-information settings in which required utilities are withheld and replaced with irrelevant text, testing whether models can distinguish missing decision-relevant information from merely additional context. We find that targeted fine-tuning substantially improves coherent decision-making and that in many situations, learning transfers across domains and framings to situations unobserved during training. Further, models trained for decidability learn to identify when action cannot be justified based on missing information. Finally, we show the value of a routed system that considers separately the recognition of decision completeness and utility-sensitive decision execution.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether language models can learn a reliable decision procedure—preserving elicited beliefs, applying utilities, and detecting missing information—via supervised fine-tuning, and whether this generalizes across domains, framings, and payoff structures.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction alone is insufficient for reliable decision-making; a model must also preserve its beliefs, apply relevant utilities, and recognize when information needed to justify an action is missing. The work asks whether language models can learn this full decision procedure from supervised fine-tuning and generalize it across domains and natural-language framings.
AI.method: Across 20 datasets, the authors isolate belief instability and decision errors by first eliciting outcome probabilities and then varying only utilities and decision framing while holding evidence fixed. Models are trained to preserve elicited beliefs while selecting the expected-utility-maximizing action, and evaluated on transfer to unseen domains, held-out framings, and different payoff structures. They introduce incomplete-information settings where required utilities are withheld and replaced with irrelevant text, testing whether models distinguish missing decision-relevant information from mere additional context.
AI.result: Targeted fine-tuning substantially improves coherent decision-making, and in many situations learning transfers across domains and framings to situations unobserved during training. Models trained for decidability learn to identify when an action cannot be justified due to missing information. A routed system that separately handles recognition of decision completeness and utility-sensitive decision execution proves valuable.
AI.conclusion: Language models can acquire a generalizable decision procedure through targeted supervised fine-tuning, including belief preservation, utility-sensitive action selection, and recognition of decision incompleteness—and decomposing these into a routed system yields further benefits.

title: IVG-UAV: An Intelligent Voice-Guided UAV System for Autonomous Ripe Fruit Harvesting with Vision-Based Classification and Adaptive Path Planning
summary: In tropical regions, their agricultural sectors remain highly dependent on manual labor for fruit harvesting. On large-scale farms, this dependency often results in significant labor cost and logistic complexities. This project presents the development and simulation of a voice-controlled Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) system designed to automate harvesting tasks in extensive plantations. The proposed system integrates speech recognition using Whisper [1] and LLM, computer vision-based ripeness classification, and adaptive path planning within a unified framework. The entire system is modeled and validated in a Gazebo simulation environment, allowing performance evaluation under controlled agricultural scenarios

AI.tldr: A voice-controlled UAV system integrating Whisper speech recognition, an LLM, computer vision ripeness classification, and adaptive path planning is developed and validated in Gazebo to automate fruit harvesting in large tropical plantations.
AI.motivation: Tropical agriculture's fruit harvesting is highly manual, causing substantial labor costs and logistical complexity on large-scale farms. Automation is needed to address this dependency.
AI.method: The system unifies Whisper-based speech recognition with an LLM, computer vision-based ripeness classification, and adaptive path planning into a single framework. It is modeled and validated in a Gazebo simulation environment under controlled agricultural scenarios.
AI.result: The system's performance is evaluated through Gazebo simulation under controlled agricultural scenarios, enabling assessment of the integrated voice, vision, and planning components.
AI.conclusion: The proposed voice-controlled UAV framework offers a simulated, validated approach to automating harvesting in extensive plantations, targeting reduced labor cost and logistical complexity, with real-world deployment as a future direction.

title: From Probabilities to Decisions: Search and Multi-Teacher Distillation with Jev
summary: Probability-only models, which TypeSafe calls System One models, return calibrated probabilities for fixed choices in milliseconds and generate no text. We study one such model, Jev, through two tasks that require decisions under tight constraints. In bullet chess, a bot that places Jev's judgment inside Stockfish search alongside an opening book and endgame tablebases climbs above a 2200 Lichess bullet rating against other bots. Live model calls are too slow for search, so we distill pairwise judgments into a compact evaluator that runs at every position. We then ask how best to spend a fixed labeling budget when an LLM, Qwen3-32B, is available as a second teacher. In chess, averaging both judges' labels beats spending the whole budget on Qwen alone by 9.6 Elo (95% interval 4.3 to 14.9), and the gain replicates on fresh openings; a second answer from the same judge is no substitute, and Jev is the strongest partner for Qwen among the models tested. In passage reranking, Jev's labels alone train a reranker that scores as high as Qwen's, from 21 minutes of API calls instead of 5.1 GPU-hours, and adding Qwen gains at most a few thousandths in ranking quality. Search supplies the lookahead, distillation makes the judgment cheap enough to use at every position, and an LLM partner pays off in chess.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Jev, a probability-only ("System One") model, and shows that distillation plus search turns its millisecond pairwise judgments into a competitive bullet-chess bot and an efficient passage reranker; a labeling budget split with an LLM teacher (Qwen3-32B) yields gains in chess but little in reranking.
AI.motivation: Probability-only models return calibrated probabilities for fixed choices in milliseconds and generate no text, making them attractive for repeated decisions under tight constraints. The authors want to know whether such a model can be harnessed for high-performance tasks (chess play, passage reranking) and how to allocate a fixed labeling budget when a generative LLM teacher is also available.
AI.method: Two constraint-heavy decision tasks. In bullet chess, Jev's judgment is embedded inside Stockfish search together with an opening book and endgame tablebases; because live model calls are too slow for search, pairwise judgments are distilled into a compact per-position evaluator. A fixed labeling budget is then compared between Jev, Qwen3-32B, and combinations (including a second answer from the same judge) across fresh openings. In passage reranking, Jev labels alone are used to train a reranker and compared against Qwen-trained rerankers in quality, API time, and GPU cost.
AI.result: The distilled Jev-in-search bot exceeds a 2200 Lichess bullet rating against other bots. Averaging both judges' labels beats spending the full budget on Qwen alone by 9.6 Elo (95% interval 4.3–14.9), replicating on fresh openings; a self-second answer is no substitute and Jev is the strongest Qwen partner among tested models. In reranking, Jev's labels alone match Qwen's reranker quality using 21 minutes of API calls versus 5.1 GPU-hours, with Qwen adding at most a few thousandths in ranking quality.
AI.conclusion: Search supplies lookahead, distillation makes the model's judgment cheap enough to apply at every position, and pairing the probability-only judge with an LLM teacher pays off in chess while offering little benefit in passage reranking.

title: TempoBridge: Language-Guided Tempo Control for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are effective at understanding what task to perform, but provide limited control over how it should be executed, such as moving quickly or slowly. We introduce TempoBridge, a lightweight framework that uses frozen VLA representations to modulate actions according to tempo cues in the instruction at each task phase, without additional tempo-conditioned robot demonstrations or tempo-specific base-policy fine-tuning. TempoBridge extracts tempo cues from contextual VLM representations, aligns them with task progress through a causal phase router, and modulates nominal motion commands during execution. Across LIBERO tasks, TempoBridge improves Tempo Success Rate from 52.6% to 89.7% under canonical tempo instructions while retaining high task success. It also preserves near-baseline performance when no tempo cue is present and generalizes to unseen tempo expressions without additional training. Experiments on a physical robot further demonstrate language-conditioned tempo modulation in real-world manipulation.

AI.tldr: TempoBridge is a lightweight, training-free framework that steers frozen VLA robots to execute tasks at instructed speeds ("quickly" or "slowly") via tempo cues extracted from VLM representations and applied to motion commands.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action models understand what to do but offer limited control over how to execute it (e.g., fast vs. slow), and achieving such tempo control typically requires tempo-conditioned demonstrations or fine-tuning of the base policy.
AI.method: TempoBridge uses frozen VLA representations, extracts tempo cues from contextual VLM representations, aligns them with task progress using a causal phase router, and modulates nominal motion commands during execution—without extra tempo-conditioned demonstrations or tempo-specific base-policy fine-tuning.
AI.result: On LIBERO tasks, Tempo Success Rate rises from 52.6% to 89.7% under canonical tempo instructions while maintaining high task success; performance stays near baseline without tempo cues, and it generalizes to unseen tempo expressions without training. Physical-robot experiments confirm real-world language-conditioned tempo modulation.
AI.conclusion: Tempo cues can be effectively decoupled from task semantics and injected post hoc into frozen VLA policies, enabling controllable execution tempo in both simulation and real-world manipulation.

title: Bookkeeping, Composition, or Unreachable Gold? Reading MemoryAgentBench's Conflict-Resolution Scores Against a Frozen Last-Write Resolver
comment: Accepted at the IAB Workshop (Interpreting Agent Behavior) at NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). 19 pages
summary: MemoryAgentBench's Conflict Resolution split is read as measuring "selective forgetting". We execute the benchmark's own rule - the newest statement about a fact wins - as a zero-learning resolver frozen on one of the four fact lists. Under the official metric the rule answers 80.25% of the questions (74.5% on the three held-out lists). Of the rest, 67 items have a released gold that the last-write graph cannot reach but overwritten statements would ("The capital of India is New Delhi." superseded by "The capital of India is Grosseto."; gold New Delhi); such items are a third of the multi-hop questions at 262K. Two long-context models and our pre-registered approximate re-implementation of the benchmark's BM25 agent, one retained run per item and outcomes only, score 84.7%, 82.6% and 41.6% on the items the rule solves against 10.4%, 11.9% and 6.0% on those 67. The failures are a reachability split plus a small parser-scope residual; the per-item split, not the aggregate, is the unit at which a score here can be read.

AI.tldr: MemoryAgentBench's Conflict Resolution split, though read as measuring "selective forgetting," is largely solved by the benchmark's own zero-learning newest-statement-wins rule (80.25% official, 74.5% on held-out lists); the residual failures concentrate on 67 "unreachable gold" items where the overwritten statement is correct, and this per-item reachability split—not the aggregate score—is the correct unit of interpretation.
AI.motivation: The paper questions the construct validity of MemoryAgentBench's Conflict Resolution split as a measure of "selective forgetting." It hypothesizes that the split may be trivially passable by the benchmark's own conflict-resolution rule without any learning or memory mechanism, which would undermine the benchmark's intended interpretation.
AI.method: The authors implement the benchmark's stated rule—the newest statement about a fact wins—as a zero-learning resolver frozen on one of the four fact lists. They evaluate it under the official metric. They then isolate the residual failures and characterize a subset of 67 items whose released gold is unreachable by the last-write graph but reachable via the overwritten (superseded) statements. They compare two long-context models and a pre-registered approximate re-implementation of the benchmark's BM25 agent, using one retained run per item with outcomes only.
AI.result: The zero-learning rule scores 80.25% under the official metric (74.5% on the three held-out lists). The 67 "unreachable gold" items constitute a third of the multi-hop questions at 262K. The two long-context models and the BM25-agent re-implementation score 84.7%, 82.6%, and 41.6% on rule-solvable items, versus 10.4%, 11.9%, and 6.0% on the 67 unreachable items. Failures decompose into a reachability split plus a small parser-scope residual.
AI.conclusion: The Conflict Resolution split predominantly measures application of a simple recency rule rather than selective forgetting or genuine memory conflict resolution. Aggregate scores obscure a bimodal structure: models succeed on rule-solvable items but fail systematically on items whose gold requires reaching superseded (overwritten) statements. The per-item reachability split, not the aggregate, is the appropriate unit for interpreting scores on this benchmark.

title: RobotAPO: Adversarial Physics Preference Optimization for Robotic Manipulation Video Generation
summary: Robotic manipulation videos are increasingly used as visual plans for embodied agents, but optimizing purely for visual plausibility often fails to capture the fragile physical manifold of real-world interactions. Even minor physics-violating errors at the interaction boundary, such as interpenetration or premature object motion, can completely invalidate the inferred timing and pose needed for downstream execution. Because standard supervised fine-tuning lacks the direct pressure to penalize these localized failures, we introduce AgiBot-PhysPref. This rigorously curated 10,000-sample preference dataset isolates condition-matched physics violations, turning the generator's own failure distribution into a foundational signal for physical consistency. Building upon this, we propose RobotAPO, an adversarial physics preference optimization framework operating in the continuous flow-matching denoising space. To prevent the policy from merely memorizing static curated failures, RobotAPO employs a lightweight adversarial counterfactual proposer that learns a condition-dependent, physical-failure-biased direction in denoising space. This encourages the model to explore and better respect the physical interaction boundary, all while maintaining a pure prompt-and-reference inference interface without requiring external structural conditioning. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that explicitly correcting these localized physics violations improves downstream robot execution from generated videos. On held-out AgiBot conditions, RobotAPO outperforms the strongest controlled internal baseline in physical consistency by 6.8% hard score and 10.0% soft score. Crucially, in real-robot replay, it translates these physical-consistency gains into a 37.4% relative improvement in task success over the strongest controlled internal baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AgiBot-PhysPref, a 10,000-sample preference dataset isolating condition-matched physics violations, and RobotAPO, an adversarial physics preference optimization framework in flow-matching denoising space, improving physical consistency (6.8% hard, 10.0% soft) and real-robot success (37.4% relative).
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation videos used as visual plans for embodied agents are typically optimized for visual plausibility, which fails to capture the fragile physical manifold of real-world interactions. Minor physics-violating errors at the interaction boundary (e.g., interpenetration, premature object motion) can invalidate inferred timing and pose for downstream execution, and standard supervised fine-tuning lacks direct pressure to penalize these localized failures.
AI.method: AgiBot-PhysPref: a rigorously curated 10,000-sample preference dataset that isolates condition-matched physics violations, turning the generator's own failure distribution into a signal for physical consistency. RobotAPO: an adversarial physics preference optimization framework operating in the continuous flow-matching denoising space, with a lightweight adversarial counterfactual proposer that learns a condition-dependent, physical-failure-biased direction in denoising space, encouraging exploration of the physical interaction boundary while maintaining a pure prompt-and-reference inference interface without external structural conditioning.
AI.result: On held-out AgiBot conditions, RobotAPO outperforms the strongest controlled internal baseline in physical consistency by 6.8% hard score and 10.0% soft score. In real-robot replay, it translates these gains into a 37.4% relative improvement in task success.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly correcting localized physics violations in generated robot manipulation videos improves downstream robot execution. RobotAPO effectively enhances physical consistency and yields substantial gains in real-robot task success.

title: FreeEvolve: Learning to Evolve Beyond Fixed Loops
summary: Agent evolvers automate the design of the prompts, skills and workflows around language model agents, yet the optimization process they follow is still designed by hand: a fixed search loop decides how candidates are evaluated, which are kept and when the search stops. We propose FREEEVOLVE, which automates this process as well. An environment specifies the goal, target agent, evaluator, data and resource limits; within these limits, the evolver itself decides what to test, how much evidence to collect, which candidates to pursue and when to stop. These decisions follow an editable evolution skill, which we improve through meta-evolution by scoring each candidate skill on the fresh target agent it produces. The optimization process thus becomes a capability learned from experience rather than a loop engineered in advance. On tau3-bench, ARC-AGI-2, ARC-AGI-3 and Terminal-Bench 2.1, FREEEVOLVE controls the evolution campaign by itself, yet improves the primary held-out metric by 13.6 points on average and matches or exceeds hand-designed evolvers. The learned process keeps improving with experience: meta-evolved skills add 6.9 points over the seed skill on fresh target agents, demonstrating transferability across environments.

AI.tldr: FREEEVOLVE automates not just agent artifact design but the optimization process itself; the evolver learns an editable "evolution skill" via meta-evolution, matching or beating hand-designed evolvers and improving held-out metrics by 13.6 points on average.
AI.motivation: Existing agent evolvers automate prompt/skill/workflow design but rely on a hand-engineered fixed search loop that dictates evaluation, selection, and stopping. The paper aims to remove this manual engineering by making the optimization process itself a learnable capability.
AI.method: An environment provides the goal, target agent, evaluator, data, and resource limits. Within these limits, the evolver autonomously decides what to test, how much evidence to gather, which candidates to pursue, and when to stop. Decisions follow an editable evolution skill, improved through meta-evolution by scoring each candidate skill on the fresh target agent it produces.
AI.result: On tau3-bench, ARC-AGI-2, ARC-AGI-3, and Terminal-Bench 2.1, FREEEVOLVE self-manages the evolution campaign, improving the primary held-out metric by 13.6 points on average and matching or exceeding hand-designed evolvers. Meta-evolved skills add 6.9 points over the seed skill on fresh target agents, showing transferability.
AI.conclusion: Treating the optimization procedure as a learned skill rather than a pre-engineered loop yields stronger and transferable agent evolution across environments, with continued gains as experience accumulates.

title: TMT: Runtime Backdoor Detection for Vision-Language-Action Policies on Unseen Tasks
summary: Backdoored vision-language-action (VLA) policies can preserve benign task performance while producing malicious actions when a trigger appears. Detecting such activation is difficult because malicious behavior can comprise individually plausible actions, while unfamiliar tasks introduce legitimate changes in observations and behavior. We introduce TMT, a runtime backdoor detector based on Token Manifold and latent Transition modeling. Trained on benign rollouts, its two branches assess input-token structure and prediction errors in adjacent-layer latent dynamics. A suspicious rollout identified by the token manifold branch, once confirmed through latent deviations, guides transition selection for subsequent monitoring. We further explore policy purification through self-distillation: a frozen copy of the backdoored policy provides benign-input actions to supervise a student on paired benign and triggered observations, without requiring a separate clean reference policy. For evaluation, we adapt traditional backdoor detectors and repurpose anomaly and failure detection methods as VLA backdoor detectors. In a post-hoc comparison with ten baselines, TMT achieves state-of-the-art backdoor detection performance on unseen tasks across three VLA backdoor attacks. Our project page is available at https://zzr42.github.io/tmt/.

AI.tldr: TMT is a runtime backdoor detector for vision-language-action policies that combines a token-manifold branch with latent transition-error modeling, trained only on benign rollouts, plus a self-distillation purification scheme; it achieves state-of-the-art detection on unseen tasks across three VLA backdoor attacks against ten baselines.
AI.motivation: Backdoored VLA policies retain benign task performance yet emit malicious actions when a trigger appears. Detection is hard because malicious actions can be individually plausible, and unseen tasks legitimately shift both observations and behavior, making clean vs. triggered behavior difficult to separate.
AI.method: TMT has two benign-trained branches: a token manifold branch checking input-token structure, and a latent transition branch measuring prediction errors in adjacent-layer latent dynamics. A rollout flagged by the token branch is confirmed via latent deviations, which then guide transition selection for subsequent monitoring. Policy purification is explored via self-distillation: a frozen backdoored policy supplies benign-input actions to supervise a student on paired benign and triggered observations, so no separate clean reference policy is needed. Evaluation adapts traditional backdoor detectors and repurposes anomaly/failure detection methods as VLA backdoor detectors, compared post-hoc against ten baselines on three attacks.
AI.result: TMT achieves state-of-the-art backdoor detection performance on unseen tasks across three VLA backdoor attacks in comparison with ten baselines.
AI.conclusion: Joint token-level and latent-dynamics modeling enables reliable runtime backdoor detection under distribution shift from unfamiliar tasks, and self-distillation offers a reference-free path to policy purification.

title: Few Bits, One Law: Toward W2A4KV2
summary: Extreme low-bit LLM compression is most challenging when weights, activations, and KV caches are quantized together: their distributions differ, and quantization errors interact throughout the network. We introduce CanonQ, a unified quantization-aware training framework that addresses these challenges by separating source canonicalization from task-aware adaptation. Fixed rotations and energy normalization map heterogeneous tensor sources to canonical coordinates, enabling frozen Gaussian-reference codebooks to be reused across layers and models. Joint training then adapts the network to the coupled errors of weight, activation, and cache quantization within a common scalar/vector interface. We bound frozen-codebook transfer error and local task loss, and derive an exact normalization-aware straight-through Jacobian that links quantization distortion to gradient bias. The strongest gains arise under joint W2A4KV2 compression: across LLaMA3-1B/3B/8B, CanonQ-Omni achieves up to 14.28x lower WikiText-2 perplexity and up to 57.9% higher mean zero-shot accuracy than prior state-of-the-art and representative quantization baselines. The benefits extend to Qwen3-1.7B, code generation, and mathematical reasoning: on instruction-tuned MobileLLM-Pro-1B at W2A16KV16, CanonQ achieves relative improvements of 41.7% in HumanEval pass@1 and 39.1% in GSM8K exact match over the strongest evaluated quantization baseline.

AI.tldr: CanonQ is a unified quantization-aware training framework for extreme low-bit LLM compression that separates source canonicalization (fixed rotations + energy normalization enabling reusable frozen Gaussian codebooks) from task-aware joint adaptation across weights, activations, and KV caches, achieving large gains under joint W2A4KV2 compression.
AI.motivation: Extreme low-bit LLM compression is hardest when weights, activations, and KV caches are quantized jointly: their distributions differ, and quantization errors interact and propagate throughout the network, challenging existing methods that treat these tensor sources separately.
AI.method: CanonQ separates source canonicalization from task-aware adaptation. Fixed rotations and energy normalization map heterogeneous tensor sources into canonical coordinates, letting frozen Gaussian-reference codebooks be reused across layers and models. Joint training then adapts the network to coupled weight/activation/cache quantization errors within a common scalar/vector interface. The authors bound frozen-codebook transfer error and local task loss, and derive an exact normalization-aware straight-through Jacobian linking quantization distortion to gradient bias.
AI.result: Under joint W2A4KV2 compression across LLaMA3-1B/3B/8B, CanonQ-Omni achieves up to 14.28x lower WikiText-2 perplexity and up to 57.9% higher mean zero-shot accuracy than prior state-of-the-art and representative quantization baselines. Gains extend to Qwen3-1.7B, code generation, and mathematical reasoning; on instruction-tuned MobileLLM-Pro-1B at W2A16KV16, it improves HumanEval pass@1 by 41.7% and GSM8K exact match by 39.1% relatively over the strongest evaluated baseline.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling source canonicalization from task-aware adaptation enables reusable frozen codebooks and effective joint low-bit quantization of weights, activations, and KV caches, with theoretical guarantees on transfer error and gradient bias, yielding substantial perplexity, accuracy, code generation, and reasoning improvements.

title: Precise SE(3) End-Effector Tracking in Whole-Body Humanoid Control
summary: Precise end-effector tracking during humanoid whole-body motion is challenging due to floating-base oscillations, gravity, dynamic coupling, and locomotion-induced disturbances. We propose ResGAC, a whole-body humanoid controller for precise end-effector pose tracking that combines geometric admittance control (GAC) with residual reinforcement learning. GAC provides structured $\SE$ task-space feedback and generates nominal arm joint-position targets, while residual RL compensates for unmodeled dynamics and coordinates locomotion and balance in the shared joint-position action space. The left-invariant geometric formulation allows the same GAC law to be used across manipulation reference frames. This enables the use of a ground-attached heading frame that preserves planar locomotion while removing pelvis roll, pitch, and heave from the manipulation reference, thereby reducing reference-induced end-effector motion during locomotion. ResGAC is validated on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across four standing end-effector tracking benchmarks, ResGAC consistently outperforms representative baselines, including SONIC, achieving lower translational and rotational errors. Real-world experiments further demonstrate reduced propagation of pelvis motion to the desired end-effector pose using the proposed ground-attached heading frame. ResGAC achieves $90\%$ success in a standing peg-in-hole task compared with $50\%$ for SONIC, and accurate world-frame $\SE$ end-effector pose tracking during lower-body motion. Experimental videos are included in the supplementary material and are also available on the project website: https://resgac.github.io/ResGAC-website/.

AI.tldr: ResGAC combines geometric admittance control with residual RL for precise end-effector pose tracking on a humanoid, validated on a real Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Precise end-effector tracking during humanoid whole-body motion is difficult due to floating-base oscillations, gravity, dynamic coupling, and locomotion-induced disturbances.
AI.method: Combines geometric admittance control (GAC), providing structured SE(3) task-space feedback and nominal arm joint-position targets, with residual RL that compensates for unmodeled dynamics and coordinates locomotion and balance in a shared joint-position action space. The left-invariant geometric formulation allows the same GAC law across manipulation frames, enabling a ground-attached heading frame that preserves planar locomotion while removing pelvis roll, pitch, and heave from the manipulation reference.
AI.result: On a real Unitree G1, ResGAC outperforms baselines including SONIC across four standing end-effector tracking benchmarks with lower translational and rotational errors. It achieves 90% success in a standing peg-in-hole task versus 50% for SONIC, and shows reduced pelvis-motion propagation using the ground-attached heading frame, plus accurate world-frame SE(3) tracking during lower-body motion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed GAC-plus-residual-RL design and ground-attached heading frame yield superior end-effector tracking and manipulation performance on real humanoid hardware.

title: AGAR: a reinforcement learning substrate for LLM program evolution
summary: Given a task and an evaluator, a language model can rewrite a candidate program while a search loop decides which rewrites survive, offering a practical route to algorithm discovery. But that loop is governed by five constants set by hand: which parent to select, how hard to mutate, how to keep diversity, what to remember, and a scalar score that never says which part of the program earned it. Reinforcement learning already has an estimator for each. The obstacle is that program evolution is not usually written down as a decision process. We formalize it as a Markov decision process whose action is the modular prefix the model is conditioned on, rather than the program it emits. Credit assignment, value estimation, adaptive exploration, and experience memory can then attach to distinct components. AGAR (Algorithm Generation As RL) provides the resulting substrate: any estimator can be replaced or switched off without changing the controller, making the transfer auditable one mechanism at a time, with no gradient training of the backend model. Across 19 tasks, two backends, and three seeds under one harness, AGAR improves on the stronger of two published baselines on most tasks, with gains concentrated in the competitive-programming family. The formalization also yields a checkable reading of prior work: these systems are implicitly zero-discount, not by choice, but because fitness is exogenous to an individual rather than a return over successors, leaving a discount factor nothing to act on.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes language-model-driven program rewriting as a Markov decision process, enabling RL estimators to replace five hand-tuned search loop constants, and introduces AGAR, which outperforms published baselines on most of 19 tasks.
AI.motivation: Program evolution for algorithm discovery is typically governed by five constants set by hand (parent selection, mutation strength, diversity maintenance, memory, and a scalar score lacking credit assignment). Although reinforcement learning offers estimators for each, program evolution has not been framed as a decision process, preventing these estimators from being applied.
AI.method: The authors formalize program evolution as an MDP whose action is the modular prefix the model is conditioned on, rather than the emitted program itself. This allows credit assignment, value estimation, adaptive exploration, and experience memory to attach to distinct components. AGAR (Algorithm Generation As RL) is the resulting substrate, where any estimator can be replaced or disabled independently without altering the controller, and no gradient training of the backend model is required.
AI.result: Across 19 tasks, two backends, and three seeds under a single harness, AGAR improves on the stronger of two published baselines on most tasks, with gains concentrated in the competitive-programming family. The formalization also provides a checkable reading of prior work: such systems are implicitly zero-discount, not by design, but because fitness is exogenous to an individual rather than a return over successors, leaving a discount factor nothing to act on.
AI.conclusion: Framing program evolution as an MDP over modular prefixes yields an auditable substrate (AGAR) in which RL estimators can be swapped or ablated one mechanism at a time, delivering empirical gains without backend gradient training and clarifying the implicit zero-discount nature of prior systems.

title: SiGNgapore - An Interactive Dataset for Sign-based Visual Navigation
summary: The future of autonomous robots in human-oriented environments depends on their ability to navigate in the absence of prebuilt maps; exploiting navigational aids, such as navigational signs, designed by humans for humans is critical for enabling autonomy. This manuscript introduces a unique dataset collected using a handheld device, at various public spaces across Singapore, representing environments that humans frequent daily, and focusing on sign-centric decision making for mapless navigation. The dataset includes RGB, sparse depth, odometry and IMU measurements of scenarios centered around navigational signs and the complex environments where they are placed. Additionally, we provide 56 long-horizon navigation missions and over 450 sign-centric scenarios. All data is provided in a human- readable format, as well as utility scripts for conversion to ROS 2. Lastly, we provide venue maps and GPS aligned scene graphs of the test environments. We discuss the potential use cases for this dataset.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a handheld-collected, multi-modal dataset of sign-centric environments across Singapore public spaces, including over 450 sign scenarios, 56 long-horizon navigation missions, and GPS-aligned scene graphs, to support mapless navigation research using human-designed navigational signs.
AI.motivation: Autonomous robots in human-oriented environments need to navigate without prebuilt maps. Human-designed navigational signs are a critical, yet underexploited, aid for enabling such mapless autonomy, and no dataset specifically targets sign-centric decision making in complex real-world public spaces.
AI.method: The authors collected a dataset using a handheld device in various public spaces across Singapore. It captures RGB, sparse depth, odometry, and IMU measurements of scenarios centered on navigational signs and their surrounding complex environments. The dataset comprises 56 long-horizon navigation missions and over 450 sign-centric scenarios, provided in human-readable format with utility scripts for conversion to ROS 2. They additionally supply venue maps and GPS-aligned scene graphs of the test environments, and discuss potential use cases.
AI.result: A multi-modal, sign-centric dataset featuring RGB, sparse depth, odometry, and IMU data; 56 long-horizon missions; 450+ scenarios; ROS 2 conversion scripts; venue maps; and GPS-aligned scene graphs, all in human-readable formats.
AI.conclusion: The dataset provides a foundation for developing and benchmarking mapless navigation systems that leverage navigational signs in human-oriented public environments, enabling sign-centric decision making for autonomous robots.

title: RLDISCOVER: LLM-driven co-evolution of reinforcement learning algorithms
summary: LLM-guided program evolution has enabled discoveries in mathematics and computational optimization, raising the prospect of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms that self-evolve to improve how agents learn. However, realizing this prospect faces two obstacles. Joint search over coupled algorithmic components is difficult to scale: simultaneous changes can disrupt learning, while isolated changes overlook their dependencies. Evaluating candidate algorithms also requires costly training, with fitness remaining uncertain across random seeds. We introduce RLDiscover, a framework for the self-evolution of model-free deep RL algorithms. Progressive Co-Evolution advances from targeted component edits to joint evolution, while Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation balances search breadth and evaluation fidelity through staged training and repeated evaluation. Experiments across SAC, PPO, and DQN on four benchmark suites show substantial improvements in mean return, with per-family median gains of 32%-84% and a peak return ratio of approximately 363x over a near-zero baseline. These gains include transitions from failed learning to successful task completion, and improvements persist when evolution starts from stronger open-source implementations. On measured SAC locomotion runs, evaluation uses approximately one-fifteenth the estimated compute required to fully evaluate the same candidate pool. Remarkably, independent searches repeatedly discover interpretable combinations of adaptive robust losses, progress-dependent value targets, and running statistics, with selected programs transferring to unseen tasks. These findings point toward a broader role for self-evolution in AI: discovering interpretable algorithms that improve how agents learn.

AI.tldr: RLDiscover self-evolves model-free deep RL algorithms via progressive co-evolution and probabilistic evaluation, yielding large, transferable, interpretable gains.
AI.motivation: LLM-guided program evolution could enable RL algorithms that self-evolve, but joint search over coupled components is hard to scale (simultaneous edits disrupt learning; isolated edits ignore dependencies) and candidate evaluation needs costly training with uncertain fitness across seeds.
AI.method: RLDiscover combines Progressive Co-Evolution, which moves from targeted component edits to joint evolution, with Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation, which uses staged training and repeated evaluation to balance search breadth and evaluation fidelity.
AI.result: Across SAC, PPO, and DQN on four benchmark suites, per-family median return gains are 32%-84%, with a peak return ratio of ~363x over a near-zero baseline; failed learning transitions to task completion, gains persist from stronger open-source implementations, and measured SAC locomotion evaluation uses ~1/15 the estimated compute of fully evaluating the same candidate pool.
AI.conclusion: Independent searches repeatedly discover interpretable combinations of adaptive robust losses, progress-dependent value targets, and running statistics, with selected programs transferring to unseen tasks, pointing toward self-evolution as a means to discover interpretable algorithms that improve how agents learn.

title: Sparse Feature Policy Unlearning Mitigates State Hallucination in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models. However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors. In this work, we study state hallucination, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved. Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur. Based on this analysis, we propose SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively. Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities. These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies.

AI.tldr: This paper studies "state hallucination" in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) robot policies and proposes SOUL, a sparse-feature-based policy unlearning method that selectively forgets hallucination-associated knowledge while retaining successful behaviors.
AI.motivation: VLA models generalize well in robotic manipulation but suffer from recurring unreliable behaviors that limit real-world deployment. The work targets "state hallucination," a failure pattern where a VLA keeps acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved.
AI.method: Analysis shows state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions; sparse autoencoders provide a mechanistic interpretation, revealing hallucination-associated sparse features activated during failures. Based on this, SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning) selectively unlearns policy knowledge tied to hallucination, using sparse features from hallucination failures and successful behaviors as explicit forgetting and retention targets.
AI.result: Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show substantially reduced hallucinated failures and improved task success, without substantially compromising existing manipulation capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable feature analysis offers a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies, enabling targeted correction of specific failure modes.

title: CM-DPO: Constraint-Margin Direct Preference Optimization for LLM Planning
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats all constraint violations equally: a $1 budget overshoot and a $1,000 overshoot induce the same training signal. It is also susceptible to length and style bias when preference pairs come from different model families. We introduce Constraint-Margin DPO (CM-DPO), which replaces DPO's binary preference signal with a continuous margin derived from a deterministic symbolic verifier and scaled by violation severity. Hard and soft constraints are separated through a lexicographic objective, ensuring hard constraints are never traded off against preferences. To supply CM-DPO with bias-reduced training pairs, we generate preference data through procedurally generated constraint profiles (DCCG) and minimal-edit distillation from a reasoning teacher (RT-MED), within a framework we call SynPlan-R. On TravelPlanner, NaturalPlan, and out-of-distribution PlanBench, an 8B model fine-tuned with CM-DPO achieves 89.2% pass rate and 93.4% solve rate, matching multi-agent systems at 13x lower latency while outperforming GPT-4o on unseen Blocksworld by 9.2 points.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Constraint-Margin DPO (CM-DPO), a variant of Direct Preference Optimization that uses continuous, severity-scaled margins from a symbolic verifier and a lexicographic hard/soft constraint objective, trained on bias-reduced pairs generated by the SynPlan-R framework (DCCG + RT-MED). An 8B model fine-tuned with CM-DPO reaches 89.2% pass rate and 93.4% solve rate on TravelPlanner, NaturalPlan, and OOD PlanBench, matching multi-agent systems at 13x lower latency and beating GPT-4o by 9.2 points on unseen Blocksworld.
AI.motivation: DPO treats all constraint violations equally, so a $1 budget overshoot and a $1,000 overshoot produce the same training signal, failing to reflect violation severity. DPO is also susceptible to length and style bias when preference pairs originate from different model families, which corrupts the preference signal.
AI.method: CM-DPO replaces DPO's binary preference signal with a continuous margin derived from a deterministic symbolic verifier and scaled by violation severity. Hard and soft constraints are separated via a lexicographic objective so hard constraints are never traded off against preferences. To supply bias-reduced training pairs, preference data is generated through procedurally generated constraint profiles (DCCG) and minimal-edit distillation from a reasoning teacher (RT-MED), together forming the SynPlan-R framework.
AI.result: On TravelPlanner, NaturalPlan, and out-of-distribution PlanBench, an 8B model fine-tuned with CM-DPO achieves 89.2% pass rate and 93.4% solve rate. It matches multi-agent systems at 13x lower latency and outperforms GPT-4o on unseen Blocksworld by 9.2 points.
AI.conclusion: CM-DPO provides a severity-aware, lexicographically constrained alternative to DPO that, combined with the SynPlan-R data generation pipeline, yields strong planning performance with substantially lower latency than comparable multi-agent systems and improved out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Not All Uncertainty Matters: Simulation-in-the-Loop Fast-Slow Reasoning for Decision-Critical Autonomous Driving System
summary: Large vision-language models (VLMs) provide powerful open-world perception and reasoning for autonomous driving, but their high computational cost and inference latency make continuous cloud-side use impractical. This motivates fast--slow collaboration, where efficient onboard modules handle real-time perception and control while cloud models provide high-level reasoning only when needed. The key challenge is deciding when cloud reasoning should influence time-critical driving decisions. Existing methods often rely on perception uncertainty, heuristic triggers, or resource-driven policies, without assessing whether resolving an uncertainty will improve planning. We propose \textbf{SIGMA}, a simulation-in-the-loop framework for task-oriented fast--slow collaboration. SIGMA embeds the planner into uncertainty assessment and evaluates how plausible scene realizations under semantic and geometric uncertainty affect feasible trajectories and planning cost. Based on these outcomes, it estimates the expected reduction in planning cost from resolving uncertainty. We further introduce expected planning gain (EPG), a decision-level metric for cloud invocation, cloud-guidance integration, and request prioritization under deadline and resource constraints. Experiments in CARLA show that SIGMA reduces unnecessary cloud interactions while improving planning, efficiency, and navigation success in static and dynamic obstacle scenarios. Compared with fixed-period collaboration, SIGMA reduces unnecessary cloud interactions by 50\%, improves navigation success by more than 6\%, and cuts finish time by up to 26.2\% in dynamic scenarios.

AI.tldr: SIGMA is a simulation-in-the-loop framework for task-oriented fast-slow collaboration in autonomous driving, using an expected planning gain (EPG) metric to decide when cloud VLM reasoning should influence time-critical driving decisions.
AI.motivation: Large VLMs enable open-world perception and reasoning for driving, but their cost and latency preclude continuous cloud-side use. Fast-slow collaboration is thus needed, where onboard modules handle real-time control and cloud models provide high-level reasoning only when needed. The core challenge is deciding when cloud reasoning should affect time-critical decisions; existing methods rely on perception uncertainty, heuristic triggers, or resource-driven policies, without assessing whether resolving an uncertainty would actually improve planning.
AI.method: SIGMA embeds the planner into uncertainty assessment and evaluates how plausible scene realizations under semantic and geometric uncertainty affect feasible trajectories and planning cost. From these outcomes it estimates the expected reduction in planning cost from resolving uncertainty. The paper introduces expected planning gain (EPG), a decision-level metric used for cloud invocation, cloud-guidance integration, and request prioritization under deadline and resource constraints.
AI.result: Experiments in CARLA show SIGMA reduces unnecessary cloud interactions while improving planning, efficiency, and navigation success in both static and dynamic obstacle scenarios. Compared with fixed-period collaboration, SIGMA reduces unnecessary cloud interactions by 50%, improves navigation success by more than 6%, and cuts finish time by up to 26.2% in dynamic scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Framing cloud invocation as a planning-oriented decision via EPG enables more effective fast-slow collaboration, cutting redundant cloud interactions and improving driving performance over fixed-period baselines.

title: Trajectory Abstraction for the Science of Language Agent Behavior
summary: Scientific studies of language agents need behavioral variables that support hypotheses across tasks and models. We formulate this research problem as learning and testing a hierarchy of trajectory abstractions. A concrete recursive procedure first measures role- and phase-indexed events, proposes temporally constrained relations, and tests their stability across conditions. It then constructs episode-level motif variables from selected relations and repeats the analysis on those variables. Explicit measurement functions connect every abstraction level to the original trajectories. Observations and randomized protocol experiments assess the resulting hypotheses, while comparisons between intervention realizations determine whether an abstraction should be retained, refined, or restricted. We derive a finite-depth bound for accepted reductions, identify protocol effects on fixed abstractions, and characterize realization disagreement and composition of abstraction error. A finite-sample test makes projected intervention consistency operational, and constructed examples illustrate motif construction and abstraction refinement. The formulation distinguishes this experimental approach from semantic taxonomies, qualitative theory induction, and behavior-model recovery. It specifies a proposed research procedure for discovering generalizable behavioral hypotheses, with literature-relative novelty assessed separately from model-relative surprise.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates the study of language agents as learning and testing a hierarchy of trajectory abstractions, using a recursive procedure that measures events, proposes relations, and builds episode-level motifs, with bounds and finite-sample tests for validation.
AI.motivation: Scientific studies of language agents require behavioral variables that generalize across tasks and models, motivating a principled abstraction framework rather than ad hoc measures.
AI.method: A recursive procedure: measure role- and phase-indexed events, propose temporally constrained relations, test stability across conditions, then build episode-level motif variables and repeat. Measurement functions link each abstraction level to original trajectories; randomized protocol experiments and intervention-realization comparisons decide whether abstractions are retained, refined, or restricted.
AI.result: A finite-depth bound for accepted reductions, characterization of protocol effects on fixed abstractions, analysis of realization disagreement and composition of abstraction error, and a finite-sample test operationalizing projected intervention consistency; constructed examples illustrate motif construction and refinement.
AI.conclusion: The formulation defines an experimental procedure for discovering generalizable behavioral hypotheses, distinct from semantic taxonomies, qualitative theory induction, and behavior-model recovery, with literature-relative novelty assessed separately from model-relative surprise.

title: Contact-Aware Imitation Learning Through Contact Factorization
summary: Generalizable contact-rich manipulation requires robots to preserve intended task behavior while adapting its physical realization to changing contact conditions. However, interaction forces can vary substantially with small changes in surface geometry, orientation, and friction, making policies trained directly on raw force measurements difficult to transfer beyond demonstrated conditions. We introduce FACE, a contact-factorized imitation learning framework that separates intended task behavior from environment-dependent contact factors. Our representation expresses interaction forces in normalized, contact-relative coordinates, while a learned contact-normal estimator and an online friction estimator infer the local contact normal and effective friction scale. Together, these estimators enable force observations to be encoded and policy outputs to be decoded into physical motion and force commands during execution. In this way, FACE adapts execution to current contact conditions while preserving the intended task behavior, without updating the policy parameters. We evaluate FACE on real-robot contact-rich manipulation under unseen variations in surface properties and geometry, demonstrating robust generalization across contact conditions through controlled comparisons with variants that adapt prior approaches to our setting. Videos and additional materials can be found on the project page: https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/face.

AI.tldr: FACE is a contact-factorized imitation learning framework that disentangles intended task behavior from environment-dependent contact factors, enabling contact-rich robot manipulation policies to generalize across unseen surface properties and geometry without policy parameter updates.
AI.motivation: Generalizable contact-rich manipulation requires robots to preserve intended task behavior while adapting their physical realization to changing contact conditions. However, interaction forces vary substantially with small changes in surface geometry, orientation, and friction, making policies trained directly on raw force measurements difficult to transfer beyond demonstrated conditions.
AI.method: FACE factorizes contact from task behavior. It represents interaction forces in normalized, contact-relative coordinates. A learned contact-normal estimator and an online friction estimator infer the local contact normal and effective friction scale. These estimators encode force observations and decode policy outputs into physical motion and force commands during execution, adapting to current contact conditions while preserving intended task behavior, without updating policy parameters.
AI.result: Evaluated on real-robot contact-rich manipulation under unseen variations in surface properties and geometry, FACE demonstrates robust generalization across contact conditions through controlled comparisons with variants that adapt prior approaches to the same setting.
AI.conclusion: Contact-factorized representation with online estimation of contact normal and friction scale enables robust generalization of imitation learning policies to unseen contact conditions without retraining, establishing a practical route toward generalizable contact-rich manipulation.

title: The Winner's Curse in LLM Self-Improvement Loops: Selection Noise, Lock-in, and Acceptance Rules
comment: 34 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables; code and saved experimental records included as ancillary files
summary: Self-improving LLM systems propose changes to themselves and keep those that score better on a small evaluation set. We treat this keep-if-better step as selection under measurement noise, model the correlated errors of the candidates in a single decision, and study empirically what happens when the evaluation set is reused. In runs where Qwen models rewrite their own instructions and every candidate is also scored on 600 held-out items, most proposals after the first are harmful, and the model gives the size of the winner's curse of a generation's best candidate. With a prior from a separate pilot, it matches the average overstatement of first-generation commits in native loops, though not setting by setting. In a pre-registered study, the final selection-set score of greedy loops exceeded held-out accuracy by 13 to 20 points with 16 selection items and by 1 to 5 points with 256. Held-out gains grew with the selection set on TREC but not on GSM8K, and the tested acceptance rules did not beat greedy acceptance over whole runs. Gains measured on the selection set also exceeded held-out gains when a current model refined a competent instruction, and in the validation scores of GEPA and MIPROv2. Scoring the starting and the current instruction on 64 items never used for selection removes the average bias of a loop's reported gain, but single estimates remain off by about 6 points. Self-improvement studies should report held-out gains with their uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the "keep-if-better" step in self-improving LLM systems as selection under measurement noise, showing that reusing a small evaluation set produces a winner's curse: reported selection-set gains systematically overstate held-out gains.
AI.motivation: Self-improving LLM pipelines accept new candidates when they score higher on a small evaluation set, but these scores are noisy and the same set is reused across generations. The paper seeks to characterize empirically how much this selection procedure inflates reported improvements relative to true held-out performance.
AI.method: The keep-if-better step is framed as selection under measurement noise with correlated errors across candidates within a single decision. Experiments use Qwen models rewriting their own instructions, with every candidate additionally scored on 600 held-out items. A pilot provides a prior for predicting the winner's curse. A pre-registered study varies selection-set size (16 vs. 256 items), datasets (TREC, GSM8K), and acceptance rules, and extends the analysis to GEPA and MIPROv2 validation scores and to a competent-instruction refinement setting. A debiasing procedure scores starting and current instructions on 64 never-selected items.
AI.result: Most proposals after the first are harmful. The prior matches the average overstatement of first-generation commits in native loops, though not setting by setting. Final selection-set scores exceed held-out accuracy by 13-20 points with 16 selection items and by 1-5 points with 256. Held-out gains grew with selection-set size on TREC but not GSM8K, and tested acceptance rules did not beat greedy acceptance over whole runs. Gains on the selection set also exceeded held-out gains for competent-instruction refinement and in GEPA/MIPROv2 validation scores. The 64-item debiasing removes average bias of a loop's reported gain, but single estimates remain off by about 6 points.
AI.conclusion: Reusing a small evaluation set in self-improving LLM loops yields systematically inflated gains due to the winner's curse. Self-improvement studies should report held-out gains together with their uncertainty rather than relying on selection-set scores alone.

title: MagCilia: A Compact Magnetociliary Tactile Sensor with 3D Force Sensing for Robotic Contact Perception and Grasping Feedback
summary: Robotic grasping and surface exploration benefit from simultaneous measurement of normal and tangential forces and from surface information obtained through contact. Here, we present a compact magnetociliary tactile sensor (MagCilia) that combines a flexible magnetic-cilia structure with a Hall sensor for 3D force sensing. Quasi-static finite element analysis is used to investigate structural deformation and magnetic responses under multidirectional loading. To reconstruct forces from the coupled magnetic channels, we propose causal history fusion regression (CHFR), which combines current magnetic-field measurements with their recent changes. Five-fold cross-validation grouped by calibration record yields root-mean-square errors of 0.40, 0.57, and 0.69 N for Fx, Fy, and Fz, respectively, with corresponding coefficients of determination of 0.93, 0.90, and 0.92. Robotic experiments demonstrate tangential-force-guided gripper adjustment and multi-axis load monitoring under external perturbations. Frequency-domain features of the reconstructed forces distinguish six surface categories with 99.39% accuracy in three-fold cross-validation grouped by acquisition session. An online robotic demonstration additionally identifies all six tested surfaces. These results demonstrate 3D force reconstruction, grasping feedback, and surface recognition using a single compact tactile unit.

AI.tldr: A compact magnetociliary tactile sensor (MagCilia) combining a magnetic-cilia structure with a Hall sensor achieves 3D force reconstruction via causal history fusion regression, enabling gripper feedback and 99.39%-accurate surface recognition.
AI.motivation: Robotic grasping and surface exploration need simultaneous normal and tangential force measurement plus contact-derived surface information, which existing compact tactile units often cannot provide together.
AI.method: The sensor pairs a flexible magnetic-cilia structure with a Hall sensor. Quasi-static finite element analysis models structural deformation and magnetic responses under multidirectional loading. Causal history fusion regression (CHFR) reconstructs forces from coupled magnetic channels by fusing current magnetic-field measurements with their recent changes. Validation uses five-fold cross-validation grouped by calibration record for force regression, three-fold cross-validation grouped by acquisition session for surface classification, and robotic grasping and online recognition experiments.
AI.result: Force reconstruction yields RMSEs of 0.40, 0.57, and 0.69 N for Fx, Fy, and Fz with R² of 0.93, 0.90, and 0.92. Robotic experiments show tangential-force-guided gripper adjustment and multi-axis load monitoring under perturbations. Frequency-domain features of reconstructed forces classify six surface categories at 99.39% accuracy, and an online demonstration identifies all six surfaces.
AI.conclusion: A single compact tactile unit can simultaneously deliver 3D force reconstruction, grasping feedback, and surface recognition.

title: We Query, Therefore We Compute: On Oracle Computation beyond the Machine, with an Application to Agents
summary:
Agentic systems use large language models (LLMs) to carry out concrete tasks. Prior work often borrows abstractions such as scheduling, caching or isolation piecemeal from operating systems, so the mechanisms it builds share little common ground, and the shared view of the two forms of agentic system, Workflows and Agents, is limited. We construct an abstract machine that provides both.
  We treat the LLM as an Oracle and extend a two-stack pushdown automaton with one instruction, which hands the Oracle a whole stack as its query and appends the answer to that same stack. The machine thus performs two computations, the Oracle's and a Turing-complete one that we call the Priestess. A stack that the program only appends to grows autoregressively, as an agent's context does. Two symmetry breakings, S in storage and T in transitions, make a Priestess program the operating system of the programs the Oracle runs, and produce the Agent and the Workflow as the two placements of a task's program.
  For internally autoregressive Oracles, the two computations synchronize at the end of every answer under certain conditions, and through that synchronization we model caching and analyse scheduling. No guarantee that holds for every Oracle can fix which content crosses between the two computations, but such a guarantee does fix the boundary itself.
  The construction V fits the machine to a von Neumann computer. To show that it is realizable, we propose ArchNights, an extended RISC-V ISA and a Linux-style operating system implementing the machine by design. ArchNights-SE runs on gem5 as a computer system, becomes an agentic system when it runs an LLM as the Oracle, and will be open source.
  Agentic systems can then be designed as computer systems are. With a foundation built and a unified view, future work can share invariants and bounds, each with its conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an abstract machine treating the LLM as an Oracle inside a two-stack pushdown automaton with one added instruction, yielding a unified foundation for Workflows and Agents via two symmetry breakings (S in storage, T in transitions), and demonstrates realizability through ArchNights, a RISC-V-based ISA and Linux-style OS.
AI.motivation: Prior work borrows OS abstractions such as scheduling, caching, and isolation piecemeal, so the resulting mechanisms share little common ground and the shared view of the two forms of agentic system, Workflows and Agents, remains limited. The paper aims to provide a common foundation giving both.
AI.method: Treat the LLM as an Oracle and extend a two-stack pushdown automaton with one instruction that hands the Oracle a whole stack as its query and appends the answer to that same stack. The machine thus performs two computations: the Oracle's and a Turing-complete one called the Priestess. Two symmetry breakings, S in storage and T in transitions, make a Priestess program the operating system of the programs the Oracle runs, producing the Agent and the Workflow as the two placements of a task's program. For internally autoregressive Oracles, the two computations synchronize at the end of every answer under certain conditions. The construction V fits the machine to a von Neumann computer, and ArchNights (an extended RISC-V ISA plus a Linux-style OS) realizes it by design.
AI.result: The two computations synchronize at the end of every answer under certain conditions, enabling modeling of caching and analysis of scheduling. No guarantee holding for every Oracle can fix which content crosses between the two computations, but such a guarantee does fix the boundary itself. ArchNights-SE runs on gem5 as a computer system and becomes an agentic system when running an LLM as the Oracle; it will be open source.
AI.conclusion: Agentic systems can be designed as computer systems are. With a foundation built and a unified view established, future work can share invariants and bounds, each with its conditions.

title: Targeted Modality Dropout for Real-Robot Manipulation Robust to Intermittent Vision Loss
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)
summary: Imitation learning policies that integrate multiple sensory modalities are prone to overreliance on a dominant modality, such as vision, during training, which can disrupt policy execution when that modality is lost at inference time. In this paper, we introduce Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), in which the dependence on each modality is estimated using attention and the most dominant modality is selectively dropped. This is combined with entropy regularization over the dependence distribution. Through real-robot evaluation using a bimanual manipulator, we show that under vision loss the success rate of the baseline policy drops substantially, whereas TMD sustains task execution. In contrast, a conventional dropout that selects the dropped modality at random, without the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), which uses attention to estimate modality dependence and selectively drops the dominant modality, combined with entropy regularization, to prevent overreliance on a single modality in multimodal imitation learning.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning policies that integrate multiple sensory modalities tend to overrely on a dominant modality (e.g., vision) during training. When that modality is unavailable at inference, policy execution breaks down. A robust solution is needed to balance modality dependence.
AI.method: TMD estimates the dependence on each modality using attention and selectively drops the most dominant modality. This is combined with entropy regularization applied over the modality dependence distribution. It is compared against a baseline and a conventional random modality dropout without entropy regularization.
AI.result: In real-robot evaluation with a bimanual manipulator, the baseline's success rate drops substantially under vision loss, whereas TMD sustains task execution. The conventional random dropout without entropy regularization fails on many tasks even without vision loss.
AI.conclusion: TMD improves robustness to modality loss in multimodal imitation learning by targeting the dominant modality and regularizing the dependence distribution, outperforming both the baseline and naive random dropout.

title: RT-Safe: Benchmarking Agent Safety in Real-Time Embodied Environment
summary: Rapid progress in AI agents has brought growing attention to agent safety, with extensive evaluation focused on digital environments. As agents move into the physical world, embodied safety becomes increasingly important: failures can cause human injury and costly hardware damage. Beyond selecting safe actions, embodied agents must also operate under real-time constraints: the physical world does not pause while an agent reasons. As pedestrians move and vehicles approach during inference, an action that appears safe at observation time may become unsafe before execution. Real-time embodied safety therefore depends on both decision quality and decision latency. We introduce RT-SAFE, a simulated urban benchmark for evaluating embodied-agent safety under real-time constraints. RT-SAFE combines navigation tasks with moving actors, environmental hazards, and traffic rules, while allowing the world to evolve throughout inference and action execution. Across eight VLMs, agents achieve high task completion yet almost never complete safely: in the hardest setting, only 0.7% of episodes finish without a safety event. More strikingly, matched static and real-time evaluations yield task completion rates of 91.3% and 94.1%, respectively, while real-time execution increases collisions by $12.3\times$. These results reveal that standard task success can mask substantial safety failures, and that decision latency itself can become a source of physical risk. Finally, we show that RT-SAFE can support offline RL training and substantially reduce collision rates while achieving strong task completion.

AI.tldr: RT-SAFE is a simulated urban benchmark that evaluates embodied-agent safety under real-time constraints, showing that high task completion often masks severe safety failures driven largely by decision latency.
AI.motivation: AI agent safety research has focused on digital environments, but as agents enter the physical world, embodied safety gains importance because failures can cause human injury and hardware damage. Embodied agents face a real-time constraint: the world keeps evolving during inference and action execution, so an action deemed safe at observation time can become unsafe by execution. Thus real-time embodied safety depends on both decision quality and decision latency.
AI.method: The authors introduce RT-SAFE, a simulated urban benchmark for evaluating embodied-agent safety under real-time constraints. RT-SAFE combines navigation tasks with moving actors, environmental hazards, and traffic rules, and allows the world to evolve throughout inference and action execution. The benchmark is used to evaluate eight VLMs, with matched static and real-time evaluations, and is also tested as a substrate for offline RL training.
AI.result: Agents achieve high task completion but almost never complete safely: in the hardest setting, only 0.7% of episodes finish without a safety event. Matched static and real-time evaluations yield task completion rates of 91.3% and 94.1% respectively, while real-time execution increases collisions by 12.3x. RT-SAFE also supports offline RL training, substantially reducing collision rates while achieving strong task completion.
AI.conclusion: Standard task success metrics can mask substantial safety failures, and decision latency itself can become a source of physical risk. RT-SAFE provides a benchmark for exposing these failures and can serve as a training substrate to improve embodied-agent safety.

title: Point It, Strike It: Direction-Conditioned Dynamic Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects
