comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Project Page: https://deformx.github.io/DeformY
summary: Goal-conditioned dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects has mainly specified goals as positions for a rope tip to reach. Many tasks, however, depend on how the tip arrives. We therefore study single-swing rope striking with goals that specify the tip's 3D position and arrival direction, across the workspace and on different ropes. This is challenging because rope dynamics are hard to model, no demonstrations exist, distinct swings reach the same goal with different reliability, and the sim-to-real gap extends beyond the rope. To address these challenges, we extend the state-of-the-art DLO simulator DeformX with GPU acceleration, a stable Cosserat rod solver, and a cross-flow aerodynamic model, yielding DeformX2.0, which is more than $20{,}000\times$ faster. We then propose TRACE (Trace-rooted Adaptive Cross-Entropy), which generates striking data by warm-starting each new target from the stored swing whose tip path passes closest to it. Its cost penalizes rope bending and abrupt tip motion to favor repeatable swings. A conditional flow-matching policy trained on this data reaches 92.1% accuracy in simulation. Finally, we propose RECAP (Residual Calibration Policy), which fits the simulator's rope and rig parameters to a few calibration swings and adapts actions with a correction policy trained in simulation. On a real robot, across three ropes, RECAP raises success within 5cm from 72% to 87% for position goals, and within 10cm and 10° from 50% to 79% for goals that also specify the arrival direction.

AI.tldr: The paper studies single-swing rope striking where goals specify both the tip's 3D position and its arrival direction. It introduces DeformX2.0 (a 20,000x faster GPU-accelerated DLO simulator), TRACE (a data generation method), and RECAP (a residual calibration policy), achieving 92.1% simulation accuracy and improving real-robot success rates.
AI.motivation: Existing goal-conditioned dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects (DLOs) mainly specifies goals as rope tip positions, ignoring how the tip arrives. Many tasks depend on the tip's arrival direction. This problem is challenging because rope dynamics are hard to model, no demonstrations exist, distinct swings reach the same goal with varying reliability, and the sim-to-real gap extends beyond the rope itself.
AI.method: The authors (1) extend the DLO simulator DeformX into DeformX2.0 with GPU acceleration, a stable Cosserat rod solver, and a cross-flow aerodynamic model; (2) propose TRACE (Trace-rooted Adaptive Cross-Entropy), which generates striking data by warm-starting each target from the stored swing whose tip path passes closest to it, with a cost penalizing rope bending and abrupt tip motion; (3) train a conditional flow-matching policy on this data; and (4) propose RECAP (Residual Calibration Policy), which fits the simulator's rope and rig parameters to a few calibration swings and adapts actions via a correction policy trained in simulation.
AI.result: DeformX2.0 is more than 20,000x faster than the baseline. The conditional flow-matching policy reaches 92.1% accuracy in simulation. On a real robot across three ropes, RECAP raises success within 5cm from 72% to 87% for position goals, and within 10cm and 10 degrees from 50% to 79% for goals that also specify the arrival direction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables goal-conditioned single-swing rope striking that specifies both tip position and arrival direction across the workspace and on different ropes, with substantial improvements in both simulation accuracy and real-robot success rates.

title: The AI Evaluation Ecosystem
summary: AI evaluation shapes the decisions of model providers, users, funders, and regulators. We argue that designing valid benchmarks requires contextualizing design choices in the dynamics of this ecosystem of actors. We develop a simulation architecture that combines rule-based market dynamics with LLM-driven strategic actors, building on advances in Generative Agent-Based Modeling (GABM). We model benchmarks, consumer needs, and provider capabilities as vectors over a six-dimensional capability space (reasoning, coding, knowledge, safety, communication, agentic), with structural information partitions across actors. As a case study, we apply this stylized simulation to explore benchmark holdout design. We find that moving from public benchmarks to private holdout benchmarks shrinks the gap between benchmark scores and user satisfaction on most benchmarks but widens it on a few, depending on where holdout weights shift scoring credit. We stress-test our findings at both the instrument and case-study level, drawing on the V&V framework of Sargent (2013) and GABM-specific evidence criteria. Beyond holdout design, our simulation is a hypothesis-generating sandbox for studying how evaluator and policy choices, in turn, reshape the ecosystem.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that valid AI benchmarks must be contextualized within the ecosystem of model providers, users, funders, and regulators, and develops a GABM simulation combining rule-based market dynamics with LLM-driven strategic actors to study benchmark holdout design.
AI.motivation: AI evaluation shapes decisions across an ecosystem of stakeholders (providers, users, funders, regulators). However, benchmark design is typically treated in isolation rather than as embedded in these actor dynamics. The authors seek to understand how benchmark design choices—specifically public vs. private holdout—interact with strategic behavior and user satisfaction.
AI.method: A simulation architecture integrating rule-based market dynamics with LLM-driven strategic actors, based on Generative Agent-Based Modeling (GABM). Benchmarks, consumer needs, and provider capabilities are represented as vectors in a six-dimensional capability space (reasoning, coding, knowledge, safety, communication, agentic), with structural information partitions across actors. A case study applies this stylized simulation to benchmark holdout design.
AI.result: Moving from public to private holdout benchmarks reduces the gap between benchmark scores and user satisfaction on most benchmarks, but widens it on a few—depending on where holdout weights shift scoring credit. Findings are stress-tested at both instrument and case-study levels using Sargent's (2013) V&V framework and GABM-specific evidence criteria.
AI.conclusion: The simulation serves as a hypothesis-generating sandbox beyond holdout design, enabling study of how evaluator and policy choices reshape the ecosystem. Holdout design effects on benchmark-user alignment are heterogeneous and weight-dependent.

title: Adaptive Code Generation for Controlling Robots
comment: International Symposium on Leveraging Applications of Formal Methods, Verification, and Validation 2026
summary: Deploying robots as Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS) in unknown and dynamic environments necessitates a transition from rigid command libraries toward intention-based autonomy, as natural language represents the only medium capable of articulating complex goals beyond the capacity of finite instruction sets. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a path toward natural language goal description, their integration introduces significant challenges: the formalization gap between imprecise intentions and executable actions, the taxonomy gap induced by unpredictable environments, and the challenge of maintaining temporal state and progress awareness. This work introduces an architectural framework that enables robotic control by leveraging generative AI. The system follows a dual-AI design: an LLM translates high-level intentions into executable program code restricted to a formal robotic library and constrained by verifiable syntax, while a Vision-Language Model (VLM) provides semantic grounding via a distillation process. To ensure robustness, the framework incorporates environment-driven replanning triggers based on geometric and semantic thresholds, complemented by continuous runtime monitoring and an adaptive planning loop. Benchmarked across frontier models, our framework architecture demonstrates that grounding generative AI in a reactive, constrained loop enables robust fulfillment of complex intentions in dynamic and unknown environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dual-AI architecture where an LLM translates high-level natural language intentions into executable program code constrained by a formal robotic library, while a VLM provides semantic grounding via distillation, enabling robust robot control in dynamic, unknown environments.
AI.motivation: Deploying robots as Complex Adaptive Systems in unknown and dynamic environments requires a shift from rigid command libraries toward intention-based autonomy, since natural language is the only medium capable of expressing complex goals beyond finite instruction sets. While LLMs offer a path toward natural language goal description, their integration faces three key challenges: the formalization gap between imprecise intentions and executable actions, the taxonomy gap caused by unpredictable environments, and maintaining temporal state and progress awareness.
AI.method: The framework follows a dual-AI design: an LLM translates high-level intentions into executable program code restricted to a formal robotic library and constrained by verifiable syntax, while a Vision-Language Model (VLM) provides semantic grounding through a distillation process. Robustness is ensured via environment-driven replanning triggers based on geometric and semantic thresholds, complemented by continuous runtime monitoring and an adaptive planning loop.
AI.result: Benchmarked across frontier models, the framework architecture demonstrates that grounding generative AI in a reactive, constrained loop enables robust fulfillment of complex intentions in dynamic and unknown environments.
AI.conclusion: Grounding generative AI within a reactive, constrained loop is an effective design principle for achieving intention-based robot autonomy in dynamic, unknown environments, addressing the formalization, taxonomy, and temporal awareness gaps.

title: SearchWorld: Spatial Value-Grounded Imagination for UAV Object Search via World Models
summary: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object search involves a closed loop of perception, decision-making, and action under partial observability. Urban environments pose several challenges: large search areas and narrow egocentric views limit coverage, dense 3D geometry constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions require identifying a specific target among distractors. Many existing methods mitigate partial observability through explicit maps or memory representations, yet remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without explicitly predicting future states. World models enable prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts. However, image-generating world models can incur high inference latency, while spatially grounded planning remains challenging for latent world models. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses from world-model learning to expert imitation and imagination-based exploration refinement. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld improves the success rate to 23.8% (19.5% for the strongest published agent) and raises oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes (19.9% success rate). By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react.

AI.tldr: SearchWorld is a recurrent state-space world model that grounds prospective imagination in explicit spatial memory (BEV exploration and obstacle maps) for autonomous UAV object search in urban environments, achieving state-of-the-art success rates on UAV-ON.
AI.motivation: Autonomous UAV object search under partial observability in urban settings faces large search areas, narrow egocentric views that limit coverage, dense 3D geometry that constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions requiring target discrimination among distractors. Existing methods handle partial observability via explicit maps or memory but remain largely reactive, reasoning only over past observations without predicting future states. World models allow prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts, yet image-generating world models have high inference latency and spatially grounded planning is hard for latent world models.
AI.method: SearchWorld is a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. It maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network leverages this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy via imagined rollouts, avoiding a separately trained scalar critic. Training proceeds in stages: world-model learning, expert imitation, then imagination-based exploration refinement.
AI.result: On UAV-ON, SearchWorld raises the success rate to 23.8% (vs. 19.5% for the strongest published agent) and increases oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes with a 19.9% success rate.
AI.conclusion: By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than reactively, improving search performance and generalization in urban object search.

title: Fast and Robust Teach-and-Repeat Navigation Using MixVPR Visual Place Recognition*
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 2025 European Conference on Mobile Robots (ECMR)
summary: Teach-and-repeat navigation systems employing advanced visual place recognition techniques for localization exhibit key attributes for long-term mobile robot navigation, such as the ability to operate in unstructured and dynamic environments. However, existing solutions based on deep-learning techniques are computationally demanding, limiting their applicability. This work introduces a novel and efficient teach-and-repeat system built on the modern visual place recognition method MixVPR. Real-world testing demonstrated its ability to operate both indoors and outdoors, achieving robustness and navigation precision comparable to other state-of-the-art systems. In addition, its lower hardware requirements make it suitable for a wide range of robotic platforms and practical applications.

AI.tldr: A novel teach-and-repeat navigation system built on MixVPR achieves efficient, robust indoor/outdoor localization with lower hardware requirements while matching state-of-the-art accuracy.
AI.motivation: Teach-and-repeat navigation systems using visual place recognition enable long-term robot navigation in unstructured and dynamic environments, but deep-learning-based solutions are computationally demanding, restricting their practical applicability.
AI.method: The work introduces an efficient teach-and-repeat system built on the modern visual place recognition method MixVPR, and validates it through real-world testing.
AI.result: Real-world testing demonstrated the system operates both indoors and outdoors, achieving robustness and navigation precision comparable to other state-of-the-art systems, with lower hardware requirements.
AI.conclusion: The system's reduced hardware demands make it suitable for a wide range of robotic platforms and practical applications.

title: Relevance Is Not Sufficiency: What Actually Closes the Evidence Gap in Long-Term Memory QA
summary:
LLM agents that interact with a user across many sessions accumulate histories that exceed their context window, so they store past interactions in an external memory and answer each question from a small set of retrieved records. Existing memory systems rank records by lexical or embedding relevance, yet the top-ranked memories can each be relevant while jointly omitting a complementary fact that the answer requires, especially for multi-session and temporal questions.
  Drawing on the distinction between relevance and sufficiency in legal evidence scholarship, we recast memory retrieval as constructing a sufficient memory set.
  To operationalize this view, we introduce a blinded LLM judgment over the retrieved set, together with Gold Hit and Turn Hit as evidence-coverage proxies. We then propose Budgeted Flat Reconstruction (BFR), which builds sufficient sets over a fixed flat memory store in two stages. Specifically, we first apply Formal Concept Analysis for Memory Selection (FCA-MS) to decompose the question into information requirements and select a compact candidate subset that jointly covers them. Then, we repeatedly acquire unseen records through deeper text search or complementary entity and session views, stopping when the budget is exhausted.
  Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show that BFR outperforms same-store adaptations of recent agent-memory systems in both answer quality and evidence coverage. Specifically, on LongMemEval-S it raises judged accuracy from 72.4% to 82.2% and Turn Hit to 91.4%.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts LLM agent memory retrieval as constructing a sufficient memory set rather than ranking records by relevance, and proposes Budgeted Flat Reconstruction (BFR) to build sufficient sets over a fixed flat memory store, improving answer quality and evidence coverage on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S.
AI.motivation: LLM agents accumulate interaction histories across sessions that exceed their context window, forcing them to store past interactions in external memory and answer questions from a small set of retrieved records. Existing memory systems rank records by lexical or embedding relevance, but jointly the top-ranked memories may omit a complementary fact required for the answer, especially for multi-session and temporal questions.
AI.method: Drawing on the relevance versus sufficiency distinction from legal evidence scholarship, the authors recast memory retrieval as constructing a sufficient memory set. They introduce a blinded LLM judgment over the retrieved set plus Gold Hit and Turn Hit as evidence-coverage proxies. They then propose Budgeted Flat Reconstruction (BFR), a two-stage method over a fixed flat memory store: first, Formal Concept Analysis for Memory Selection (FCA-MS) decomposes the question into information requirements and selects a compact candidate subset jointly covering them; second, it repeatedly acquires unseen records via deeper text search or complementary entity and session views until the budget is exhausted.
AI.result: On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, BFR outperforms same-store adaptations of recent agent-memory systems in both answer quality and evidence coverage. On LongMemEval-S it raises judged accuracy from 72.4% to 82.2% and Turn Hit to 91.4%.
AI.conclusion: Reframing memory retrieval around sufficiency, operationalized through Budgeted Flat Reconstruction over a flat memory store, yields more complete evidence sets and better answers than relevance-ranked retrieval baselines.

title: Design optimization of tendon-driven robots considering tendon wrapping and shortcut
summary: This study proposes a multi-objective optimization method for tendon-driven arm design, addressing the inherent trade-off between joint torque and arm thickness through tendon wrapping and shortcut effects. We formulate the problem to simultaneously maximize torque and minimize thickness, solved using NSGA-II. The algorithm optimizes tendon routing, pulley configurations, and attachment points. Results reveal Pareto-optimal designs with effective moment arm expansion via strategic shortcuts, providing practical guidelines for compact high-torque arms. The optimized configurations demonstrate non-trivial patterns beyond conventional design intuition, offering new insights for engineering efficient robotic systems.

AI.tldr: A multi-objective optimization (NSGA-II) framework for tendon-driven arm design that trades off joint torque against arm thickness by jointly optimizing tendon routing, pulley configurations, and attachment points.
AI.motivation: Tendon-driven arm design faces an inherent trade-off between achievable joint torque and arm thickness, driven by tendon wrapping and shortcut (routing) effects. Conventional design intuition does not provide a systematic way to navigate this trade-off, so a principled optimization approach is needed.
AI.method: The design problem is formulated as a multi-objective optimization maximizing joint torque while minimizing arm thickness. It is solved using NSGA-II, with the decision variables comprising tendon routing, pulley configurations, and tendon attachment points.
AI.result: Optimization yields a set of Pareto-optimal designs. Effective moment-arm expansion is achieved through strategic tendon shortcuts. The optimized configurations exhibit non-trivial patterns that deviate from conventional design intuition.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical design guidelines for compact, high-torque tendon-driven arms and offers new insights for engineering efficient robotic systems.

title: TopoGraphRAG-Bench: Evaluating Multimodal GraphRAG on Layout-Grounded Evidence Reasoning
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Real-world documents distribute evidence across text, tables, figures, and captions within complex page layouts. Answering complex questions over such documents therefore requires more than retrieving relevant passages: systems must recover the evidence topology that connects heterogeneous evidence units. Existing GraphRAG evaluations remain largely text-centered, while multimodal document RAG benchmarks assess cross-modal retrieval and generation without directly evaluating recovery of the intended evidence topology. We introduce TOPOGRAPHRAG-BENCH, a layout-grounded benchmark for multimodal evidence reasoning in GraphRAG, comprising 2,024 questions over 201 long, visually rich documents. Questions are constructed bottom-up from text, figure, and table evidence units under three controlled topologies: single-hop retrieval, bridge-chain reasoning, and multi-source synthesis. To ensure that questions preserve their intended structure, we apply counterfactual validation for shortcut resistance, modality necessity, and evidence necessity. We evaluate text-only GraphRAG, page-level visual retrieval, and multimodal GraphRAG systems using retrieval, generation, and topology-aware reasoning metrics. Multimodal GraphRAG systems achieve the strongest overall performance, but still fail when visual-textual evidence alignment or multi-unit composition is incomplete. Text-only GraphRAG struggles when key dependencies are grounded in figures or tables, while page-level visual retrieval lacks the fine-grained structure needed for topology recovery. These findings motivate GraphRAG systems that move beyond text-derived entity relation graphs to explicitly model document layouts, cross-modal evidence alignment, and the reasoning roles of evidence units. Code and data are available at https://richardlrc.github.io/TopoGraphRAG-Bench/.

AI.tldr: TOPOGRAPHRAG-BENCH is a layout-grounded benchmark for multimodal evidence reasoning in GraphRAG, with 2,024 questions over 201 visually rich documents spanning three controlled evidence topologies, used to reveal that current systems fail to recover cross-modal evidence structure.
AI.motivation: Real-world documents distribute evidence across text, tables, figures, and captions in complex layouts, so complex QA requires recovering the evidence topology connecting heterogeneous evidence units rather than just retrieving passages. Existing GraphRAG evaluations are largely text-centered, and multimodal document RAG benchmarks assess cross-modal retrieval/generation without directly evaluating recovery of the intended evidence topology.
AI.method: The authors introduce TOPOGRAPHRAG-BENCH, comprising 2,024 questions over 201 long, visually rich documents. Questions are built bottom-up from text, figure, and table evidence units under three controlled topologies: single-hop retrieval, bridge-chain reasoning, and multi-source synthesis. Counterfactual validation is applied to enforce shortcut resistance, modality necessity, and evidence necessity. They evaluate text-only GraphRAG, page-level visual retrieval, and multimodal GraphRAG using retrieval, generation, and topology-aware reasoning metrics.
AI.result: Multimodal GraphRAG achieves the strongest overall performance but still fails when visual-textual evidence alignment or multi-unit composition is incomplete. Text-only GraphRAG struggles when key dependencies are grounded in figures or tables, while page-level visual retrieval lacks the fine-grained structure needed for topology recovery.
AI.conclusion: Current GraphRAG systems must move beyond text-derived entity relation graphs to explicitly model document layouts, cross-modal evidence alignment, and the reasoning roles of evidence units. Code and data are available at https://richardlrc.github.io/TopoGraphRAG-Bench/.

title: NAViLoss: An Underwater Navigation-Aware Dual-Residual Objective for Physics-Consistent Learning
summary: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) commonly rely on inertial navigation systems (INS) aided by Doppler velocity logs (DVLs) for reliable underwater navigation. Accurate DVL velocity estimation is therefore essential for successful operation. Recent learning-based methods have demonstrated improved DVL velocity estimation, particularly under degraded measurement conditions. However, their training objectives typically rely on conventional regression losses that are highly sensitive to large residuals and corrupted observations. Additionally, they do not explicitly account for the physical consistency and measurement uncertainty associated with the underlying sensing process. To address these limitations, this paper introduces navigation-aware loss (NAViLoss), a robust and uncertainty-aware objective function for learning-based AUV velocity estimation. NAViLoss jointly penalizes the velocity-estimation residual in the navigation-state domain and the beam-consistency residual in the DVL measurement domain. Its bounded formulation limits the influence of large residuals, while an adaptive mechanism regulates the uncertainty in beam geometry. Furthermore, NAViLoss is integrated with a DeepONet architecture to form a novel NAVi-DeepONet model for seamless estimation of an underwater vehicle's velocity. Lastly, our model is evaluated using approximately 10,000m of semi-synthetic AUV experimental data collected during multiple real-world sea trials. Experimental results demonstrate a 44% improvement in velocity-estimation accuracy compared with conventional and learning-based baselines. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of navigation-aware and uncertainty-adaptive loss design for robust learning-based underwater velocity estimation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes NAViLoss, a robust and uncertainty-aware loss function for learning-based AUV velocity estimation from DVL data, integrated with a DeepONet architecture (NAVi-DeepONet), achieving 44% accuracy improvement over baselines on ~10,000m of semi-synthetic sea-trial data.
AI.motivation: AUV navigation relies on INS aided by DVLs, making accurate DVL velocity estimation essential. Recent learning-based methods improve estimation under degraded conditions, but their training objectives use conventional regression losses that are highly sensitive to large residuals and corrupted observations, and they ignore the physical consistency and measurement uncertainty of the sensing process.
AI.method: The authors introduce NAViLoss, a robust, uncertainty-aware objective that jointly penalizes the velocity-estimation residual in the navigation-state domain and the beam-consistency residual in the DVL measurement domain. Its bounded formulation limits the influence of large residuals, and an adaptive mechanism regulates uncertainty in beam geometry. NAViLoss is integrated with a DeepONet architecture to form the NAVi-DeepONet model for velocity estimation.
AI.result: Evaluated on approximately 10,000m of semi-synthetic AUV experimental data from multiple real-world sea trials, the model achieves a 44% improvement in velocity-estimation accuracy compared with conventional and learning-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the effectiveness of navigation-aware and uncertainty-adaptive loss design for robust learning-based underwater velocity estimation.

title: DUDA-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Multimodal Data-Driven Urban Diagnosis
summary: Urban diagnosis integrates heterogeneous observations to identify urban problems, localize affected areas, and investigate contributing factors, informing evidence-based urban planning and management. However, its reliance on labor-intensive, case-specific expert workflows limits scalability and reuse, motivating the exploration of agent-based execution. To evaluate this capability, we introduce DUDA-Bench, a hierarchical and interactive benchmark that formalizes data-driven urban diagnosis as a multi-stage agent workflow. It comprises 86 atomic and 22 workflow tasks spanning four analytical stages, grounded in multimodal data from 12 cities covering five urban problem types. Evaluations of seven backbone models and five agent systems reveal a substantial gap between isolated analytical competence and end-to-end diagnosis, with system benefits varying across backbones. Trajectory analysis shows that unresolved evidence gaps propagate across stages, while successful recovery involves revising assumptions and actions using feedback. These findings highlight limitations in coordinating analytical capabilities across stages, particularly adaptive planning, evidence integration, and verification. More broadly, DUDA-Bench provides a framework for translating expert analytical workflows into hierarchical agent tasks and process-aware evaluation, supporting systematic assessment of end-to-end analytical capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DUDA-Bench, a hierarchical, interactive benchmark that formalizes data-driven urban diagnosis as a multi-stage agent workflow to evaluate agent-based execution of urban diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Urban diagnosis relies on labor-intensive, case-specific expert workflows that limit scalability and reuse, motivating exploration of agent-based execution. However, the capability of agents to perform end-to-end urban diagnosis is not yet systematically evaluated.
AI.method: DUDA-Bench comprises 86 atomic and 22 workflow tasks across four analytical stages, grounded in multimodal data from 12 cities covering five urban problem types. Seven backbone models and five agent systems are evaluated, complemented by trajectory analysis.
AI.result: A substantial gap exists between isolated analytical competence and end-to-end diagnosis, with system benefits varying across backbones. Trajectory analysis shows unresolved evidence gaps propagate across stages, while successful recovery involves revising assumptions and actions using feedback.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight limitations in coordinating analytical capabilities across stages, especially adaptive planning, evidence integration, and verification. DUDA-Bench offers a framework for translating expert analytical workflows into hierarchical agent tasks and process-aware evaluation.

title: Do Better Visual Representations Always Lead to Better End-to-End Autonomous Driving?
summary: Visual foundation models (VFMs) are increasingly integrated into end-to-end autonomous driving for their powerful representations, yet it remains unclear when these representations improve driving performance. To investigate this question, we introduce ViRA, a planner-agnostic visual representation alignment framework that keeps the planner architecture and inference cost unchanged. Our study reveals three findings: (1) VFM-guided visual representations consistently improve driving performance across diverse end-to-end planners, with gains extending to zero-shot closed-loop evaluation. (2) The choice of VFM target matters for planning performance, and alignment to a different VFM can further benefit planners with pre-trained VFM encoders. (3) Auxiliary perception supervision reduces sensitivity to VFM target selection, narrowing the EPDMS spread across five targets from 2.7 to 0.5 points and potentially compensating for less effective VFM targets. Guided by these findings, we develop ViRA-Diffusion, a diffusion-based planner trained without auxiliary perception supervision, which achieves 92.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest, outperforming recent methods in our comparison by at least 1.9 points. The results motivate jointly considering target selection and planner supervision when integrating VFMs into end-to-end autonomous driving. The results and demo are available at https://github.com/OpenDriveLab/ViRA.

AI.tldr: Visual foundation model (VFM) representations can consistently improve end-to-end driving performance; the choice of VFM target and the presence of auxiliary perception supervision jointly shape gains, motivating a planner called ViRA-Diffusion.
AI.motivation: VFMs are increasingly used in end-to-end autonomous driving for their powerful representations, but it remains unclear when these representations actually improve driving performance. The paper systematically investigates this question.
AI.method: Introduces ViRA, a planner-agnostic visual representation alignment framework that keeps planner architecture and inference cost unchanged. It studies three factors: VFM-guided representation effects across diverse planners, VFM target choice, and auxiliary perception supervision. Based on the findings, develops ViRA-Diffusion, a diffusion-based planner trained without auxiliary perception supervision.
AI.result: (1) VFM-guided representations consistently improve driving performance across diverse end-to-end planners, including zero-shot closed-loop evaluation. (2) VFM target choice matters for planning, and aligning to a different VFM can further benefit planners with pre-trained VFM encoders. (3) Auxiliary perception supervision reduces sensitivity to VFM target selection, narrowing the EPDMS spread across five targets from 2.7 to 0.5 points. ViRA-Diffusion achieves 92.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest, outperforming recent methods by at least 1.9 points.
AI.conclusion: Target selection and planner supervision should be jointly considered when integrating VFMs into end-to-end autonomous driving. Code and demo are available at the provided repository.

title: From Plausible Hierarchies to Useful Taxonomies: Evaluating Agentic Harnesses on Customer Feedback
summary: Taxonomies are the symbolic representations through which AI systems organize evidence, aggregate patterns, and answer questions over large document collections. Over customer feedback, the category tree decides how every record is counted and routed, which problems get seen, and which team owns them. Agentic harnesses now make it easy to generate a plausible-looking hierarchy, and such trees are checked today with generic, individually scoped checks: each name fits its description, sits under the right parent, and stays distinct from its siblings. We ask a more operational question: when is a generated hierarchy actually useful as a production taxonomy? We build six taxonomies over two proprietary feedback corpora (1,940 and 5,000 records): for each corpus, a production reference and two repeated runs of the same harness under identical inputs. All six pass every generic naming and structure check, and a deeper product-coverage check even prefers the generated trees. Yet in every generated tree at least 97.7% of leaf names merely restate an ancestor's name (13.9% and 2.9% in the references), and in one, three of every four records fall under multiple top-level categories. We introduce two families of whole-tree metrics: structural discriminators test whether a tree's shape was learned from the data or imposed by its generator; team partitionability tests whether branches split feedback into groups teams can own. Trees the generic checks rate as equally correct differ by 27 percentage points in cross-branch leakage, and only one of the two beats a random split. Surface plausibility is an insufficient measure of taxonomy quality: evaluation must measure the whole tree as well as each node.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that surface-level, node-by-node checks are insufficient for evaluating AI-generated taxonomies; whole-tree metrics reveal that hierarchies passing all generic checks can still be structurally degenerate (up to 97.7% redundant leaf names) and operationally unusable for routing feedback, differing by 27 percentage points in cross-branch leakage.
AI.motivation: Taxonomies are symbolic representations through which AI systems organize evidence, aggregate patterns, and answer questions over large document collections. In customer feedback, the category tree determines how records are counted and routed, which problems surface, and which team owns them. Agentic harnesses now easily generate plausible-looking hierarchies, and these are validated only with generic, individually scoped checks (name fits description, correct parent, distinct from siblings). The authors ask a more operational question: when is a generated hierarchy actually useful as a production taxonomy?
AI.method: The authors build six taxonomies over two proprietary feedback corpora (1,940 and 5,000 records): for each corpus, one production reference plus two repeated runs of the same generation harness under identical inputs. They then introduce two families of whole-tree metrics: (1) structural discriminators, which test whether a tree's shape was learned from the data or imposed by its generator; and (2) team partitionability, which tests whether branches split feedback into groups that teams can own. They evaluate all six trees against both generic node-level checks and these new whole-tree metrics, including a product-coverage check and a random-split baseline.
AI.result: All six taxonomies pass every generic naming and structure check, and a deeper product-coverage check even prefers the generated trees over the references. However, in every generated tree at least 97.7% of leaf names merely restate an ancestor's name, versus 13.9% and 2.9% in the reference taxonomies, and in one generated tree three of every four records fall under multiple top-level categories. Trees that generic checks rate as equally correct differ by 27 percentage points in cross-branch leakage, and only one of the two generated trees beats a random split on team partitionability.
AI.conclusion: Surface plausibility is an insufficient measure of taxonomy quality. Evaluation must measure the whole tree as well as each individual node, since generic node-level checks cannot detect structural redundancy or operational unusability for routing and ownership assignment.

title: RoboPace: Contact-Aware Time-Optimal Retiming for Action-Chunk Policies
summary: Robot manipulation data collection has been shifting from teleoperation toward robot-free demonstrations, through interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) or directly from human hands. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on such data inherit the demonstrator's timing. Yet human timing does not directly transfer to robots: compliant hands tolerate fast contact, whereas robots may overshoot due to actuator and tracking limitations; conversely, robots can move faster in free space. This motivates a unified approach that reconciles execution speed with contact safety. We present RoboPace, an online retiming layer that preserves the policy's geometric path while adapting its timing, respecting the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. It adapts execution speed based on predicted contact, jointly accounting for contact-dependent speed limits and the robot's motion constraints. The method requires no policy retraining and operates in real time. Across three contact-rich tasks on a dual-arm robot, faster uniform execution and physical-limit-only retiming largely fail. RoboPace instead achieves higher overall success than slow uniform execution while completing four of five commands in approximately half the time, retaining the reliability of slow execution without its time cost.

AI.tldr: RoboPace is a real-time, retraining-free retiming layer that preserves a VLA policy's geometric path while adapting execution timing to the target robot's kinematic and dynamic limits, using predicted contact to balance speed against contact safety, achieving high success in about half the time of slow uniform execution on three contact-rich dual-arm tasks.
AI.motivation: Data collection for robot manipulation is shifting from teleoperation to robot-free demonstrations (e.g., UMI or human hands), so VLA policies inherit human timing. Human timing does not transfer directly to robots: compliant hands tolerate fast contact while robots may overshoot due to actuator and tracking limits, yet robots can move faster in free space. This mismatch motivates unifying execution speed with contact safety.
AI.method: An online retiming layer that preserves the policy's geometric path while adapting its timing. It adapts execution speed based on predicted contact, jointly accounting for contact-dependent speed limits and the robot's motion constraints. It requires no policy retraining and operates in real time.
AI.result: On three contact-rich tasks with a dual-arm robot, faster uniform execution and physical-limit-only retiming largely fail. RoboPace achieves higher overall success than slow uniform execution while completing four of five commands in roughly half the time, retaining slow execution's reliability without its time cost.
AI.conclusion: Reconciling execution speed with contact safety via contact-aware online retiming yields reliable and substantially faster contact-rich manipulation without retraining the underlying VLA policy.

title: Let the Library Speak: Self-Advertised Method Selection for Formal Proving
summary: LLM-based formal provers can retrieve relevant lemmas and prior proofs, but relevance alone does not say whether a mathematical method can be used on the current theorem. A method has prerequisites, a target, an intended action, and obligations that its use leaves to prove. Methods that look equally related to a theorem may therefore differ substantially in whether they offer a plausible next step. We formulate this as an applicability-aware method-selection problem and introduce self-advertisement: before candidates are ranked, a model generates a problem-specific proposal for each one, stating what part of the goal it targets, what action it would take, and what conditions that action requires. We organize 82 reusable methods from Putnam 2000-2014 as Method Contracts, which pair applicability descriptions with Mathlib anchors, a checked example or scaffold, and expected proof obligations. A single batched call elicits proposals across the library; vague or unsupported proposals are demoted, yielding a ranked shortlist accompanied by inspectable claims about each candidate's use. We analyze when similarity-based representations cannot distinguish methods with different applicability, how errors in applicability estimates affect shortlist quality, and what a checked scaffold guarantees under its stated assumptions. Against lexical, embedding, and embedding-plus-LLM reranking baselines, self-advertisement achieves 95.0% hit@5 on Putnam 2015-2025, compared with 84.2% for the strongest reranker. On IMO ProofBench, it achieves 91.7% compared with 88.3%. These results indicate improved coverage of annotated methods in the retrieved shortlists, particularly on Putnam.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates lemma/method selection for LLM-based formal provers as an applicability-aware problem and proposes "self-advertisement," where a model generates problem-specific proposals describing each candidate method's target, action, and prerequisites before ranking, achieving 95.0% hit@5 on Putnam 2015-2025 and 91.7% on IMO ProofBench.
AI.motivation: Retrieving relevant lemmas and prior proofs by relevance alone does not indicate whether a mathematical method is actually usable on the current theorem, since methods carry prerequisites, targets, intended actions, and residual obligations. Equally "related" methods can differ greatly in whether they offer a plausible next step, so method selection must be applicability-aware rather than purely similarity-based.
AI.method: The authors formalize applicability-aware method selection and introduce self-advertisement: before ranking, a model produces a problem-specific proposal for each candidate stating the targeted goal part, the action it would take, and required conditions. They curate 82 reusable methods from Putnam 2000-2014 as Method Contracts, pairing applicability descriptions with Mathlib anchors, a checked example or scaffold, and expected proof obligations. A single batched call elicits proposals across the library; vague or unsupported proposals are demoted, producing a ranked shortlist with inspectable claims about each candidate's use. They also analyze when similarity-based representations fail to distinguish methods with different applicability, how applicability-estimation errors affect shortlist quality, and what a checked scaffold guarantees under stated assumptions.
AI.result: Against lexical, embedding, and embedding-plus-LLM reranking baselines, self-advertisement reaches 95.0% hit@5 on Putnam 2015-2025 versus 84.2% for the strongest reranker, and 91.7% on IMO ProofBench versus 88.3%. This indicates improved coverage of annotated methods in retrieved shortlists, particularly on Putnam.
AI.conclusion: Applicability-aware selection via self-advertisement improves retrieval shortlists for formal provers, delivering markedly higher hit rates than similarity-based and reranking baselines, with the largest gains on Putnam, and yields inspectable justifications for each candidate's proposed use.

title: YUBI-STAG: Contact and Semantic-Rich Alignment for VLAs via Automated Video-Language Grounding
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models acquire broad manipulation capabilities via large-scale pretraining, yet eliciting them through language requires fine-grained alignment between instructions and physical interactions. Existing robot demonstrations typically provide only coarse task descriptions, omitting how actions are executed, including which gripper acts, which object is contacted, and how it is grasped and moved. We introduce YUBI-STAG, a framework for Spatio-Temporal Annotation and Grounding that automatically enriches manipulation demonstrations with interaction-rich semantics to align pretrained VLAs with fine-grained manipulation language. Combining contact-object segmentation with vision-language models, YUBI-STAG annotates object identities, attributes and states, per-gripper actions, bimanual coordination, and spatially grounded interactions. To address YUBI-STAG's reliance on localized sequences and multi-stage VLM inference, we distill it into YUBI-VLM. YUBI-VLM directly recovers action structure and annotations from raw, unsegmented video in few inference calls and operates from wrist views alone. We evaluate both frameworks on YUBI-STAG-Bench across temporal, semantic, and spatial grounding tasks. YUBI-VLM retains much of YUBI-STAG's annotation accuracy with fewer inference calls and shorter runtime while generalizing to unseen manipulations. Finally, post-training VLA policies on these annotations aligns them with fine-grained language and contact-aware structure. Bimanual experiments demonstrate improved performance and instruction following, including control over object identity, acting gripper, target location, and spatial relations absent from original labels.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces YUBI-STAG and its distilled variant YUBI-VLM, frameworks that automatically annotate manipulation demonstrations with fine-grained spatio-temporal and interaction semantics to better align pretrained VLAs with detailed manipulation language.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action models possess broad manipulation capabilities from large-scale pretraining, but leveraging them via language demands fine-grained alignment between instructions and physical interactions. Existing robot demonstrations only supply coarse task descriptions, omitting execution details such as which gripper acts, which object is contacted, and how it is grasped and moved.
AI.method: The authors propose YUBI-STAG, which combines contact-object segmentation with vision-language models to annotate object identities, attributes, states, per-gripper actions, bimanual coordination, and spatially grounded interactions. To overcome YUBI-STAG's reliance on localized sequences and multi-stage VLM inference, they distill it into YUBI-VLM, which recovers action structure and annotations directly from raw, unsegmented video in few inference calls and works from wrist views alone.
AI.result: Evaluated on YUBI-STAG-Bench across temporal, semantic, and spatial grounding tasks, YUBI-VLM retains much of YUBI-STAG's annotation accuracy with fewer inference calls and shorter runtime while generalizing to unseen manipulations. Post-training VLA policies on these annotations aligns them with fine-grained language and contact-aware structure; bimanual experiments show improved performance and instruction following, including control over object identity, acting gripper, target location, and spatial relations absent from original labels.
AI.conclusion: Automatic, interaction-rich semantic annotation of demonstrations effectively aligns pretrained VLAs with fine-grained manipulation language, and distillation into a single efficient VLM preserves accuracy while improving efficiency and generalization.

title: Efficient Reasoning with Flow Language Models
summary: Flow Language Models (FLMs) have emerged as a continuous-state alternative to discrete diffusion language models, yet the role of their continuous representations in reasoning remains unclear. We investigate this question by comparing the reasoning efficiency of FLMs and discrete diffusion models, measured by solution accuracy under matched denoising steps. Unlike discrete diffusion, which passes categorical states between denoising steps, FLMs evolve a continuous sequence representation throughout denoising and decodes it into discrete tokens only at the end. Our theoretical analysis shows, from a superposition perspective, how information retained in these continuous states can benefit reasoning. Intermediate-state interventions provide further empirical support for this theoretical account, showing that removing information about alternative candidates reduces subsequent solution recovery. Together, these findings show that FLMs allow evidence for multiple candidates to persist and inform subsequent reasoning before a discrete answer is produced. Furthermore, our experiments on maze planning and Sudoku tasks show that FLMs achieve greater reasoning efficiency in the few-step regime: FLMs achieves higher sequence accuracy than discrete diffusion baselines at matched model sizes and small denoising steps. On maze planning tasks, FLMs can also achieve comparable accuracy with smaller models. For example, on Maze15, FLM reaches the 95\% accuracy target at 64 denoising steps with 36.5\% fewer parameters than MDLM. These findings point to continuous state spaces as a promising foundation for reasoning models that require fewer refinement steps.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the role of continuous representations in Flow Language Models (FLMs) for reasoning, showing theoretically and empirically that continuous states preserve superposition of candidate evidence, yielding higher reasoning efficiency than discrete diffusion in few-step regimes.
AI.motivation: FLMs have emerged as a continuous-state alternative to discrete diffusion language models, but the role of their continuous representations in reasoning remains unclear. The paper aims to clarify whether and how continuous state evolution benefits reasoning compared to discrete diffusion, which passes categorical states between denoising steps.
AI.method: The authors compare reasoning efficiency of FLMs and discrete diffusion models under matched denoising steps. They provide a theoretical analysis from a superposition perspective on how information retained in continuous states benefits reasoning, and conduct intermediate-state interventions to test the account empirically. Experiments cover maze planning and Sudoku tasks, comparing sequence accuracy at matched model sizes and small denoising steps.
AI.result: FLMs achieve greater reasoning efficiency in the few-step regime, attaining higher sequence accuracy than discrete diffusion baselines at matched model sizes and small denoising steps. Intermediate-state interventions show that removing information about alternative candidates reduces subsequent solution recovery. On maze planning tasks, FLMs can match accuracy with smaller models, e.g., on Maze15, FLM reaches 95% accuracy at 64 denoising steps with 36.5% fewer parameters than MDLM.
AI.conclusion: Continuous state spaces allow evidence for multiple candidates to persist and inform subsequent reasoning before a discrete answer is produced. This points to continuous state spaces as a promising foundation for reasoning models that require fewer refinement steps.

title: ΔWAM: Distilling Action Tangent Fields into World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAM) improve robot policies by augmenting sparse action supervision with dense future prediction. However, much of the predictable future is dominated by appearance and scene persistence rather than action-dependent dynamics. We observe that several recent WAM designs, including optical flow, motion-centric representations, and latent actions, can be understood from a common perspective in which world supervision becomes more efficient as it contains a higher proportion of action-relevant variation. Based on this insight, we introduce Action Tangent Fields, which reformulate world supervision through a local Taylor expansion of how actions induce changes in future dynamics. We represent future dynamics in Residual-VAE space, where the future latent remains recoverable from the current latent and its residual, and use a strong action-conditioned world model (ACWM) to probe the local correspondence between action variations and residual-world variations. This local first-order structure is distilled into the WAM to guide its denoising supervision toward dynamics that are more tightly coupled to action, rather than merely predictable from appearance. Across LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and RoboTwin2.0-Plus, our method consistently improves robustness to lighting, background, camera, layout, and other environmental perturbations. Despite using no large-scale embodied pretraining, it achieves stronger robustness under several distribution shifts than pretrained policies. We further distill multi-step VideoDiT denoising into a single step for efficient inference. Our results suggest that effective WAM supervision should remain information-rich while concentrating its predictive capacity on the directions along which actions change the future.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Action Tangent Fields, a World Action Model supervision scheme that reformulates future prediction as a local Taylor expansion of action-induced changes in future dynamics, concentrating world supervision on action-relevant variation to improve robot policy robustness under environmental distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: World Action Models (WAM) use dense future prediction to augment sparse action supervision, but much of the predictable future reflects appearance and scene persistence rather than action-dependent dynamics, making world supervision inefficient. The authors observe that recent WAM designs (optical flow, motion-centric representations, latent actions) can be unified under one view: world supervision becomes more efficient as it captures a higher proportion of action-relevant variation.
AI.method: Action Tangent Fields reformulate world supervision via a local (first-order) Taylor expansion of how actions induce changes in future dynamics. Future dynamics are represented in Residual-VAE space, where the future latent is recoverable from the current latent plus its residual. A strong action-conditioned world model (ACWM) probes the local correspondence between action variations and residual-world variations. This local first-order structure is distilled into the WAM to steer its denoising supervision toward dynamics tightly coupled to action rather than merely appearance-predictable. Multi-step VideoDiT denoising is further distilled into a single step for efficient inference.
AI.result: Across LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and RoboTwin2.0-Plus, the method consistently improves robustness to lighting, background, camera, layout, and other environmental perturbations. Despite using no large-scale embodied pretraining, it achieves stronger robustness under several distribution shifts than pretrained policies.
AI.conclusion: Effective WAM supervision should remain information-rich while concentrating predictive capacity on the directions along which actions change the future. Focusing world supervision on action-relevant dynamics yields more robust policies and enables efficient single-step inference via denoising distillation.

title: RSI-Forge: From Research Papers to Environments for Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Environments are the foundation of recursive self-improvement: they provide the problems agents work on and the feedback used to evaluate progress. Yet constructing challenging research environments with reliable evaluation still depends on domain experts, limiting their scale and disciplinary coverage. We introduce RSI-Forge, a multi-agent pipeline that turns published papers into executable environments for self-improvement. Three agents coordinate construction, reproduction, and review to produce tasks with automated evaluators; each paper's method is independently reimplemented to establish a baseline score. We present 210 environments across 18 fields, including 90 reviewed by independent human domain experts. Both experts and agent judges give high ratings to the potential for improving the provided starting solutions and the evaluators' ability to distinguish solution quality, whereas experts are more critical of shortcut resistance, faithfulness to the source paper, and whether a single idea can exhaust a task. To validate their use for repeated improvement, we evaluate four models over 3 successive attempts on 120 environments, with each attempt inheriting prior code and notes while model weights remain fixed. At least one model improves after the first attempt in 84% of environments. Models also outperform the reproduced paper methods in 68 of the 120 environments, demonstrating room for gains beyond these baselines. Transcript analysis identifies work beyond parameter tuning in 95% of these successful attempts. Analysis of the resulting trajectories shows that models scoring lower on these tasks explore less, more often accept gains smaller than the reported standard error, and rely more heavily on tuning to the development set. RSI-Forge provides a scalable approach to constructing research environments for training and evaluating self-improving agents.

AI.tldr: RSI-Forge is a multi-agent pipeline that converts published papers into executable research environments with automated evaluators, yielding 210 environments across 18 fields, and demonstrates that models can iteratively improve over successive attempts.
AI.motivation: Recursive self-improvement depends on challenging research environments with reliable evaluation, but constructing them requires domain experts, limiting scale and disciplinary coverage.
AI.method: A multi-agent pipeline where three agents coordinate construction, reproduction, and review to produce tasks with automated evaluators; each paper's method is independently reimplemented to establish a baseline score. Four models are then evaluated over 3 successive attempts on 120 environments, each inheriting prior code and notes with fixed weights.
AI.result: 210 environments across 18 fields, 90 reviewed by independent human experts. Experts and agent judges rate improvement potential and evaluator discrimination highly, but experts are more critical of shortcut resistance, faithfulness, and single-idea exhaustion. At least one model improves after the first attempt in 84% of environments; models outperform reproduced paper methods in 68/120. Transcript analysis finds work beyond parameter tuning in 95% of successful attempts. Lower-scoring models explore less, accept gains below reported standard error, and over-rely on development-set tuning.
AI.conclusion: RSI-Forge offers a scalable approach to constructing research environments for training and evaluating self-improving agents.

title: AeroEval: Staged Program and Execution Validation for AI-Generated Drone Missions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate drone programs from natural-language mission descriptions, but syntactically valid programs may still violate user intent, environmental constraints, and mission-level behavior. This problem is pronounced in cyber-physical applications, where correctness depends on the interaction among generated code, mobile sensing, environmental geometry, event-driven analytics, and physical execution. Existing drone code-generation systems primarily use prompt guardrails or simulator outcomes and provide limited failure localization. We present AeroEval, an agent-assisted middleware for staged validation of AI-generated drone missions. AeroEval combines deterministic program analysis with context-grounded LLM agents. It first validates program syntax, platform API usage, and mission intent, and then evaluates the realized behavior using execution trajectories, mission requirements, and environmental context. Each stage returns structured failure information for iterative regeneration. In our evaluation using 20 navigation tasks and five analytical mission types over AirSim and Gazebo simulators, AeroEval improves navigation success from 55% to 95%. In a stagewise ablation study, our Code and Trajectory Validators by themselves achieve mean run-level success rates of 44% and 56%, respectively, while the full AeroEval pipeline achieves 88%; the stages detect complementary failures in program structure, API usage, mission intent, obstacle avoidance, altitude, coverage, and event-driven transitions and the guided regeneration corrects for them. Across the main analytics missions, AeroEval increases aggregate run-level success from 34% for one-shot AeroGen to 88% within the regeneration budget. These results demonstrate the benefit of combining program-level and execution-grounded agentic validation for AI-generated drone applications in the evaluated environment.

AI.tldr: AeroEval is an agent-assisted middleware that performs staged validation of AI-generated drone missions by combining deterministic program analysis with context-grounded LLM agents, improving navigation success from 55% to 95% and analytics success from 34% to 88%.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate drone programs from natural-language mission descriptions, but syntactically valid programs may still violate user intent, environmental constraints, and mission-level behavior. This is critical in cyber-physical applications where correctness depends on interactions among generated code, mobile sensing, environmental geometry, event-driven analytics, and physical execution. Existing drone code-generation systems rely mainly on prompt guardrails or simulator outcomes and offer limited failure localization.
AI.method: AeroEval couples deterministic program analysis with context-grounded LLM agents in a staged pipeline. Stage one validates program syntax, platform API usage, and mission intent; stage two evaluates realized behavior using execution trajectories, mission requirements, and environmental context. Each stage returns structured failure information to support iterative regeneration.
AI.result: Evaluated on 20 navigation tasks and five analytical mission types across AirSim and Gazebo, AeroEval raises navigation success from 55% to 95%. In a stagewise ablation, Code and Trajectory Validators alone reach mean run-level success of 44% and 56%, while the full pipeline reaches 88%. The stages detect complementary failures in program structure, API usage, mission intent, obstacle avoidance, altitude, coverage, and event-driven transitions, and guided regeneration corrects them. For analytics missions, AeroEval lifts aggregate run-level success from 34% (one-shot AeroGen) to 88% within the regeneration budget.
AI.conclusion: Combining program-level and execution-grounded agentic validation benefits AI-generated drone applications in the evaluated environment, offering structured failure localization and effective iterative regeneration.

title: LLM-Enabled UAV Dispatch: A System-Level Survey and Taxonomy
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) dispatch is beginning to move beyond isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation toward system-level coordination supported by semantic reasoning and LLM-based interfaces. This survey provides a unified characterization of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems that bridges semantic intent, symbolic decision-making, and physical UAV execution. Rather than treating LLMs as standalone add-ons, we conceptualize them as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer connecting human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules. We organize the literature into four representative dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. For each paradigm, we analyze its decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. We further examine how LLMs support semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation. We discuss the implications of these paradigms for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements, and identify open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency. This survey provides a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems.

AI.tldr: This survey unifies LLM-enabled UAV dispatch into a semantic orchestration layer, organized into four dispatch paradigms, and reviews LLM roles, system trade-offs, and open challenges for safety-critical deployment.
AI.motivation: UAV dispatch is shifting from isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation toward system-level coordination enabled by semantic reasoning and LLM interfaces. However, the literature lacks a unified characterization bridging semantic intent, symbolic decision-making, and physical UAV execution. This survey addresses that gap for safety-critical UAV dispatch systems.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize LLMs not as standalone add-ons but as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer linking human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules. They organize the literature into four dispatch paradigms—pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch—and analyze each along decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. They further examine LLM support for semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation.
AI.result: The survey characterizes each paradigm's decision logic, architecture, and control flow, and maps LLM capabilities onto dispatch functions. It discusses paradigm implications for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements, and identifies open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency.
AI.conclusion: The survey offers a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems, framing LLMs as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer and highlighting verification, feasibility, and deployment challenges for future work.

title: On-Demand Robotic Assembly via Differentiable Geometric Part Repair
summary: Transitioning from a digital design to a robotic assembly process currently requires months of expert manual tuning to reconcile part geometries with robotic constraints. This paper presents an end-to-end, autonomous pipeline for the design and physical construction of bespoke wooden assemblies. A generative AI agent translates user prompts into initial 3D geometries, balancing the visual fidelity of the design with select physical constraints. The assemblability of the design is further improved by a gradient-based repair stage that backpropagates through a graph attention network surrogate to adjust component geometries. In addition to correcting for disjointed and overlapping components, we demonstrate hardware-specific corrections, differentiably optimizing the geometry of components to enable robot screwdriving for 86.7% of 60 novel natural language inputs, significantly outperforming prior work by a factor of ten. For ten of the structures, we physically demonstrate assemblability with two UR5e robots. This work marks a meaningful step toward on-demand robotic manufacturing, enabling the rapid production of customized, low-volume goods.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an end-to-end autonomous pipeline that goes from natural language prompts to physically assembled bespoke wooden structures, using a generative AI agent plus a gradient-based repair stage on a graph attention network surrogate.
AI.motivation: Translating a digital design into a robotic assembly process currently demands months of expert manual tuning to reconcile part geometries with robotic constraints, which blocks on-demand, low-volume customized manufacturing.
AI.method: A generative AI agent converts user prompts into initial 3D geometries, balancing visual fidelity against selected physical constraints. A gradient-based repair stage then backpropagates through a graph attention network surrogate to adjust component geometries, correcting disjointed and overlapping parts as well as applying hardware-specific corrections, differentiably optimizing geometry so that components support robot screwdriving.
AI.result: The pipeline enables robot screwdriving for 86.7% of 60 novel natural language inputs, outperforming prior work by a factor of ten. For ten of the structures, assemblability was physically demonstrated with two UR5e robots.
AI.conclusion: The work represents a meaningful step toward on-demand robotic manufacturing, enabling rapid production of customized, low-volume goods.

title: MIMESIS: Learning User Simulators as Training Environments for Interactive Agents
summary: Training and evaluating interactive language agents typically requires rich user interactions, yet collecting human feedback is expensive and difficult to scale. Simulated users offer a scalable alternative, but they must both resemble real user behavior and provide useful learning experiences for agents. In contrast, most agent-training frameworks rely on off-the-shelf assistant LLMs, whose helpfulness can make them overly cooperative, explicit, and behaviorally homogeneous compared with real users. We introduce MIMESIS, a purpose-built user simulator trained on human conversations with explicit reasoning supervision and 13 realistic behavioral patterns derived from real user interactions. Empirically, our 9B model achieves a SOUL-Index of 65.7, surpassing the strongest frontier model. Compared with Claude-Opus-5, the strongest baseline on RealUserSim and SimulatorArena, MIMESIS improves behavioral fidelity by 13.4 points and reduces Turing distance by 3.6 points, respectively. We then freeze the simulator and train an agent by interacting with the frozen simulator using multi-turn reinforcement learning. Across eight environments, training with MIMESIS yields better agent performance than training with GPT-5.5 under all nine unseen user simulators, demonstrating stronger generalization to new user simulators. Moreover, we propose Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation (CSD), which leverages simulator-generated private reasoning traces and subsequent utterances as feedback on how well the agent addresses user needs. A coach converts this information into concise coaching notes that describe how the agent can better anticipate user needs and adapt its behavior over the course of an interaction. CSD turns this feedback into dense, token-level supervision beyond sparse task rewards, yielding further gains across all nine evaluation user models.

AI.tldr: MIMESIS is a purpose-built user simulator trained on human conversations with explicit reasoning supervision and 13 realistic behavioral patterns, which outperforms frontier models in behavioral fidelity and enables more generalizable agent training via multi-turn RL, further boosted by Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation (CSD).
AI.motivation: Training and evaluating interactive language agents needs rich user interactions, but human feedback is costly and hard to scale. Existing simulated users based on off-the-shelf assistant LLMs tend to be overly cooperative, explicit, and behaviorally homogeneous, failing to resemble real users or provide useful learning experiences.
AI.method: The authors introduce MIMESIS, a purpose-built user simulator trained on human conversations with explicit reasoning supervision and 13 realistic behavioral patterns derived from real interactions (a 9B model). They freeze the simulator and train an agent via multi-turn reinforcement learning against it. They also propose Coached On-Policy Self-Distillation (CSD), which uses simulator-generated private reasoning traces and subsequent utterances as feedback; a coach converts these into concise coaching notes, turning them into dense token-level supervision beyond sparse task rewards.
AI.result: The 9B MIMESIS achieves a SOUL-Index of 65.7, surpassing the strongest frontier model. Versus Claude-Opus-5, the strongest baseline on RealUserSim and SimulatorArena, MIMESIS improves behavioral fidelity by 13.4 points and reduces Turing distance by 3.6 points. Across eight environments, agents trained with MIMESIS outperform those trained with GPT-5.5 under all nine unseen user simulators. CSD yields further gains across all nine evaluation user models.
AI.conclusion: A purpose-built user simulator with explicit reasoning supervision and realistic behavioral patterns improves behavioral fidelity and produces agents that generalize better to new user simulators. CSD provides dense token-level supervision from simulator feedback, delivering additional gains, highlighting the value of simulator-driven, feedback-rich agent training.

title: End-to-End Autonomous Generation of Human Assembly Plans
summary: Turning a CAD design into an assembly plan is still largely done by hand, requiring engineers to reason about geometric feasibility, tool access, stability, and the ergonomics of human assembly. In this work, we encode long-established design for assembly (DfA) principles into a contained, end-to-end approach for generating assembly plans. Our approach takes only a mesh assembly and produces either a step-by-step assembly manual or a structured failure report, requiring no joint metadata, fastener annotations, or additional information. Four major components of a manufacturing plan are addressed autonomously: an assembly tool list, the assembly sequence and subassemblies, an assembly manual, and design feedback for improving assemblability. For determining the sequence plan, we systematically disassemble the object in a physics simulator and apply a cost function that encodes DfA principles. Manual generation, tool labelling, and assembly feedback rely primarily on multimodal large language models. Compared with a baseline that always removes the outermost part first from Tian et al., DfA-aware sequence planning reduces simulated assembly time, measured with a robot-arm assembly-time proxy, by 35% on 136 assemblies of 5 to 30 parts. The correct tool is selected for 88.6% of assembly steps. A vision-language model judge compares the generated manuals against ablated variants, identifying which page elements carry the information a reader needs. The presented approach and open-source code are available for use by engineers or AI agents looking to rapidly accelerate the creation of manufacturing plans for a given product design.

AI.tldr: This work encodes design-for-assembly (DfA) principles into an end-to-end pipeline that takes only a mesh assembly and autonomously produces an assembly tool list, sequence/subassemblies, an assembly manual, and assemblability feedback.
AI.motivation: Turning a CAD design into an assembly plan is still largely manual, requiring engineers to reason about geometric feasibility, tool access, stability, and human ergonomics. Existing approaches also typically need joint metadata, fastener annotations, or other extra information.
AI.method: The approach requires only a mesh assembly. The sequence plan is obtained by systematically disassembling the object in a physics simulator and applying a cost function that encodes DfA principles. Manual generation, tool labelling, and assembly feedback rely primarily on multimodal large language models.
AI.result: Compared with a baseline (Tian et al.) that always removes the outermost part first, DfA-aware sequence planning reduces simulated assembly time (robot-arm proxy) by 35% on 136 assemblies of 5 to 30 parts. The correct tool is selected for 88.6% of assembly steps. A vision-language model judge compares generated manuals against ablated variants, identifying which page elements carry needed information.
AI.conclusion: The method autonomously addresses four components of a manufacturing plan and is released as open-source code for engineers or AI agents to accelerate manufacturing-plan creation.

title: The Attribution Blind Spot: Layerwise Trajectory Diagnostics for Source Reliance in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
summary: A retrieval-augmented model can match a document without relying on it.
