Controlled knowledge conflicts make source choice observable and let us ask a second question that prediction alone cannot answer: which internal-state properties define useful intervention directions? We study paired hidden-state changes with Latent Trajectory Shift (LTS), a signed projection onto a training-fitted first principal component (PC1), and keep verified training exposure separate from behavioral source choice. Across the evaluated conflicts, state-change magnitude is often the stronger predictor, whereas signed PC1 is the stronger selective controller: equal-norm interventions change source preference while better preserving non-target behavior, and the frozen direction transfers across the tested datasets and aligned model pairs. A same-system OLMo study further combines positive choice and control results with inconclusive exposure detection at the achieved power. The central result is a separation: representations that diagnose what a model will choose need not be the representations that best control that choice.

AI.tldr: State-change magnitude often predicts a retrieval-augmented model's source choice better, but a signed Latent Trajectory Shift (PC1 projection) is the stronger selective controller of that choice, revealing that diagnostic and control representations can differ.
AI.motivation: A retrieval-augmented model can match a document without relying on it, so prediction alone is insufficient. Controlled knowledge conflicts make source choice observable and raise a second question: which internal-state properties define useful intervention directions. The work also aims to keep verified training exposure separate from behavioral source choice.
AI.method: The authors study paired hidden-state changes using Latent Trajectory Shift (LTS), a signed projection onto a training-fitted first principal component (PC1). They compare state-change magnitude against signed PC1 and test equal-norm interventions, non-target behavior preservation, and transfer of the frozen direction across datasets and aligned model pairs. A same-system OLMo study is also conducted.
AI.result: Across evaluated conflicts, state-change magnitude is often the stronger predictor, whereas signed PC1 is the stronger selective controller: equal-norm interventions change source preference while better preserving non-target behavior, and the frozen direction transfers across the tested datasets and aligned model pairs. The OLMo study combines positive choice and control results with inconclusive exposure detection at the achieved power.
AI.conclusion: The central result is a separation: representations that diagnose what a model will choose need not be the representations that best control that choice.

title: Enhancing Robotic Perception and Adaptability through Sensor Fusion and Origami-Inspired Designs
summary: Compact mobile robots must recover scene geometry under changing lighting and surface texture while working within tight payload and cost limits. We present a compact mobile robot that uses origami-inspired wheels for locomotion and active control of its sensing geometry. As the wheels move between terrain-adaptive configurations, the changing chassis pitch sweeps a 2D LiDAR through intermediate elevations; held wheel positions provide a chosen viewing angle. An IMU accounts for chassis attitude, and a fusion node projects LiDAR returns into the RGB-D depth stream supplied to RTAB-Map. The arrangement uses the wheel actuation already present on a sub-300 USD, sub-2 kg prototype to extend the scanner's viewing geometry. We assess depth fusion in a textureless indoor corridor and an outdoor sunlit area, with three runs per sensor configuration in each setting. Mean full-frame invalid-depth fractions fell from 21% to 11% indoors and from 48% to 18% outdoors. The prototype combines improved depth coverage with a continuously adjustable LiDAR viewpoint using the same actuation that reconfigures its wheels.

AI.tldr: A sub-300 USD, sub-2 kg origami-wheeled mobile robot uses its wheel actuation to sweep and hold a 2D LiDAR's viewing geometry, fusing LiDAR returns into the RGB-D stream for RTAB-Map; mean invalid-depth fraction drops from 21% to 11% indoors and 48% to 18% outdoors.
AI.motivation: Compact mobile robots must recover scene geometry under changing lighting and surface texture while constrained by tight payload and cost budgets. Conventional fixed sensor rigs struggle in textureless or sunlit scenes, so a low-cost way to extend sensing geometry is needed.
AI.method: Origami-inspired wheels provide locomotion and active control of sensing geometry. As wheels move between terrain-adaptive configurations, changing chassis pitch sweeps a 2D LiDAR through intermediate elevations; held wheel positions set a chosen viewing angle. An IMU accounts for chassis attitude, and a fusion node projects LiDAR returns into the RGB-D depth stream supplied to RTAB-Map. The arrangement reuses existing wheel actuation on a sub-300 USD, sub-2 kg prototype.
AI.result: Depth fusion assessed in a textureless indoor corridor and an outdoor sunlit area, three runs per sensor configuration per setting. Mean full-frame invalid-depth fractions fell from 21% to 11% indoors and from 48% to 18% outdoors.
AI.conclusion: The prototype achieves improved depth coverage with a continuously adjustable LiDAR viewpoint, using the same actuation that reconfigures its wheels, within tight payload and cost limits.

title: Cognitive Schemas, Laws and Tasks
summary:
This paper asks how explicit representations can support reusable cognitive schemas in knowledge-based problem solving. We develop a structural framework in which schemas are organized by the information and relations required for their use, rather than introduced as unrelated primitives. The framework also distinguishes context-dependent relations from more stable structures that can be reused across different representations.
  Tasks are described through the information available, the unknowns to be determined, and the constraints that admissible solutions must satisfy. This makes it possible to separate limitations of the representation from limitations of the solving procedure. In particular, we distinguish inconsistency, underdetermination, and contextual insufficiency, where the current representation lacks distinctions or relations required by the external task meaning. We also show formally when a reduction of representation preserves the task-relevant solution structure.
  The resulting task--schema interface offers a structured way to describe representational conditions relevant to problem solving. It supports the reuse and stabilization of derived knowledge while remaining independent of the particular mechanism used to generate candidate solutions. This may provide a useful component for future solver architectures that combine structured knowledge, verification, and learned proposal mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structural framework for organizing reusable cognitive schemas by the information and relations needed for their use, distinguishing stable structures from context-dependent relations. Tasks are characterized by available information, unknowns, and constraints, enabling separation of representational limits from procedural limits via inconsistency, underdetermination, and contextual insufficiency, with formal conditions for structure-preserving reductions. The resulting task–schema interface is solver-agnostic and may inform architectures combining structured knowledge, verification, and learned proposal mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Explicit representations are needed to support reusable cognitive schemas in knowledge-based problem solving, but schemas are often introduced as unrelated primitives rather than being systematically organized by their functional requirements. A principled framework is needed to clarify when representational limitations—as opposed to limitations of the solving procedure—account for failures in problem solving.
AI.method: A structural framework organizes schemas according to the information and relations required for their use, and separates context-dependent relations from stable, reusable structures. Tasks are described by available information, unknowns to be determined, and constraints on admissible solutions. The framework distinguishes inconsistency, underdetermination, and contextual insufficiency, and provides formal conditions under which a reduction of representation preserves the task-relevant solution structure.
AI.result: The framework yields a task–schema interface that describes representational conditions relevant to problem solving, supports reuse and stabilization of derived knowledge, and remains independent of the particular mechanism used to generate candidate solutions.
AI.conclusion: The task–schema interface may serve as a component for future solver architectures that combine structured knowledge, verification, and learned proposal mechanisms.

title: Towards Accurate End-Effector Localization for UMI-Style Robotic Manipulation Teaching
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. Project page: https://mild-web.github.io
summary: Robot demonstration learning requires accurate and temporally complete end-effector localization during close-range manipulation and camera occlusion. Existing SLAM benchmarks emphasize navigation motions, whereas manipulation datasets prioritize policy learning over localization evaluation. We introduce MILD, a Manipulation-Interface Localization Dataset with real-world and simulation sequences. The real-world subset provides 86 sensor sequences from Insta360 X5 and Insight9 across 15 repeated tabletop tasks, calibration assets, and a per-execution robot end-effector reference trajectory. The simulation subset, MILD-Sim, extends task coverage in Isaac Sim for controlled manipulation-replay studies. Benchmarking visual-inertial and fiducial-aided systems on instrumented real-world recordings reveals large differences in both TCP-relative trajectory error and temporal coverage, even under the same nominal task. To support marker-augmented teaching workspaces without a pre-surveyed fiducial map, we present AprilVINS, which combines fisheye visual-inertial estimation with sequence-local AprilTag geometry and separates prior admission from guarded export of the jointly optimized state. On Insta360 AprilTag4 recordings, AprilVINS(full) under a unified protocol with sequence-specific profiles reaches millimeter-level SE(3)-aligned TCP-relative APE RMSE with high time completion and lower reported error than the tested routes under their respective protocols, whereas fisheye VIO without tag factors remains at centimeter scale. Ablations separate accuracy from exportability, and a MILD-Sim replay study provides task-specific tolerance references for interpreting those error magnitudes. Together, MILD and AprilVINS provide a diagnostic benchmarking framework for UMI-style demonstration collection. Code, datasets, and evaluation manifests will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MILD, a manipulation-focused localization dataset (real-world + Isaac Sim), and AprilVINS, a fisheye visual-inertial system fused with sequence-local AprilTag geometry, forming a diagnostic benchmark for end-effector localization in robot demonstration collection.
AI.motivation: Robot demonstration learning needs accurate, temporally complete end-effector localization during close-range manipulation and camera occlusion. Existing SLAM benchmarks target navigation, while manipulation datasets focus on policy learning rather than localization evaluation, leaving a gap in benchmarking localization for UMI-style demonstration collection.
AI.method: The work builds MILD: 86 real-world sensor sequences from Insta360 X5 and Insight9 over 15 repeated tabletop tasks, with calibration assets and per-execution end-effector reference trajectories, plus MILD-Sim in Isaac Sim for controlled manipulation-replay. It benchmarks visual-inertial and fiducial-aided systems, and proposes AprilVINS, combining fisheye visual-inertial estimation with sequence-local AprilTag geometry, separating prior admission from guarded export of the jointly optimized state.
AI.result: On Insta360 AprilTag4 recordings under a unified protocol, AprilVINS(full) reaches millimeter-level SE(3)-aligned TCP-relative APE RMSE with high time completion and lower reported error than tested routes under their own protocols, while fisheye VIO without tag factors stays at centimeter scale. Ablations decouple accuracy from exportability, and the MILD-Sim replay study gives task-specific tolerance references.
AI.conclusion: MILD and AprilVINS together provide a diagnostic benchmarking framework for UMI-style demonstration collection. Code, datasets, and evaluation manifests are to be released upon acceptance.

title: Ream: Unfolding Mutual Awareness in Human-Agent Workspaces
summary: As AI agents work alongside humans in shared workspaces, a mutual awareness challenge arises: agents act at speeds that outpace human monitoring, and users' evolving interests are not always expressed in chat. This challenge is especially pressing in literature review, where both parties retrieve, read, and synthesize a growing body of papers. We present Ream, a literature review workspace that supports mutual awareness through structured artifacts, bidirectional engagement tracking, and localized visualizations. Users can see each party's activity within these documents, and agents can retrieve the same history to guide their work. In studies with eighteen researchers, participants used these traces to inspect evidence, steer agents, communicate through annotations, and reflect on their research focus. Shared histories also helped agents build on earlier work. These findings inform how engagement traces within shared documents can support transparency, personalized assistance, and coordination in human-agent knowledge work.

AI.tldr: Ream is a literature review workspace that enables mutual awareness between humans and AI agents via structured artifacts, bidirectional engagement tracking, and localized visualizations, allowing both parties to view and reuse each other's activity histories.
AI.motivation: AI agents act faster than humans can monitor, and users' evolving interests are not always expressed in chat, creating a mutual awareness gap. This is especially pressing in literature review, where both parties retrieve, read, and synthesize a growing body of papers.
AI.method: The authors designed Ream, a literature review workspace with three key mechanisms: structured artifacts, bidirectional engagement tracking, and localized visualizations. Users can see each party's activity within shared documents, and agents can retrieve the same history to guide their work. They conducted studies with eighteen researchers.
AI.result: Participants used the engagement traces to inspect evidence, steer agents, communicate through annotations, and reflect on their research focus. Shared histories also helped agents build on earlier work.
AI.conclusion: Engagement traces within shared documents can support transparency, personalized assistance, and coordination in human-agent knowledge work.

title: Juno: Taming Predictive Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict masked or future observations in representation space, offering a natural source of predictive latents for vision-language-action (VLA) models. Yet making these latents useful across pretraining, policy learning, and deployment requires addressing three failures: mismatch with embodiment-specific control, interference with action learning, and teacher miscalibration under distribution shifts. We introduce Juno, a unified framework built around one action-conditioned JEPA that serves as a control-aligned representation backbone, a predictive teacher, and an adaptable dynamics model. During pretraining, we train it on embodiment-matched trajectories and use a dynamic CLS loss to transfer motion-weighted patch dynamics to a compact global state. During policy learning, we fuse current-frame JEPA patches into VLA perception and use a decoupled reasoning branch with separate transformation parameters to distill future latent states for action generation. During deployment, we adapt the world model on all observed transitions, including failed rollouts, freeze the adapted teacher, and re-align the policy on verified executions using LoRA adapters and a trainable action head, without expert corrections or task rewards. On SimplerEnv, Juno raises average success from $60.9\%$ to $68.5\%$ over Qwen3GR00T, the strongest baseline, and test-time adaptation further reaches $72.7\%$; on a real robot, it retains $70\%$--$75\%$ success under background, height, and object shifts where the base policy collapses to $0\%$.

AI.tldr: Juno is a unified VLA framework built on a single action-conditioned JEPA serving as a control-aligned representation backbone, predictive teacher, and adaptable dynamics model, addressing embodiment mismatch, action-learning interference, and teacher miscalibration. It improves SimplerEnv success from 60.9% to 68.5% (72.7% with test-time adaptation) and retains 70–75% real-robot success under distribution shifts where the base policy collapses to 0%.
AI.motivation: JEPAs predict masked or future observations in representation space, offering predictive latents for VLA models, but three failures block their usefulness across pretraining, policy learning, and deployment: (1) mismatch with embodiment-specific control, (2) interference with action learning, and (3) teacher miscalibration under distribution shifts. The paper aims to resolve all three within one framework.
AI.method: Juno centers on one action-conditioned JEPA reused in three roles. Pretraining: train on embodiment-matched trajectories with a dynamic CLS loss that transfers motion-weighted patch dynamics to a compact global state. Policy learning: fuse current-frame JEPA patches into VLA perception and use a decoupled reasoning branch with separate transformation parameters to distill future latent states for action generation. Deployment: adapt the world model on all observed transitions including failed rollouts, freeze the adapted teacher, and re-align the policy on verified executions via LoRA adapters and a trainable action head, without expert corrections or task rewards.
AI.result: On SimplerEnv, Juno raises average success from 60.9% to 68.5% over the strongest baseline Qwen3GR00T, and test-time adaptation reaches 72.7%. On a real robot, it retains 70%–75% success under background, height, and object shifts where the base policy collapses to 0%.
AI.conclusion: A single action-conditioned JEPA can simultaneously act as a control-aligned representation backbone, predictive teacher, and adaptable dynamics model, yielding consistent gains in simulation and markedly improved robustness to real-world distribution shifts without expert corrections or task rewards.

title: Reliability of LLM Judges for Evaluating Entity Alignment
summary: Entity Alignment (EA) identifies equivalent entities across knowledge graphs and is critical for knowledge base integration and ontology merging. Evaluating EA systems at scale requires expensive expert annotation, making systematic assessment across diverse domains practically infeasible. LLM-as-judge evaluation offers a potentially scalable alternative, yet its reliability for structured prediction tasks like EA remains unstudied. We present the first systematic benchmarking study across three frontier models, three datasets, and four EA systems, using perturbation bias diagnostics, meta-evaluation across all dataset-judge-prompt combinations, and counterfactual label-flip tests. We identify anchor bias, a failure mode in which judges invert discrimination when the system's decision label is visible. Label exposure causally collapses judge discrimination (J-ROC-AUC 0.12-0.87), while a label-free protocol recovers near-ceiling capability on distinctive-name datasets (0.93-1.00) and significant recovery on biomedical pairs (0.93-0.95). Counterfactual experiments confirm causality (FSR 53-99%) and reveal a frontier model paradox: stronger judges exhibit greater label sensitivity, not less. A blinded two-annotator human evaluation (102 pairs, Cohen's kappa=0.902) confirms this mechanism directly. We release the first biomedical EA benchmark (MeSH-SNOMED CT, 15K pairs) and a reproducible auditing framework for LLM judge reliability in EA. Code and data are available at https://github.com/vaibhavalakshmiravideshik/llm-as-a-judge-entity-alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic benchmarking study of LLM-as-judge reliability for entity alignment (EA), identifying a novel "anchor bias" failure mode where exposing the system's decision label collapses judge discrimination, and proposing a label-free protocol as a mitigation.
AI.motivation: Evaluating EA systems at scale requires expensive expert annotation, making systematic cross-domain assessment practically infeasible. LLM-as-judge evaluation offers a scalable alternative, but its reliability for structured prediction tasks such as EA remains unstudied.
AI.method: The authors benchmark three frontier models across three datasets and four EA systems using perturbation bias diagnostics, meta-evaluation over all dataset-judge-prompt combinations, and counterfactual label-flip tests. A blinded two-annotator human evaluation (102 pairs, Cohen's kappa=0.902) validates the mechanism, and a new biomedical EA benchmark (MeSH-SNOMED CT, 15K pairs) plus a reproducible auditing framework are released.
AI.result: The study identifies anchor bias: label exposure causally collapses judge discrimination (J-ROC-AUC 0.12-0.87), while a label-free protocol recovers near-ceiling capability on distinctive-name datasets (0.93-1.00) and significant recovery on biomedical pairs (0.93-0.95). Counterfactual experiments confirm causality (FSR 53-99%) and reveal a frontier model paradox: stronger judges exhibit greater label sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: LLM-as-judge evaluation for EA is unreliable under label-visible protocols due to anchor bias, and stronger frontier models are not immune—they are more susceptible. A label-free protocol substantially mitigates the issue, and the released benchmark and auditing framework enable reproducible reliability assessment for EA judges.

title: Many Ways to Succeed: Diversity-Driven RL Fine-Tuning for VLA Generalization
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies through closed-loop experience, yet generalization beyond the fine-tuning distribution remains limited. Our analysis reveals a selective reshaping of exploration: RL contracts behavior globally, yet diversifies successful trajectories, elicits success with fewer rollouts, and covers more of the latent task-valid solution space than supervised fine-tuning. Broader successful-mode coverage may provide alternative strategies under distribution shifts. Inspired by this, we introduce DRIVE (Diversity-driven RL fIne-tuning for VLA gEneralization), which turns successful-behavior diversity into an explicit RL objective. DRIVE groups rollouts under matched task conditions, compares their trajectories with temporal alignment, and derives a success-conditioned intrinsic reward from relative behavioral diversity. This design encourages broader coverage of feasible solutions without rewarding diverse failures or superficial timing differences. Across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill3, and RoboTwin 2.0, DRIVE improves the average out-of-domain (OOD) performance over vanilla RL fine-tuning by 5.3 points on $π_0$ and 2.0 points on $π_{0.5}$. On a dual-arm AgileX PiPER-X platform, DRIVE further increases average OOD success from 64.1% to 73.3% (+9.2 points), demonstrating gains that persist under physical deployment.

AI.tldr: DRIVE is a diversity-driven RL fine-tuning method for VLA policies that uses a success-conditioned intrinsic reward based on relative behavioral diversity to improve out-of-distribution generalization.
AI.motivation: RL fine-tuning improves VLA policies via closed-loop experience, but generalization beyond the fine-tuning distribution remains limited. Analysis shows RL contracts behavior globally yet diversifies successful trajectories and covers more of the latent task-valid solution space, suggesting broader successful-mode coverage enables alternative strategies under distribution shifts.
AI.method: DRIVE groups rollouts under matched task conditions, compares their trajectories with temporal alignment, and derives a success-conditioned intrinsic reward from relative behavioral diversity. This encourages broader coverage of feasible solutions without rewarding diverse failures or superficial timing differences.
AI.result: Across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill3, and RoboTwin 2.0, DRIVE improves average OOD performance over vanilla RL fine-tuning by 5.3 points on π0 and 2.0 points on π0.5. On a dual-arm AgileX PiPER-X platform, it raises average OOD success from 64.1% to 73.3% (+9.2 points).
AI.conclusion: Turning successful-behavior diversity into an explicit RL objective yields consistent OOD generalization gains that persist under physical deployment.

title: DrugTargetWorld: A Synthetic Biobank for Training and Benchmarking AI Scientists
comment: 34 pages main text, 92 pages supplementary material; 6 main figures. Project: https://DrugTargetWorld.vercel.app. Code: https://github.com/sammargolis/DrugTargetWorld. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/sammargolis/DrugTargetWorld-assets
summary: Drug target discovery requires distinguishing molecules that causally drive disease from those that are merely associated with it. Training and evaluating AI agents to perform this workflow end-to-end is difficult because real world biobanks lack known causal ground truth and participant-level data is access controlled. We introduce DrugTargetWorld, a framework that procedurally generates simulated biobanks, or "worlds," with known but concealed causal structure. Each world contains genotypes, proteins, health records, outcomes, and synthetic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for 54,000 participants. Agents must construct a disease phenotype, identify causal driver proteins, infer the beneficial direction of modulation, and optionally conduct virtual 'wet lab' experiments. We evaluated nine agents in 540 episodes across 20 cardiovascular worlds and three experimental budgets. Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol achieved the highest mean composite scores, 39.98 and 35.38 of 100, respectively, and both recovered 64% of causal drivers on average. However, no agent reliably distinguished misleading non-causal proteins, and performance remained limited by the integrative judgments required to connect phenotype construction, causal evidence, and intervention decisions. By making each world's causal structure known to the evaluator but hidden from the agent, DrugTargetWorld turns end-to-end drug target discovery into a scalable training and evaluation problem with verifiable reward.

AI.tldr: DrugTargetWorld procedurally generates simulated biobanks with hidden causal structure, turning end-to-end drug target discovery into a scalable, verifiable-reward benchmark; nine agents scored poorly (best 39.98/100), recovering 64% of causal drivers but failing on misleading non-causal proteins.
AI.motivation: Drug target discovery requires separating causally disease-driving molecules from merely associated ones. Training and evaluating AI agents end-to-end is hard because real biobanks lack known causal ground truth, and participant-level data is access-controlled.
AI.method: The authors introduce DrugTargetWorld, a framework that procedurally generates simulated biobanks ("worlds") with known but concealed causal structure. Each world includes genotypes, proteins, health records, outcomes, and synthetic MRI for 54,000 participants. Agents must construct a disease phenotype, identify causal driver proteins, infer the beneficial direction of modulation, and optionally run virtual wet-lab experiments. Evaluation covered nine agents over 540 episodes across 20 cardiovascular worlds and three experimental budgets.
AI.result: Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol achieved the highest mean composite scores, 39.98 and 35.38 out of 100, each recovering 64% of causal drivers on average. No agent reliably distinguished misleading non-causal proteins, and performance was limited by the integrative judgments linking phenotype construction, causal evidence, and intervention decisions.
AI.conclusion: By making each world's causal structure known to the evaluator but hidden from the agent, DrugTargetWorld converts end-to-end drug target discovery into a scalable training and evaluation problem with verifiable reward.

title: Borrowed Eyes: Markerless Nano-UAV Flight with an Active Quadruped Observer
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ICRA 2027
summary: Nano unmanned aerial vehicles (nano-UAVs) can navigate confined spaces that larger robots cannot, but their payload capacity severely limits the sensors and compute available for self-localization in global navigation satellite system (GNSS)-denied environments. We present a vision-based system that localizes a nano-UAV from a quadruped robot with an arm-mounted camera. The quadruped tracks the drone, estimates its position in its own coordinate system using segmentation masks and depth, and transmits that position over a real-time radio link. To ensure continuous tracking, we developed a perception-aware nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) that dynamically adjusts the quadruped's body and arm to maximize the drone's visibility, treating observation reliability as a primary control objective. Relying solely on this external estimate, the nano-UAV executed predefined trajectories from takeoff to landing with a median 3D localization error of 59 mm. The system demonstrates robustness against short visual occlusions by smoothly transitioning to onboard inertial flight when line-of-sight is temporarily lost. Ultimately, this framework allows a quadruped to offload the localization burden of a nano-UAV, enabling inspection of complex spaces that neither robot could navigate alone.

AI.tldr: A quadruped with an arm-mounted camera localizes a nano-UAV via vision and streams its position over a radio link, using a perception-aware NMPC that repositions the body and arm to keep the drone visible; the nano-UAV flies on this external estimate with 59 mm median 3D error and falls back to onboard inertial flight during brief occlusions.
AI.motivation: Nano-UAVs can access confined spaces inaccessible to larger robots, but their stringent payload limits restrict onboard sensing and computation, making self-localization impossible in GNSS-denied environments. Offloading localization to an external, more capable robot is therefore desirable.
AI.method: A quadruped robot is equipped with an arm-mounted camera and tracks the nano-UAV, estimating its position in the quadruped's coordinate frame from segmentation masks and depth data, then transmitting the estimate over a real-time radio link. A perception-aware nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) dynamically adjusts both the quadruped's body pose and arm configuration, treating observation reliability (drone visibility) as a primary control objective to maintain continuous tracking.
AI.result: Relying solely on the external estimate, the nano-UAV executed predefined trajectories from takeoff to landing with a median 3D localization error of 59 mm. The system also showed robustness to short visual occlusions by smoothly switching to onboard inertial flight when line-of-sight was temporarily lost.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables a quadruped to offload the localization burden of a nano-UAV, allowing collaborative inspection of complex spaces that neither robot could navigate alone.

title: World Potential Model: Pretrained World Knowledge as Progress Potentials
summary: Long-horizon language agents often receive supervision only from terminal task outcomes, leaving little signal for distinguishing productive intermediate behavior from stagnation or even regression. Rather than learning a separate value function or process reward model for every task, we ask whether pretrained models can recognize task progress from their existing world knowledge. We formalize this capability with a World Potential Model (WPM), a goal-conditioned evaluator of task-relative realized progress in agent contexts. In ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, off-the-shelf pretrained models substantially outperform chance at recovering realized-progress structure without task-specific evaluator fine-tuning. We further anchor these progress judgments to task-specific milestones to obtain scalar world potentials, whose temporal differences provide process-sensitive step-level credit for policy optimization. Under matched comparisons, WPM-guided optimization improves success over outcome-only GRPO across all evaluated configurations. Together, these results provide initial evidence that pretrained world knowledge can support reusable realized-progress evaluation and provide useful supervision for long-horizon agents.

AI.tldr: Pretrained models can recognize task progress from existing world knowledge, enabling a reusable World Potential Model (WPM) that provides process-level credit for long-horizon agent policy optimization.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon language agents rely on terminal outcome supervision, which offers sparse signal and fails to distinguish productive intermediate behavior from stagnation or regression. Prior approaches typically require learning a separate value function or process reward model per task.
AI.method: The authors formalize a World Potential Model (WPM): a goal-conditioned evaluator of task-relative realized progress in agent contexts, leveraging pretrained world knowledge rather than task-specific evaluator fine-tuning. Progress judgments are anchored to task-specific milestones to yield scalar world potentials, whose temporal differences supply process-sensitive step-level credit for policy optimization.
AI.result: In ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, off-the-shelf pretrained models substantially outperform chance at recovering realized-progress structure without task-specific fine-tuning. Under matched comparisons, WPM-guided optimization improves success over outcome-only GRPO across all evaluated configurations.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained world knowledge can support reusable realized-progress evaluation and provide useful supervision for long-horizon agents, offering an alternative to task-specific value functions or process reward models.

title: Decoding Neural Population Dynamics through Robotic Analog
summary: Animal evidence shows that precise voluntary movements arise from rotational neural population dynamics in motor cortex, but their physical effects remain unknown. We developed a robotic analog of biological motor systems with artificial muscles, multimodal sensors, and a neural network controller trained via reinforcement learning. The robotic analog exhibited accurate movements, robustness to damage, and neural population dynamics akin to animals. This task-driven, embodied model illuminates the causal link between neural population dynamics and motor outcomes. We discovered that neural rotations generate oscillatory maneuvers orthogonal to the reaching direction, optimizing trajectory adjustments, which is confirmed by primate neural data. The model also revealed counterintuitive neural energy principles under sensor and motor redundancies, and striking Eureka moments during motor learning, bridging biological and artificial systems. These findings provide new perspectives on how neural dynamics contribute to accurate and flexible movement, inspiring future intelligent robots with animal-like mobility.

AI.tldr: A bio-inspired robotic arm with artificial muscles and a reinforcement-learning neural controller reproduces animal-like rotational neural population dynamics, revealing that these rotations drive orthogonal oscillatory maneuvers that optimize reaching, and uncovering neural energy principles and "Eureka" learning moments.
AI.motivation: Animal evidence links precise voluntary movement to rotational neural population dynamics in motor cortex, but the physical/causal effects of these dynamics on motor outcomes remain unknown. Bridging this gap requires an embodied system where neural dynamics and their behavioral consequences can be directly manipulated and observed.
AI.method: The authors built a robotic analog of biological motor systems featuring artificial muscles, multimodal sensors, and a neural network controller trained via reinforcement learning, creating a task-driven, embodied model that can be compared against primate neural recordings.
AI.result: The robot achieved accurate movements and robustness to damage while exhibiting neural population dynamics akin to animals. Neural rotations were found to generate oscillatory maneuvers orthogonal to the reaching direction, optimizing trajectory adjustments—a finding confirmed by primate neural data. The model also revealed counterintuitive neural energy principles under sensor and motor redundancies, and striking Eureka moments during motor learning.
AI.conclusion: The embodied model establishes a causal link between neural population dynamics and motor outcomes, offering new perspectives on how neural dynamics enable accurate, flexible movement and inspiring future intelligent robots with animal-like mobility.

title: Dual- versus Single-Suggestion AI Support for Radiographic Interpretation in Residents: Randomized Multireader Study
summary:
Purpose: To compare dual- and single-suggestion AI support for radiographic interpretation by residents, particularly when the shared AI suggestion was incorrect.
  Materials and Methods: This prospective, multicenter, randomized three-arm reader study was conducted at three hospitals in China from July to September 2026 (ChiCTR2600129243). After specialty stratification, 132 residents with fewer than 3 years of clinical experience were randomized 1:1:1 to GPT-5.4 alone (group A), GPT-5.4 plus Kimi-K2.6 (group B), or GPT-5.4 plus Gemini-3.6 Flash (group C); 123 were analyzed. Participants interpreted 60 radiographs before and after AI support. The primary outcome was accuracy change. Welch ANOVA and Holm-adjusted t tests compared support conditions; HC3 linear models assessed specialty interaction.
  Results: Among 123 residents (mean age, 24.1 years +/- 1.4; 65 women), radiology residents showed greater accuracy improvement with dual- than single-suggestion support (B-A, 6.69 percentage points [95% CI, 0.97-12.40]; C-A, 7.87 percentage points [95% CI, 1.64-14.11]; Holm-adjusted P = .030 for both), whereas accuracy change did not differ in non-radiology residents (P = .20). When GPT-5.4 was incorrect, AI-assisted accuracy was higher with dual- than single-suggestion support in radiology residents (40.1% and 40.4% vs 20.0%) and non-radiology residents (31.3% and 31.0% vs 12.1%) (all Holm-adjusted P < .001). The dual-suggestion effect differed by specialty (interaction difference, 10.44 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.36-16.52; P < .001).
  Conclusion: Dual-suggestion support may mitigate the influence of erroneous AI suggestions, with greater accuracy improvement observed in radiology but not non-radiology residents.

AI.tldr: This randomized three-arm reader study (123 residents, 60 radiographs each, pre/post AI support) compared dual-suggestion (GPT-5.4 + Kimi-K2.6 or Gemini-3.6 Flash) versus single-suggestion (GPT-5.4 alone) AI support. Dual-suggestion support improved accuracy more than single-suggestion in radiology residents (about +7-8 percentage points) but not in non-radiology residents, and largely mitigated the harmful effect of an incorrect shared AI suggestion, especially in radiology residents.
AI.motivation: Residents frequently rely on AI suggestions for radiographic interpretation, and a single erroneous AI suggestion can mislead them. Providing two independent AI suggestions (dual-suggestion support) may reduce over-reliance on any one potentially wrong output, but it was unclear whether dual-suggestion support outperforms single-suggestion support, whether benefits differ by specialty, and how each performs specifically when the shared AI suggestion is incorrect.
AI.method: Prospective, multicenter, randomized three-arm reader study at three Chinese hospitals (July-September 2026; ChiCTR2600129243). After specialty stratification, 132 residents (<3 years clinical experience) were randomized 1:1:1 to GPT-5.4 alone (A), GPT-5.4 + Kimi-K2.6 (B), or GPT-5.4 + Gemini-3.6 Flash (C); 123 analyzed. Each interpreted 60 radiographs before and after AI support. Primary outcome: accuracy change. Welch ANOVA and Holm-adjusted t tests compared support conditions; HC3 linear models assessed specialty interaction.
AI.result: Among 123 residents (mean age 24.1 +/- 1.4 years; 65 women), radiology residents improved more with dual- than single-suggestion support (B-A: 6.69 percentage points [95% CI, 0.97-12.40]; C-A: 7.87 [1.64-14.11]; Holm-adjusted P = .030 both), while non-radiology residents showed no difference (P = .20). When GPT-5.4 was incorrect, AI-assisted accuracy was higher with dual- than single-suggestion support in radiology residents (40.1% and 40.4% vs 20.0%) and non-radiology residents (31.3% and 31.0% vs 12.1%) (all Holm-adjusted P < .001). The dual-suggestion effect differed by specialty (interaction difference, 10.44 percentage points [4.36-16.52]; P < .001).
AI.conclusion: Dual-suggestion AI support may mitigate the influence of erroneous AI suggestions, yielding greater accuracy improvement in radiology residents than non-radiology residents. The benefit appears most pronounced when the shared AI suggestion is wrong, suggesting dual-suggestion designs as a safeguard against AI-induced errors, though specialty-dependent effects warrant further investigation.

title: Tactile Reconstruction of Contact Task Frames and Forces for Hybrid Force/Motion Control
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables. Video: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLejKMZmW8AvI. Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23209032
summary: Hybrid force/motion control requires knowledge of the interaction force and of a task frame defining the force- and motion-controlled directions. These quantities are usually obtained from force/torque sensing or model-based residuals, often assuming also a nominal environment model. This work addresses the online estimation of the contact force and a possibly time-varying task frame using only soft optical tactile sensing, under the assumption of locally planar contact with a negligible contact moment. The proposed method maps a single image of the deformed elastomer of a soft optical tactile sensor to observable contact variables: indentation depth, two surface-to-sensor tilt angles, and 3D contact force, each with a per-sample uncertainty estimate. The mapping is learned through a self-labeling acquisition procedure, in which a manipulator imposes controlled contacts while an auxiliary Force/Torque sensor is used offline to provide ground-truth labels. The tactile measurement is then fused with robot proprioceptive data in an Extended Kalman Filter, producing a continuously updated estimate of the contact task frame and of the interaction force. Control experiments with a DigiTac sensor mounted on a UR10 manipulator demonstrate closed-loop contact force regulation against a flat rigid board in linear and angular motion by a human operator, with touch as the only exteroceptive feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper estimates contact force and a time-varying task frame online using only soft optical tactile sensing, assuming local planar contact with negligible moment. A learned per-pixel mapping from elastomer images to contact variables (indentation, two tilt angles, 3D force with uncertainty) is fused with proprioception in an EKF, enabling closed-loop force regulation with touch as sole exteroceptive feedback.
AI.motivation: Hybrid force/motion control needs interaction force and a task frame defining force- and motion-controlled directions. These are typically obtained from force/torque sensing or model-based residuals, often requiring a nominal environment model. The authors aim to remove this dependence by using only soft optical tactile sensing.
AI.method: The method maps a single image of the deformed elastomer to observable contact variables: indentation depth, two surface-to-sensor tilt angles, and 3D contact force, each with a per-sample uncertainty estimate. The mapping is learned via self-labeling acquisition, where a manipulator imposes controlled contacts and an auxiliary F/T sensor provides offline ground-truth labels. Tactile measurements are fused with robot proprioceptive data in an Extended Kalman Filter to continuously estimate the contact task frame and interaction force.
AI.result: Control experiments with a DigiTac sensor on a UR10 manipulator achieve closed-loop contact force regulation against a flat rigid board in linear and angular motion induced by a human operator, using touch as the only exteroceptive feedback.
AI.conclusion: Contact force and a possibly time-varying task frame can be estimated online from soft optical tactile sensing alone, under locally planar contact with negligible contact moment, enabling effective closed-loop force control without force/torque sensing, model-based residuals, or a nominal environment model.

title: Learning Situation-Conditioned Thinking Policies for Long-Term LLM Agents
summary: Long-running autonomous agents must reuse accumulated reasoning experience without allowing explicit historical memory and LLM context to grow indefinitely. However, existing memory mechanisms mainly retrieve, summarize, or compress past content and do not directly learn when particular kinds of thinking should be activated or discover new thinking knowledge from temporally dispersed experiences. This paper proposes a situation-conditioned thinking memory framework that transforms historical reasoning experience into a lightweight policy for predicting what should be thought about in the current situation, while leaving detailed reasoning to a large language model. Situations may represent temporal or spatiotemporal evolution rather than only current states. Temporary experiences are also periodically analyzed across multiple independent episodes to identify repeated long-range regularities, which are consolidated into new thinking knowledge and further internalized by the lightweight policy. Experiments show that the learned policy achieves 1.000 F1 on temporal-rule generalization, improves DeepSeek reasoning F1 from 0.789 to 0.868, reduces online processing time from 0.3636 ms to 0.0382 ms per query at 30,000 historical situations, and reaches 1.000 relation-discovery F1 and future-thinking accuracy after sufficient repeated cross-experience evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a situation-conditioned thinking memory framework that converts historical reasoning experience into a lightweight policy predicting what to think in the current situation, while delegating detailed reasoning to an LLM, and periodically consolidating cross-episode regularities into new thinking knowledge.
AI.motivation: Long-running autonomous agents must reuse accumulated reasoning experience without letting explicit historical memory and LLM context grow indefinitely. Existing memory mechanisms mainly retrieve, summarize, or compress past content; they do not directly learn when particular kinds of thinking should be activated, nor discover new thinking knowledge from temporally dispersed experiences.
AI.method: A situation-conditioned thinking memory framework transforms historical reasoning experience into a lightweight policy that predicts what should be thought about in the current situation, leaving detailed reasoning to a large language model. Situations may represent temporal or spatiotemporal evolution rather than only current states. Temporary experiences are periodically analyzed across multiple independent episodes to identify repeated long-range regularities, which are consolidated into new thinking knowledge and further internalized by the lightweight policy.
AI.result: The learned policy achieves 1.000 F1 on temporal-rule generalization, improves DeepSeek reasoning F1 from 0.789 to 0.868, reduces online processing time from 0.3636 ms to 0.0382 ms per query at 30,000 historical situations, and reaches 1.000 relation-discovery F1 and future-thinking accuracy after sufficient repeated cross-experience evidence.
AI.conclusion: Transforming historical reasoning experience into a lightweight situation-conditioned thinking policy, combined with periodic cross-episode consolidation of long-range regularities into new thinking knowledge, enables efficient and generalizable memory reuse for long-running autonomous agents.

title: Video-to-Model: Automatic Modeling of Deformable Linear Objects
summary: This paper presents a video-to-model framework for automatically modeling the motion of a deformable suture thread from an input video. We utilize a recently developed CBF--CLF--QP numerical model that simplifies the characterization of deformable string motion through the selection of a small number of parameters. A perception module first localizes and tracks the thread in video, producing an ordered sequence of thread nodes. The observed thread motion is then processed by a spatio-temporal CNN network that estimates the effective parameters of a structured CBF--CLF--QP model. These parameters are used to simulate the thread under a user-defined needle velocity input. Experiments using unseen thread configurations and motion demonstrate that the framework can reliably reconstruct the thread behavior from video, automatically configure the structured model, and reproduce the expected thread motion with low tracking error. The proposed approach reduces the need for manual parameter tuning and provides a step toward automatic video-based modeling of deformable linear objects.

AI.tldr: A video-to-model framework that automatically models the motion of a deformable suture thread by using a spatio-temporal CNN to estimate parameters of a structured CBF-CLF-QP numerical model, reducing manual tuning.
AI.motivation: Modeling the motion of deformable suture threads typically requires manual tuning of parameters, which is difficult and time-consuming. There is a need to automatically configure such models from observed data, in particular from video, to model deformable linear objects without relying on burdensome manual parameter tuning.
AI.method: The framework combines a perception module with learning and simulation. The perception module localizes and tracks the thread in video, producing an ordered sequence of thread nodes. The observed thread motion is processed by a spatio-temporal CNN that estimates the effective parameters of a structured CBF-CLF-QP model, which simplifies characterization of deformable string motion through a small number of parameters. These learned parameters are then used to simulate the thread under a user-defined needle velocity input.
AI.result: Experiments using unseen thread configurations and motion show that the framework reliably reconstructs the thread behavior from video, automatically configures the structured model, and reproduces the expected thread motion with low tracking error.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach reduces manual parameter tuning and provides a step toward automatic video-based modeling of deformable linear objects.

title: SafeEvo: Deciphering the Safety Alignment Mechanism and Evolution in Language Models
summary: Safety interpretability advances the study of Large Language Model (LLM) alignment from behavioral constraints driven by data or algorithms towards a deeper understanding of internal mechanisms. However, existing works have focused primarily on safety-related representations, attention heads, or neurons after alignment, while largely overlooking the safety mechanisms in pretrained-only models and their evolution across alignment checkpoints. To address this, we propose SafeEvo, an interpretability framework from the circuit (sparse subgraphs of an LLM) perspective. SafeEvo first applies an optimization-based extraction algorithm to identify weak refusal circuits in pretrained base LLMs that can independently express refusal behavior. Causally ablating these circuits completely eliminates the base model's refusal of harmful inputs. SafeEvo then traces the evolution of refusal circuits across successive alignment checkpoints and finds that their structures change progressively, suggesting that the alignment tax may result from refusal-circuit updates affecting utility-related parameters. To validate this, SafeEvo introduces Safety Circuit Alignment (SCA), which confines safety updates to the refusal circuits. Experiments across three LLMs and two alignment algorithms show that, on average, SCA outperforms vanilla alignment in three aspects: \textbf{(1) stronger alignment}, lowering harmfulness score by 63.21\%; \textbf{(2) less over-refusal}, yielding a 58.44\% decrease in refusal rates for benign queries; and \textbf{(3) better utility}, retaining 99.58\% of the original model capabilities.

AI.tldr: SafeEvo is a circuit-level interpretability framework that finds weak refusal circuits in pretrained base LLMs and traces their evolution across alignment checkpoints, then uses Safety Circuit Alignment (SCA) to confine safety updates to these circuits.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretability work on LLM safety focuses on safety-related representations, attention heads, or neurons after alignment, largely overlooking safety mechanisms in pretrained-only models and how these mechanisms evolve across alignment checkpoints.
AI.method: SafeEvo applies an optimization-based extraction algorithm to identify weak refusal circuits (sparse subgraphs) in pretrained base LLMs that can independently express refusal behavior, and causally ablates them to test their role. It then traces refusal-circuit evolution across successive alignment checkpoints. Building on this, it introduces Safety Circuit Alignment (SCA), which confines safety updates to the refusal circuits.
AI.result: Causal ablation of the refusal circuits completely eliminates the base model's refusal of harmful inputs. Refusal circuit structures change progressively across alignment checkpoints, suggesting the alignment tax may stem from refusal-circuit updates affecting utility-related parameters. Across three LLMs and two alignment algorithms, SCA on average lowers harmfulness score by 63.21%, decreases refusal rates for benign queries by 58.44%, and retains 99.58% of original model capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Refusal behavior is localized in identifiable circuits present in base LLMs and evolves during alignment; confining safety updates to these circuits (SCA) yields stronger alignment, less over-refusal, and better utility retention than vanilla alignment.

title: Distributed Motion Planning for Multi-Robot Systems under Topological Constraints
summary: Efficient and distributed coordination of mobile robots is one of the main challenges in multi-robot systems. Topological constraints, often expressed as topological braids, are a popular tool to encode complex coordination patterns between multiple mobile robots, as they offer a compact and abstract representation of the desired qualitative relation between the space-time trajectories of the robots. However, execution of joint motion plans encoded as braid-based topological constraints via distributed controllers is challenging, with existing approaches, generally based on the execution of one braid generator at a time, producing slow and suboptimal trajectories. We propose a distributed controller based on Model Predictive Control (MPC) to efficiently execute braid-based topological specifications. Rather than directly tracking the braid specification, we propose to use winding numbers, which are topological invariants for braids, as a proxy. This has the twofold benefit of converting braids into a continuous function, which can be easily tracked by an MPC controller through an appropriate term in the cost function, and of decoupling the global braid specification into a set of pairwise specifications, which can be tracked distributedly through the solution of only local MPC problems. To maintain global coordination, we propose a consensus-based progress estimation approach, which allows the robots to synchronize their motion toward the desired specification. We validate the proposed approach in simulation and in real-world experiments, where we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and the improvement over existing approaches in terms of execution speed and control effort.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a distributed Model Predictive Control (MPC) approach to efficiently execute braid-based topological specifications for multi-robot coordination. Winding numbers—topological invariants of braids—serve as a continuous proxy for the braid specification, enabling decoupling into pairwise local MPC problems and consensus-based progress synchronization. Simulations and real-world experiments show faster execution and reduced control effort versus existing methods.
AI.motivation: Efficient, distributed coordination of mobile robots is a core challenge in multi-robot systems. Braids compactly encode complex coordination patterns as qualitative space-time relations, but executing braid-encoded joint motion plans via distributed controllers is hard: existing methods typically execute one braid generator at a time, yielding slow and suboptimal trajectories.
AI.method: A distributed MPC controller executes braid-based topological specifications. Instead of directly tracking the braid, winding numbers (topological invariants of braids) are used as a proxy. This (i) converts the braid into a continuous function trackable by MPC via a cost-function term, and (ii) decouples the global braid specification into pairwise specifications solved distributively as local MPC problems. A consensus-based progress estimation scheme synchronizes robot motion toward the desired specification.
AI.result: Validation in simulation and real-world experiments demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach and improvement over existing approaches in terms of execution speed and control effort.
AI.conclusion: Winding-number-based MPC, combined with pairwise decoupling and consensus-based progress estimation, enables efficient distributed execution of braid-based topological specifications, outperforming prior generator-by-generator methods in speed and control effort.

title: How Do Agentic LLMs Decide to Call Tools? A Tool-Call Vector Shaped by Suppression
summary: Tool calling, invoking external tools on demand, is central to agentic LLMs, yet the mechanism that decides whether a model calls a tool or responds directly remains poorly understood. Agentic prompts are long and heavily scaffolded, combining role instructions, tool schemas, format templates, and the user's request across hundreds of tokens, creating a noisy, highly entangled context in which no single controllable variable for mechanistic analysis is obvious. To obtain such a variable, we propose a method that converts complex agentic prompts into minimal contrastive pairs in which a single request verb determines the tool-call decision: replacing an execution-verb (e.g., \textit{write}) with an analysis-verb (e.g., \textit{discuss}) reliably flips the decision, suggesting it is mediated by a compact internal state. We construct 500 such paired prompts across Python, Java, and C++ (300 for mechanistic analysis, 200 held out for evaluation). We trace the decision to a vector, $μ_Δ$, that is both causally necessary and sufficient and generalizes beyond the discovery prompts to native multi-turn $τ^2$-Bench trajectories and verb-free requests. Behavioral ablations show that the scaffold establishes a tool-call prior; Transcoder decomposition then reveals that analysis verbs suppress this prior through features signaling that tool use is unnecessary, whereas execution verbs largely leave it intact. Downstream scaffold-reading attention heads and MLP features read out the resulting state, and the same mechanism recurs across seven models from the Qwen, Mistral, and Granite families. Our code is available at https://github.com/XijieGo/MI4ToolCalling.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a compact, causally necessary and sufficient internal vector that mediates tool-call decisions in agentic LLMs, discovered by converting heavily scaffolded prompts into minimal verb-contrastive pairs and validated across seven models.
AI.motivation: Tool calling is central to agentic LLMs, but the mechanism deciding whether a model calls a tool or responds directly is poorly understood. Agentic prompts are long and heavily scaffolded, combining role instructions, tool schemas, format templates, and user requests, producing a noisy, entangled context with no obvious single controllable variable for mechanistic analysis.
AI.method: They convert complex agentic prompts into minimal contrastive pairs in which a single request verb determines the tool-call decision (execution-verb vs. analysis-verb, e.g., write vs. discuss), constructing 500 paired prompts across Python, Java, and C++ (300 for mechanistic analysis, 200 held-out). They trace the decision to a vector μ_Δ that is causally necessary and sufficient, then use behavioral ablations, Transcoder decomposition, and analysis of scaffold-reading attention heads and MLP features.
AI.result: Replacing an execution verb with an analysis verb reliably flips the decision, indicating mediation by a compact internal state. μ_Δ is causally necessary and sufficient and generalizes beyond discovery prompts to native multi-turn τ²-Bench trajectories and verb-free requests. Behavioral ablations show the scaffold establishes a tool-call prior; Transcoder decomposition reveals analysis verbs suppress this prior via features signaling tool use is unnecessary, whereas execution verbs leave it intact. The same mechanism recurs across seven models from the Qwen, Mistral, and Granite families.
AI.conclusion: Tool-call decisions are mediated by a compact, causally necessary and sufficient internal vector that generalizes across prompts, benchmarks, and model families, with the scaffold setting a tool-call prior that analysis verbs suppress and execution verbs preserve, read out by scaffold-reading attention heads and MLP features.

title: RealtimeWAM: How Fast Can I Run My World Action Model?
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) combine visual dynamics modeling with action generation, but their high inference latency limits responsive robot control. Recent efforts accelerate inference by removing explicit future-video generation at test time, as in FastWAM, an approach that requires a specially tailored architectural design. More general caching strategies exploit feature redundancy, but redundancy alone does not capture the changing computational demands of closed-loop control. To address these challenges, we present RealtimeWAM, a general, training-free framework that coordinates parallel execution with adaptive computation for low-latency inference across diverse WAM architectures. We exploit layerwise dependencies to overlap observation processing with prediction. However, concurrent branches still compete for GPU resources, limiting the benefit of parallel execution. We therefore adapt computation throughout the pipeline through selective reuse, caching observation features in visually stable regions and reusing Transformer residuals while reserving additional refinement for small predicted adjustments. We evaluate RealtimeWAM on FastWAM and OpenWAM across RoboTwin, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus. On an RTX 4090, measured mean inference latencies are 24.09 and 63.09 ms, corresponding to average speedups of 8.90$\times$ and 10.67$\times$. Average success rates are 82.75% and 87.41%, respectively, within 0.02 and 0.53 percentage points of native inference. Across five real-world tasks, RealtimeWAM improves average success rates over native inference by 17.2 and 37.2 percentage points on FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively.

AI.tldr: RealtimeWAM is a training-free framework that combines parallel execution with adaptive computation to enable low-latency inference for World Action Models in robot control, achieving ~9-11x speedups with minimal success-rate loss.
AI.motivation: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly model visual dynamics and action generation, but their high inference latency impedes responsive closed-loop robot control. Prior acceleration methods are limited: FastWAM requires a bespoke architecture, and generic caching strategies relying solely on feature redundancy fail to capture the dynamic computational demands of closed-loop control.
AI.method: RealtimeWAM is a general, training-free framework that coordinates parallel execution with adaptive computation. It exploits layerwise dependencies to overlap observation processing with prediction, and, to mitigate GPU resource contention between concurrent branches, performs adaptive computation via selective reuse—caching observation features in visually stable regions and reusing Transformer residuals while allocating extra refinement to small predicted adjustments.
AI.result: Evaluated on FastWAM and OpenWAM across RoboTwin, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus on an RTX 4090, RealtimeWAM achieves mean inference latencies of 24.09 ms and 63.09 ms, i.e., average speedups of 8.90x and 10.67x. Success rates are 82.75% and 87.41%, within 0.02 and 0.53 percentage points of native inference. On five real-world tasks, it improves average success rates over native inference by 17.2 and 37.2 percentage points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: RealtimeWAM provides a general, architecture-agnostic, training-free acceleration approach that substantially reduces WAM inference latency for responsive robot control while preserving or even improving task success rates.

title: Automatically Building and Updating a Knowledge Graph of MLIP Models
summary: Complementing the many efforts in providing semantic representations of concepts, notions, and entities in materials science, we report and illustrate a process by which we can automatically build a knowledge graph of the fast evolving field of machine learning applied to the prediction of material properties, focusing on MLIP (Machine Learning Interatomic Potential). This LLM-based process relies on multiple steps, from information extraction in documents and articles to a validation loop using SHACL constraints to detect and correct errors. It is carried out on a model-by-model basis, focusing on the consistency of representation, therefore enabling an iterative construction where the addition of new models is facilitated. We illustrate the process by showing a few interesting aspects that can be queried from a knowledge graph built from the models listed in the Matbench Discovery leaderboard.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-based pipeline that automatically constructs a knowledge graph for the MLIP (Machine Learning Interatomic Potential) domain, using multi-step information extraction and a SHACL-based validation loop, demonstrated on models from the Matbench Discovery leaderboard.
AI.motivation: Materials science already has substantial work on semantic representations of concepts, notions, and entities, but the rapidly evolving subfield of machine learning applied to material property prediction—specifically Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIP)—lacks a structured, machine-readable representation. Building such a representation manually is impractical given the field's fast growth, motivating an automated, model-by-model approach that supports incremental construction.
AI.method: An LLM-based, multi-step process: information extraction from documents and articles, followed by a validation loop using SHACL (Shapes Constraint Language) constraints to detect and correct errors. The pipeline operates on a model-by-model basis, prioritizing consistency of representation, which enables iterative construction in which new models can be easily added.
AI.result: A knowledge graph of the MLIP field was automatically built from the models listed in the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, and the paper illustrates several interesting aspects that can be queried from this graph.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LLM-based process can automatically and iteratively construct a consistent knowledge graph for a fast-moving research area such as MLIP, and such a graph supports meaningful queries, demonstrating the feasibility of scalable, incremental semantic representation in materials science.

title: Lifelong small-object navigation in changing object layouts: a benchmark and method
summary: Household robots need to continually navigate to different objects in the same environment, many of which are small and portable, such as tools and toys. Their small visual footprint and frequent occlusion make reliable observation difficult, and they may be moved by people without the robot observing the changes. We formulate this challenging task as Lifelong Small-object Navigation in Changing Object Layouts (LiSoNav-COL). Agents must seek suitable viewpoints for reliable observation, accumulate and reuse scene knowledge to efficiently locate subsequent targets, and update outdated memory after object relocation. To eliminate the need for prior scene scanning, we also require agents to start navigation with empty scene memory. Although practical, this task still lacks benchmarks designed around its defining assumptions. To bridge this gap, we introduce LiSoNav-Eval, a dedicated benchmark spanning 28 indoor scenes with 45 small-object categories. Its lifelong navigation sequences include both unchanged and relocated targets to evaluate memory reuse and adaptation to object relocation. To address this challenging task, we propose a navigation method based on multi-view Inspection with Viewpoint-Anchored Memory, dubbed IVAM-Nav. IVAM-Nav actively observes supporting surfaces from complementary viewpoints for reliable small-object perception and anchors the resulting memory to their observation viewpoints, supporting relational memory reuse and revalidation under similar viewing conditions. Extensive experiments on LiSoNav-Eval demonstrate favorable performance of IVAM-Nav against representative methods. Benchmark analyses also show that smaller objects, larger environments, and longer relocation distances pose greater challenges. The dataset and code are available here.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LiSoNav-COL, a task of lifelong small-object navigation in changing object layouts, along with a benchmark LiSoNav-Eval (28 scenes, 45 small-object categories) and a method IVAM-Nav that uses multi-view inspection with viewpoint-anchored memory to locate small, occluded, movable objects without prior scene scanning.
AI.motivation: Household robots must repeatedly navigate to small, portable objects (tools, toys) in the same environment. Such objects have small visual footprints, are frequently occluded, and may be moved unobserved, making reliable observation and efficient re-localization hard. Existing benchmarks do not reflect these defining assumptions, and methods typically rely on prior scene scanning rather than starting with empty memory.
AI.method: The authors formulate LiSoNav-COL, requiring agents to seek suitable viewpoints, accumulate and reuse scene knowledge, and update outdated memory after relocation, starting from empty scene memory. They build LiSoNav-Eval, covering 28 indoor scenes and 45 small-object categories, with lifelong sequences containing both unchanged and relocated targets. They propose IVAM-Nav, which actively observes supporting surfaces from complementary viewpoints for reliable small-object perception and anchors memory to observation viewpoints, enabling relational memory reuse and revalidation under similar viewing conditions.
AI.result: On LiSoNav-Eval, IVAM-Nav achieves favorable performance compared with representative methods. Benchmark analyses show that smaller objects, larger environments, and longer relocation distances pose greater challenges.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a task and benchmark for lifelong small-object navigation under changing object layouts, and demonstrates that viewpoint-anchored multi-view memory is effective. Dataset and code are released.

title: MeshSIPP: Efficient Lattice Planning in Dynamic Environment
summary: Autonomous navigation in dynamic environments requires computing spatiotemporal trajectories that satisfy non-holonomic motion constraints. When the trajectories of the moving obstacles are predictable or known, a promising approach is to rely on the combination of state lattices constructed from precomputed feasible motion primitives and Safe Interval Path Planning -- a search-based algorithm with strong theoretical guarantees. While this approach yields feasible paths, the rich primitive sets needed for smooth navigation induce a large branching factor, which becomes costly when coupled with time-dependent obstacle intervals. To this end, we present MeshSIPP, an efficient planner that removes the computational bottleneck by exploiting the fact that many primitives sweep the same regions and can therefore be validated together. MeshSIPP propagates primitives as spatial bundles, screens them with lightweight bounding-interval checks, and defers the expensive exact departure-time search until a primitive reaches its terminal state. A time-aware pruning rule additionally discards redundant space-time branches early in the search. We prove that the resulting search is complete and optimal. Extensive experiments over more than 6,000 benchmark instances and real-time ROS~2 simulations show that MeshSIPP achieves up to a 3$\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art spatiotemporal planners.

AI.tldr: MeshSIPP is an efficient spatiotemporal planner for autonomous navigation that speeds up Safe Interval Path Planning over state lattices by validating motion primitives in spatial bundles, using lightweight bounding-interval checks, deferring exact departure-time search, and applying time-aware pruning, while preserving completeness and optimality.
AI.motivation: Autonomous navigation in dynamic environments requires spatiotemporal trajectories satisfying non-holonomic constraints. Combining state lattices of precomputed feasible motion primitives with Safe Interval Path Planning yields feasible, theoretically grounded paths, but the large branching factor of rich primitive sets becomes expensive when combined with time-dependent obstacle intervals, creating a computational bottleneck.
AI.method: MeshSIPP exploits that many primitives sweep the same regions and can be validated together. It propagates primitives as spatial bundles, screens them with lightweight bounding-interval checks, defers expensive exact departure-time search until a primitive reaches its terminal state, and adds a time-aware pruning rule that discards redundant space-time branches early.
AI.result: Experiments over more than 6,000 benchmark instances and real-time ROS 2 simulations show MeshSIPP achieves up to a 3x speedup over state-of-the-art spatiotemporal planners, with proven completeness and optimality.
AI.conclusion: MeshSIPP removes the computational bottleneck of lattice-based Safe Interval Path Planning in dynamic environments by bundling and deferring primitive validation, enabling faster complete and optimal spatiotemporal planning.

title: Do Vision-Language-Action Models Understand Instructions? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study on Language Grounding
summary: Vision-Language-Action models are designed to generalise across environments and task descriptions, raising the question of whether their action generation actually depends on the language instruction, or whether they largely rely on visual cues and superficial correlations. Robustness to variance in the visual and linguistic observation space is critical for real-world deployment, yet VLAs lack explicit grounding modules and instead rely on the intrinsic language grounding capabilities of their Vision-Language model backbones. For this reason, we conduct a controlled mechanistic interpretability study on the language grounding capabilities of two state-of-the-art Vision-Language-Action models, $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7, by applying activation and attribution patching to the residual stream of the action generation modules. We systematically corrupt the task instruction of input samples of the LIBERO benchmark following five strategies: synonym replacement, semantic scaling, directional corruption, random object substitution, and empty string. Our experiments find that both models are comparatively insensitive to abstract rephrasing and to referencing non-existent objects, but react strongly to empty task descriptions and, especially, to directional language. During action generation, this sensitivity is concentrated in different loci for each model: mainly in the early, periodic cross-attention layers for GR00T N1.7, versus distributed across the earliest and selected later layers for $π_{0.5}$. For GR00T N1.7, directional perturbations drive some of the largest causal effects while leaving the internal representational geometry comparatively unchanged, a dissociation we do not observe clearly for $π_{0.5}$. Finally, the reliability of attribution patching is model-dependent: it closely tracks activation patching for GR00T N1.7 but not for $π_{0.5}$.

AI.tldr: This paper mechanistically probes whether two state-of-the-art Vision-Language-Action models ($\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7) genuinely ground their actions in language, using activation and attribution patching under five instruction-corruption strategies on LIBERO.
AI.motivation: VLAs are expected to generalise across environments and task descriptions, but it is unclear whether their action generation truly depends on the language instruction or mainly relies on visual cues and superficial correlations. Since VLAs lack explicit grounding modules and depend on the intrinsic grounding ability of their VLM backbones, this question matters for robustness under visual and linguistic variance in real-world deployment.
AI.method: A controlled mechanistic interpretability study of two VLAs, $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7, applying activation and attribution patching to the residual stream of the action generation modules. Task instructions of LIBERO input samples are systematically corrupted via five strategies: synonym replacement, semantic scaling, directional corruption, random object substitution, and empty string.
AI.result: Both models are relatively insensitive to abstract rephrasing and to non-existent object references, but react strongly to empty instructions and especially to directional language. Sensitivity is localised differently per model: mainly early periodic cross-attention layers for GR00T N1.7, versus distributed across earliest and selected later layers for $\pi_{0.5}$.
