For GR00T N1.7, directional perturbations produce some of the largest causal effects while leaving internal representational geometry largely unchanged, a dissociation not clearly observed for $\pi_{0.5}$. Attribution patching reliability is model-dependent: it closely tracks activation patching for GR00T N1.7 but not for $\pi_{0.5}$.
AI.conclusion: Language grounding in VLAs is partial and structured: models tolerate lexical and referential noise yet depend heavily on directional and non-empty instructions, with model-specific loci of causal influence. The dissociation between causal effect and representational change, and the model-dependent validity of attribution patching, indicate that grounding conclusions require caution and per-model validation.

title: Shared and structured inputs undermine collective random choice by reasoning AI agents
summary: Random selection is widely used in resource allocation and auditing, making reliable implementation essential for AI-agent systems. Behavioural tests across six reasoning models uncovered threshold and divisibility rules used in identifier-based choices. For threshold-following GPT-6 Sol and Gemini 3.8 Flash, single-agent measurements prospectively predicted correlated participation under shared identifiers and biased participation under distinct identifiers with common timestamp bits. Changing dates, formats and identifier labels revealed when these predictions held. Explicit instructions to randomize independently reduced but did not eliminate shared-input correlation. To test implications for oversight, we asked four models to select customer requests randomly for human review. GPT-6 Sol approached the target rate while selecting predictably from identifiers; the others rarely selected requests. All four closely followed supplied random draws. These findings expose collective and audit vulnerabilities that selection rates alone miss, making input-dependent bias, correlation and predictability central targets for agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: Behavioural tests reveal that reasoning models implement "random" selection via deterministic identifier rules, producing correlated and biased participation, and undermining audit fairness.
AI.motivation: Random selection underpins resource allocation and auditing, so its reliable implementation is critical for AI-agent systems. Yet it is unclear whether LLM-based agents actually select randomly or exploit hidden identifier patterns.
AI.method: Behavioural tests across six reasoning models probing identifier-based choices; single-agent measurements prospectively predicting multi-agent participation under shared vs. distinct identifiers with common timestamp bits; variations in dates, formats and identifier labels; explicit randomization instructions; and an oversight simulation where four models selected customer requests for human review, compared against supplied random draws.
AI.result: Threshold and divisibility rules drove identifier-based choices. GPT-6 Sol and Gemini 3.8 Flash showed correlated participation under shared identifiers and bias under distinct identifiers sharing timestamp bits. These predictions held or broke depending on dates, formats and labels. Explicit independence instructions reduced but did not eliminate shared-input correlation. GPT-6 Sol neared the target review rate while selecting predictably from identifiers; other models rarely selected requests. All four closely followed supplied random draws.
AI.conclusion: Selection rates alone are insufficient; input-dependent bias, correlation and predictability should be primary targets in evaluating agent randomness.

title: Design of a Fully Actuated 4-DOF Robotic Finger With Joint-Specific Hybrid Remote Actuation
comment: 10 pages, 10 figures. This manuscript has been submitted for possible publication
summary: This paper presents a fully actuated 4-DOF robotic finger using a joint-specific hybrid remote-actuation architecture. The metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint is driven by two coordinated rigid-link transmission sets, whereas the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints are independently actuated by closed-loop wire transmissions incorporating circular rolling-contact joints (RCJs). A larger transmission radius is used at the PIP joint than at the DIP joint. The RCJ wire geometry maintains the total wire-loop length during joint rotation, and the DIP wire routing is designed so that PIP motion does not affect its differential actuation for a fixed MCP configuration. The distal wire transmission, MCP linkage, and fingertip kinematics are analytically modeled. In experiments, the transmission behavior was quantitatively evaluated from the ball-screw displacements measured using ArUco-marker tracking. MCP actuation produced measurable displacements of the PIP and DIP transmission units, whereas isolated PIP and DIP actuation with the MCP fixed supported the intended mechanical decoupling between the distal transmissions. The mean peak fingertip forces under isolated MCP, PIP, and DIP actuation were 21.28 N, 9.22 N, and 5.75 N, respectively. The resulting finger postures were also examined using objects of different geometries and sizes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fully actuated 4-DOF robotic finger using a joint-specific hybrid remote-actuation architecture, combining rigid-link transmissions at the MCP joint with closed-loop wire transmissions and rolling-contact joints at the PIP and DIP joints, achieving mechanical decoupling of the distal transmissions.
AI.motivation: To achieve independent, fully actuated control of a multi-DOF robotic finger, conventional monolithic actuation schemes struggle with transmission coupling between joints. A joint-specific architecture is needed to decouple distal joints and enable precise, independent actuation while maintaining compact remote transmission.
AI.method: A 4-DOF robotic finger is designed with a hybrid remote-actuation architecture: the MCP joint is driven by two coordinated rigid-link transmission sets, while the PIP and DIP joints are independently actuated by closed-loop wire transmissions using circular rolling-contact joints (RCJs), with a larger transmission radius at the PIP than the DIP. The RCJ wire geometry maintains constant total wire-loop length during rotation, and the DIP wire routing decouples PIP motion from differential actuation at fixed MCP. Distal wire transmission, MCP linkage, and fingertip kinematics are analytically modeled. Transmission behavior is quantitatively evaluated via ball-screw displacements measured with ArUco-marker tracking.
AI.result: MCP actuation produced measurable displacements of the PIP and DIP transmission units, whereas isolated PIP and DIP actuation with the MCP fixed confirmed the intended mechanical decoupling between the distal transmissions. Mean peak fingertip forces under isolated MCP, PIP, and DIP actuation were 21.28 N, 9.22 N, and 5.75 N, respectively. Resulting finger postures were also examined using objects of different geometries and sizes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed joint-specific hybrid remote-actuation architecture enables a fully actuated 4-DOF robotic finger with mechanically decoupled distal transmissions, demonstrated by the measured decoupling behavior, quantified fingertip force capabilities, and validated grasping postures across varied objects.

title: Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving via Agent Orchestration in Program Verification
summary: Program verification establishes software correctness through machine-checkable proofs constructed in theorem provers. It's a guarantee especially valuable for code generated by large language models (LLMs), which is fluent but carries no assurance of correctness. Almost all existing provers, however, pursue pass rates alone at whatever sampling or search budget it takes, and overlook the success-vs-cost frontier; yet real software often carries hundreds of interdependent proof obligations, so what matters at scale is not whether one theorem can be proved, but how many can be proved economically. We introduce CoCo-Prover, which formalizes cost-efficient program proving as metalevel decision-making under cost, grounded on two-level proof graphs: an AND/OR proof hypergraph within each declaration is joined to a lemma-dependency graph across declarations; and at each step, it answers two questions: which open goals to select, and which actions to purchase on these goals. Selection stays symbolic as a topological pass over the proof graphs. Action choice is agent orchestration via metalevel decision-making: an agentic router treats every bounded specialist invocation as a separately priced, best-effort computation, matching heterogeneous specialist agents together with configurations, under evolved routing rules as evidence accumulates. On five program verification benchmarks in Lean 4 including function-level CLEVER, VERINA, and AlgoVeri, and repository-level NTP4VC and Vero, we show that CoCo-Prover achieves a better success-vs-cost frontier than baselines including frontier coding agents and state-of-the-art LLM-based provers: it achieves the best solve rate on every benchmark and up to 100% on two benchmarks. It also reduces cost by up to 30.9% compared to the strongest baseline with the strongest LLM in our evaluation.

AI.tldr: CoCo-Prover formalizes cost-efficient program proving as metalevel decision-making over two-level proof graphs, achieving the best success-vs-cost frontier across five Lean 4 benchmarks and up to 100% solve rate while reducing cost by up to 30.9%.
AI.motivation: Existing provers optimize pass rates only, ignoring the success-vs-cost frontier. Real software carries hundreds of interdependent proof obligations, so at scale, how many theorems can be proved economically matters more than whether one theorem can be proved.
AI.method: CoCo-Prover frames cost-efficient program proving as metalevel decision-making under cost, grounded on two-level proof graphs: an AND/OR proof hypergraph within each declaration joined to a cross-declaration lemma-dependency graph. At each step it decides which open goals to select and which actions to purchase. Goal selection is symbolic (a topological pass over the proof graphs); action choice uses agent orchestration, where an agentic router treats each bounded specialist invocation as separately priced, best-effort computation, matching specialist agents with configurations under evolved routing rules as evidence accumulates.
AI.result: On five Lean 4 benchmarks (function-level CLEVER, VERINA, AlgoVeri; repository-level NTP4VC, Vero), CoCo-Prover achieves a better success-vs-cost frontier than baselines including frontier coding agents and state-of-the-art LLM-based provers, attaining the best solve rate on every benchmark and up to 100% on two, while reducing cost by up to 30.9% versus the strongest baseline with the strongest LLM.
AI.conclusion: CoCo-Prover demonstrates that treating proof search as cost-aware metalevel decision-making over two-level proof graphs yields superior success-vs-cost tradeoffs, making economical large-scale verification of LLM-generated code feasible.

title: Benchmarking Behavioral Steerability in Behavior Foundation Models
summary: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) are emerging as a paradigm for translating human intentions into executable humanoid behaviors. As these models evolve beyond behavior generation toward general-purpose behavioral systems, a fundamental question arises: can they be reliably steered according to user intentions? In this paper, we introduce the concept of behavioral steerability, defined as the ability of BFMs to faithfully generate behaviors that satisfy user-specified intentions. To study this capability, we present RoboSteer, the first benchmark for behavioral steerability in BFMs. RoboSteer organizes behavioral steerability into a three-level hierarchy-Conditional Steering, Constraint Steering, and Compositional Steering-and establishes a unified evaluation framework supported by a large-scale multimodal motion corpus. Using RoboSteer, we conduct the first large-scale empirical study of behavioral steerability across 9 existing BFMs. We view behavioral steerability as more than a capability for controlling motion: it concerns how embodied systems translate human intentions into purposeful actions. We hope RoboSteer will advance research on intention realization as a foundation for general-purpose embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: RoboSteer is introduced as the first benchmark for evaluating behavioral steerability in Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs), organizing it into a three-level hierarchy (Conditional, Constraint, and Compositional Steering), and applied in a large-scale empirical study of 9 existing BFMs.
AI.motivation: As BFMs evolve from behavior generation toward general-purpose behavioral systems, it becomes essential to know whether they can be reliably steered according to user intentions; the paper frames this as "behavioral steerability," a capability not previously systematically studied or benchmarked.
AI.method: The authors define behavioral steerability, then build RoboSteer, a benchmark with a unified evaluation framework supported by a large-scale multimodal motion corpus. The benchmark organizes steerability into a three-level hierarchy: Conditional Steering, Constraint Steering, and Compositional Steering. They use it to run a large-scale empirical study across 9 existing BFMs.
AI.result: The first large-scale empirical evaluation of behavioral steerability across 9 existing BFMs is conducted, providing a systematic comparison under a unified framework.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral steerability is framed as more than motion control: it concerns how embodied systems translate human intentions into purposeful actions. The authors hope RoboSteer advances research on intention realization as a foundation for general-purpose embodied intelligence.

title: System Switch: When Should a Fast Decision Model Stop and Think?
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Code, prompts and data: https://github.com/dexmac221/doomgemma (branch system-switch)
summary: Dual-process agents pair a fast policy with a slow deliberative model. In real-time settings the slow model usually runs continuously; in turn-based agents and robot planners it is invoked on events such as uncertainty or a detected failure. We study a fast learned actor that takes every decision and hands control to a reasoning vision-language model only when a gate opens, while the game keeps running. We use closed-loop Doom and the new open "System One" typed-decision models, served through a common llama.cpp interface. On 900 held-out questions, (i) zero-shot decision models from 0.15B to 9B parameters choose to collect items 1.6-1.8 times more often than chance among their errors, in any option order, although the order changes some models' accuracy; (ii) accuracy, calibration and sensitivity (how well confidence separates right from wrong answers) are distinct: models of similar accuracy differ widely in AUROC, and the confidence of the most sensitive one tracks which kinds of situation it fails, not which answers are wrong; (iii) offline, deferring the least confident 30% of decisions to a reasoning model gains over random deferral in proportion to the actor's AUROC (rank correlation 0.87); with actor and rate chosen on held-out games the gain is +0.13 [0.08, 0.18] with doomLaya's option order and +0.08 [0.02, 0.14] with shuffled options, and reasoning carries about half of it; (iv) in closed loop (33 games, three seeds) no variant reaches the exit. Committing to plans, the reasoner's or a fixed explore rule's, opens more doors and makes an actor that stands still play; with the rule the agent dies more often. Told that some doors need keys, the reasoner takes ordinary doors for locked ones, which the state cannot tell apart; without that knowledge it goes back to collecting. We release code, prompts, data and logs.

AI.tldr: Dual-process agents pair a fast policy with a slow deliberative model. In real-time settings the slow model usually runs continuously; in turn-based agents and robot planners it is invoked on events such as uncertainty or a detected failure. We study a fast learned actor that takes every decision and hands control to a reasoning vision-language model only when a gate opens, while the game keeps running.
AI.motivation: In real-time settings, slow deliberative models typically run continuously, whereas in turn-based agents and robot planners they are invoked only on events such as uncertainty or detected failure. This raises the question of how a fast learned actor should hand off control to a reasoning model via a gate while the environment keeps running.
AI.method: The authors use closed-loop Doom and new open "System One" typed-decision models, served through a common llama.cpp interface. They evaluate zero-shot decision models from 0.15B to 9B parameters on 900 held-out questions, examining choice bias, accuracy, calibration, sensitivity (AUROC), and deferral to a reasoning model. They test offline deferral of the least confident 30% of decisions and closed-loop performance on 33 games with three seeds, including plan commitment and knowledge of locked doors.
AI.result: (i) Zero-shot decision models choose to collect items 1.6–1.8 times more often than chance among their errors, in any option order, though order changes some models' accuracy. (ii) Accuracy, calibration, and sensitivity are distinct: models of similar accuracy differ widely in AUROC, and the most sensitive model's confidence tracks which kinds of situation it fails, not which answers are wrong. (iii) Offline, deferring the least confident 30% of decisions to a reasoning model gains over random deferral in proportion to the actor's AUROC (rank correlation 0.87); with actor and rate chosen on held-out games the gain is +0.13 [0.08, 0.18] with doomLaya's option order and +0.08 [0.02, 0.14] with shuffled options, and reasoning carries about half of it. (iv) In closed loop (33 games, three seeds) no variant reaches the exit. Committing to plans, the reasoner's or a fixed explore rule's, opens more doors and makes a stationary actor play; with the rule the agent dies more often. Told that some doors need keys, the reasoner mistakes ordinary doors for locked ones, which the state cannot distinguish; without that knowledge it reverts to collecting.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that confidence-based gating can yield measurable deferral gains proportional to actor AUROC, but no closed-loop variant reaches the exit. Plan commitment improves door opening and elicits play from a stationary actor, while the explore rule increases deaths, and explicit knowledge about locked doors degrades reasoning by causing ordinary doors to be treated as locked.

title: Making Task Abstractions Executable: Control-Aware Layout Repair for a Fixed Controller
summary: A task abstraction can specify the intended events while its spatial layout prevents a fixed agent and controller from completing them. Starting from a supplied structured task record, we compile whole-task tracking, clearance, and actuation requirements into auditable affine layout constraints. We repair only declared continuous coordinates, preserving event order, timing, topology, and the controller. A most-violated-row update admits conditional finite-certification and net-displacement bounds; a same-compiler quadratic projection separates the representation from the optimizer. On three researcher-authored task abstractions, both backends certify all three layouts and complete all 300 fresh paired rollouts per backend. A risk-target sweep also exposes fixed event tests that the chosen certificate cannot satisfy through layout edits alone.

AI.tldr: The paper compiles task-level tracking, clearance, and actuation requirements into auditable affine layout constraints and repairs only declared continuous coordinates, preserving event order, timing, topology, and controller. A most-violated-row update yields conditional finite-certification and net-displacement bounds, with a same-compiler quadratic projection separating representation from optimizer; both backends certify three layouts and complete 300 paired rollouts each.
AI.motivation: A task abstraction can define intended events, yet its spatial layout may make those events impossible for a fixed agent and controller to complete. The work targets repairing the layout while keeping the task semantics and controller unchanged, and it aims to provide a certifiable, auditable compilation pipeline rather than an unverified optimization heuristic.
AI.method: Starting from a supplied structured task record, the method compiles whole-task tracking, clearance, and actuation requirements into auditable affine layout constraints. It repairs only declared continuous coordinates while preserving event order, timing, topology, and the controller. A most-violated-row update provides conditional finite-certification and net-displacement bounds, and a same-compiler quadratic projection decouples the representation from the optimizer, allowing alternative backends.
AI.result: On three researcher-authored task abstractions, both backends certify all three layouts and complete all 300 fresh paired rollouts per backend. A risk-target sweep further exposes fixed event tests that the chosen certificate cannot satisfy through layout edits alone.
AI.conclusion: The approach turns layout repair into an auditable affine-constraint problem with certification and bounded displacement, and it is validated across backends and many paired rollouts. Its limitation is that certain fixed event tests remain unsatisfiable by layout edits alone under the selected certificate, which defines the boundary of what layout repair can guarantee.

title: A Tale of Two Error Categories: Exploring Concealed Trade-Offs in the Errors of Automated Judges in Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantifiers
summary: The wide adoption of LLMs across broad NLG applications heightens the importance of providing users with the means to avert errors and hallucinations. Uncertainty quantification is poised to fill that gap; with low uncertainty (high confidence), as a proxy for correctness, allowing users to be selective (e.g., reject low-confidence, likely incorrect responses). Correlation between confidence and correctness then serves as a useful criterion for evaluation of uncertainty quantifiers (UQs). But in NLG, where diverse responses can be adequate to a prompt, obtaining reliable correctness judgements is not simple, especially without human intervention. Errors in automated judgement are hardly avoidable and known to diminish the reliability of evaluation protocols (Santilli et al., 2025; Ielanskyi et al., 2025). In a meta-analysis of published work, we show that automated judgement is the present norm. Besides, automated judgements are rarely validated against human ones, and the validation of the UQ evaluation they automate is even rarer. With experiments in question answering, using 4 LLMs, human and automated judgements and 7 popular UQs, we find that i) a judge's performance can only coarsely predict the observed impact of its errors on the reliability of UQ evaluation, and that ii) judgement errors tend to misrepresent informative UQs most. We link these observations to patterns of correlation between confidence and categories of judgement error.

AI.tldr: This meta-analysis and experiment study show that automated correctness judgements, now the norm in evaluating uncertainty quantifiers (UQs) for LLM NLG, are rarely validated against human judgements; using 4 LLMs, 7 UQs, and question answering, it finds judge performance only coarsely predicts the impact of judgement errors on UQ evaluation reliability, and that such errors most misrepresent informative UQs.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are widely adopted in NLG, uncertainty quantification is used to let users be selective—rejecting low-confidence, likely incorrect responses—with confidence-correctness correlation serving as the evaluation criterion for UQs. However, in NLG, diverse responses can be adequate, so reliable correctness judgements are hard without human intervention, and errors in automated judgement are unavoidable and known to undermine evaluation protocols.
AI.method: A meta-analysis of published work to characterize current judgement practices, plus experiments in question answering using 4 LLMs, human and automated correctness judgements, and 7 popular UQs, examining the relationship between confidence and categories of judgement error.
AI.result: Automated judgement is the present norm; automated judgements are rarely validated against human ones, and validation of the UQ evaluation they automate is even rarer. Empirically, (i) a judge's performance only coarsely predicts the observed impact of its errors on UQ evaluation reliability, and (ii) judgement errors tend to misrepresent informative UQs most; these patterns are linked to correlations between confidence and categories of judgement error.
AI.conclusion: The findings caution against relying on unvalidated automated judgements in UQ evaluation and highlight how judgement error patterns, tied to confidence, can specifically distort assessments of the most informative uncertainty quantifiers.

title: Temporal Visuo-Tactile Learning for Dexterous Grasp Stability
summary: Humans can grasp everyday objects with almost perfect success rates using fingertip tactile feedback, yet much of the robotic grasping literature emphasizes vision-based grasp selection with parallel grippers. In this work, we systematically investigate how high-resolution, dynamic tactile sensing contributes to grasp stability prediction and model-guided grasping in dexterous robotic hands. To this end, we collected a dataset of 10,000 grasp trials across 200 objects using a multi-fingered robotic hand equipped with four Digit 360 tactile sensors, recording external vision, proprioception, and tactile streams throughout each grasp. With this dataset, we trained end-to-end temporal multimodal models to predict post-lift stability from pre-lift grasp observations and compared sensing modalities and encoding backbones. Experimental results and controlled input ablations show that incorporating touch, and particularly high-resolution, dynamic touch, improves grasp stability prediction. Finally, we deployed the learned predictor as an online stability gate on the real robot, where visuo-tactile model-guided regrasping improved the success rate among executed lifts by 10.5 percentage points over a non-tactile gate. These results show how rich fingertip sensing and expressive temporal models that capture the dynamics of touch can support learned grasping with multi-fingered hands without explicit contact or force modeling, providing a scalable data-driven path from tactile experience toward stable dexterous manipulation. The dataset is publicly available at https://lasr-lab.github.io/dexterous-grasp-stability/.

AI.tldr: This work shows that high-resolution, dynamic fingertip tactile sensing, combined with temporal multimodal models, improves grasp stability prediction and enables visuo-tactile model-guided regrasping for dexterous robotic hands.
AI.motivation: Humans achieve near-perfect grasping via fingertip tactile feedback, but robotic grasping research predominantly relies on vision-based grasp selection with parallel grippers, underusing tactile sensing in dexterous hands. The authors aim to systematically quantify how high-resolution, dynamic tactile sensing contributes to grasp stability prediction and model-guided grasping.
AI.method: They collected a dataset of 10,000 grasp trials over 200 objects using a multi-fingered robotic hand equipped with four Digit 360 tactile sensors, recording external vision, proprioception, and tactile streams. They trained end-to-end temporal multimodal models to predict post-lift stability from pre-lift observations, and compared sensing modalities and encoding backbones via controlled input ablations. The learned predictor was then deployed as an online stability gate for regrasping on the real robot.
AI.result: Incorporating touch—especially high-resolution, dynamic touch—improved grasp stability prediction. In real-robot deployment, visuo-tactile model-guided regrasping raised the success rate among executed lifts by 10.5 percentage points over a non-tactile gate.
AI.conclusion: Rich fingertip sensing and expressive temporal models capturing touch dynamics can support learned grasping with multi-fingered hands without explicit contact or force modeling, offering a scalable data-driven path from tactile experience to stable dexterous manipulation. The dataset is publicly released.

title: From Expert-Guided Proof Search to Automated Open-Problem Solving
comment: Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI), NeurIPS 2026
summary: Large language models are increasingly contributing to mathematical research, where progress often depends on efficient proof search, incremental improvements and careful verification. We describe Bolzano, a multi-agent open-source system that uses parallel prover agents with a verifier agent and maintains a human-readable research state. Initial manual use on expert-selected problems yielded 8 results whose proofs were checked by domain experts. Motivated by these case studies, we ran Bolzano without problem-specific human guidance on about 3,800 open problems extracted from four sets of papers, solving about 200 open problems. One experiment used papers accepted to STOC 2026, a top conference in theoretical computer science. There, we answered four questions raised in the papers, as confirmed by their authors.

AI.tldr: Bolzano, a multi-agent open-source system combining parallel prover agents with a verifier agent and a human-readable research state, solves ~200 open problems from ~3,800 extracted from four paper sets, with expert-verified proofs and author-confirmed answers.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly contribute to mathematical research, where progress hinges on efficient proof search, incremental improvements, and careful verification; a system is needed to scale automated proof search while preserving verifiability.
AI.method: Bolzano is a multi-agent open-source system using parallel prover agents alongside a verifier agent, maintaining a human-readable research state. It was first applied manually on expert-selected problems, then run without problem-specific human guidance on ~3,800 open problems extracted from four sets of papers.
AI.result: Initial manual use produced 8 domain-expert-checked results. The unguided run on ~3,800 open problems solved about 200. In one experiment using papers accepted to STOC 2026, four questions raised in the papers were answered and confirmed by their authors.
AI.conclusion: Bolzano demonstrates that multi-agent LLM systems with built-in verification can autonomously address open mathematical problems at scale, yielding expert- and author-validated results.

title: Energy-Efficient Gait Adaptation via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Quadrupedal Locomotion Across Diverse Terrains
comment: 9 pages. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027. Ammar Issa, Anubhav Singh, and Anton Tsaritsin contributed equally
summary: While energy efficiency is a critical objective for legged-robot locomotion control, achieving low energy consumption while maintaining robust performance across different velocity ranges and terrain conditions remains a key challenge. This is particularly true for end-to-end RL policies, where gait generation, motion execution, and energy optimization are tightly coupled, leading to high sensitivity to reward design. In this work, we propose a hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) framework that separates a high-frequency policy for stable and robust joint-level motion execution from low-frequency gait adaptation that explicitly minimizes the cost of transport (CoT). The three-stage Isaac-based training procedure enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with improved tracking accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency. The learned hierarchy exhibits automatic speed-dependent gait adaptation, transitioning from pacing at low speeds to trotting at higher speeds. We validate the proposed approach in simulation against representative single-policy and hierarchical locomotion baselines, demonstrating reduced CoT over a broad range of commanded velocities, while maintaining robust locomotion across flat, uneven rough, and inclined terrains. We further demonstrate its practical feasibility through zero-shot deployment on a physical Unitree AlienGo quadruped.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hierarchical RL framework for legged-robot locomotion that decouples high-frequency joint-level motion execution from low-frequency gait adaptation explicitly minimizing cost of transport (CoT), achieving energy-efficient, robust, zero-shot sim-to-real locomotion with automatic speed-dependent gait transitions.
AI.motivation: Energy efficiency is critical for legged-robot locomotion, yet achieving low energy consumption while maintaining robustness across velocity ranges and terrains remains challenging. This is especially problematic for end-to-end RL policies, where gait generation, motion execution, and energy optimization are tightly coupled, making them highly sensitive to reward design.
AI.method: A hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) framework separates a high-frequency policy for stable and robust joint-level motion execution from a low-frequency gait adaptation policy that explicitly minimizes cost of transport (CoT). A three-stage Isaac-based training procedure enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: The approach yields improved tracking accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency. The learned hierarchy shows automatic speed-dependent gait adaptation, transitioning from pacing at low speeds to trotting at higher speeds. Against representative single-policy and hierarchical locomotion baselines in simulation, it reduces CoT over a broad range of commanded velocities while maintaining robust locomotion on flat, uneven rough, and inclined terrains. Zero-shot deployment on a physical Unitree AlienGo quadruped demonstrates practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling motion execution from energy-aware gait adaptation via hierarchy offers an effective route to energy-efficient, robust legged locomotion, validated in simulation and through zero-shot deployment on real hardware.

title: SkillForge: Co-Evolving Skills and Agents via Dynamic Skill Lifecycles
summary: Memory-augmented reinforcement learning strengthens LLM agents' ability to solve complex long-horizon tasks. Skills are one such form of memory, pairing instructions with an applicability condition over task types. However, retaining every skill indiscriminately as the policy improves lets obsolete or harmful entries accumulate and mislead the agent. We propose SkillForge, an agentic RL method that compiles and evolves the skill library through a fitness-driven skill lifecycle of trial, active, stable, and retired states, so that the skills and the model co-evolve throughout training. A pre-RL evaluation phase first uses the base model's own rollouts to pre-retire low-fitness skills, yielding a filtered library that then seeds supervised fine-tuning. Reinforcement learning takes over from this checkpoint, and at each iteration selective retirement, stabilization, and LLM-guided mutation continue to forge the skill library alongside policy optimization. Across multiple interactive agent benchmarks, SkillForge achieves the highest aggregate success rate, delivering up to 7.8% relative improvement over the strongest baseline while keeping the skill library compact throughout training. We introduce SkillFurnace, a dataset of 5k+ annotated records bundling retirement-filtered SFT trajectories, evolved skill libraries with fitness annotations, and retirement events with human-annotated failure categories to support research on skill quality and lifecycle management.

AI.tldr: SkillForge is an agentic RL method that manages a dynamically evolving skill library via a fitness-driven lifecycle (trial, active, stable, retired), enabling skills and the policy to co-evolve. It achieves the highest aggregate success rate on interactive agent benchmarks with up to 7.8% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, while keeping the library compact. A companion dataset, SkillFurnace, is released.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented RL, where skills pair instructions with applicability conditions, helps LLM agents solve complex long-horizon tasks. However, retaining every skill indiscriminately as the policy improves causes obsolete or harmful entries to accumulate and mislead the agent, degrading performance.
AI.method: SkillForge compiles and evolves the skill library through a fitness-driven lifecycle of trial, active, stable, and retired states. A pre-RL evaluation phase uses the base model's own rollouts to pre-retire low-fitness skills, producing a filtered library that seeds supervised fine-tuning. RL then takes over from this checkpoint, and each iteration applies selective retirement, stabilization, and LLM-guided mutation alongside policy optimization.
AI.result: Across multiple interactive agent benchmarks, SkillForge achieves the highest aggregate success rate, with up to 7.8% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, while keeping the skill library compact throughout training.
AI.conclusion: The fitness-driven skill lifecycle enables skills and the model to co-evolve, yielding a compact, high-quality library and superior agent performance. The authors release SkillFurnace, a dataset of 5k+ annotated records (retirement-filtered SFT trajectories, evolved skill libraries with fitness annotations, and retirement events with human-annotated failure categories) to support research on skill quality and lifecycle management.

title: Hall Effect-Based Tactile Force Detection Sensor for Robot-Assisted Minimally Invasive Surgery
summary: Robotic minimally invasive surgery has revolutionized surgical practice. However, as the surgeons are mechanically separated from the surgical tools, loss of tactile feedback occurs. We present a compact force sensor with three, millimeter scale sensing elements (taxels) that can be affixed to the grasping face of a robotic surgical tool. The sensor features a miniaturized design using Hall effect sensors and magnets embedded in a deformable elastomer contact layer. Sensor calibration is achieved with a 6 degree of freedom (DoF) parallel robot. Each taxel can detect applied normal and shear forces with average RMSE of 2.133 kPa. The calibrated sensor was validated on phantom and ex vivo porcine tissue, demonstrating tactile sensing during retraction as well as slip. This work introduces a small-scale Hall effect based tactile sensor, enabling sensing for force-sensitive robotic surgical applications.

AI.tldr: A compact 3-taxel Hall effect-based tactile sensor for robotic surgical tools detects normal and shear forces with 2.133 kPa average RMSE, validated on phantom and ex vivo porcine tissue.
AI.motivation: Robotic minimally invasive surgery separates surgeons from surgical tools, causing loss of tactile feedback. A small-scale force sensor is needed to restore tactile sensing for force-sensitive robotic surgical applications.
AI.method: The authors designed a compact sensor with three millimeter-scale sensing elements (taxels) affixable to a robotic surgical tool's grasping face. It uses Hall effect sensors and magnets embedded in a deformable elastomer contact layer. Calibration was performed with a 6-DoF parallel robot.
AI.result: Each taxel detects applied normal and shear forces with an average RMSE of 2.133 kPa. The calibrated sensor was validated on phantom and ex vivo porcine tissue, demonstrating tactile sensing during retraction and slip.
AI.conclusion: The work introduces a small-scale Hall effect-based tactile sensor, enabling tactile sensing for force-sensitive robotic surgical applications.

title: Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents
summary: Self-evolving tool-integrated agents learn from tasks and feedback generated within their own training loop. A Curriculum Agent generates tasks, while an Executor Agent learns from self-consistency signals through reinforcement learning. However, relying solely on the current Executor for feedback has two limitations: group-relative advantages vanish under full consensus, while uncertainty-based curriculum rewards favor disagreement without showing whether the generated tasks support further learning. These limitations motivate an additional reference beyond the current Executor. We propose \textit{AnchorLoop}, which introduces a frozen copy of the previous iteration's Executor as a historical reference and reuses it on both sides of the training loop. For the Executor, the anchor provides a cross-reference advantage that evaluates current outputs against both current and historical majority answers. For the Curriculum, it provides an agreement-based reference based on differences in sampled majority agreement. Since the Executor and anchor have identical parameters during Curriculum training, this comparison serves as a proxy for task selection rather than evidence of inter-version improvement or correctness. Across 13 reasoning benchmarks, AnchorLoop improves over Agent0 by 2.5\% on mathematical reasoning and 2.8\% on general reasoning tasks. It also maintains higher effective-advantage variance and continues improving in later iterations as the unanchored baseline shows diminishing gains. These results demonstrate the benefit of introducing a lightweight historical reference into self-evolving tool-integrated agents without external task or answer supervision.

AI.tldr: AnchorLoop introduces a frozen previous-iteration Executor as a historical "anchor" reference reused on both the Executor and Curriculum sides of a self-evolving tool-integrated agent's training loop, yielding gains over Agent0 across 13 reasoning benchmarks without external supervision.
AI.motivation: In self-evolving tool-integrated agents, the Curriculum Agent generates tasks and the Executor Agent learns from self-consistency signals via RL. Relying only on the current Executor for feedback is limiting: group-relative advantages vanish under full consensus, and uncertainty-based curriculum rewards favor disagreement without indicating whether generated tasks actually support further learning. This motivates adding a reference beyond the current Executor.
AI.method: AnchorLoop adds a frozen copy of the previous iteration's Executor as a historical reference and reuses it on both sides of the training loop. For the Executor, the anchor provides a cross-reference advantage that evaluates current outputs against both current and historical majority answers. For the Curriculum, it provides an agreement-based reference derived from differences in sampled majority agreement. Since the Executor and anchor share identical parameters during Curriculum training, this comparison acts as a proxy for task selection rather than evidence of inter-version improvement or correctness.
AI.result: Across 13 reasoning benchmarks, AnchorLoop improves over Agent0 by 2.5% on mathematical reasoning and 2.8% on general reasoning tasks. It also maintains higher effective-advantage variance and continues improving in later iterations, whereas the unanchored baseline shows diminishing gains.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the benefit of introducing a lightweight historical reference into self-evolving tool-integrated agents without external task or answer supervision.

title: MultiFly: A Real-World Multimodal Aerial Dataset with Annotation-Efficient Label Transfer and Cross-Modal Semantic Consistency
summary: We introduce MultiFly, a real-world, low-altitude UAV dataset for semantic perception across RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar modalities. MultiFly provides 17,272 synchronized samples from four suburban scenes with frame-wise annotations for 15 semantic classes, together with calibration and GNSS-RTK/IMU measurements. To avoid costly and inconsistent modality-specific annotation, we propagate labels from only 115 manually annotated RGB images through shared geometric representations to all four modalities. This approach generates semantic labels for 17,157 additional RGB images, 17,272 thermal images, 840M LiDAR points, and 3.4M radar points. Transferred annotations achieve 89.93% average agreement with held-out manual annotations, and 90.94% average semantic consistency across all six modality pairs. We further establish semantic segmentation benchmarks for all four modalities, revealing distinct architectural behavior for dense LiDAR and sparse radar data. Taken together, MultiFly provides a scalable foundation for multimodal aerial perception and, to the best of our knowledge, the first public real-world low-altitude aerial benchmark that combines consistent frame-wise semantic annotations for RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar. Data at https://github.com/markus-42/multifly.

AI.tldr: MultiFly is the first public real-world low-altitude UAV dataset with consistent frame-wise semantic annotations across RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar, containing 17,272 synchronized samples and annotation propagation from only 115 manual RGB images.
AI.motivation: Aerial multimodal perception lacks real-world benchmark datasets with consistent semantic labels across diverse sensing modalities. Annotating each modality separately is costly and leads to inconsistent labels, so a scalable, geometry-based labeling strategy is needed.
AI.method: The authors collect 17,272 synchronized samples from four suburban scenes over RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar, with calibration and GNSS-RTK/IMU measurements and 15 semantic classes. Labels are propagated from 115 manually annotated RGB images to all modalities via shared geometric representations, yielding labels for 17,157 additional RGB images, 17,272 thermal images, 840M LiDAR points, and 3.4M radar points. Semantic segmentation benchmarks are established for all four modalities.
AI.result: Transferred annotations reach 89.93% average agreement with held-out manual annotations and 90.94% average semantic consistency across all six modality pairs. Benchmarks reveal distinct architectural behavior for dense LiDAR versus sparse radar data.
AI.conclusion: MultiFly offers a scalable foundation for multimodal aerial perception and is, to the authors' knowledge, the first public real-world low-altitude aerial benchmark combining consistent frame-wise semantic annotations for RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar. Data are available at the provided GitHub link.

title: LiveMACE: Process-Aware Evaluation of LLM Agent Capabilities in Evolving Markets
summary: Evaluating agents by outcomes alone can obscure the capabilities that produce them. This problem is especially pronounced in evolving environments, where outcomes reflect a closed-loop interaction between agent behavior and changing external conditions. We introduce LiveMACEBench, a process-aware benchmark that uses live financial markets as a naturally evolving testbed for persistent LLM agents. Five frontier LLMs operate along continuous trajectories under matched Tool Use, Persistent Memory, Rule Following, and Multi-Agent Collaboration configurations. We evaluate them through both realized outcomes and mechanism-specific diagnostics derived from complete decision traces. Across 30 days of live evaluation, we find a pronounced outcome-capability gap: realized returns often diverge from capability-specific measurements, and similar outcomes can arise from markedly different patterns of mechanism use. Trace-level diagnostics further expose distinct bottlenecks across capabilities, demonstrating that mechanism access, effective mechanism use, and downstream performance are not interchangeable measures of agent capability. LiveMACEBench makes this distinction measurable, turning live markets from a performance leaderboard into a diagnostic environment for agent capability

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LiveMACEBench, a process-aware benchmark using live financial markets as an evolving testbed for persistent LLM agents, evaluating five frontier LLMs over 30 days via both realized outcomes and trace-level mechanism diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Evaluating agents solely by outcomes obscures the underlying capabilities producing them, especially in evolving environments where outcomes arise from closed-loop interaction between agent behavior and changing external conditions. Mechanism access, effective use, and performance are often conflated.
AI.method: LiveMACEBench uses live financial markets as a naturally evolving testbed. Five frontier LLMs operate along continuous trajectories under matched configurations of Tool Use, Persistent Memory, Rule Following, and Multi-Agent Collaboration. Evaluation combines realized outcomes with mechanism-specific diagnostics derived from complete decision traces.
AI.result: Over 30 days of live evaluation, a pronounced outcome-capability gap emerges: realized returns frequently diverge from capability-specific measurements, and similar outcomes can arise from markedly different patterns of mechanism use. Trace-level diagnostics expose distinct bottlenecks across capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Mechanism access, effective mechanism use, and downstream performance are not interchangeable measures of agent capability. LiveMACEBench makes this distinction measurable, turning live markets from a performance leaderboard into a diagnostic environment for agent capability.

title: Semantic-Aware Predictive Mapping for Exploration and Navigation
summary: Predictive mapping can support robotic exploration and navigation by estimating unseen geometric layouts from partial occupancy observations. However, occupancy-only representations may fail to distinguish semantically different structures with similar geometry. This is particularly relevant for indoor doors, which may appear as occupied cells like walls but indicate possible connected rooms or corridors beyond the observed region. This work investigates whether semantic door cues improve predictive geometric occupancy mapping around such ambiguous regions. We modify a subset of the CogniPlan dataset by inserting door-induced ambiguities into partial occupancy maps while keeping the ground-truth layouts unchanged. We compare a geometry-only control model with a semantic-cued model trained on the same modified dataset, where the semantic-cued model receives an additional door channel. Evaluation uses L1 error, F1 score, and Intersection over Union (IoU) over both the full map and a 10-pixel door-region mask. Full-map performance remains broadly similar between models, but localized door-region results show a clear qualitative improvement: L1 decreases from 0.004342 to 0.000025, while F1 and IoU improve from 0.031311 and 0.015905 to 1.000000 and 1.000000, respectively. These results suggest that semantic cues can improve predictive occupancy completion in regions where geometric observations alone are ambiguous.

AI.tldr: Adding semantic door cues to a predictive occupancy mapping model yields substantially better localized completion around door-induced ambiguities, while full-map performance stays largely unchanged.
AI.motivation: Predictive mapping helps robot exploration by inferring unseen geometry from partial occupancy observations. However, occupancy-only representations cannot distinguish structures with similar geometry but different semantics—especially indoor doors, which appear as occupied cells like walls yet may signal connected rooms or corridors beyond the observed region. The work asks whether semantic door cues improve predictive geometric occupancy mapping in such ambiguous areas.
AI.method: The authors modify a subset of the CogniPlan dataset by inserting door-induced ambiguities into partial occupancy maps while leaving ground-truth layouts unchanged. They compare a geometry-only control model against a semantic-cued model trained on the same modified dataset, where the semantic-cued model receives an additional door channel. Evaluation uses L1 error, F1, and IoU over both the full map and a 10-pixel door-region mask.
AI.result: Full-map performance is broadly similar across models. In the localized door-region mask, the semantic-cued model shows clear qualitative improvement: L1 drops from 0.004342 to 0.000025, while F1 and IoU rise from 0.031311 and 0.015905 to 1.000000 and 1.000000, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Semantic cues can improve predictive occupancy completion in regions where geometric observations alone are ambiguous, particularly around doors.

title: Think Before You Paint: Recursive Latent Reasoning for Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion models generate realistic images but often fail on visual reasoning tasks, such as filling in a Sudoku or drawing the path through a maze. When a discrete symbolic representation is available, recursive methods such as the Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) solve even hard instances of these puzzles. We ask how such reasoning can be carried over to pixels, where no symbolic representation is available. We propose Painter-Thinker (PaTh): a small recursive network (the Thinker) reasons over a grid of learned tokens that encode the noisy image and the conditioning, refines a latent state within every denoising step, and steers a frozen diffusion model (the Painter) through ControlNet adapters. The Thinker is trained with the standard reconstruction loss alone, without symbolic targets, a solver, or a verifier. PaTh solves 92.5% of hard MNIST Sudoku puzzles (prior best 75%) and 71.2% of extreme ones (prior best 4.1%), with 10M parameters against 82M for a standard diffusion model. It also improves on mazes, Queens, and CLEVR scenes with specified spatial relations, and its advantage grows with problem size. Diagnostic experiments show that PaTh recovers from injected mistakes that the diffusion model cannot repair, especially when many cells are wrong. Together, these results show that reasoning mechanisms developed for symbolic data can be integrated into pixel-space diffusion without symbolic supervision, opening a path toward generating data under increasingly complex constraints.

AI.tldr: PaTh couples a small recursive "Thinker" network with a frozen diffusion "Painter" (via ControlNet) to solve pixel-space visual reasoning puzzles without symbolic supervision, achieving large gains on hard/extreme Sudoku, mazes, Queens, and CLEVR.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models produce realistic images but struggle at visual reasoning tasks like Sudoku or mazes. Recursive symbolic methods (e.g., Tiny Recursive Model) solve such puzzles well, but no symbolic representation exists in pixel space. The paper asks whether symbolic-style reasoning mechanisms can be transferred to pixels.
AI.method: PaTh: a small recursive Thinker reasons over learned tokens encoding the noisy image and conditioning, refining a latent state within each denoising step, and steers a frozen diffusion Painter through ControlNet adapters. Trained with reconstruction loss only—no symbolic targets, solver, or verifier.
AI.result: Solves 92.5% of hard MNIST Sudoku (prior best 75%) and 71.2% of extreme ones (prior best 4.1%), using 10M parameters vs 82M for a standard diffusion model. Also improves mazes, Queens, and CLEVR spatial-relation scenes, with advantage growing with problem size. Diagnostics show PaTh recovers from injected mistakes the diffusion model cannot repair, especially with many wrong cells.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning mechanisms developed for symbolic data can be integrated into pixel-space diffusion without symbolic supervision, opening a path toward generating data under increasingly complex constraints.

title: OpenViTac: Learning and Benchmarking Visuo-Tactile Policies in a Unified Sim-and-Real Framework
summary: Tactile feedback provides embodied agents with physical information beyond visual observations, enabling more reliable interaction with the real world. However, despite the rapid progress of vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policies, there remains a lack of unified benchmarks for evaluating tactile-enabled robot manipulation across simulation and the real world. To address this gap, we introduce OpenViTac, a visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark for evaluating robot policies across simulation and the real world. OpenViTac organizes contact-rich manipulation into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions and provides paired simulation-real-world settings for consistent evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies. Building upon this benchmark, we investigate how different tactile representations and integration strategies affect the performance of pretrained VLA models. Correspondingly, we introduce OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework that combines the best-performing representation and integration strategy. Furthermore, we leverage the paired benchmark setting to study sim-real co-training and analyze factors affecting cross-domain policy learning. Together, OpenViTac provides a unified platform for evaluating and advancing visuo-tactile robot manipulation.

AI.tldr: OpenViTac is a unified visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark for evaluating robot policies across simulation and the real world, organizing contact-rich manipulation into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions and providing paired sim-real settings; it also introduces OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework, and studies sim-real co-training for cross-domain policy learning.
AI.motivation: Tactile feedback provides embodied agents with physical information beyond visual observations, enabling more reliable real-world interaction. Despite rapid progress in vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policies, there is a lack of unified benchmarks for evaluating tactile-enabled robot manipulation across both simulation and the real world.
AI.method: OpenViTac organizes contact-rich manipulation into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions and provides paired simulation-real-world settings for consistent evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies. The authors investigate how different tactile representations and integration strategies affect pretrained VLA model performance, introduce OpenVTLA (a tactile augmentation framework combining the best-performing representation and integration strategy), and leverage the paired benchmark to study sim-real co-training and analyze factors affecting cross-domain policy learning.
AI.result: OpenViTac enables consistent evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies, identifies best-performing tactile representation and integration strategies via OpenVTLA, and provides analysis of sim-real co-training and factors influencing cross-domain policy learning.
AI.conclusion: OpenViTac provides a unified platform for evaluating and advancing visuo-tactile robot manipulation.

title: Outperformance Inverse Optimization: Learning Objective Functions that Outperform Agent Decisions
summary: Inverse optimization estimates the weights of an objective function that explain observed decisions as optimal solutions, and is used in a variety of fields. For mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), existing methods aim to reproduce the observations as optimal solutions, and thus learn compromise weights when the observations are suboptimal. We propose outperformance inverse optimization, which instead seeks weights that induce, at each state, an optimal solution outperforming the observed action in every component. We give a loss function that can be evaluated with forward-problem oracles alone and is thus applicable to MILPs, together with gradient-based and DC optimization algorithms for minimizing it. For weights inducing a unique outperforming optimal solution at all observations, we prove that the probability of failing to induce such a solution at a new state (the generalization error) is bounded by a quantity inversely proportional to the number of observations, and that this bound is tight in the number of observations up to logarithmic factors. In experiments on synthetic and real data, the proposed methods improve the prediction of solutions outperforming the actions over existing methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes "outperformance inverse optimization" for MILPs, which learns weights that induce optimal solutions outperforming observed actions in every component rather than reproducing suboptimal observations. It introduces a forward-oracle-only loss, gradient and DC algorithms, proves a tight generalization bound, and demonstrates improved prediction on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: Existing inverse optimization methods for MILPs aim to reproduce observations as optimal solutions. When observations are suboptimal, this leads to learning compromise weights, which is undesirable. The authors seek an alternative that yields solutions strictly better than the observed actions.
AI.method: The paper formalizes outperformance inverse optimization, seeking weights that induce, at each state, an optimal solution outperforming the observed action in every component. It designs a loss function evaluable using only forward-problem oracles (thus applicable to MILPs), and develops gradient-based and DC (difference-of-convex) optimization algorithms to minimize this loss.
AI.result: For weights inducing a unique outperforming optimal solution at all observations, the authors prove the generalization error at a new state is bounded by a quantity inversely proportional to the number of observations, and that this bound is tight in the number of observations up to logarithmic factors. Experiments on synthetic and real data show improved prediction of outperforming solutions versus existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Outperformance inverse optimization offers a principled and computationally practical alternative to standard inverse optimization for MILPs, with theoretical generalization guarantees and empirical gains in predicting solutions that outperform observed actions.

title: NeRFifyMesh: Optimizing Neural Radiance Fields from Textured Meshes for Robotics Scene Building
summary: In robotics, scene representation plays a pivotal role in understanding and interacting with the environment. The advent of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and its variants, as a novel representation, has opened a new frontier of research. In applications such as semantic mapping and simulation, roboticists aim to build scenes using multiple NeRF models, each representing an object. While extensive datasets of 3D mesh models already exist, there is an urgent need to develop tools to convert these assets to NeRF models for rapid algorithm development and testing. This paper presents a new pipeline for converting existing mesh models to NeRF representations by artificially generating a ground truth point-based radiance field through sampling mesh geometry and texture. This approach alleviates the need for camera-based sampling or rendering multi-view images of the original mesh to train the NeRF model. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates that our method yields comparable rendering quality to the baselines. Additionally, the application of this representation is shown by constructing unified NeRF scenes and performing collision simulations with extracted geometry.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a pipeline that converts existing 3D mesh models into NeRF representations by artificially generating ground-truth point-based radiance fields via sampling mesh geometry and texture, avoiding camera-based sampling or multi-view rendering for training.
AI.motivation: In robotics, scene representation is central to understanding and interacting with the environment. NeRF and its variants offer a novel representation, and roboticists aim to build scenes from multiple object-level NeRF models for tasks like semantic mapping and simulation. Although extensive datasets of 3D mesh models already exist, tools to convert these assets into NeRF models are urgently needed for rapid algorithm development and testing.
AI.method: The pipeline converts mesh models to NeRF by directly generating a ground-truth point-based radiance field through sampling the mesh geometry and texture. This bypasses the conventional need for camera-based sampling or rendering multi-view images of the original mesh to train the NeRF model.
AI.result: Extensive benchmarking shows that the method achieves rendering quality comparable to the baselines. The representation's applicability is further demonstrated by constructing unified NeRF scenes and performing collision simulations using geometry extracted from them.
AI.conclusion: The proposed conversion pipeline provides an effective means of turning existing mesh assets into NeRF models, yielding competitive rendering quality and supporting downstream robotic applications such as unified scene construction and collision simulation.

title: NL2Hull: A Natural Language-Driven Constrained Ship Design Decision Framework
summary: Ship-form design combines smooth geometric representation, local shape editing, and constraints on the resulting hull. We present the Natural-Language-to-Hull Framework (NL2Hull Framework), which formulates ship-form editing as a typed discrete decision problem and connects language decisions to numerical geometry. Its Constrained Free-Form Deformation Engine (CFFD Engine) represents hull waterlines with non-uniform rational B-splines (NURBS), applies free-form deformation (FFD) to their control points, reconstructs the hull, and checks geometric constraints. We construct the Ship Design Decision Dataset (SDD Dataset) with 134,558 cleaned records and evaluate compared models on its subset Ship Design Decision Benchmark (SDDBench), containing 5,000 records and 43,496 typed questions. We propose Chip, a constrained ship-design decision model for processing natural-language requests. Chip reaches 95.90\% question accuracy and 99.32\% FFD exact match, with a negative log-likelihood of 0.0951, an expected calibration error of 0.0032, and a Brier score of 0.0551. The NL2Hull Framework provides a reproducible interface for evaluating language-based ship-form decisions while identifying the geometry and continuous-control components that require further development. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/wenhuahuo/NL2Hull.

AI.tldr: The NL2Hull Framework casts natural-language ship-form editing as a typed discrete decision problem, linking language decisions to NURBS-based numerical geometry, and introduces the Chip model with the SDD dataset and SDDBench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Ship-form design requires combining smooth geometric representation, local shape editing, and hull constraints; there is a need for a reproducible interface that connects natural-language requests to numerical geometry for evaluating language-based ship-form decisions.
AI.method: The framework formulates ship-form editing as a typed discrete decision problem. Its Constrained Free-Form Deformation Engine (CFFD Engine) represents hull waterlines with NURBS, applies FFD to control points, reconstructs the hull, and checks geometric constraints. The SDD Dataset (134,558 cleaned records) is built, with the SDDBench subset (5,000 records, 43,496 typed questions). The Chip constrained ship-design decision model processes natural-language requests.
AI.result: Chip achieves 95.90% question accuracy and 99.32% FFD exact match, with negative log-likelihood 0.0951, expected calibration error 0.0032, and Brier score 0.0551.
AI.conclusion: The NL2Hull Framework offers a reproducible interface for evaluating language-based ship-form decisions while identifying geometry and continuous-control components that need further development. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/wenhuahuo/NL2Hull.

title: RoboQuest: Generalist Physical Agents that Search, Inspect and Test
summary: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have made them capable generalist physical agents for a range of manipulation tasks. However, successful operation in an unfamiliar environment may require an agent to seek task-relevant information through interaction when it is absent from the observations: it may need to determine where a relevant object is, inspect an unobserved property, or discover the effect of an unfamiliar tool. We thus introduce RoboQuest, a benchmark for goal-directed embodied exploration, where agents must actively acquire task-relevant information through physical interaction, use the resulting evidence to adapt subsequent actions, and autonomously decide when to commit to task completion. RoboQuest comprises ten mobile manipulation tasks centered on three forms of uncertainty: search, manipulation-based inspection, and interactive testing. We evaluate five frontier multimodal agents through a common visuomotor interface, as well as a $π_{0.5}$ policy fine-tuned on the full-episode demonstrations we release. The best agent succeeds in only 23\% of the episodes, and the fine-tuned policy almost never succeeds. Isolated tests of the execution skills the tasks are built from, with the hidden information supplied, show that the agents can carry out most of the required actions, and our failure analysis attributes only a minority of the failures to execution. Our failure analysis further finds that the agents often stop exploring too early as they make decisions before observing the required evidence for task completion. We also find that agents rarely prevent or repair the disturbances caused by their exploration. Moreover, learning by trial and error remains difficult for most models.

AI.tldr: RoboQuest is a new benchmark of ten mobile manipulation tasks for goal-directed embodied exploration, where agents must actively gather task-relevant information via interaction and decide when to act. Frontier multimodal agents succeed in at most 23% of episodes, and mostly fail due to premature commitment rather than execution errors.
AI.motivation: Multimodal foundation models are increasingly capable generalist physical agents, but operating in unfamiliar environments often requires acquiring task-relevant information absent from observations—locating objects, inspecting unobserved properties, or discovering how unfamiliar tools behave. Existing evaluations do not test this active, goal-directed information acquisition.
AI.method: The authors introduce RoboQuest, a benchmark for goal-directed embodied exploration comprising ten mobile manipulation tasks organized around three forms of uncertainty: search, manipulation-based inspection, and interactive testing. They evaluate five frontier multimodal agents through a common visuomotor interface, plus a π0.5 policy fine-tuned on released full-episode demonstrations. They additionally run isolated tests of the constituent execution skills with hidden information supplied, and perform a failure analysis.
AI.result: The best agent succeeds in only 23% of episodes, and the fine-tuned π0.5 policy almost never succeeds. Isolated skill tests with hidden information provided show agents can perform most required actions, and failure analysis attributes only a minority of failures to execution. Failures predominantly stem from agents stopping exploration too early—deciding before observing the evidence needed for completion—along with rarely preventing or repairing disturbances caused by exploration, and difficulty learning by trial and error.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier multimodal agents are substantially limited in goal-directed embodied exploration: their bottleneck is not low-level execution but the active acquisition of task-relevant information, appropriate timing of commitment, and management of exploration-induced disturbances, highlighting key open challenges for generalist physical agents.

title: Where Can a Decision Model Diagnose HVAC Faults? Reasoning Demand, Physical Representation, and Robustness Under Shift
comment: 58 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Submitted to Energy and Buildings
summary: Artificial intelligence supports building operations in several forms, each with its own barrier. Expert rules must be tuned for every system, supervised models need labeled data that buildings rarely record, and language models return free text that requires human-in-the-loop checking, since their stated confidence is unreliable. A newer kind of pretrained model, here called a decision model, returns a probability for every allowed answer, so one model could serve many decisions without training. This study answers three open questions for fault diagnosis in heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems: which decisions such a model can make, what input it needs, and whether its probabilities hold when conditions change. On 128 fault days from four public datasets of real equipment, faults are graded by the reasoning their diagnosis demands, with data given raw, as physical features, or with Brick topology. The decision model Jev, open language models, and a supervised model face nine tests that change season, control configuration, or building. Given physical features, Jev and the larger open model diagnosed faults whose evidence one feature carries, but not faults that need operating context. Under shift they kept their accuracy and calibration, while the supervised model lost 0.33 macro-F1 yet led or tied within a building. Their probabilities still needed correction, and detection was weak. The study maps which faults a decision model can diagnose and from what input, and supports a division of work in which code computes the physics and the model ranks candidate faults for an operator.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates a pretrained "decision model" (Jev) for HVAC fault diagnosis on 128 fault days from four public real-equipment datasets, comparing it with open language models and a supervised model across nine distribution-shift tests. It assesses which faults such a model can diagnose, what input (raw data, physical features, or Brick topology) it needs, and whether its probabilities hold under changing conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing AI approaches for building operations each face barriers: expert rules require per-system tuning, supervised models need labeled data that buildings rarely record, and language models return free text requiring human checking because their stated confidence is unreliable. A newer class of pretrained "decision model" that returns a probability for every allowed answer could serve many decisions without training, but open questions remain about which decisions it can make, what input it needs, and whether its probabilities remain valid when conditions change.
AI.method: On 128 fault days from four public datasets of real equipment, faults are graded by the reasoning their diagnosis demands, with data provided raw, as physical features, or with Brick topology. The decision model Jev, open language models, and a supervised model are subjected to nine tests that alter season, control configuration, or building.
AI.result: Given physical features, Jev and the larger open model diagnosed faults whose evidence a single feature carries, but not faults requiring operating context. Under shift, they maintained accuracy and calibration, while the supervised model lost 0.33 macro-F1 yet led or tied within a building. Their probabilities still required correction, and detection was weak.
AI.conclusion: The study maps which faults a decision model can diagnose and from what input, and supports a division of labor in which code computes the physics while the model ranks candidate faults for an operator.

title: RobotWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Robot Use Across Diverse Tasks and Embodiments
summary: General-purpose agents increasingly write code, use tools, and complete complex digital tasks, raising the question of how far these capabilities carry into the physical world. To investigate this, we introduce RobotWorld, a challenging simulation testbed for robot use: turning instructions and observations into physical task execution through robot interfaces. Its 84 tasks span manipulation, mobile manipulation, locomotion, driving, and aerial control, with explicit interaction budgets and executable success checks. By analysing task outcomes alongside execution traces, we identify both the capabilities that transfer and the gaps that prevent reliable completion. Furthermore, we find that current agents can construct sophisticated perception and control workflows, including image segmentation, camera calibration, spatial estimation, and dynamics-based computation. These capabilities, however, do not consistently compose into successful behaviour: agents lose task-relevant object states despite reaching commanded poses, fail to correct ineffective actions, recover too late, or mistake unfinished tasks for completion. This uneven transfer also differs across models: Astra succeeds more often on spatial and constrained-contact goals, whereas Opus 5.5 succeeds more often on continuous-balance and timed-interaction goals. By linking these outcomes to execution behaviour, RobotWorld provides both a rigorous proving ground and an empirical account of the remaining capability gaps, thereby establishing concrete targets for training and designing more reliable physical-world agents.

AI.tldr: RobotWorld is a simulation testbed of 84 robotic tasks (manipulation, mobile manipulation, locomotion, driving, aerial control) with explicit interaction budgets and executable success checks, used to measure how far general-purpose agents' code/tool-use capabilities transfer to physical task execution and to identify the specific capability gaps that remain.
AI.motivation: General-purpose agents increasingly write code, use tools, and complete complex digital tasks, but it is unclear how far these capabilities carry into the physical world. A rigorous testbed is needed to quantify transfer and expose failure modes.
AI.method: RobotWorld simulation testbed: turning instructions and observations into physical execution via robot interfaces. Includes 84 tasks across five domains with explicit interaction budgets and executable success checks. Analysis combines task outcomes with execution traces to correlate success with behaviour.
AI.result: Agents can build sophisticated perception and control workflows (image segmentation, camera calibration, spatial estimation, dynamics-based computation), but these do not consistently compose into successful behaviour. Observed failures: loss of task-relevant object states despite reaching commanded poses, failure to correct ineffective actions, late recovery, and premature completion claims. Transfer is uneven across models: Astra performs better on spatial and constrained-contact goals, Opus 5.5 on continuous-balance and timed-interaction goals.
AI.conclusion: RobotWorld serves as both a rigorous proving ground and an empirical account of remaining capability gaps, providing concrete targets for training and designing more reliable physical-world agents.

title: AgentTime: Can Agents Estimate and Control Their Own Runtime?
summary: An essential control of AI agents is their ability to manage runtime. This ability requires a sense of time-awareness, to predict and estimate wall-clock time and to control their own actions.
