Prior work has focused on time-awareness, but duration-following and control in native agent harnesses remain unexplored. We present AgentTime, a benchmark for testing whether agents can work for a requested duration, predict their runtime, and estimate elapsed time afterward. It comprises 222 tasks from 18 sources spanning coding, computer use, agentic work, and automated research. Duration-following experiments append a single instruction specifying how long to work, with requests ranging from about a minute to multiple days. Accuracy on these instructions varies substantially: Fable 5.1 in Claude Code deviates from requested runtimes by a typical factor of 2.9$\times$, compared with only 1.2$\times$ for GPT-6 Astra in Codex. However, matching the requested runtime does not, by itself, establish continued work on the task. Among 158 reviewed Astra runs with classifiable transcripts, 14 explicitly slept after appearing to finish. In forecasting experiments, predictions tend to overestimate natural runtimes. In retrospective experiments, removing temporal information more than doubles deviation for Sol and Astra and nearly doubles it for Fable. An agent's ability to complete a task does not guarantee that it can control its own time or work for the whole requested duration. For agents to run reliably, safely, and autonomously over long horizons, we require the evaluation of both.

AI.tldr: AgentTime is a 222-task benchmark across 18 sources that evaluates whether AI agents can follow requested runtimes, predict their own runtime, and estimate elapsed time, revealing large deviations and "sleeping" behavior in harnesses like Claude Code and Codex.
AI.motivation: Runtime management is an essential control capability for AI agents, requiring time-awareness to predict wall-clock time, estimate elapsed time, and govern their own actions. Prior work addressed time-awareness, but duration-following and self-time control within native agent harnesses remain unexplored.
AI.method: AgentTime comprises 222 tasks from 18 sources spanning coding, computer use, agentic work, and automated research. It has three experiment types: (1) duration-following, where a single instruction specifies how long to work (requests range from about a minute to multiple days); (2) forecasting, where agents predict natural runtimes; and (3) retrospective estimation of elapsed time, including ablations that remove temporal information.
AI.result: Duration-following accuracy varies substantially: Fable 5.1 in Claude Code deviates from requested runtimes by a typical factor of 2.9x, versus 1.2x for GPT-6 Astra in Codex. Matching runtime does not imply continued work: among 158 reviewed Astra runs with classifiable transcripts, 14 explicitly slept after appearing to finish. Forecasting tends to overestimate natural runtimes. Removing temporal information more than doubles deviation for Sol and Astra and nearly doubles it for Fable.
AI.conclusion: Task completion does not guarantee an agent can control its own time or work for the entire requested duration. Reliable, safe, long-horizon autonomous agents require evaluation of both task ability and runtime control.

title: AirGroundVLN: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Goal-Oriented Air-Ground Collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Goal-oriented Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to locate and reach targets described in natural language without prescribed routes. Air--ground collaboration is valuable for tasks requiring both wide-area search and fine-grained localization. However, systematic study of goal-oriented air--ground collaborative VLN remains limited by the lack of large-scale, diverse benchmarks and two core challenges: 1) substantial differences between aerial and ground views, together with useful observations becoming unavailable as navigation proceeds, make it difficult to maintain spatially consistent context across platforms and over time; and 2) asymmetric spatial observability makes ground perception locally detailed but spatially limited and aerial perception broad but locally coarse, limiting the reliability of single-platform planning. To address these limitations, we introduce AirGroundVLN, a benchmark containing 10,281 navigation episodes and 955 target instances across 19 Unreal Engine environments, with seen/unseen splits and an aerial-visibility protocol for systematic evaluation. Alongside the benchmark, we propose AG-CoNAV, a trainable reference framework comprising two key components: Spatiotemporally Anchored Collaborative Memory (SACM) and Aerial-Guided Regional-to-Local Planning (AGRLP). SACM maintains and retrieves spatially consistent historical context across aerial and ground observations. Meanwhile, AGRLP combines regional aerial guidance with fine-grained ground navigation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of AG-CoNAV and establish AirGroundVLN as a comprehensive benchmark for future exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AirGroundVLN, a large-scale benchmark for goal-oriented air-ground collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), and AG-CoNAV, a trainable framework with SACM and AGRLP components to address cross-platform spatial consistency and asymmetric observability challenges.
AI.motivation: Goal-oriented VLN requires agents to locate and reach targets described in natural language without prescribed routes. Air-ground collaboration suits tasks needing wide-area search plus fine-grained localization, but systematic study is limited by the lack of large-scale, diverse benchmarks and two core challenges: (1) aerial-ground view differences and loss of useful observations over time hinder maintaining spatially consistent context across platforms and time; (2) asymmetric spatial observability makes ground perception locally detailed but spatially limited, and aerial perception broad but locally coarse, reducing single-platform planning reliability.
AI.method: The authors introduce AirGroundVLN, a benchmark with 10,281 navigation episodes and 955 target instances across 19 Unreal Engine environments, including seen/unseen splits and an aerial-visibility protocol. They also propose AG-CoNAV, a trainable reference framework with two components: Spatiotemporally Anchored Collaborative Memory (SACM), which maintains and retrieves spatially consistent historical context across aerial and ground observations, and Aerial-Guided Regional-to-Local Planning (AGRLP), which combines regional aerial guidance with fine-grained ground navigation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of AG-CoNAV and establish AirGroundVLN as a comprehensive benchmark for future exploration.
AI.conclusion: AirGroundVLN provides a systematic evaluation platform for goal-oriented air-ground collaborative VLN, and AG-CoNAV offers an effective trainable framework addressing cross-platform spatiotemporal consistency and asymmetric observability, enabling future research in this direction.

title: Successive Training Stages and Large Language Model Persuasion: Effects of Misalignment, Supervised Fine-Tuning, and Preference Optimization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be tuned to influence human attitudes, yet the respective contributions of successive post-training stages remain un-clear. This study examines how three successive training stages affect LLM persuasiveness: (1) misalignment through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on conspiracy data, (2) additional persuasive SFT on argumentative data, and (3) Identity Preference Optimization (IPO), a preference-optimization method. A total of 835 participants recruited on Prolific were randomly assigned to five between-subject conditions (neutral text, conspiracy-trained model, persuasion-trained model, preference-optimized model, and GPT-4) and were exposed to texts on 10 divisive political issues, personalized from their individual profiles in all model conditions. Attitude change was measured as the difference between pre- and post-exposure positions on continuous Likert scales and analyzed with an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). A significant condition x baseline-attitude interaction, F (4, 825) = 5.33, p < .001, indicated that training effects depended on participants' initial attitudes. Persuasive SFT produced greater attitude change than conspiracy training alone, d = 0.30, whereas IPO provided no additional benefit, d = 0.03, and GPT-4 did not differ from neutral text, d = --0.01. These results show that targeted supervised training on persuasive data increases LLM persuasiveness, whereas preference optimization yields no significant gains beyond it.

AI.tldr: This study isolates the contributions of successive post-training stages to LLM persuasiveness, finding that persuasive supervised fine-tuning significantly increases attitude change over conspiracy-based misalignment training, while Identity Preference Optimization adds no further benefit.
AI.motivation: LLMs can be tuned to influence human attitudes, but the respective contributions of successive post-training stages (misalignment SFT, persuasive SFT, and preference optimization) to persuasiveness remain unclear. The study aims to disentangle these stage-wise effects.
AI.method: 835 Prolific participants were randomly assigned to five between-subject conditions (neutral text, conspiracy-trained model, persuasion-trained model, preference-optimized model, and GPT-4) and exposed to personalized texts on 10 divisive political issues. Attitude change was measured via pre-/post-exposure Likert-scale differences and analyzed with ANCOVA.
AI.result: A significant condition x baseline-attitude interaction emerged, F(4, 825) = 5.33, p < .001, indicating training effects depended on initial attitudes. Persuasive SFT produced greater attitude change than conspiracy training alone (d = 0.30), whereas IPO provided no additional benefit (d = 0.03), and GPT-4 did not differ from neutral text (d = -0.01).
AI.conclusion: Targeted supervised training on persuasive data increases LLM persuasiveness, while preference optimization yields no significant gains beyond it. Successive post-training stages contribute non-uniformly to persuasive capability.

title: RFPO: Rectified Flow Policy Optimization for Embodied Control
summary: Flow-based policies provide an expressive framework for continuous robot control, but their iterative ODE integration incurs substantial inference cost. Naively reducing the integration budget can severely degrade control, since policies optimized under full-step execution are not explicitly constrained to remain reliable under coarse numerical integration. We refer to this mismatch as the few-step discretization gap. To address this problem, we introduce RFPO, a flow-policy optimization framework for reliable few-step execution. Reward-aware online Reflow rectifies student-induced transport paths during on-policy learning, making the resulting policy more robust to coarse integration. A frozen Gaussian PPO controller supplies complementary action-space supervision at full and intermediate integration budgets, while the deployed policy remains a single flow student executed with one Euler step. Across Unitree Go2, Boston Dynamics Spot, Unitree H1, and Unitree G1, RFPO consistently preserves full-step control performance under one-step execution, with one-step returns remaining within 2.4% of their corresponding 64-step values across both zero and random initialization. On Unitree Go2, one-step execution retains 98.5% of the 64-step reward while reducing onboard mean inference latency from 4.39 ms to 0.08 ms, yielding a 54.9x speedup. Real-robot experiments further validate stable one-step locomotion. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/RFPO. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/RFPO.

AI.tldr: RFPO is a flow-policy optimization framework that enables reliable one-step Euler inference for continuous robot control by closing the few-step discretization gap via reward-aware online Reflow and frozen Gaussian PPO supervision.
AI.motivation: Flow-based policies are expressive for continuous robot control but require iterative ODE integration, incurring high inference cost. Naively shrinking the integration budget degrades control because policies trained under full-step execution are not constrained to stay reliable under coarse numerical integration, a mismatch the authors term the few-step discretization gap.
AI.method: RFPO combines reward-aware online Reflow, which rectifies student-induced transport paths during on-policy learning to make the policy robust to coarse integration, with a frozen Gaussian PPO controller that provides complementary action-space supervision at full and intermediate integration budgets. The deployed policy is a single flow student executed with one Euler step.
AI.result: Across Unitree Go2, Boston Dynamics Spot, Unitree H1, and Unitree G1, RFPO preserves full-step control performance under one-step execution, with one-step returns within 2.4% of 64-step values for both zero and random initialization. On Unitree Go2, one-step execution retains 98.5% of the 64-step reward while cutting onboard mean inference latency from 4.39 ms to 0.08 ms (54.9x speedup). Real-robot experiments confirm stable one-step locomotion.
AI.conclusion: RFPO effectively addresses the few-step discretization gap, enabling fast, single-step flow-policy deployment without sacrificing control quality, and is validated in simulation across multiple robot platforms and on real hardware.

title: From Expected Harmfulness to Likelihood: A Probabilistic Reformulation of Jailbreaking LLM Agents
summary: When the harmfulness of an LLM agent's output can be quantified, a natural jailbreaking objective is to maximize expected harmfulness over admissible input modifications. An alternative approach constructs or selects harmful target outputs and modifies the input to increase their likelihood. We establish a precise connection between these two approaches through a probabilistic reformulation. Specifically, we show that the gradient of the logarithm of expected harmfulness with respect to the input equals the expected input gradient of the model's log-likelihood under a harmfulness reweighted output distribution. This identity provides a unified interpretation of expected harmfulness and target likelihood optimization. Building on this connection, we propose OPUR, a sampling distribution designed to generate highly harmful target outputs and use the resulting samples to guide likelihood-based input optimization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the resulting method in jailbreaking LLM agents.

AI.tldr: The paper unifies two jailbreaking objectives—maximizing expected harmfulness and maximizing target-output likelihood—via a probabilistic identity, and proposes OPUR, a harmfulness-reweighted sampling distribution that guides likelihood-based input optimization for effective jailbreaking.
AI.motivation: Two natural jailbreaking objectives exist for LLM agents: (1) directly maximizing expected harmfulness over admissible input modifications, and (2) selecting or constructing harmful target outputs and modifying inputs to raise their likelihood. These approaches appear distinct, and it is unclear how they relate or which is preferable.
AI.method: A probabilistic reformulation establishes that the gradient of the log expected harmfulness w.r.t. the input equals the expected input gradient of the model's log-likelihood under a harmfulness-reweighted output distribution. This identity unifies the two objectives. Based on it, the authors propose OPUR, a sampling distribution that generates highly harmful target outputs, whose samples then guide likelihood-based input optimization.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the resulting method in jailbreaking LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: Expected-harmfulness optimization and target-likelihood optimization are two views of the same underlying problem, and the proposed OPUR-guided likelihood-based input optimization is an effective jailbreaking strategy for LLM agents.

title: FoldBack: Self-Correcting Masked Generative Policy for Long-Horizon Garment Folding
summary: We present FoldBack, a self-correcting masked generative policy for long-horizon garment folding. Existing long-trajectory policies may continue after a missed or slipped grasp even when the garment has not reached the intended configuration. We structure FoldBack's recovery mechanisms around three inference-time decisions: when to refine and verify, how to roll back, and where and how to retry. FoldBack aligns refinement and grasp verification with pick-and-place events, returns the robot to a retryable pre-grasp configuration while preserving successful grasps, and selectively regenerates the failed segment and selected future actions while avoiding previous failed grasp locations. To our knowledge, FoldBack is the first editable full-trajectory policy to unify these decisions, enabling failed interactions to be detected, undone, and repaired before execution continues, without recovery demonstrations or base-policy retraining. Across 33 real garments from six categories, FoldBack achieves 75.2% final folding success and 0.837 final-mask IoU, versus 45.7% and 0.689 for the strongest prior baseline.

AI.tldr: FoldBack is a self-correcting masked generative policy for long-horizon garment folding that detects, undoes, and repairs failed grasps at inference time without recovery demonstrations or retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing long-trajectory garment-folding policies keep executing after a missed or slipped grasp even when the garment has not reached its intended configuration, lacking mechanisms to detect, undo, and repair failures mid-execution.
AI.method: FoldBack structures recovery around three inference-time decisions: when to refine and verify, how to roll back, and where/how to retry. It aligns refinement and grasp verification with pick-and-place events, returns the robot to a retryable pre-grasp configuration while preserving successful grasps, and selectively regenerates the failed segment plus selected future actions while avoiding previously failed grasp locations. It is an editable full-trajectory policy requiring no recovery demonstrations or base-policy retraining.
AI.result: On 33 real garments across six categories, FoldBack reaches 75.2% final folding success and 0.837 final-mask IoU, compared to 45.7% and 0.689 for the strongest prior baseline.
AI.conclusion: FoldBack is, to the authors' knowledge, the first editable full-trajectory policy to unify refine-verify, rollback, and retry decisions, enabling failed interactions to be detected, undone, and repaired before execution continues.

title: What the Sleeve Feels: Explainable Machine Learning for Textile Pressure-Based Postural Screening
summary: Pressure-sensing smart textiles convert body-surface contact into a dense, image-like signal closely tied to posture and movement, making them a promising low-cost route to wearable posture screening. Realizing that promise, however, requires more than classification accuracy: a deployable system must generalize to wearers unseen during training, expose the physical evidence behind its decisions, and tolerate the small donning offsets that occur whenever a garment is removed and re-worn. This paper addresses these three requirements jointly using a knitted piezoresistive sleeve worn on the forearm as a testbed. We regroup fine-grained everyday activities into three coarser screening categories (neutral, potentially undesirable, and functional or transitional), engineer 29 interpretable pressure-distribution features spanning global intensity, spatial center of pressure, quadrant asymmetry, distribution complexity, and short-horizon temporal change, and evaluate under a strict subject-wise split. A tuned XGBoost classifier reaches 0.818 accuracy, 0.788 balanced accuracy, and 0.801 macro F1 on unseen test subjects, with tight frame-level bootstrap 95% intervals of about plus-minus 0.01 and a subject-to-subject standard deviation near 0.06 under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. A simple 2D-CNN baseline trained on raw frames achieves broadly similar performance, showing that hand-engineered features are not left behind by a learned spatial representation on this task. SHAP-based explanation, a feature-group ablation, per-activity error analysis inside the pooled undesirable class, class-mapping sensitivity, and a simulated donning-rotation stress test together locate what the model relies on, where it degrades, and why, directly targeting the generalization, interpretability, and robustness gaps that determine whether such a system is deployable.

AI.tldr: A knitted piezoresistive forearm sleeve is used to screen daily activities into three coarse posture categories, using 29 interpretable pressure-distribution features and a tuned XGBoost model evaluated under a strict subject-wise split, with SHAP explanation, ablation, error analysis, and a simulated donning-rotation stress test.
AI.motivation: Pressure-sensing smart textiles offer a low-cost route to wearable posture screening, but deployability requires more than classification accuracy: generalization to unseen wearers, interpretable physical evidence for decisions, and robustness to small donning offsets when a garment is removed and re-worn. This paper targets these three requirements jointly.
AI.method: Using a knitted piezoresistive sleeve worn on the forearm, the authors regroup fine-grained everyday activities into three coarser screening categories (neutral, potentially undesirable, and functional/transitional), engineer 29 interpretable pressure-distribution features spanning global intensity, spatial center of pressure, quadrant asymmetry, distribution complexity, and short-horizon temporal change, and evaluate under a strict subject-wise split. They compare a tuned XGBoost classifier against a simple 2D-CNN baseline trained on raw frames, and apply SHAP-based explanation, a feature-group ablation, per-activity error analysis within the pooled undesirable class, class-mapping sensitivity, and a simulated donning-rotation stress test.
AI.result: The tuned XGBoost classifier reaches 0.818 accuracy, 0.788 balanced accuracy, and 0.801 macro F1 on unseen test subjects, with tight frame-level bootstrap 95% intervals of about ±0.01 and subject-to-subject standard deviation near 0.06 under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. The 2D-CNN baseline on raw frames achieves broadly similar performance, indicating hand-engineered features are not left behind by a learned spatial representation on this task.
AI.conclusion: The analysis locates what the model relies on, where it degrades, and why, directly targeting the generalization, interpretability, and robustness gaps that determine whether such a smart-textile posture screening system is deployable.

title: LLA-MPPI: Rapidly Adaptive Whole-body Control of Legged Robots with GPU-Accelerated Parallel Simulations
comment: The first two authors are co-first authors (contributed equally to the work)
summary: Real-time whole-body controllers for legged robots typically plan through a fixed nominal model and degrade when the deployed dynamics change. Adaptive methods typically require a model structure that contact dynamics do not provide, or they need offline training for each anticipated condition. We present Look-back and Look-ahead Adaptive Model Predictive Path Integral control (LLA-MPPI). The method converts whole-body adaptation into selection over a bank of GPU-batched contact simulators with different physical or structural parameters. Windowed prediction errors select the simulator that best explains recent motion. A whole-body MPPI planner optimizes controls through the selected model. The framework requires no offline training, and its selected hypotheses are physically interpretable. Across four simulated tasks, it achieves 97.5% success while the strongest baseline reaches 74% and an oracle with the true model reaches 98.5%. Hardware validation on a Unitree Go2 shows the robot walking under a payload added mid-run, walking after one leg is disabled, and pushing a box to its goal while increasing its mass on the fly. Code, videos, and project details are available at: https://lla-control.github.io

AI.tldr: LLA-MPPI adapts whole-body legged robot control online by selecting among a bank of GPU-batched contact simulators with differing parameters, using windowed prediction errors, and planning with MPPI through the selected model—no offline training required.
AI.motivation: Real-time whole-body controllers for legged robots rely on a fixed nominal model and degrade when deployed dynamics change. Adaptive methods either require a model structure that contact dynamics do not provide or need offline training per anticipated condition.
AI.method: Look-back and Look-ahead Adaptive Model Predictive Path Integral control (LLA-MPPI) converts whole-body adaptation into selection over a bank of GPU-batched contact simulators with different physical or structural parameters. Windowed prediction errors select the simulator that best explains recent motion; a whole-body MPPI planner then optimizes controls through the selected model.
AI.result: Across four simulated tasks, LLA-MPPI achieves 97.5% success versus 74% for the strongest baseline and 98.5% for an oracle with the true model. Hardware validation on a Unitree Go2 shows walking with a payload added mid-run, walking after one leg is disabled, and pushing a box to its goal while increasing its mass on the fly.
AI.conclusion: LLA-MPPI enables training-free, physically interpretable online whole-body adaptation for legged robots, approaching oracle performance and transferring to hardware.

title: Learning to Accumulate Knowledge with Mutual Information
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve their performance by reusing knowledge distilled from past interactions. However, curating new experiences into a knowledge bank that becomes more useful as it grows remains challenging. Effective knowledge accumulation should limit redundant overlap among entries and ensure that new knowledge contributes beyond what the bank already provides. Yet training a curator with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on standalone task success can reinforce general guidance even when it duplicates existing knowledge. Therefore, we propose Knowledge Weaver, a reinforcement learning framework that trains a language model to curate reusable knowledge from agent trajectories. We couple feedback inspired by token-wise mutual information (MI) with marginal success rewards to guide knowledge accumulation. Together, these signals encourage the curator to preserve distinct information from experience and produce entries that improve task success when added to existing knowledge. Standalone success rewards also favor entries that are useful on their own. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Knowledge Weaver achieves mean success rates of 54.0\% and 42.0\% with k=10 retrieved entries, exceeding GRPO by 16.9 and 18.7 percentage points, respectively. Its knowledge banks also outperform the evaluated prompt-based and established banks, including human-written banks, in overall ALFWorld success rate and WebShop score with the executor frozen. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/LaoKuiZe/Knowledge-Weaver.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Knowledge Weaver, a reinforcement learning framework that trains a language model curator to distill reusable knowledge from LLM agent trajectories, using token-wise mutual information signals and marginal success rewards to build knowledge banks that grow more useful as they expand.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can improve by reusing knowledge from past interactions, but curating experiences into a knowledge bank that becomes more useful as it grows is hard. Effective accumulation must limit redundant overlap among entries and ensure new knowledge contributes beyond what the bank already provides. Training a curator with GRPO on standalone task success can reinforce general guidance even when it duplicates existing knowledge, failing to ensure marginal contribution.
AI.method: Knowledge Weaver couples feedback inspired by token-wise mutual information (MI) with marginal success rewards to guide knowledge accumulation. These signals encourage the curator to preserve distinct information from experience and produce entries that improve task success when added to existing knowledge, while standalone success rewards favor entries useful on their own. The framework trains a language model to curate reusable knowledge from agent trajectories via reinforcement learning.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop, Knowledge Weaver achieves mean success rates of 54.0% and 42.0% with k=10 retrieved entries, exceeding GRPO by 16.9 and 18.7 percentage points, respectively. Its knowledge banks also outperform evaluated prompt-based and established banks, including human-written banks, in overall ALFWorld success rate and WebShop score with the executor frozen.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge Weaver demonstrates that combining mutual-information-inspired feedback with marginal success rewards enables a trained curator to accumulate non-redundant, complementary, and reusable knowledge, yielding knowledge banks that surpass GRPO and human-written baselines. The codebase is publicly available.

title: CMP-IRRT*: A Perception-Assisted Height-Adaptive Planner for Quadruped Robots
comment: Accepted at the 18th Asian Conference on Machine Learning (ACML 2026)
summary: Quadruped robots can traverse low obstacles, but many 2D planning pipelines still model obstacles as binary occupied regions and rely on sampling-based search that can be inefficient under a limited budget. We propose a perception-assisted height-adaptive planning framework based on CMP-IRRT*, a Channel Mamba PointNet-guided Informed RRT* planner. Given a calibrated top-view RGB observation, the perception module estimates obstacle regions and converts depth predictions into a ground-relative height map. The planner then performs height-conditioned collision checking, treating high obstacles as blocked while allowing low obstacles to be traversed, and uses the CMP guide to bias sampling toward promising regions while retaining standard free-space and informed sampling fallbacks. Experiments on 2D planning benchmarks show that CMP-IRRT* reduces explored nodes and iterations compared with classical and neural-guided baselines, and a controlled ablation supports the contribution of the Mamba-based guide. In constructed traversability-aware scenarios, the proposed planner reduces path length by up to 16.3% when low obstacles are traversable, and a Unitree Go2 demonstration further shows executable bypassing and traversal behaviors. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/MingfanZhao/height-adaptive-planner.

AI.tldr: CMP-IRRT* is a Channel Mamba PointNet-guided Informed RRT* planner with a perception-assisted height-adaptive framework: it estimates obstacle regions and a ground-relative height map from a top-view RGB image, then lets the planner treat high obstacles as blocked and low obstacles as traversable, with a neural guide biasing sampling.
AI.motivation: Many 2D planning pipelines still model obstacles as binary occupied regions and rely on sampling-based search that can be inefficient under a limited budget, despite quadruped robots being able to traverse low obstacles.
AI.method: A perception module estimates obstacle regions from a calibrated top-view RGB observation and converts depth predictions into a ground-relative height map. The planner performs height-conditioned collision checking (high obstacles blocked, low obstacles traversable) and uses a Channel Mamba PointNet (CMP) guide to bias sampling toward promising regions, while retaining standard free-space and informed sampling fallbacks.
AI.result: On 2D planning benchmarks, CMP-IRRT* reduces explored nodes and iterations versus classical and neural-guided baselines; a controlled ablation supports the contribution of the Mamba-based guide. In traversability-aware scenarios, path length is reduced by up to 16.3% when low obstacles are traversable; a Unitree Go2 demonstration shows executable bypassing and traversal behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The height-adaptive, perception-assisted CMP-IRRT* framework improves sampling efficiency and path quality for quadruped navigation by exploiting traversable low obstacles, with code publicly available.

title: Loud Failures, Quiet Failures: Fault Detection and Recovery in Tool-Using Language Model Agents
summary: Tool-using agents are usually scored on whether they finish a task while the tools work. Deployments are less forgiving: services time out, endpoints disappear, parameter names change, and results come back well formed but wrong. Prior work has shown that language models over-trust tool outputs that fail silently; we ask how that over-trust plays out across the stages of failure handling in multi-turn agents. Wrapping the executable environments of an established function-calling benchmark in a fault-injection layer, we inject one of four typed faults at a controlled point in the trajectory and record whether the agent notices, changes plan, recovers the task, or repeats itself. Six models from three families, half of them reasoning variants, ran 1,920 trials over 24 multi-step tasks. Agents treat a failure as a problem in 91.3% of trials when the tool returns an explicit error, but in 58.8% of trials when it returns a plausible wrong value, against a 26.8% rate of reporting problems when nothing was wrong. Reasoning models are not better placed: paired against instruct siblings, they notice less (-9.3 points, p < .001) and change plan more (+10.4 points, p < .001), and recovery is unchanged (p = .512). Because agents are stochastic, two fault-free runs of the same task end in the same state only 63.3% of the time; against that baseline, only a missing tool clearly lowers recovery (39.9%), while timeouts, schema drift, and corruption stay within run-to-run variation. After a fault, agents return to the same tool three or more times in a row in up to 22.2% of trials, though strictly identical repeats are rare. A prompt line asking the agent to check each result did not move detection. Agents respond to the error channel rather than to the content of what a tool returns, so failures that stay inside the expected format pass through.

AI.tldr: Multi-turn tool-using agents detect explicit tool errors 91.3% of the time but plausible-but-wrong outputs only 58.8%, and reasoning variants detect failures less than instruct siblings; only a missing tool clearly reduces recovery beyond baseline stochasticity.
AI.motivation: Deployed agents face unreliable tools (timeouts, disappearing endpoints, renamed parameters, well-formed but incorrect results), and prior work shows language models over-trust silently failing tool outputs. The paper asks how this over-trust unfolds across the stages of failure handling—detection, replanning, recovery, and repetition—in multi-turn agents, and whether reasoning models are better placed to cope.
AI.method: The authors wrap the executable environments of an established function-calling benchmark in a fault-injection layer, injecting one of four typed faults (missing tool, timeout, schema drift, corruption) at a controlled point in the trajectory and recording whether the agent notices, changes plan, recovers, or repeats itself. Six models from three families, half reasoning variants, ran 1,920 trials over 24 multi-step tasks, with fault-free runs as a run-to-run variation baseline.
AI.result: Agents treat a failure as a problem in 91.3% of trials for explicit errors but only 58.8% for plausible wrong values, against a 26.8% false-alarm rate when nothing was wrong. Reasoning models notice less than instruct siblings (-9.3 points, p < .001) and change plan more (+10.4 points, p < .001), with recovery unchanged (p = .512). Fault-free runs of identical tasks converge to the same state only 63.3% of the time; against that baseline, only a missing tool clearly lowers recovery (39.9%), while timeouts, schema drift, and corruption stay within run-to-run variation. Agents return to the same tool three or more times in up to 22.2% of trials, though strictly identical repeats are rare. A prompt line instructing the agent to check each result did not improve detection.
AI.conclusion: Agents respond to the error channel rather than to the content of what a tool returns, so failures that stay inside the expected format pass through. Because over-trust is tied to signal presence rather than output plausibility, and reasoning variants offer no advantage, prompt-level reminders are insufficient; the authors call for mechanism-level handling of silent and semantic tool failures.

title: Robotic Boomerang Throwing via Model-Based Release Design
summary: Throwing objects that generate aerodynamic lift can greatly extend robot throwing beyond ballistic flight. A returning boomerang is a challenging example because its flight depends strongly on the release velocity, attitude, and spin, while robotic manipulators cannot readily reproduce the rapid motions used in human throwing. We present a model-based framework for robotic boomerang throwing centered on the release state. We identify the boomerang flight dynamics in stages to predict how flight changes across design variations. To systematically design the robot throwing motion, we screen candidate parameters according to how strongly and consistently they control release spin under uncertain contact conditions. These models are then used to design the throwing motion and boomerang for a 6-DoF manipulator with limited joint speeds. To our knowledge, this is the first robotic manipulator to generate a returning boomerang flight. In the demonstrated returning trial, the boomerang is released at 51 rad/s (8.1 rev/s), reaches 2.03 m from the robot base, and returns to touch down 0.31 m from the base. The successful release differs significantly from the measured human throws, showing that a robot need not imitate human throwing motion to achieve a returning flight. The project page is available at https://robot-boomerang.github.io

AI.tldr: A model-based framework enables a 6-DoF robotic manipulator to throw a returning boomerang, achieving a flight that reaches 2.03 m and returns to 0.31 m from the base, released at 51 rad/s.
AI.motivation: Aerodynamic-lift throwing extends robot throwing beyond ballistic flight, but a returning boomerang is challenging because its flight depends strongly on release velocity, attitude, and spin, while robotic manipulators cannot readily reproduce the rapid motions used in human throwing.
AI.method: The framework centers on the release state. Boomerang flight dynamics are identified in stages to predict how flight changes across design variations. Candidate parameters are screened by how strongly and consistently they control release spin under uncertain contact conditions. These models then guide design of the throwing motion and boomerang for a 6-DoF manipulator with limited joint speeds.
AI.result: In the demonstrated returning trial, the boomerang is released at 51 rad/s (8.1 rev/s), reaches 2.03 m from the robot base, and returns to touch down 0.31 m from the base. The successful release differs significantly from measured human throws.
AI.conclusion: To the authors' knowledge, this is the first robotic manipulator to generate a returning boomerang flight. It shows that a robot need not imitate human throwing motion to achieve a returning flight.

title: HGP:An on-device personalized agent memory via hybrid graph storage
summary: LLM-based agents face challenges in personalized interactive tasks due to heterogeneous, multi-typed, and implicitly constrained long-term traces. Existing memory mechanisms struggle with accurate routing and retrieval, especially on-device where personalization is critical. Most methods use single-vector representations, blurring type distinctions and relational structure. We propose HGP, a hybrid graph memory framework. HGP employs a lightweight self-enhancement classifier for personalized memory routing and constructs episodic, semantic, and procedural memories as graphs. It also extracts working memory as a state trajectory to capture current state and implicit constraints, ensuring reliable decision-making. The classifier reduces large-model calls, enabling on-device deployment, while graph storage enables accurate retrieval and incremental user profile refinement. Experiments on two benchmarks show that on PAL-Set solution selection, HGP achieves an S-score of 35.58, nearly 7 points above the strongest baseline. Code and data are at https://github.com/Ouan6/HGP-.git.

AI.tldr: HGP is a hybrid graph memory framework for LLM-based agents that enables personalized on-device memory routing, typed graph memories (episodic, semantic, procedural), and working-memory state trajectories, improving personalized interactive task performance.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with personalized interactive tasks because of heterogeneous, multi-typed, and implicitly constrained long-term traces. Existing memory mechanisms have difficulty with accurate routing and retrieval, especially on-device where personalization matters most, and most rely on single-vector representations that blur type distinctions and relational structure.
AI.method: HGP combines a lightweight self-enhancement classifier for personalized memory routing with graph-structured episodic, semantic, and procedural memories. It additionally extracts working memory as a state trajectory to capture current state and implicit constraints for reliable decision-making. The classifier cuts large-model calls for on-device deployment, while graph storage supports accurate retrieval and incremental user profile refinement.
AI.result: On two benchmarks, HGP achieves an S-score of 35.58 on PAL-Set solution selection, nearly 7 points above the strongest baseline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ouan6/HGP-.git.
AI.conclusion: HGP addresses heterogeneous, multi-typed, implicitly constrained long-term memory for personalized LLM agents by structuring memory as typed graphs and adding a routing classifier and working-memory trajectory, yielding substantial gains while remaining suitable for on-device deployment.

title: Agentic RSR: Real-to-Sim-to-Real through Scene Reconstruction and Execution-Grounded Robot Policies
summary: A simulation of a real robot workspace must preserve task-relevant interactions, while policies developed in it must operate on observations available to the real robot. Yet scene reconstruction and policy development are often treated separately. We present Agentic Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Agentic RSR), a framework that links scene reconstruction, policy development, and real-robot execution through the same manipulation task. Given a workspace video, a task description, and a known robot model, an agent recovers metric scale, iteratively refines the scene using visual feedback, and checks task-relevant interactions in MuJoCo. A coding agent then develops an executable policy, progressing from privileged object poses to visual observations and randomized simulation. The policy can interleave multiple observations and actions within one invocation, while the agent uses execution feedback to continue, retry, or revise its approach. A shared task-level interface carries the policy and accumulated experience to the real robot, where fresh observations and safety checks guide execution. Across 18 reconstructed scenes involving two robots, the mean four-view Depth MAE against reference depth estimates is 0.1057 m, the mean Lab $ΔE_{76}$ is 11.04, and the mean grayscale SSIM is 0.6990. In real-robot experiments, the aggregate task success rate reaches 80% of the simulation task success rate, indicating substantial retention of simulated performance on hardware. Code and reconstructed scene data will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: Agentic RSR is a framework that unifies scene reconstruction, policy development, and real-robot execution through a shared manipulation task, achieving real-world success at 80% of simulated performance across 18 reconstructed scenes.
AI.motivation: Simulated robot workspaces must preserve task-relevant interactions, and policies developed in simulation must use observations available to the real robot. However, scene reconstruction and policy development are typically treated as separate stages, limiting transfer from simulation to hardware.
AI.method: Given a workspace video, task description, and known robot model, an agent recovers metric scale, iteratively refines the scene via visual feedback, and verifies task-relevant interactions in MuJoCo. A coding agent then builds an executable policy, advancing from privileged object poses to visual observations and randomized simulation. The policy can interleave multiple observations and actions per invocation, with the agent using execution feedback to continue, retry, or revise. A shared task-level interface transfers the policy and accumulated experience to the real robot, where fresh observations and safety checks guide execution.
AI.result: Across 18 reconstructed scenes with two robots: mean four-view Depth MAE 0.1057 m, mean Lab ΔE76 11.04, mean grayscale SSIM 0.6990. Real-robot aggregate task success reaches 80% of simulation success rate, showing substantial retention of simulated performance on hardware.
AI.conclusion: Linking reconstruction, policy development, and deployment via a shared task interface enables effective real-to-sim-to-real transfer. Code and reconstructed scene data will be publicly released.

title: SkillSandbox: Skill Verification via Dynamic Scenario Synthesis
summary: Self-evolving agents distill task-solving experience into skills for future reuse, but these skills can encode incorrect procedures or non-transferable knowledge. It is therefore critical to verify each skill's reusability: whether its guidance remains useful beyond the experience from which it was distilled. Such verification requires observing how a skill affects execution in new tasks, yet existing tasks may not expose the situations where the target skill can actually be exercised. To construct such situations, we propose SkillSandbox, a framework that dynamically synthesizes a task and its environment for each skill that are skill-relevant yet novel. A Proposer specifies the conditions to preserve and the source-specific details to vary, a Builder constructs an executable scenario, and a Verifier compares executions with and without the skill. The Verifier assesses executability, utility, and efficiency to assign a Keep or Reject verdict, determining whether the skill enters the library. Across ALFWorld and WebShop with three models, SkillSandbox consistently yields the strongest downstream performance and improved execution efficiency. Further analyses examine whether these gains reflect accurate assessment of skill reusability and identify which components of SkillSandbox contribute to them.

AI.tldr: SkillSandbox synthesizes skill-relevant yet novel tasks and environments to verify whether each distilled skill's guidance is reusable, assigning Keep or Reject verdicts; it consistently yields the strongest downstream performance and efficiency across ALFWorld and WebShop with three models.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents distill task-solving experience into reusable skills, but these skills can encode incorrect procedures or non-transferable knowledge. It is therefore critical to verify each skill's reusability—whether its guidance remains useful beyond the experience from which it was distilled. Existing tasks may not expose the situations where a target skill can actually be exercised, so such situations must be constructed.
AI.method: SkillSandbox dynamically synthesizes a skill-relevant yet novel task and environment for each skill. A Proposer specifies the conditions to preserve and the source-specific details to vary, a Builder constructs an executable scenario, and a Verifier compares executions with and without the skill. The Verifier assesses executability, utility, and efficiency to assign a Keep or Reject verdict, determining whether the skill enters the library.
AI.result: Across ALFWorld and WebShop with three models, SkillSandbox consistently yields the strongest downstream performance and improved execution efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Further analyses examine whether the gains reflect accurate assessment of skill reusability and identify which components of SkillSandbox contribute to them.

title: HuMBLE: Human Motion-Driven Behavior Learning for Embodied Locomotion
summary: Despite recent advances in humanoid locomotion, controllers optimized for command tracking and robustness tend to produce mechanical gaits, whereas controllers tied to human motion data often fail to generalize to commands outside the data distribution. This work introduces a learning framework that balances these competing objectives to synthesize real-time steerable, robust, and biomimetic locomotion policies from human data. Using an in-house curated locomotion dataset covering diverse speeds and directions, we first learn a natural locomotion prior policy through a teacher-student distillation process. Specifically, we train a full-body reference-conditioned policy with Reinforcement Learning (RL), then distill it into a lightweight prior policy conditioned solely on proprioception and a planar torso-velocity steering command. Next, we fine-tune the prior policy with multi-task RL to expand command coverage and robustness beyond the data distribution, pairing a goal-conditioned task that tracks arbitrary commands with a reference-guided task that tracks the human data as an explicit style regularizer. We validate our framework on three humanoid robots: the Boston Dynamics Atlas R1, Atlas D1, and Unitree G1. Experimental results demonstrate robust performance across real-world scenarios, including direct user-controlled locomotion in indoor and outdoor environments, and integration as the locomotion layer within hierarchical control stacks. Benchmarks against Tabula Rasa RL policies trained without human data and ablation studies confirm that our framework yields a lightweight, deployable policy that reconstructs coordinated whole-body behavior from a steering command, retaining the human gait characteristics while remaining robust and fully steerable.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a learning framework that produces real-time steerable, robust, and biomimetic humanoid locomotion policies by combining a human-data prior policy (via teacher-student distillation) with multi-task RL fine-tuning, validated on three humanoid robots in real-world scenarios.
AI.motivation: Humanoid locomotion controllers face a trade-off: RL controllers optimized for command tracking and robustness yield mechanical gaits, while human-motion-data-driven controllers fail to generalize beyond the data distribution. The work aims to balance these competing objectives.
AI.method: Using a curated locomotion dataset of diverse speeds and directions, the authors first learn a natural locomotion prior policy via teacher-student distillation: a full-body reference-conditioned RL policy is distilled into a lightweight prior policy conditioned only on proprioception and a planar torso-velocity steering command. The prior is then fine-tuned with multi-task RL, combining a goal-conditioned task (tracking arbitrary commands) and a reference-guided task (tracking human data as an explicit style regularizer) to expand command coverage and robustness.
AI.result: The framework was validated on Boston Dynamics Atlas R1, Atlas D1, and Unitree G1. It achieved robust performance in real-world settings, including direct user-controlled indoor and outdoor locomotion and integration as the locomotion layer in hierarchical control stacks. Benchmarks against Tabula Rasa RL policies (trained without human data) and ablation studies confirmed a lightweight, deployable policy that reconstructs coordinated whole-body behavior from a steering command.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework yields a lightweight, deployable locomotion policy that retains human gait characteristics while remaining robust and fully steerable, effectively balancing biomimetic style with command-tracking generalization.

title: RewardWeaver: Long-Horizon Interactive Learning for Language Agents via Self-Evolving Reward Adaptation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has driven substantial progress in domains where task outcomes can be reliably evaluated, but long-horizon interaction remains challenging due to sparse terminal feedback and difficult credit assignment. Process rewards provide denser supervision, yet the capabilities most relevant for training can change as the policy evolves: a behavior that is easy to evaluate or frequently deficient need not be the bottleneck currently limiting task success. We introduce RewardWeaver, a self-evolving reward adaptation framework for language agents in long-horizon interaction. RewardWeaver maintains a validated capability space in which the semantics of admitted Rubrics remain fixed, and closes the loop between policy optimization, task evaluation, failure attribution, and reward adaptation. After each training stage, it performs outcome-grounded backward attribution on low-outcome trajectories, aggregates recurrent and policy-controlled capability bottlenecks, and dynamically selects the corresponding process rewards for the next stage. Recurrent failures not covered by the existing capability space trigger a separate, controlled expansion procedure. We evaluate REWARDWEAVER on SOTOPIA, Amazon?HistoryPrice, and a newly constructed Sales Benchmark. Across social interaction, bilateral bargaining, and domain-specific sales, REWARDWEAVER establishes new state-of-the-art (SOTA) results. Ablations further demonstrate the importance of dynamic reward allocation, failure-grounded attribution, and stable semantics for admitted capabilities.

AI.tldr: RewardWeaver is a self-evolving reward adaptation framework that closes the loop between policy optimization, task evaluation, failure attribution, and reward adaptation, dynamically selecting process rewards to target current capability bottlenecks for long-horizon language agents.
AI.motivation: RLVR struggles in long-horizon interaction due to sparse terminal feedback and hard credit assignment. Process rewards give denser supervision, but the capabilities that actually limit task success shift as the policy evolves, so a statically chosen or merely easy-to-evaluate behavior may not be the current bottleneck.
AI.method: RewardWeaver maintains a validated capability space with fixed semantics for admitted Rubrics. After each training stage it performs outcome-grounded backward attribution on low-outcome trajectories, aggregates recurrent and policy-controlled capability bottlenecks, and dynamically selects corresponding process rewards for the next stage. Recurrent failures uncovered by the existing capability space trigger a separate, controlled expansion procedure.
AI.result: Evaluated on SOTOPIA, Amazon-HistoryPrice, and a newly constructed Sales Benchmark, RewardWeaver achieves new SOTA across social interaction, bilateral bargaining, and domain-specific sales. Ablations confirm the importance of dynamic reward allocation, failure-grounded attribution, and stable semantics for admitted capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Adapting process rewards to the policy's evolving capability bottlenecks, while keeping admitted capability semantics stable, is effective for long-horizon language-agent training.

title: Factorized Tactile Representation and Control for Sim-to-Real Manipulation
summary: Tactile sim-to-real learning must bridge simulated contact and device-specific sensor responses while preserving information needed for control. We propose a factorized tactile representation and control framework that maps normal force and contact patch to an effective contact response recoverable from sensor readings. The response is separated into contact geometry, force distribution, and temporal contact change, with representation-specific encoding and randomization. A Tactile Gated Policy preserves these representations separately through control and operates over all mask configurations without retraining. We evaluate the approach through response reconstruction, spatial alignment, force regulation, and contact-rich adversarial peg insertion in simulation and the real world, enabling the utility and transfer reliability of different tactile representations to be assessed independently. The approach achieves <1 mm contact localization, 1.69 N force-tracking error on unseen geometries, and a 35% improvement in real-world adversarial peg insertion over the unfactorized response, with different tactile representations benefiting different interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a factorized tactile representation and control framework that separates the effective contact response into contact geometry, force distribution, and temporal contact change, enabling sim-to-real transfer and robust control across sensor mask configurations.
AI.motivation: Tactile sim-to-real learning must bridge the gap between simulated contact and device-specific sensor responses while retaining control-relevant information; a single entangled representation cannot capture the distinct roles of different tactile features or generalize across sensors and masking.
AI.method: A factorized tactile representation maps normal force and contact patch to an effective contact response recoverable from sensor readings, decomposed into contact geometry, force distribution, and temporal contact change, each with representation-specific encoding and randomization. A Tactile Gated Policy preserves these representations separately through control and handles all mask configurations without retraining.
AI.result: Evaluated via response reconstruction, spatial alignment, force regulation, and contact-rich adversarial peg insertion in simulation and the real world: <1 mm contact localization, 1.69 N force-tracking error on unseen geometries, and a 35% improvement in real-world adversarial peg insertion over an unfactorized response, with different tactile representations benefiting different interactions.
AI.conclusion: Factorizing tactile representations improves sim-to-real transfer and control reliability, and allows the utility of individual tactile representations to be assessed independently per interaction.

title: UniSkill: Learning Actor-Aligned Skill Proposals for an Evolving Policy
summary: Large language model agents can improve across tasks by retaining reusable skills distilled from prior interactions. Recent work jointly optimizes task execution and skill extraction, enabling the policy and skillbank to co-evolve. However, as the actor continues learning, rewarding skill proposals through their reuse in subsequent training steps may conflate skill benefits with actor improvement, while directly testing each proposed skill requires costly additional actor rollouts. In this paper, we introduce UniSkill, which uses a shared policy to interact with the environment and propose skillbank edits (Add, Update, or No Edit) from the resulting trajectories. Specifically, the actor learns from environment rewards, while contrastive action feedback guides skill proposal learning. This feedback provides an actor-alignment signal by measuring how replacing the retrieved skill with a proposed skill changes the current actor's action log-likelihood gap between previously collected successful and failed trajectories from the same task, thereby avoiding new rollouts for each proposal. Since proposal-level feedback may suppress an otherwise appropriate edit operation when the proposed skill content scores poorly, we further apply skill-edit support regularization to preserve exploration. Empirically, UniSkill achieves strong performance, reaching 98.4% success on ALFWorld and 84.7% on WebShop while maintaining stable joint training. Further ALFWorld experiments show that UniSkill remains effective when the shared policy uses a smaller backbone. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LimOkii/UniSKill.

AI.tldr: UniSkill uses a single shared policy to both execute tasks and propose skillbank edits, learning skill proposals via contrastive action feedback (no extra rollouts) plus skill-edit support regularization, achieving 98.4% on ALFWorld and 84.7% on WebShop with stable joint training.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can improve by retaining reusable skills from prior interactions, and recent work co-evolves the policy and skillbank by jointly optimizing execution and skill extraction. However, rewarding skill proposals through their reuse in later training conflates skill benefits with overall actor improvement, while directly testing each proposed skill needs costly additional actor rollouts. This motivates a way to evaluate skill proposals without extra rollouts and without confounding skill quality with actor progress.
AI.method: UniSkill employs a shared policy that interacts with the environment and proposes skillbank edits (Add, Update, or No Edit) from resulting trajectories. The actor is trained on environment rewards, while skill proposal learning is guided by contrastive action feedback. This feedback yields an actor-alignment signal by measuring how replacing the retrieved skill with a proposed skill changes the current actor's action log-likelihood gap between previously collected successful and failed trajectories of the same task, thereby avoiding new rollouts per proposal. Since proposal-level feedback can suppress an otherwise appropriate edit when the proposed skill content scores poorly, skill-edit support regularization is applied to preserve exploration.
AI.result: UniSkill reaches 98.4% success on ALFWorld and 84.7% on WebShop while maintaining stable joint training. Additional ALFWorld experiments show it remains effective when the shared policy uses a smaller backbone.
AI.conclusion: A single shared policy can jointly execute tasks and propose skillbank edits, with contrastive action feedback providing a rollout-free, actor-aligned learning signal for skill proposals, and skill-edit support regularization preserving exploration. This yields strong, stable joint training and robustness to smaller backbones, with implementation released at https://github.com/LimOkii/UniSKill.

title: Rephrase Before You Act: Characterizing and Mitigating Language Sensitivity in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are strikingly sensitive to instruction phrasing and do not inherit the language robustness of the vision-language models they are built on. A one-word edit can move success by tens of points: $π_{0.5}$ turns on a LIBERO stove 100% of the time for "switch on the stove" and 2% for "switch on the hot plate", and a $π_0$ checkpoint finetuned with rephrase augmentation still shows swings of up to 61 points. We characterize this sensitivity with statistically tested single-edit swings and an oracle phrase search, which shows that phrasing alone nearly closes the 21-point gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks. We then reduce it without modifying the policy. Because the sensitivity is systematic, it can be expressed as explicit rules: we score many phrasings of a few training tasks, have a large language model distill the evidence into ten to twenty rephrasing rules, and at deployment rewrite each incoming instruction once under these rules. The rules improve the frozen $π_0$ by 16 to 27% relative on twelve held-out tasks across adversarial, VLM-generated, and human-generated phrasings, with gains concentrated on out-of-distribution tasks. The pipeline replicates on $π_{0.5}$ and LIBERO, lifting in-finetune success from 93.6% to 97.8%. The method requires no retraining and no per-step verification, and applies zero-shot to unseen tasks and instructions. Project website: https://sttawm.github.io/rephrase-before-you-act

AI.tldr: VLAs are highly sensitive to instruction phrasing; distilling rephrasing rules via an LLM and rewriting instructions once at deployment improves frozen policies by 16-27% relative without retraining.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action models inherit less language robustness than their VLM backbones: small phrasing edits (e.g., "stove" vs. "hot plate") cause large success-rate swings, even with rephrase augmentation. The paper aims to characterize and mitigate this sensitivity without modifying the policy.
AI.method: The authors quantify sensitivity via statistically tested single-edit swings and an oracle phrase search. They then score many phrasings of a few training tasks, use an LLM to distill the evidence into 10-20 rephrasing rules, and at deployment rewrite each incoming instruction once under these rules before feeding it to the frozen policy.
AI.result: Rules improve the frozen π0 by 16-27% relative on twelve held-out tasks across adversarial, VLM-generated, and human-generated phrasings, with gains concentrated on out-of-distribution tasks. The pipeline replicates on π0.5 and LIBERO, raising in-finetune success from 93.6% to 97.8%. Phrasing alone nearly closes the 21-point ID/OOD gap in oracle search.
AI.conclusion: Because the phrasing sensitivity is systematic, it can be captured as explicit rules and corrected by a single instruction rewrite at deployment. The approach requires no retraining and no per-step verification, and applies zero-shot to unseen tasks and instructions.

title: Agentic AI-Assisted Modeling for Production Scheduling: Assessment in Constraint Programming
summary: Developing optimization models for production scheduling requires substantial expert effort. Research on large language models (LLMs) has followed two directions: specialized approaches for automated modeling, mostly for mixed-integer linear programming, which often rely on dedicated training or problem-specific architectures that limit industrial deployment; and agentic artificial intelligence for operational decision support, which generally assumes that the optimization model already exists. This study bridges both directions by assessing whether general-purpose LLMs, orchestrated as agents without task-specific training, can formulate and implement constraint programming models from natural-language problem descriptions. Singleagent and multi-agent architectures are integrated with a Model Context Protocol server that provides context-aware retrieval of solver documentation to mitigate hallucinations during implementation. Both are compared with a direct LLM baseline on six industry-oriented problems covering flow-shop, job-shop, flexible job-shop and resource-constrained warehouse scheduling, using three LLMs and assessing modeling accuracy, execution success, latency and token consumption. Formulation proves largely within reach of current LLMs, whereas implementation is the main barrier. The multi-agent workflow raises the share of scripts that run correctly as generated from 14.8% with a direct LLM call to 59.3%, reaching 80.6% on the four less complex problems, while tightly coupled intralogistics models remain an open challenge.

AI.tldr: General-purpose LLM agents without task-specific training are assessed on formulating and implementing constraint programming models from natural-language scheduling problems, using a Model Context Protocol server for solver documentation retrieval; multi-agent orchestration lifts execution from 14.8% to 59.3%.
AI.motivation: Building optimization models for production scheduling demands substantial expert effort. Existing research splits into automated modeling (mostly MILP, relying on dedicated training or problem-specific architectures that hinder industrial deployment) and agentic AI for operational decision support (which presumes the model already exists). A gap remains in assessing whether general-purpose LLMs, used as agents without task-specific training, can formulate and implement constraint programming models from natural-language descriptions.
AI.method: Single-agent and multi-agent architectures are integrated with a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server providing context-aware retrieval of solver documentation to mitigate hallucination during implementation. These are compared against a direct LLM baseline on six industry-oriented problems: flow-shop, job-shop, flexible job-shop, and resource-constrained warehouse scheduling. Three LLMs are used, with evaluation of modeling accuracy, execution success, latency, and token consumption.
AI.result: Formulation is largely within reach of current LLMs, but implementation is the main barrier. The multi-agent workflow raises the share of scripts that run correctly as generated from 14.8% (direct LLM call) to 59.3%, and reaches 80.6% on the four less complex problems. Tightly coupled intralogistics models remain an open challenge.
AI.conclusion: General-purpose LLM agents without task-specific training can formulate constraint programming models from natural-language scheduling descriptions, with formulation largely attainable while implementation is the bottleneck. Multi-agent orchestration with MCP-based solver documentation retrieval substantially improves execution success, though tightly coupled intralogistics scheduling remains unsolved.

title: Long-WAM: Scaling the Context of World-Action Models
summary: Real-time robot control demands enough visual history to infer motion and task progress, but processing that history can delay action. We present Long-WAM, a model-system framework for scaling the context of causal world-action models under real-time control constraints. Our central finding is that access to history is not the same as using it: longer histories pay off far more when the video foundation is pretrained autoregressively (AR). We first learn causal prediction from robot and egocentric videos without action labels, then preserve this history-to-future structure during world-action adaptation. On RoboCasa GR-1, increasing context from 0.0 to 19.2 seconds raises success from 63.3% to 78.7%, whereas a bidirectionally pretrained initialization shows no net gain; robot-domain AR pretraining further raises peak success on GR-1 and LIBERO-Long. Long-WAM also achieves the best results among compared methods on LIBERO-Long, RoboTwin 2.0, and DOMINO. Streaming observation encoding, asynchronous execution, and hardware-specific acceleration enable deployment on RTX 5090, DGX Spark, and Jetson AGX Thor without dropping future prediction; on RTX 5090, each action chunk, including future-video latent prediction, takes 107.4 ms. Real-time deployment on Unitree G1 and YAM supports dynamic and long-horizon manipulation, including 95% success on dynamic cup stacking, where Pi0.5 and Fast-WAM succeed in none of 20 trials. As a memory-informed executor, Long-WAM also complements higher-level planning in composite tasks.

AI.tldr: Long-WAM scales the context of causal world-action models under real-time control, showing that longer visual history helps only when the video foundation is pretrained autoregressively, reaching 78.7% success on RoboCasa GR-1 with 19.2s context and real-time deployment on multiple hardware platforms.
AI.motivation: Real-time robot control needs enough visual history to infer motion and task progress, but processing such history can delay action. There is a tension between longer context (better inference of motion/task progress) and real-time latency constraints. The paper investigates how to scale context for causal world-action models without sacrificing real-time deployment.
AI.method: Long-WAM is a model-system framework for scaling the context of causal world-action models. It first learns causal prediction from robot and egocentric videos without action labels, then preserves the history-to-future structure during world-action adaptation. Key insight: access to history is not the same as using it. Longer histories pay off far more when the video foundation is pretrained autoregressively (AR). The system employs streaming observation encoding, asynchronous execution, and hardware-specific acceleration to enable real-time deployment on RTX 5090, DGX Spark, and Jetson AGX Thor.
AI.result: On RoboCasa GR-1, increasing context from 0.0 to 19.2 seconds raises success from 63.3% to 78.7%, whereas a bidirectionally pretrained initialization shows no net gain. Robot-domain AR pretraining further raises peak success on GR-1 and LIBERO-Long. Long-WAM achieves the best results among compared methods on LIBERO-Long, RoboTwin 2.0, and DOMINO. On RTX 5090, each action chunk, including future-video latent prediction, takes 107.4 ms. Real-time deployment on Unitree G1 and YAM supports dynamic and long-horizon manipulation, including 95% success on dynamic cup stacking, where Pi0.5 and Fast-WAM succeed in none of 20 trials.
AI.conclusion: Long-WAM demonstrates that scaling context for causal world-action models is effective when the video foundation is pretrained autoregressively, and that streaming encoding, asynchronous execution, and hardware acceleration allow real-time deployment without dropping future prediction. As a memory-informed executor, Long-WAM also complements higher-level planning in composite tasks.

title: GAGR-Lab: Evaluating Joint Spatial-Geometric and Analytic Function Reasoning
summary: Joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning requires translating a perceived spatial configuration into a symbolic function whose executed curve satisfies geometric constraints. We present GAGR-Lab, a framework for measuring this capability through Cartesian game scenes, explicit function semantics, and authoritative Rust trajectory execution. It distinguishes spatial perception, metric grounding, geometric relations, function interpretation, function construction, and constrained synthesis. We specify four configurable scene-difficulty presets and a prospective 24-cell diagnostic design, while reporting only the subset actually evaluated. A bounded pilot of one hosted model (Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct) using two API credentials as execution replicas yields 72 balanced games with 432 attempts, 429 valid provider responses, and no target hits; exploratory ordinary-function prompt variants also fail to hit, while the structured localization interface yields no scoreable outputs. A privileged analytic search control independently succeeds on 600 directional cases from 300 generated scenes, with exact repeatability and 1,200 successful vertical-reflection or translation checks. The framework separates serving reliability, symbolic compliance, and geometric success, and preserves exact model-visible inputs and realized paths. A staged protocol outlines diagnostic calibration, held-out replication, multi-model comparison, and paired robustness tests. The contribution is an operational research framework with an executed pilot and a clearly identified prospective study plan; the full difficulty matrix and comparative model results remain untested.

AI.tldr: GAGR-Lab measures joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning via Cartesian game scenes, explicit function semantics, and Rust trajectory execution across six capability stages; a pilot with Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct produced no target hits, while a privileged analytic control succeeded, with the full difficulty matrix left untested.
AI.motivation: Joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning requires translating a perceived spatial configuration into a symbolic function whose executed curve satisfies geometric constraints, a capability not yet systematically measured.
AI.method: GAGR-Lab framework using Cartesian game scenes, explicit function semantics, and authoritative Rust trajectory execution; six distinguished capabilities (spatial perception, metric grounding, geometric relations, function interpretation, function construction, constrained synthesis); four configurable scene-difficulty presets and a prospective 24-cell diagnostic design; a bounded pilot with one hosted model (Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct) over two API credentials as execution replicas, plus exploratory prompt variants and a structured localization interface; a privileged analytic search control; and separation of serving reliability, symbolic compliance, and geometric success while preserving exact model-visible inputs and realized paths.
AI.result: Pilot: 72 balanced games, 432 attempts, 429 valid provider responses, zero target hits; ordinary-function prompt variants also fail; structured localization interface yields no scoreable outputs. Analytic control: success on 600 directional cases from 300 generated scenes, exact repeatability, 1,200 successful vertical-reflection or translation checks.
AI.conclusion: The work is an operational research framework with an executed pilot and a clearly identified prospective study plan; a staged protocol outlines diagnostic calibration, held-out replication, multi-model comparison, and paired robustness tests, but the full difficulty matrix and comparative model results remain untested.

title: RoboPrompt: Intuitive Robot Policy Steering with Sparse Human Input
summary: End-to-end robot policies trained through imitation learning remain constrained by limited data diversity, making reliable zero-shot deployment in real-world settings challenging. Shared-autonomy methods enable human correction through teleoperation, but specialized hardware and operator training hinder deployment at scale. Other approaches incorporate human guidance as additional policy inputs, often requiring architectural changes and dedicated training for steerability, which limits their applicability across policies. We present RoboPrompt, a general-purpose, lightweight robot policy steering system that enables users to guide policy behavior through intuitive, sparse inputs, including drawn traces, target points, and coarse directional instructions. RoboPrompt decouples human-intention translation from the underlying policy: a reusable module converts human guidance into action drafts, which are refined through the diffusion or flow-matching dynamics of the base policy. By controlling action generation in noise space, RoboPrompt balances human intent with the policy prior without modifying the base policy architecture or fine-tuning it for steerability. Experiments demonstrate effective steering across Diffusion Policy, $π_{0.5}$, and FastWAM. We further use steered rollouts for online policy improvement through DAgger. After 2-3 rounds of iteration, average success rates increase by 15.5\% for $π_{0.5}$ across three tasks and by 21.3\% across three policies(Diffusion Policy, $π_{0.5}$, FastWAM) on the Insert Bread task, while average human intervention counts decrease by 44.0\% (2.86 to 1.60) and 81.9\% (2.60 to 0.47), respectively.

AI.tldr: RoboPrompt is a lightweight, policy-agnostic steering system that converts sparse human guidance (traces, target points, directions) into action drafts refined via the base policy's diffusion/flow-matching dynamics in noise space, requiring no architecture changes or steerability fine-tuning, and enabling online improvement via DAgger.
