AI.motivation: End-to-end imitation-learned robot policies suffer from limited data diversity, hindering reliable zero-shot real-world deployment. Existing remedies are limited: shared-autonomy teleoperation requires specialized hardware and trained operators, while guidance-as-input methods need architectural changes and dedicated steerability training, restricting applicability across policies.
AI.method: RoboPrompt decouples human-intention translation from the base policy. A reusable module translates intuitive sparse inputs—drawn traces, target points, and coarse directional instructions—into action drafts. These drafts are refined through the diffusion or flow-matching dynamics of the base policy by controlling action generation in noise space, balancing human intent with the policy prior without modifying the base architecture or fine-tuning for steerability.
AI.result: Effective steering is demonstrated across Diffusion Policy, π0.5, and FastWAM. Steered rollouts support online policy improvement via DAgger: after 2–3 rounds, average success rates increase by 15.5% for π0.5 across three tasks and by 21.3% across three policies on the Insert Bread task, while average human intervention counts decrease by 44.0% (2.86 to 1.60) and 81.9% (2.60 to 0.47), respectively.
AI.conclusion: RoboPrompt offers a general-purpose, lightweight steering mechanism that works across multiple modern policies without architectural modification or steerability training, and it enables data-efficient online policy improvement through human-guided rollouts.

title: OOM-RL II: Reality Is an Oracle, Not a Debugger Provenance-Constrained Diagnosis in Continually Evolving Agent-Engineered Systems
comment: 38 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables. Supplementary Dataset S1: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23215521. Follow-up to arXiv:2604.11477
summary: Reality may establish that an outcome occurred without identifying which evolving procedure produced it or why. This distinction matters in production ML systems whose code, configuration, and artifacts change while external feedback accumulates. We examine it in a human-directed, agent-engineered quantitative trading system, using oracle to mean an external source of realized outcomes rather than a complete correctness specification. Across one year, the account gained and outperformed a broad market index, while annual alpha was not statistically distinguishable from zero under the main retrospective specification. Retrospectively selected subperiods include adverse relative performance and conditional candidate-level weakness under declared approximate references. Engineering records document changes during the episode, and complete recommendation-to-runtime binding is unavailable. The archive does not establish a common frozen instance or a unique cause. The case motivates an outcome--diagnosis gap: outcome evidence, evaluated-object identity, and causal explanation support distinct claims. We distinguish frozen instances, pre-specified adaptive procedures, and ad-hoc development; organize archive-relative claim identifiability and an evidence hierarchy; and propose a prospective production-binding protocol. An illustrative compatible-history example shows how factual binding can resolve a recommendation's referent without supplying its counterfactual effect. The protocol is proposed rather than prospectively validated. External feedback constrains outcome claims, while provenance and additional identification structure determine the resolution of diagnosis.

AI.tldr: The paper examines a human-directed, agent-engineered quantitative trading system over one year, where the account gained and beat a broad market index, yet annual alpha was statistically indistinguishable from zero under the main retrospective specification. It introduces an outcome–diagnosis gap, distinguishing outcome evidence, evaluated-object identity, and causal explanation as supporting distinct claims, and proposes a prospective production-binding protocol (not prospectively validated).
AI.motivation: Reality may establish that an outcome occurred without identifying which evolving procedure produced it or why. This distinction matters in production ML systems whose code, configuration, and artifacts change while external feedback accumulates. The work addresses the problem that complete recommendation-to-runtime binding is unavailable and archives rarely establish a common frozen instance or a unique cause.
AI.method: A case study of a human-directed, agent-engineered quantitative trading system, using "oracle" to mean an external source of realized outcomes rather than a complete correctness specification. The authors analyze one year of engineering records, retrospective specifications, and conditional candidate-level evaluations, then frame an outcome–diagnosis gap: outcome evidence, evaluated-object identity, and causal explanation support distinct claims. They distinguish frozen instances, pre-specified adaptive procedures, and ad-hoc development; organize archive-relative claim identifiability and an evidence hierarchy; and propose a prospective production-binding protocol, illustrated with a compatible-history example.
AI.result: Across one year, the account gained and outperformed a broad market index, but annual alpha was not statistically distinguishable from zero under the main retrospective specification. Retrospectively selected subperiods show adverse relative performance and conditional candidate-level weakness under declared approximate references. Engineering records document changes during the episode, and complete recommendation-to-runtime binding is unavailable; the archive does not establish a common frozen instance or a unique cause. An illustrative compatible-history example shows factual binding can resolve a recommendation's referent without supplying its counterfactual effect.
AI.conclusion: The case motivates an outcome–diagnosis gap in which outcome evidence, evaluated-object identity, and causal explanation support distinct claims. External feedback constrains outcome claims, while provenance and additional identification structure determine the resolution of diagnosis. The proposed prospective production-binding protocol is put forward rather than prospectively validated.

title: Stale, Misattributed, or Late: Where Personal Memory Fails Before Generation
summary: Personal memory for language agents is usually judged by whether the final an- swer is correct. That score hides errors that arise before generation: the memory block may contain an obsolete value, a fact about the wrong person, or no use- ful fact before the serving deadline. We measure these failures directly. Using Personal Fact Memory (PFM) as a reference layer, we find that temporal validity is primarily a property of memory construction in our setting. On a controlled revision benchmark, serving only the active value of each correctly keyed slot eliminates observed stale exposure; without update resolution, 70.3% of prompts expose a superseded value. Once retrievers share the same active store and par- ticipant information, participant-aware BM25 is equivalent to the reference ranker within a prespecified 0.02 margin. The harder problem is assigning revisions to the right slot. Missed merges leave stale values active, whereas false merges silently remove current values; four LLM key assigners achieve higher key re- call than a rule extractor yet produce lower clean-retrieval rates, and open-domain merge recall on LongMemEval never exceeds 0.062. Misattribution survives va- lidity filtering: an entity posterior reduces same-name exposure on controlled data but cannot distinguish identically named speakers in LoCoMo. Two frozen lan- guage models reproduce prompt errors in generated text. Retrieval latency varies across rankers, but prompt prefill dominates turn-level latency on our hardware. These results argue for evaluating agent memory before generation, separating stored-state validity, identity resolution, abstention, and serving latency.

AI.tldr: Agent memory is typically scored only on final-answer correctness, which conceals pre-generation failures such as obsolete values, wrong-person facts, and missing facts. This paper measures these failures directly using Personal Fact Memory (PFM), showing that temporal validity is mainly a construction property, that merge/key-assignment (not retrieval) is the hard bottleneck, and that misattribution survives validity filtering.
AI.motivation: Correctness-only evaluation of personal memory for language agents hides errors occurring before generation: memory blocks may hold a superseded value, a fact about the wrong entity, or no useful fact before the serving deadline. The paper argues for diagnosing memory at the stored-state level before generation rather than relying on the single end score.
AI.method: Using Personal Fact Memory (PFM) as a reference layer, the authors measure memory failures directly across controlled revision benchmarks, LongMemEval, and LoCoMo. They test active-value-only serving vs. update resolution, compare participant-aware BM25 against a reference ranker under a prespecified 0.02 margin, contrast four LLM key assigners with a rule extractor via key recall and clean-retrieval rate, apply an entity posterior for misattribution, and probe two frozen language models for prompt errors in generated text, plus analyze retrieval vs. prompt-prefill latency.
AI.result: On a controlled revision benchmark, serving only the active value of each correctly keyed slot eliminates observed stale exposure, whereas without update resolution 70.3% of prompts expose a superseded value. With a shared active store and participant information, participant-aware BM25 matches the reference ranker within the 0.02 margin. Key assignment is harder: missed merges leave stale values active, false merges silently remove current values; four LLM key assigners beat a rule extractor on key recall but yield lower clean-retrieval rates, and open-domain merge recall on LongMemEval never exceeds 0.062. Misattribution persists after validity filtering—an entity posterior reduces same-name exposure on controlled data but cannot separate identically named speakers in LoCoMo. Two frozen language models reproduce prompt errors in generated text. Retrieval latency varies across rankers, but prompt prefill dominates turn-level latency.
AI.conclusion: The findings argue for evaluating agent memory before generation and for separating four distinct concerns: stored-state validity, identity resolution, abstention, and serving latency.

title: AI Safety Considerations for Agents With Limited Time to Act
summary: In the wake of the increasingly public discussion about AI alignment, recent work has tried to propose specific AI architectures that behave safely. However, the proposed arguments that seemingly demonstrate proved alignment mostly neglect the environment the agent needs to act in. We discuss theoretical bounds for agent-agnostic safety guarantees in environments that can only be partially observed and within which an action is required within limited time. We introduce two realistic scenarios, one with an infinite state space and one with signal mixture. In these scenarios, we prove that even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behaviour. It will be argued that for any proof of AI safety or alignment, the environment and associated safe actions need to be specifically considered together with the agent.

AI.tldr: The paper proves theoretical bounds showing that in partially observable, time-constrained environments, even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behavior, so AI alignment proofs must jointly consider the agent and its environment.
AI.motivation: Recent AI alignment work has proposed specific architectures claimed to provably behave safely. However, these arguments largely neglect the environment in which the agent must act. The authors aim to expose this gap by examining whether agent-agnostic safety guarantees are possible in realistic environments.
AI.method: The authors analyze theoretical bounds for agent-agnostic safety guarantees under partial observability and limited action time. They construct two realistic scenarios: one with an infinite state space and one involving signal mixture, and use these to test whether a perfect agent can guarantee safe behavior.
AI.result: In both scenarios, the authors prove that even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behavior. This holds despite the agent being idealized, demonstrating the impossibility of environment-independent safety guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Any proof of AI safety or alignment must specifically consider the environment and its associated safe actions together with the agent; agent-agnostic alignment claims are insufficient.

title: The Handover Problem: Governing Autonomy Transitions in Human-AI Collaboration
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Human-Machine Systems
summary:
Human-machine systems rarely operate at a fixed level of AI autonomy. As operators and AI systems collaborate over time, control must shift: the AI can take on more responsibility when collaboration is stable, maintain its current role when evidence is ambiguous, or return control to the human when conditions deteriorate. Existing work on adaptive automation, supervisory control, trust in automation, and deskilling explains parts of this problem, but provides no auditable, multi-signal criterion for governing when autonomy should change across multi-cycle workflows.
  We formalise this challenge as the Handover Problem: deciding, at each operational cycle, whether to escalate, maintain, or revert AI autonomy while keeping the process reversible, recoverable, and auditable. We introduce the Handover Readiness Score (HRS), a transparent composite measure that integrates four signal dimensions: operator readiness, human-AI trust, learning stability, and operational performance. It is combined with a hysteresis-based transition policy that requires sustained positive evidence before increasing autonomy but reverts promptly when conditions worsen.
  Across software engineering and manufacturing domains, the HRS and hard safety guards address complementary failure regimes: guards enforce immediate corrective action when a single indicator breaches a critical threshold, while the HRS detects the slow, multi-signal erosion of operator readiness that no individual guard can observe. The framework establishes autonomy handover as a governance problem requiring explicit, composite, and auditable criteria. This provides a conceptual and formal foundation that adaptive automation research has not previously provided.

AI.tldr: The paper formalises the "Handover Problem" of deciding when to escalate, maintain, or revert AI autonomy across multi-cycle human-AI workflows, and introduces the Handover Readiness Score (HRS)—a transparent four-signal composite measure paired with a hysteresis-based transition policy.
AI.motivation: Human-machine systems rarely operate at a fixed AI autonomy level; control must shift over time. Existing work on adaptive automation, supervisory control, trust in automation, and deskilling explains parts of this problem but offers no auditable, multi-signal criterion for governing when autonomy should change across multi-cycle workflows.
AI.method: The authors formalise the Handover Problem as a per-cycle decision to escalate, maintain, or revert AI autonomy while keeping the process reversible, recoverable, and auditable. They introduce the Handover Readiness Score (HRS), a transparent composite measure integrating operator readiness, human-AI trust, learning stability, and operational performance, combined with a hysteresis-based transition policy requiring sustained positive evidence before increasing autonomy but reverting promptly when conditions worsen.
AI.result: Across software engineering and manufacturing domains, the HRS and hard safety guards address complementary failure regimes: guards enforce immediate corrective action when a single indicator breaches a critical threshold, while the HRS detects the slow, multi-signal erosion of operator readiness that no individual guard can observe.
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes autonomy handover as a governance problem requiring explicit, composite, and auditable criteria, providing a conceptual and formal foundation that adaptive automation research has not previously provided.

title: RoboJEPA: Scaling Robotic Latent World Models
summary: Latent world models have shown a remarkable ability to predict future states and to plan in the real world. In practice, however, we lack a principled way to estimate how their capabilities scale with model size, data, and compute, an open problem that slows progress in the field. In this work we present RoboJEPA, a world model based on the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) and trained on a large-scale dataset spanning 12 robotic embodiments. We show that RoboJEPA's imagination error, the error of its latent rollouts, follows a second-order power law in compute, allowing us to predict model quality well beyond the scale at which the law is fit. We further show that downstream robotic planning performance improves predictably with compute, and that imagination error is strongly correlated with it, making it a reliable proxy for real-robot evaluation. Finally, we demonstrate that latent world models can be deployed zero-shot as robotic agents, planning toward a single goal image to solve tasks requiring long-horizon planning on real hardware. We release all model checkpoints together with our training and robot deployment code. To our knowledge, this is the first work to establish scaling laws for multi-embodiment robotic world models trained on real robot data, and RoboJEPA, at 8B parameters, is the largest JEPA predictor model trained to date.

AI.tldr: RoboJEPA is a JEPA-based latent world model trained on 12 robotic embodiments (~8B params) that exhibits second-order compute scaling laws in imagination error, enabling predictable downstream planning performance and zero-shot long-horizon real-robot deployment.
AI.motivation: The field lacks a principled way to estimate how latent world model capabilities scale with model size, data, and compute, which slows progress. Scaling laws that are well-established in language modeling have not been established for multi-embodiment robotic world models trained on real robot data.
AI.method: The authors build RoboJEPA on the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), training it on a large-scale dataset covering 12 robotic embodiments, and analyze how its imagination error (the error of latent rollouts) scales with compute. They correlate this error with downstream robotic planning performance and deploy the model zero-shot as a robotic agent that plans toward a single goal image to solve long-horizon manipulation tasks on real hardware.
AI.result: RoboJEPA's imagination error follows a second-order power law in compute, allowing prediction of model quality well beyond the scale at which the law is fit. Downstream planning performance improves predictably with compute, and imagination error is strongly correlated with it, making it a reliable proxy for real-robot evaluation. The model also performs zero-shot long-horizon planning on real hardware from a single goal image. All model checkpoints, training code, and robot deployment code are released.
AI.conclusion: This is, to the authors' knowledge, the first work establishing scaling laws for multi-embodiment robotic world models trained on real robot data, and RoboJEPA at 8B parameters is the largest JEPA predictor model trained to date. Imagination error serves as a scalable, reliable proxy for real-robot evaluation.

title: Open-MMUnlearning: Unifying Methods and Evaluation for MLLM Unlearning
summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become more capable and widely deployed, concerns about privacy and safety have become increasingly pressing. Machine unlearning offers one approach to addressing these concerns by removing designated information from trained models while preserving unrelated capabilities. However, fragmented implementations and evaluation protocols, incomplete robustness testing, and limited understanding of metric reliability make progress in MLLM unlearning difficult to assess systematically. We introduce Open-MMUnlearning, an open-source, extensible framework that integrates target-model preparation, multimodal data processing, unlearning, and evaluation through shared interfaces and structured configurations. The framework supports five benchmarks spanning privacy, safety, and copyright, eight MLLMs from four model families, and twelve unlearning methods. Its evaluation suite jointly assesses forgetting effectiveness, retained utility, and robustness to model interventions, adversarial inputs, and membership inference attacks. Using a common evaluation protocol, we compare ten representative unlearning methods. In this comparison, GD and MIP-Editor tie for the highest overall score: GD achieves the highest Forget Quality, while MIP-Editor preserves more Model Utility. We further introduce a metric meta-evaluation protocol that tests faithfulness using models with controlled exposure to target knowledge and robustness under quantization and relearning. Among the thirteen evaluated metrics, BLEU achieves the highest aggregate reliability score. KS-Test attains the highest faithfulness AUC but performs less well on robustness. Together, the framework and these findings support reproducible comparison of MLLM unlearning methods and systematic assessment of evaluation reliability.

AI.tldr: Open-MMUnlearning is an open-source, extensible framework for multimodal LLM unlearning that unifies target preparation, data processing, unlearning, and evaluation across 5 benchmarks, 8 MLLMs, and 12 methods. Under a shared protocol, GD and MIP-Editor tie for top overall score, and a meta-evaluation of 13 metrics finds BLEU most reliable overall while KS-Test leads in faithfulness.
AI.motivation: As multimodal large language models grow more capable and widely deployed, privacy and safety concerns intensify. Machine unlearning can remove designated information while preserving unrelated capabilities, but fragmented implementations, inconsistent evaluation protocols, incomplete robustness testing, and unclear metric reliability impede systematic progress in MLLM unlearning.
AI.method: The authors build Open-MMUnlearning, an open-source, extensible framework integrating target-model preparation, multimodal data processing, unlearning, and evaluation via shared interfaces and structured configurations. It supports five benchmarks (privacy, safety, copyright), eight MLLMs from four families, and twelve unlearning methods. Its evaluation suite jointly measures forgetting effectiveness, retained utility, and robustness to model interventions, adversarial inputs, and membership inference attacks. Ten representative methods are compared under a common protocol, plus a metric meta-evaluation protocol testing faithfulness with controlled-exposure models and robustness under quantization and relearning.
AI.result: Under the shared protocol, GD and MIP-Editor tie for highest overall score: GD attains the highest Forget Quality, whereas MIP-Editor better preserves Model Utility. Among thirteen evaluated metrics, BLEU reaches the highest aggregate reliability score; KS-Test achieves the highest faithfulness AUC but weaker robustness.
AI.conclusion: The framework and findings together enable reproducible comparison of MLLM unlearning methods and systematic assessment of evaluation reliability.

title: Reasoning-Token Spikes Under Prompted Untruthful Responding in Large Language Models
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Code: https://github.com/Wakaranaino/token-spike-project ; Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21895296
summary: Monitoring the chain-of-thought of reasoning artificial intelligence (AI) models remains a key approach to detecting deception and other forms of misbehavior in such models. However, semantic chain-of-thought monitoring depends on reasoning traces being legible and sufficiently faithful to the underlying computations that produced the model's behavior, not to mention accessible. Moreover, there is increasing evidence that chain-of-thought outputs may soon become illegible or unfaithful, if they even remain accessible. Based on cognitive load theory, we investigate a lower-bandwidth signal -- the number of reasoning tokens generated -- which does not require access to the content of the reasoning trace. Three reasoning-capable large language models answered 210 multiple-choice questions -- across analytic, descriptive, and normative reasoning types as well as moral and non-moral domains -- under system prompts instructing them to respond truthfully, falsely, or without regard for truth. Across all three models, truth-directed responding elicited fewer reasoning tokens than both lie-directed and truth-indifferent responding. These findings show that explicitly prompted untruthful response policies can produce robust group-level differences in test-time reasoning-token use. While not yet establishing reasoning-token count as a detector of spontaneous deception or general misalignment, our results are a proof of concept that it can serve as a simple, content-independent candidate signal for differentiating untruthful from truthful model behavior when raw reasoning traces are unavailable or unreliable. Future work should test instance-level detection rates, out-of-distribution generalization, learned deceptive policies, hidden objectives, and robustness under adversarial pressure.

AI.tldr: Reasoning-token count, a content-independent, low-bandwidth signal, is higher when LLMs are prompted to lie or respond truth-indifferently than when prompted to answer truthfully, across three models and 210 multiple-choice questions.
AI.motivation: Semantic chain-of-thought monitoring for detecting deception depends on reasoning traces being legible, faithful, and accessible, but such traces may soon become illegible or unfaithful. A monitoring signal that does not rely on trace content is therefore needed.
AI.method: Grounded in cognitive load theory, the authors use the number of reasoning tokens generated as a lower-bandwidth signal. Three reasoning-capable LLMs answered 210 multiple-choice questions spanning analytic, descriptive, and normative reasoning types and moral/non-moral domains, under system prompts directing truthful, false, or truth-indifferent responding.
AI.result: Across all three models, truth-directed responding elicited fewer reasoning tokens than both lie-directed and truth-indifferent responding, yielding robust group-level differences in test-time reasoning-token use.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly prompted untruthful response policies produce robust group-level differences in reasoning-token use. This is a proof of concept for reasoning-token count as a simple, content-independent candidate signal for distinguishing untruthful from truthful behavior when raw traces are unavailable or unreliable, though it does not yet establish the metric as a detector of spontaneous deception or general misalignment.

title: SOTA: Stock Options Trading Agents Guided by Option-Implied Return Distributions
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Agenthon Workshop
summary: As option markets grow and AI advances, agentic systems for option trading are gaining increasing attention. Language-model-based agents can reason over contextual information such as news, but option trading presents a particularly challenging decision problem: a single stock can have thousands of contracts, and the agent must decide both which contracts to trade and how to combine them. Existing approaches often sidestep this complexity by restricting the policy to a fixed strategy structure, such as a straddle, limiting their ability to switch strategies as market conditions change. We present SOTA (Stock Options Trading Agents), an agentic trading framework for structured option-strategy selection. SOTA abstracts the large option universe into strategy-level decisions while deterministic resolvers handle portfolio implementation. We develop SOTA by post-training Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. SOTA is evaluated on options on nine large-cap U.S. equities and SPY against rule-based and machine-learning strategy selectors in the same trading environment. Over a six-month out-of-sample period, SOTA earns an 18.3% total return with a Sharpe ratio of 1.60 and a maximum drawdown of 8.96%. We also document an asymmetric role of news: news improves frontier-teacher trajectories, but retaining news during reinforcement learning reduces out-of-sample return from 18.3% to -2.7%.

AI.tldr: SOTA is an agentic framework that abstracts a large option universe into strategy-level decisions resolved deterministically, trained via SFT then RL on Qwen3.8-27B, achieving 18.3% return, 1.60 Sharpe, and 8.96% max drawdown over six months out-of-sample.
AI.motivation: Option trading is a challenging decision problem: a single stock has thousands of contracts, requiring the agent to choose both which contracts to trade and how to combine them. Existing language-model agents sidestep this by restricting the policy to a fixed strategy structure (e.g., a straddle), limiting their ability to adapt strategies as market conditions change.
AI.method: SOTA (Stock Options Trading Agents) abstracts the large option universe into strategy-level decisions while deterministic resolvers handle portfolio implementation. It is built by post-training Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, and evaluated on options on nine large-cap U.S. equities and SPY against rule-based and machine-learning strategy selectors in the same trading environment.
AI.result: Over a six-month out-of-sample period, SOTA earns an 18.3% total return with a Sharpe ratio of 1.60 and a maximum drawdown of 8.96%. An asymmetric role of news is documented: news improves frontier-teacher trajectories, but retaining news during reinforcement learning reduces out-of-sample return from 18.3% to -2.7%.
AI.conclusion: Abstracting the option universe into strategy-level decisions with deterministic resolution enables flexible, adaptable option-strategy selection by a post-trained LLM agent, outperforming fixed-structure and baseline selectors. The findings also caution that news, while helpful for teacher trajectories, can degrade RL-trained out-of-sample performance if retained during reinforcement learning.

title: RunningTab: Direct Workspace Interaction with Environment-Side Tabs
summary: Much knowledge work produces new deliverables from files a workspace already holds, and LLM agents are beginning to take such work over. Through direct corpus interaction, an agent can search and read any of those files from a terminal with no indexing, and producing a deliverable from many of them in this way is what we call direct workspace interaction (DWI). Reaching the files, however, is only half the task: nothing keeps track of what the task asks for, what has been read, and what was listed but never opened, all of which slip through the context window without leaving a trace, so an agent may extract a figure and still deliver a report without it. To address this, we present RunningTab, a framework that equips direct workspace interaction with an environment-side tab: a per-task record of what the task still owes, kept by the environment alongside the agent. Specifically, the agent adds its requirements, while the environment records every file read as an excerpt with its provenance and every listed but unopened file as a candidate; the agent can then see each requirement beside its best-matching excerpts and top unopened candidates, resolve it against matching content or set it aside with a reason, and, should it try to finish with requirements still open, receive them in a finish check. We validate RunningTab on three benchmarks with three LLMs, where it consistently outperforms plain DWI and baselines that keep the record in the model, while its tab usually holds the values a deliverable needs once seen.

AI.tldr: RunningTab is an environment-side per-task tab that tracks outstanding requirements, read excerpts with provenance, and unopened candidates during direct workspace interaction, enabling agents to resolve each requirement against matching content or explicitly set it aside before finishing. It outperforms plain DWI and model-side record-keeping baselines across three benchmarks and three LLMs.
AI.motivation: Much knowledge work produces deliverables from files already in a workspace, and LLM agents increasingly take this on via direct workspace interaction (DWI), searching and reading files from a terminal without indexing. However, mere file access is insufficient: nothing tracks what the task requires, what has been read, or what was listed but never opened. These elements slip through the context window without a trace, so an agent may extract a figure yet still deliver a report missing it.
AI.method: RunningTab equips DWI with an environment-side tab—a per-task record of what the task still owes, maintained by the environment alongside the agent. The agent adds its requirements; the environment records every file read as an excerpt with provenance and every listed-but-unopened file as a candidate. The agent then sees each requirement beside its best-matching excerpts and top unopened candidates, resolves it against matching content or sets it aside with a reason, and receives a finish check listing any requirements still open if it attempts to conclude.
AI.result: Validated on three benchmarks with three LLMs, RunningTab consistently outperforms plain DWI and baselines that keep the record in the model. Its tab typically holds the values a deliverable needs once seen.
AI.conclusion: Externalizing task-state tracking to the environment, rather than relying on the model's context, improves LLM agents' ability to produce complete deliverables from existing workspace files. The tab's design—pairing requirements with matched excerpts and unopened candidates, plus a finish check—reliably captures the values deliverables require.

title: Before They Can Solve: Predicting Post-Training Coding-Agent Performance from Base Models
summary: How can we predict which base checkpoint is worth an expensive round of agentic post-training? End-to-end pass@$K$ tests whether successful behavior already appears in a base model's distribution, but it is a poor fit for agentic coding: many base checkpoints cannot reliably produce the well-formed tool invocation required to complete a task end-to-end. Single-shot or short-horizon tasks avoid these tool-calling failures by collapsing a multi-step interaction into a fixed prompt and a single patch, but they sidestep the core capability we care about: maintaining coherent state over many tool-using steps as the repository evolves. To bridge this gap, we treat successful post-trained agent trajectories as a lookahead signal of base-model potential. Replaying each trajectory and rerunning tests after every code-changing step identifies the decisive step: the first step whose cumulative patch flips the repository from failing to passing, certifying that the recorded action solves the task given the prior context. Motivated by a coverage principle for agentic traces, we build three screens at this step that do not require a base checkpoint to drive the harness from a cold start: (i) Decisive-Action BPB (bits per byte) measures the probability mass on the certified action, (ii) Patch MCQ tests the checkpoint's choice between that action and alternatives rejected by the same verifier, and (iii) prefix-conditioned pass@$K$ evaluates support for functionally-correct generations and credits any continuation that the tests accept. Across ten pairs of public base and post-trained models, all three screens rank the cohort in close agreement with post-trained SWE-bench Verified pass@$1$. As our methods need only a benchmark's successful trajectories and its verifier, they can be applied to turn future agentic coding benchmarks into base-model evaluations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using successful post-trained agent trajectories as a "lookahead signal" to screen base checkpoints for agentic coding potential. By replaying trajectories and isolating the "decisive step," three cold-start-free screens (Decisive-Action BPB, Patch MCQ, prefix-conditioned pass@K) rank model cohorts in close agreement with post-trained SWE-bench Verified pass@1.
AI.motivation: Predicting which base checkpoint is worth expensive agentic post-training is difficult. End-to-end pass@K fails for agentic coding because many base checkpoints cannot reliably produce the well-formed tool invocations needed to complete a task end-to-end. Single-shot or short-horizon tasks avoid these tool-calling failures by collapsing multi-step interaction into a fixed prompt and single patch, but they sidestep the core capability of interest: maintaining coherent state over many tool-using steps as the repository evolves.
AI.method: The authors treat successful post-trained agent trajectories as a lookahead signal of base-model potential. Each trajectory is replayed with tests rerun after every code-changing step to identify the decisive step: the first step whose cumulative patch flips the repository from failing to passing, certifying that the recorded action solves the task given prior context. Motivated by a coverage principle for agentic traces, three screens are built at this step that require no cold-start harness driving by the base checkpoint: (i) Decisive-Action BPB (bits per byte) measuring probability mass on the certified action; (ii) Patch MCQ testing the checkpoint's choice between that action and verifier-rejected alternatives; and (iii) prefix-conditioned pass@K evaluating support for functionally-correct generations while crediting any test-accepted continuation.
AI.result: Across ten pairs of public base and post-trained models, all three screens rank the cohort in close agreement with post-trained SWE-bench Verified pass@1.
AI.conclusion: The proposed screens reliably predict base-model agentic coding potential without requiring cold-start harness execution. Because the methods need only a benchmark's successful trajectories and its verifier, they can be applied to turn future agentic coding benchmarks into base-model evaluations.

title: EmbodiedRSI: Active Continual Robot Learning Through Hypothesis-Guided Co-Evolution
summary: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Further improvements often require post-training on substantial robot data, which can be costly to collect through methods such as teleoperation. Agentic harnesses can adapt around the model, but current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue. We introduce EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving agentic harness that autonomously decides where to explore next and turns the resulting physical interaction into improved code and skills. EmbodiedRSI realizes this through a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture, in which competing code and skill hypotheses are maintained in a Hypothesis Graph. Value-of-Information Experiment Selection chooses physical experiments that can distinguish these hypotheses. Their outcomes guide Code-Skill Co-Evolution. The Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory, and Reward-Grounded Memory Learning selects effective memory according to their value for later Fast-System improvement. On RoboCasa365, EmbodiedRSI reaches 77.0% overall success and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen, compared with 40.1% for the best baseline. EmbodiedRSI also reaches 86.8% overall success on LIBERO-Pro. Beyond benchmark performance, EmbodiedRSI transfers zero-shot to real-world robot, achieving 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.

AI.tldr: EmbodiedRSI is a self-evolving agentic harness that improves robot foundation model performance by turning physical interaction into better code and skills. Using a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture, a Hypothesis Graph, Value-of-Information experiment selection, and reward-grounded memory learning, it achieves 77.0% success on RoboCasa365 (71.3% on Composite-Unseen) versus 40.1% for the strongest baseline, 86.8% on LIBERO-Pro, and 71.3% zero-shot on real-world robots.
AI.motivation: Robot foundation models have strong visuomotor control but degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Improving them usually requires costly post-training on large teleoperated robot datasets. Existing agentic harnesses adapt around the model, but self-evolving variants use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue.
AI.method: EmbodiedRSI is a self-evolving agentic harness with a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture. Competing code and skill hypotheses are maintained in a Hypothesis Graph. Value-of-Information Experiment Selection picks physical experiments that best discriminate between hypotheses, and their outcomes drive Code-Skill Co-Evolution. The Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory, while Reward-Grounded Memory Learning retains memories according to their value for later Fast-System improvement.
AI.result: On RoboCasa365, EmbodiedRSI attains 77.0% overall success and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen, compared with 40.1% for the best baseline. It reaches 86.8% overall success on LIBERO-Pro. It also transfers zero-shot to a real-world robot, achieving 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.
AI.conclusion: EmbodiedRSI demonstrates that a self-evolving agentic harness with efficient experiment selection and memory learning can substantially outperform baselines on robot benchmarks and transfer zero-shot to real-world robot tasks, offering a data-efficient alternative to costly robot post-training.

title: Validity Without Ground Truth: What Stated-Preference Economics Offers the Evaluation of Language Models
summary: Many of the questions now put to large language models have no correct answer to score against: what a policy is worth, which option a user should choose, how to weigh competing values. Stated-preference economics has faced this problem for decades. It judges survey responses without knowing the true value, through a framework of validity and related concepts: content, construct, and criterion validity, reliability, incentive compatibility, and consequentiality. We argue that this framework is a general method for evaluating language models, and we set out what each concept means for LLM evaluation. We demonstrate the approach using a published water-quality stated preference economic valuation survey (Vossler et al. 2023) administered to six models. In this economic application, the validity tests take the form of predictions from economic theory: demand should slope down, and willingness to pay should respond to the scope of the good and to income. The tests separate the models sharply. Two older models fail the most basic test at a household income level of \$75,000, and the two newest pass every test of theoretical validity we can score, but diverge on convergent validity. Passing validity tests shows that a model's answers are coherent, not that they are correct.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using stated-preference economics' validity framework (content, construct, criterion validity, reliability, incentive compatibility, consequentiality) as a general method for evaluating LLMs on questions lacking ground truth, demonstrating it on a water-quality valuation survey with six models where theory-based validity tests sharply separate model performance.
AI.motivation: Many LLM queries—such as the worth of a policy, which option a user should choose, or how to weigh competing values—have no correct answer to score against. Standard accuracy-based evaluation is therefore inapplicable. Stated-preference economics has long confronted this exact problem of judging responses without knowing the true value.
AI.method: The authors adapt the stated-preference validity framework to LLM evaluation, specifying what content, construct, and criterion validity, reliability, incentive compatibility, and consequentiality mean for language models. They apply this approach using a published water-quality stated-preference economic valuation survey (Vossler et al. 2023) administered to six models, operationalizing validity tests as predictions from economic theory: downward-sloping demand, and willingness to pay responsive to the scope of the good and to income.
AI.result: The validity tests separate the models sharply. Two older models fail the most basic test at a household income level of $75,000, while the two newest models pass every scoreable test of theoretical validity but diverge on convergent validity.
AI.conclusion: The stated-preference validity framework offers a general method for evaluating LLMs on questions without ground truth. However, passing validity tests shows only that a model's answers are coherent, not that they are correct.

title: RECAST: Learning to Compute the Right Context through Adaptive Evidence Routing
summary: Large language models are increasingly applied to tasks grounded in long, heterogeneous information sources. Conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) relies on fixed similarity-based retrieval, while agentic variants adapt queries and tool use but remain largely retrieval-centric. However, in many tasks, the evidence required for a solution is not explicitly present in any single source item. Instead, it must be derived through filtering, aggregation, or computation across multiple source items. In this work, we introduce RECAST (Routing Evidence through Computation, Access, and Synthesized Tools), a learned framework that formulates evidence construction as a sequential decision process over heterogeneous retrieval and computation operations, allowing evidence to be actively derived rather than merely retrieved. A lightweight RouterLM iteratively selects and formulates primitive operations or specifies customized operations for a frozen CompilerLM to translate into executable code. Once it judges the evidence sufficient, RouterLM passes the accepted evidence to a frozen AnswerLM to produce the final solution. We train RouterLM with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by group relative policy optimization (GRPO). Across six heterogeneous benchmark families, RECAST achieves a mean success rate of 75.6%, outperforming the strongest large-model baseline by 15.9%. Moreover, training enables the Qwen3.5-9B RouterLM to outperform a training-free Gemini 3.5 Flash RouterLM by 5.0%. On three held-out benchmarks, RECAST improves over the strongest baseline by 15.0% on average, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization across tasks and heterogeneous source representations.

AI.tldr: RECAST reframes evidence construction for long-source tasks as a sequential decision process over retrieval and computation, using a trained RouterLM that directs a frozen CompilerLM to build executable operations and a frozen AnswerLM to solve. It beats the strongest large-model baseline by 15.9% on six benchmark families and generalizes strongly to three held-out benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Conventional RAG relies on fixed similarity-based retrieval, and agentic RAG variants mainly adapt queries and tool use but stay retrieval-centric. In many tasks the needed evidence is not explicitly present in any single source item and must instead be derived via filtering, aggregation, or computation across multiple items, which retrieval alone cannot provide.
AI.method: RECAST formulates evidence construction as a sequential decision process over heterogeneous retrieval and computation operations. A lightweight RouterLM iteratively selects and formulates primitive operations or specifies customized operations, which a frozen CompilerLM translates into executable code. When the RouterLM judges the evidence sufficient, it passes the accepted evidence to a frozen AnswerLM for the final solution. RouterLM is trained with supervised fine-tuning followed by group relative policy optimization (GRPO).
AI.result: Across six heterogeneous benchmark families, RECAST reaches a mean success rate of 75.6%, exceeding the strongest large-model baseline by 15.9%. Training lets a Qwen3.5-9B RouterLM outperform a training-free Gemini 3.5 Flash RouterLM by 5.0%. On three held-out benchmarks, it improves over the strongest baseline by 15.0% on average.
AI.conclusion: Actively deriving evidence through learned routing over computation and access operations, rather than merely retrieving it, substantially improves performance and yields strong zero-shot generalization across tasks and heterogeneous source representations.

title: SciExam for ENSO: Can AI Agents Build Climate Models?
summary: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out open-ended scientific research, yet their results are usually graded against a known answer, a rubric, or a language-model reviewer, none of which can tell whether a new scientific model is valid. The AI Science Exam for El Nino-Southern Oscillation (SciExam for ENSO) is a benchmark in which agents build low-order stochastic models of ENSO, the dominant mode of interannual climate variability, from real observations. Within a six-hour budget, agents process the observations, write their own diagnostics, which are then frozen, and develop a model using only these diagnostics as feedback. Hidden graders then test whether the model reproduces ENSO's statistics, recovers unobserved variables, and forecasts held-out years, and score a published model in the same way. Across twelve agent systems, six produce models that score higher than the published model, mainly through better reconstruction and forecasting. The simplified forms of the stronger models are each compatible with one of the two competing explanations of ENSO's warm-cold asymmetry, an open debate that the task never mentions. Controlled runs of the top system under varied information suggest that its scores do not come from recalling the dated observational record and that the information it receives shapes how it builds its model. SciExam for ENSO can thus evaluate agent research where no answer is known, and the results suggest that agents can already build competitive models whose structures bear on questions that scientists still debate.

AI.tldr: SciExam for ENSO is a benchmark where AI agents build low-order stochastic ENSO models from real observations within a six-hour budget, using self-written, frozen diagnostics as sole feedback; hidden graders test statistics reproduction, unobserved-variable recovery, and held-out forecasting. Six of twelve agent systems outperform a published model, and their simplified structures bear on a live scientific debate never mentioned in the task.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of language-model agents on open-ended scientific research rely on known answers, rubrics, or language-model reviewers, none of which can establish whether a newly proposed scientific model is valid. There is a need for a benchmark that grades genuine model-building against reality rather than against a pre-specified solution.
AI.method: Agents are given real ENSO observations and a six-hour budget. They process the data, write their own diagnostics, which are then frozen, and develop a low-order stochastic ENSO model using only those diagnostics as feedback. Hidden graders then assess whether the model reproduces ENSO statistics, recovers unobserved variables, and forecasts held-out years. A published model is scored under the identical protocol, and controlled runs vary the information provided to the top system. Twelve agent systems are evaluated.
AI.result: Six of the twelve agent systems produce models scoring higher than the published model, chiefly via better reconstruction and forecasting. The simplified forms of the stronger models each align with one of the two competing explanations of ENSO's warm-cold asymmetry, a debate the task never references. Controlled runs under varied information indicate the top system's scores do not stem from recall of the dated observational record, and that the information received shapes how it constructs its model.
AI.conclusion: SciExam for ENSO demonstrates that agents can be evaluated on scientific research where no answer is known, and that current agents can already build competitive models whose structures speak to questions scientists still debate.
